title: Ohio Duty-Shifting Runs One Direction Only
bodyText: You can agree to take on your tenant's obligations. Your tenant cannot agree to take on yours. R.C. 5321.13(A) makes the whole of Chapter 5321 non-waivable except through division (F), and (F) permits only one move: the landlord assuming the tenant's 5321.05 duties. There is no route in the other direction. So a clause making the tenant responsible for a duty Chapter 5321 assigns to you is void, however it is worded and whatever the tenant agreed to. R.C. 5321.13(E) closes the obvious workaround by barring any agreement that lets you receive rent free of the obligation to comply with 5321.04.

title: Drug Activity Is a Duty to Act, Not an Option - And Ignoring It Is a Crime
bodyText: In most situations Ohio leaves eviction to your discretion. Drug activity is the exception. Under R.C. 5321.17(C) and 5321.04(A)(9), once you have actual knowledge of - or reasonable cause to believe - that the tenant, a household member, or a guest has committed a controlled-substance offence connected with the premises, you SHALL give the three-day termination notice under 5321.17(C) and, if the tenant does not leave, SHALL promptly bring an eviction action. But 'actual knowledge or reasonable cause to believe' is a defined term here, not your own suspicion. R.C. 1923.02(A)(6)(a)(i) supplies it: a search warrant naming the tenant or person and describing the premises, executed by a law enforcement officer who found a controlled substance it described, and an officer then telling you of the violation. This is framed as a landlord obligation, not a landlord right, and the matching eviction ground sits at 1923.02(A)(6). Serving the 5321.17(C) notice also satisfies the ordinary three-day notice requirement under 1923.04(B), so no second notice is needed. R.C. 1923.051 puts this track on an accelerated schedule. Note what you do NOT need: the notice may be given whether or not the tenant or other person has been charged with, has pleaded guilty to, or has been convicted of anything. That warrant-and-police-notice chain is the trigger, and once you have it the statute says you SHALL act. The statute deems you to know when the chain is complete; whether anything less can supply that knowledge is unsettled, and no case law was read. Short of the chain, treat drug activity as an ordinary breach of a written lease term, which you may act on (R.C. 1923.02(A)(9)), and do not serve a notice that claims the mandatory track. There is a second, sharper reason to act. Under R.C. 2925.13 an owner, lessee, occupant, or person having custody, control, or supervision of premises who KNOWINGLY PERMITS them to be used for the commission of a felony drug abuse offence commits permitting drug abuse - a first-degree misdemeanour, and a fifth-degree felony where the underlying offence is trafficking or manufacturing, or where you had actual knowledge that Schedule I or II manufacturing chemicals were involved. So the same facts that trigger your Chapter 5321 duty can also expose you personally to criminal charges if you sit on them. Watch how the two standards differ. Chapter 5321's duty waits for the warrant chain; R.C. 2925.13 asks only whether you 'knowingly permit' the premises to be used for a felony drug offence, and it does not wait for a warrant. So knowing of drug activity can expose you criminally before the civil duty fires. Acting on what you know, through a lease-breach notice and eviction, is what keeps you out of the second statute.

title: Never Name a Minor on an Ohio Eviction Complaint
bodyText: If you list a minor tenant as a defendant on an eviction complaint alongside a parent or adult guardian, the court SHALL dismiss the action without prejudice and SHALL order you to pay the minor tenant's reasonable attorneys' fees. Naming every occupant is ordinary practice in most states; in Ohio it costs you the filing and the other side's legal bill. A 'minor tenant' is a tenant under eighteen who is not emancipated. Note that this fee award is statutory, so Ohio's general ban on attorney-fee agreements does not protect you from it.

title: Ohio Prescribes the Words of Your Notice
bodyText: Most states tell you how long to wait. Ohio also tells you what to say. Every notice you give to recover residential premises must contain, printed or written in a conspicuous manner, the following statement verbatim: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." Serve it at least three days before you file, by certified mail return receipt requested, by personal delivery, or by leaving it at the tenant's usual place of abode or at the premises. A notice missing this exact language will not support the action.

title: Electing Out of the Civil Rights Commission Can Cost You More
bodyText: If the Ohio Civil Rights Commission issues a housing discrimination complaint against you, you - not just the complainant - may elect to move the matter into common pleas court. Think before you do. In the administrative track the commission MAY award damages and fees, and the civil penalty is capped ($10,000, rising to $25,000 with one prior violation in five years and $50,000 with two or more in seven). In court, R.C. 4112.055(D) says the court SHALL award actual damages, reasonable attorneys' fees, court costs, expert witness fees and other litigation expenses, and MAY add punitive damages - with no cap and a right to a jury. Electing out trades a capped penalty for uncapped exposure. The election must be mailed certified, return receipt requested, within thirty days of the notice.

title: Ohio's Alarm Duty Comes From Code - Except in a High-Rise
bodyText: For an ordinary Ohio rental there is no smoke-alarm or carbon-monoxide-alarm statute telling you what to install. The duty reaches you indirectly: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires you to comply with the building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety, and R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) preserves local codes from Chapter 5321's preemption - so the answer for any given property is in the applicable building and fire code and the local ordinance, not in the landlord-tenant chapter. There is one direct statute, and it is narrow. R.C. 3781.104 requires an automatic smoke detection system in an existing apartment or condominium building over seventy-five feet tall that lacked one: a board-approved detector in each dwelling unit just outside every sleeping room, with alarms clearly audible in all bedrooms with the doors closed, plus detector spacing rules for the parts of the building outside the units. For that statute an apartment building is one where at least seventy-five per cent of the units are residential and let on other than a transient basis, which excludes a hotel but expressly includes a college or university dormitory. Below seventy-five feet, R.C. 3781.104 does not apply and you are back to the codes. For a one-, two- or three-family dwelling, the Residential Code of Ohio sets the alarm rules for new construction and for work that needs an approval (Ohio Adm.Code 4101:8-3-01, sections 314 and 315). Smoke alarms go in each sleeping room, outside each sleeping area and on each story. Carbon monoxide alarms go outside each sleeping area where the unit has a fuel-fired appliance or an attached garage. That code does not by itself make you retrofit a house where no approved work is done. But alarms the code required when installed must be kept working, and the owner is responsible for that (Ohio Adm.Code 4101:8-1-01, section 113.2). Whether the Ohio Fire Code's retrofit rules reach your building turns on text this library has not read.

title: Ohio Voids Attorney-Fee Clauses Both Ways
bodyText: A prevailing-party or fee-shifting clause does nothing for you in Ohio. R.C. 5321.13(C) provides that no agreement to pay the landlord's OR the tenant's attorney's fees shall be recognised in any residential rental agreement, or in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant. Making the clause mutual does not rescue it - mutuality is the fix in some states, and it is irrelevant here. Hedging it with 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' does not rescue it either; the statute says such an agreement is not recognised, so the sentence is inoperative at best and misleading to a tenant at worst. Fees are still available to either side where a STATUTE awards them - 5321.15(C), 5321.04(B), 5321.16(C) and 4112.055(D) all do - because those are statutory awards, not agreements.

title: Two Cure Windows Before a Bounced Payment Costs Anything
bodyText: Ohio gives you no statutory returned-check fee cap - the $30-or-10% figure you will find quoted in Ohio lease templates is R.C. 1319.16, which caps what a COLLECTION AGENCY may charge, and 1319.12(A)(2) excludes a landlord collecting its own account. Your fee rides on the lease. As for going after the tenant: recovery under R.C. 2307.61 requires a THEFT OFFENCE, which means purpose to defraud plus knowledge - insufficient funds alone is not one. On top of that the tenant has two cure windows you cannot contract away: paying within ten days of notice of dishonour defeats the presumption of knowledge (2913.11(C)(2)), and paying within thirty days of your written demand bars the civil action outright (2307.61(D)). And 2307.61(B) cuts back at you - if you pursue costs and fees and the tenant wins, you pay the tenant's fees and defence costs.

title: Taking Rent After Your Notice Can Void It
bodyText: No Ohio statute decides this. Chapters 5321 and 1923 say nothing about accepting rent after a notice; the rule comes from Ohio's appeals courts, and the cases below are leads, not opinions this library read in full. In the courts' view the line is about WHICH PERIOD the money covers. Accepting rent for obligations already incurred at the time of your three-day notice does not waive it. Accepting rent for a FUTURE period after serving the notice has been held to waive the notice, so you cannot proceed on it and must start over (King v. Dolton, 9th Dist., 2003-Ohio-2423; Bristol Court v. Jones, 4th Dist. 1994; Premiere Mgt. v. Nutt, 3d Dist., 2010-Ohio-1255). Holding the payment is not a safe middle ground: one court treated a landlord who sat on checks without telling the tenant they were not being accepted, then cashed them, as having accepted them (N. Face Properties v. Lin, 12th Dist., 2013-Ohio-2281). If you do not want the money, say so in writing and return it. Two further cautions from the cases: a pattern of quietly accepting late or partial rent can waive the due date in your lease, and accepting the current month's rent BEFORE you serve the notice can jeopardise the action too (OZ Property Mgt. v. Williams, 12th Dist., 2025-Ohio-318). Do not count on a 'no waiver' clause in your lease to save you, because courts treat the three-day notice as a condition of the eviction court's jurisdiction, which a contract cannot supply. The cautious course is the same whatever a later court says: after you serve a notice, accept nothing for any period after it unless you mean to drop the notice.

title: Selling the Property Does Not Get You Off the Deposit
bodyText: Ohio has no statute transferring deposit liability to a buyer, and no safe harbour for doing it properly - unlike states where handing the deposit over plus notifying the tenant relieves you. Ohio's appeals courts treat a security deposit as a personal obligation in the nature of a PLEDGE between you and your tenant (Castlebrook, Ltd. v. Dayton Properties, 2d Dist. 1992, following Tuteur v. P. & F. Enterprises, 8th Dist. 1970; leads, not read in full). The liability to return it does not run with the property. It stays with you unless the buyer either assumes the obligation or receives a credit on the purchase price for the deposits. So the thing that protects you is not moving the money - it is what the purchase and sale agreement says. Get the deposits itemised in the PSA and on the rent roll, name them, and confirm assumption or a price credit in writing. Pet and other deposits count, and get missed.

title: Ohio Gives You No Way to Deal With Left-Behind Belongings
bodyText: If a tenant leaves possessions behind, Ohio hands you nothing. There is no notice-and-disposal procedure for an ordinary residential tenancy - the detailed machinery of notice, valuation affidavit, county auditor sign-off and sale in R.C. 1923.12 to 1923.14 applies only to manufactured home parks. Meanwhile R.C. 5321.15(B) forbids you from seizing a tenant's furnishings or possessions for rent except under a court order, and 5321.15(C) exposes you to actual damages plus reasonable attorneys' fees if you do. The practical consequence is that there is no statutory step you can follow that makes disposal safe, so get a court order, or get the property out through the writ process rather than on your own initiative.

title: Ohio Has Seven Different Small-Landlord Thresholds
bodyText: There is no general 'small landlord' concept in Ohio law. Seven separate provisions use seven different size tests, so you have to check the one attached to the duty in front of you. Fair housing under Chapter 4112 has NO small landlord exemption from its core housing prohibitions - every landlord is covered regardless of size. The rent-escrow remedy at R.C. 5321.07(C) does not reach a landlord party to agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units WHO GIVES WRITTEN NOTICE OF THAT FACT. That exemption withdraws only the escrow section: your R.C. 5321.04 duties stay, and so do the tenant's damages, counterclaim and other remedies (see edu-landlord-breach-remedy-oh). The active-duty stay at R.C. 1923.062(C) does not apply to a landlord operating fewer than four residential premises. The waste receptacle duty at R.C. 5321.04(A)(5) applies only where you are party to agreements covering four or more dwelling units in the same structure. And the nuisance receivership scheme at R.C. 3767.41 - under which a court can put a receiver in possession of your building, let the receiver collect the rents, and make the receiver's spending a first lien ahead of your mortgage - reaches every residential property EXCEPT one that is owner-occupied and contains three or fewer units. A pool at a dwelling housing no more than three families, used only by its residents and their guests, is a private residential pool and not a public swimming pool under Chapter 3749 (R.C. 3749.01(F) and (G)). And the fair housing design-and-construct accessibility duty reaches only 'covered multifamily dwellings' - buildings of four or more units with an elevator, and ground floor units in other buildings of four or more units - first occupied on or after June 30, 1992 (R.C. 4112.02(H)(22)). Read those seven tests carefully: they are not variations on one rule. One counts dwelling units, one counts premises, one counts units in the same structure, one adds a written-notice condition you can fail, one turns on whether you live there yourself, one counts families, one also turns on when the building was first occupied, and one does not exist. Never reuse a size-keyed clause across provisions.

title: Most Ohio Limits You Expect Do Not Exist
bodyText: Ohio is a thin-statute state on money terms. There is no security deposit cap, no late fee cap, no returned check fee cap that binds a landlord, no holdover damages formula, and no required mold, radon, bed bug, meth, asbestos or flood disclosure. Mandated lease content is almost as thin: R.C. 5321.18 requires every written rental agreement to contain the name and address of the owner and of the owner's agent, and federal law requires the lead paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing. There is one more, and it applies only if you are an institution: R.C. 5321.031 requires a college or university letting to a student tenant to specify in the written agreement the conditions under which it may be terminated and the institution's notice and hearing procedures. That freedom is real but it is not unlimited: R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause or limit its application, and it is the only ceiling on every one of these terms. Set numbers you could defend to a judge, because nothing else will do it for you.

title: Ohio Sets No Rent-Increase Notice Period
bodyText: Chapter 5321 contains no rent-increase notice provision at all. The '30 days' you will see quoted everywhere is R.C. 5321.17(B), which is the notice required to TERMINATE a month-to-month tenancy - a different thing. For a periodic tenancy the practical route to a higher rent is to terminate on the statutory notice and offer new terms. For a fixed-term written lease, the rent is whatever the lease says for the term, and a mid-term increase needs the tenant's agreement. If you want a defined mid-term or renewal increase mechanic, it has to be in the lease, because the statute will not supply one.

title: Two Ohio Defaults You Are Allowed to Contract Around
bodyText: Most of Ohio's landlord-tenant rules cannot be waived - R.C. 5321.13(A) makes the whole of Chapter 5321 non-waivable except in one narrow direction. But two rules that matter to you sit OUTSIDE Chapter 5321, and both are default rules you may contract around. R.C. 5301.11 says a tenant whose building is destroyed or made unfit for occupancy through no fault of their own stops owing rent - 'unless otherwise expressly provided by written agreement or covenant' - and the tenant must surrender possession to get the benefit. And Ohio's duty to re-rent after a tenant abandons comes from case law that applies 'barring contrary contract provisions'. Because neither lives in Chapter 5321, 5321.13(A) does not protect them. R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability still does. Under the default, rent already owed before the damage stays due, and the tenant stops owing rent only by surrendering possession of all of what remains; they can't stop paying while leaving belongings there or otherwise keeping possession. One practical consequence is worth planning for: under the R.C. 5301.11 default on its own, the tenant stops owing rent and surrenders, but a fixed Term keeps running, so the tenant may claim a right to move back in once you have repaired. The library offers an optional clause that lets you end a fixed-term lease where the home is destroyed or cannot reasonably be repaired within a period you set, while leaving the tenant's R.C. 5301.11 rights untouched and stopping rent from the date the home became unfit. What the library does not offer is the other thing R.C. 5301.11 appears to permit - a term keeping rent running after the home becomes unfit. On its face the statute lets a written agreement do that, but R.C. 5321.13(E) bars any agreement letting a landlord receive rent free of the R.C. 5321.04 duties, and R.C. 5321.04 cannot be waived at all, so such a term would collide with Chapter 5321 even though R.C. 5301.11 sits outside it. A landlord who wants that term should write their own clause and take advice first.

title: Ohio Private Tow-Away Zones Have Hard Sign Rules
bodyText: Before a towing service may remove a vehicle from your rental property without the vehicle owner's permission, the property must be a valid private tow-away zone. Ohio sets the signs by statute: at least eighteen inches by twenty-four inches, visible from every entrance to the property, and stating that it is a tow-away zone, who may park there (for residential property, tenants and their guests), the property address or business name, the hours of enforcement if it is not around the clock, a telephone number and the address where a towed vehicle can be recovered, and a warning that an unclaimed vehicle may lose its title. You may modify existing signs with stickers or addenda rather than replacing them. Only the property owner or an authorized agent may order a tow, and the towing service must hold a written contract with you. If the vehicle owner arrives before the vehicle is actually removed, they may reclaim it for no more than half the removal fee. Get the signs wrong and the tow is unlawful: the vehicle owner may sue under R.C. 4513.611.

title: If Utilities Are In Your Name, A Tenant Can Redirect Your Rent
bodyText: Where you are the utility customer of record - master-metered buildings, or any unit where you include utilities in the rent - an unpaid bill is not just your problem with the utility. Before disconnecting, the utility gives you fourteen days' notice and then attempts a separate ten-day notice to each tenant unit and posts notice conspicuously on the building. That ten-day notice tells your tenants their options, and two of them cost you money. A tenant may stop the disconnection by paying an amount equal to the current month's bill, which the utility credits to your account. Or a tenant may use the rent-deposit remedy under R.C. 5321.07 to deposit rent with the court and ask the court to spend it on the utility bill - so the rent you were owed pays the utility instead. If you are the one asking for disconnection, you get ten days' notice and you are liable for everything consumed in that period. Separately, between November 15 and April 15 the utility must give your occupants five days' notice before shutting off, and must tell them about state and federal bill-payment aid.

title: A No-Firearms Clause Does Not Bind a Licensed Ohio Tenant
bodyText: Do not put a handgun ban in an Ohio residential lease expecting it to work. R.C. 2923.126(C)(3)(b) provides that a landlord may not prohibit or restrict a tenant who holds a concealed handgun license, or the tenant's guest while the tenant is present, from lawfully carrying or possessing a handgun on the residential premises, for any rental agreement entered into on or after September 9, 2008. The restriction runs against you, not the tenant, so a lease term to the contrary is simply unenforceable against a licensee. It is narrower than it first looks: the protection is written for a licensee and for that licensee's guest while the licensee is present, and it covers lawful carrying and possession of a handgun.

title: A Tenant Or Neighbor Can Put Your Building Into Receivership
bodyText: Ohio's habitability remedies are not the only exposure for a building in poor condition. Under R.C. 3767.41 a municipal corporation, a township, a neighbor, a tenant, or a nonprofit housing organization may bring a civil action alleging that the building is a public nuisance on grounds of structural safety, habitability, fire hazard or inadequate maintenance. If you have refused or failed to abate, the court must first offer your mortgagees, lienholders and other interested parties, in order of priority, the chance to do the work; only if none is willing and able, or one does not proceed with due diligence, may it appoint a receiver who takes possession and control of the building, collects the rents and income, may evict tenants, pays operating expenses and liens, hires managing agents and carries out rehabilitation work. Approved receiver expenditures and fees become a first lien on the building, superior to all prior and subsequent liens including tax liens, and the property can be sold to satisfy them. Owner-occupied buildings with three or fewer units are excluded.

title: Ohio Requires No Radon Disclosure To A Tenant
bodyText: Ohio imposes no radon testing, mitigation or disclosure duty on a residential landlord toward a tenant. Ohio does regulate radon, but only the professionals: R.C. Chapter 3723 licenses radon testers, mitigation specialists, mitigation contractors and laboratories. Nothing in it reaches the landlord-tenant relationship. Do not be misled by R.C. 5302.30: that is the residential property disclosure form for SALES, and it does not apply to a lease.

title: Ohio Has No Residential Bed Bug Statute
bodyText: Ohio imposes no bed bug disclosure duty and sets no treatment timeline for residential rental property. Bed bugs in an Ohio rental are handled through the general habitability duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(1)-(2) and the tenant's own duties in R.C. 5321.05, not through a dedicated statute. Ohio's bed bug provisions sit in the hotel chapter and do not reach a residential tenancy.

title: Ohio Has No Mold Disclosure Or Remediation Statute
bodyText: Ohio requires no mold disclosure to a tenant and sets no mold remediation standard for residential rental property. A mold complaint is handled under the general habitability duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(1)-(2), with the tenant's rent-escrow remedy under R.C. 5321.07 as the enforcement route. There is no Ohio mold-professional licensing scheme and no mold chapter.

title: Ohio Gives A Tenant No Right To Install EV Charging
bodyText: Ohio has no right-to-charge law, on a full-text search of the whole Revised Code run on 2026-09-27 (statutes only; the Administrative Code and case law were not searched). A residential tenant has no statutory right to install an electric vehicle charging station, and a landlord has no statutory duty to permit or accommodate one. Whether a tenant may install or use charging equipment is a matter for the lease and for R.C. 5321.06, which lets the parties agree to any term not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or other law. Local zoning and building codes may still govern the installation itself.

title: Ohio Gives A Domestic Violence Victim No Statutory Way Out
bodyText: Ohio has no statewide domestic violence lease-termination right, no DV anti-termination protection, and no DV lock-change duty. A survivor who leaves early remains liable on the lease under ordinary contract principles, and a landlord may pursue the remaining rent, subject only to the common-law duty to mitigate. Seven other states in this library give the survivor a statutory release; Ohio does not. Tenants in federally subsidised housing are covered by the federal Violence Against Women Act instead, which is a separate regime.

title: Ohio Has No Right-To-Call-Emergency-Services Statute
bodyText: Ohio gives a tenant no statutory, non-waivable right to summon police or emergency services. R.C. 5321.02's retaliation protection is close but narrower, and its trigger list is closed: complaining to a governmental agency about a code violation materially affecting health and safety, complaining to the landlord about a R.C. 5321.04 violation, or joining with other tenants to bargain collectively. Calling 911 is on none of those. So a landlord who penalises a tenant for repeated emergency calls faces no specific statutory bar in Ohio - and because Ohio also has no domestic violence tenancy protection, a survivor making repeated calls has no state-law shield either.

title: No Ohio Source-Of-Income Rule, With One Disability Exception
bodyText: Ohio's fair housing statute, R.C. 4112.02(H), does not list source of income or receipt of housing assistance as a protected class, and Ohio has no statewide voucher-acceptance mandate. There is one exception worth knowing, and it is easy to trip over. OAC 4112-5-07(A)(1)(c) makes it unlawful disability discrimination to refuse to consider the sources of a DISABLED applicant's income, or to subject that applicant's source of income or ability to generate income to automatic discounting in whole or in part, because of the disability. So a blanket 'no vouchers' or 'wages only' screening rule applied to an applicant whose income is disability-related benefits can become a disability claim even though Ohio has no general source-of-income protection. Several Ohio cities do protect source of income by ordinance.

title: Ohio Has No Servicemember Residential Lease Termination
bodyText: Ohio gives a servicemember no state-law right to terminate a residential lease on military orders. Two Ohio provisions come close and neither does it. R.C. 1349.02 lets a deployed servicemember or spouse terminate a lease, but it is confined to MOTOR VEHICLE leases - read the definition before relying on it. R.C. 1923.062 gives a deployed tenant a stay or adjustment of an eviction action, not a termination, it runs 90 days unless justice requires otherwise, it reaches only rental agreements entered on or after May 18 2005, and it does not apply to a landlord operating fewer than four residential premises. A servicemember's actual termination right in Ohio is the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which R.C. 5321.04(A)(10) separately requires you to comply with.

title: Ohio Does Not Regulate Immigration-Status Inquiries By Landlords
bodyText: Ohio has no statute prohibiting a landlord from asking about immigration or citizenship status, and no immigrant tenant protection act. R.C. 4112.02(H) protects national origin and ancestry, and R.C. 4112.02(H)(8) bars making inquiries, eliciting information, keeping records or using application forms concerning national origin or ancestry in connection with a lease - so an inquiry framed around national origin is already unlawful. But Ohio has nothing like the immigration-status-specific prohibitions some states have enacted, and nothing barring disclosure of status to third parties.

title: Ohio Requires No Meth-Contamination Disclosure - But Permitting Drug Abuse Is A Crime
bodyText: Ohio imposes no duty to disclose to a prospective tenant that a property was used to manufacture methamphetamine or was otherwise drug-contaminated, and sets no decontamination standard for residential rental property. Four states in this library have such a disclosure; Ohio does not. What Ohio has instead runs the other way, against you: under R.C. 2925.13 an owner, lessee, occupant or person having custody, control or supervision of premises or real estate, including vacant land, who KNOWINGLY PERMITS it to be used for the commission of a felony drug abuse offence commits permitting drug abuse, a first-degree misdemeanour, rising to a fifth-degree felony where the underlying offence is manufacturing or trafficking or involves Schedule I or II manufacturing chemicals with actual knowledge.

title: Two Ohio Lease Terms That Are Never Recognised
bodyText: Two clauses that appear in ordinary lease forms have no effect at all in Ohio, and no amount of careful drafting saves them. R.C. 5321.13(D): no agreement by a tenant to the exculpation or limitation of ANY liability of the landlord arising under law, or to indemnify the landlord, shall be recognised in any rental agreement or other agreement. That reaches the whole familiar family - 'Landlord shall not be liable for', 'Tenant releases Landlord from', 'Tenant agrees to indemnify, defend and hold Landlord harmless', and a hold-harmless buried in a pet, parking, storage or utilities clause. Making it mutual does not help. Narrowing it to a specific risk does not help. Hedging it with 'to the extent permitted by law' does not help either, because the statute does not limit such a clause, it declines to recognise it. R.C. 5321.13(B): no warrant of attorney to confess judgment is recognised in any rental agreement, or in any other landlord-tenant agreement for the recovery of rent or damages. A cognovit provision in an Ohio residential lease is dead on arrival. What you use instead is insurance, not drafting: require the tenant's renter's insurance, carry your own liability cover, and rely on the statutory allocation of duties in R.C. 5321.04 and 5321.05 rather than trying to contract out of it.

title: Ohio Has Two Cure Tracks, and Picking the Wrong One Loses the Case
bodyText: Before you terminate for a tenant breach, work out which track the breach is on, because Ohio has two and they carry different notice periods. TRACK ONE - the tenant broke a duty R.C. 5321.05 imposes, and the breach materially affects health and safety. R.C. 5321.11 requires written notice specifying the act or omission and stating a termination date NOT LESS THAN THIRTY DAYS after the tenant receives it, and the tenant may cure within that window. This is not advisory: R.C. 1923.02(A)(8) says that before commencing an action on that ground, notice shall be given and compliance secured with 5321.11. It is a condition precedent to filing, so a shorter notice does not merely weaken your case, it defeats it. TRACK TWO - the tenant broke an obligation your written lease imposes, with no health-and-safety dimension. R.C. 1923.02(A)(9) carries no 5321.11 requirement, so whatever period your lease sets is the period that governs. But (A)(9) reaches only an obligation imposed by a WRITTEN rental agreement, so a tenant under an oral tenancy has no Track Two. Then, on either track, the separate three-day notice to leave the premises under R.C. 1923.04(A) still has to be served before you file, in the words the statute prescribes. Two exceptions run on their own clocks: nonpayment of rent needs no cure period, and drug activity under 5321.05(A)(9) is carved out of 5321.11 entirely and, once the search-warrant chain that R.C. 1923.02(A)(6)(a)(i) defines is complete, goes to the mandatory three-day notice under 5321.17(C) (see edu-mandatory-drug-termination-oh). The practical trap: many breaches sit in both buckets at once, and if a court reads yours as Track One after you noticed it as Track Two, you filed on a defective notice. When it is genuinely arguable, give thirty days.

title: How An Ohio Tenant Forces Repairs: Rent Escrow
bodyText: Ohio does not give tenants a repair-and-deduct right. It gives them the courthouse. If you fail an obligation under R.C. 5321.04 or under the lease, the tenant may give you written notice specifying the acts, omissions or code violations, sent to the person or place where rent is normally paid. If you then fail to remedy within a reasonable time considering the severity, or within thirty days, whichever is sooner - and the tenant is current on rent - the tenant may do one of three things: deposit all rent due and thereafter becoming due with the clerk of the municipal or county court; apply to the court for an order that you remedy the condition, which can include an order reducing the rent until you do or an order spending the deposited rent on the repair; or terminate the rental agreement. Two carve-outs work in your favour. The remedy does not reach a landlord who is party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and who gives written notice of that fact, and it does not apply to a dwelling occupied by a student tenant.

title: Ohio Retaliation: The Three Triggers And What It Costs
bodyText: An Ohio landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by raising the rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession, because the tenant did any of three things: complained to an appropriate governmental agency about a violation of a building, housing, health or safety code that materially affects health and safety; complained to you about a violation of R.C. 5321.04; or joined with other tenants to negotiate or deal collectively with you about the terms and conditions of the tenancy. If you retaliate, the tenant may use it as a defence to your possession action, recover possession, or terminate the rental agreement - and may recover actual damages together with reasonable attorney's fees. What you may still do: R.C. 5321.02(C) expressly preserves a rent increase that reflects the cost of improvements you installed or an increase in your other costs of operating the property. Document that basis before you raise the rent of a tenant who has just complained.

title: Never Shut Off Utilities Or Change The Locks In Ohio
bodyText: Ohio bans self-help recovery of possession outright, and the ban is written broadly. Under R.C. 5321.15(A) no landlord may initiate ANY act - the statute names terminating utilities or services, excluding the tenant from the premises, and threatening any unlawful act - for the purpose of recovering possession, other than through the procedures in R.C. Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321. Under division (B) you may not seize a tenant's furnishings or possessions to recover rent except under a court order. This applies to a tenant whose right to possession has already ended, not just a current tenant. Division (C) makes you liable in a civil action for ALL damages caused, together with reasonable attorney's fees. There is no de minimis version of this: turning off the water on a holdover tenant is the conduct the section was written to stop.

title: Ohio Preempts Local Rent Control, With Findings Attached
bodyText: Ohio forecloses local rent control about as firmly as any state in this library. R.C. 5321.19 bars a political subdivision from enacting, adopting, renewing, maintaining, enforcing or continuing any charter provision, ordinance, resolution, rule or other measure that conflicts with Chapter 5321, or that regulates the rights and obligations of parties to a rental agreement that the chapter regulates, including by imposing or requiring rent control or rent stabilization. R.C. 5321.20 then adds a legislative-findings section devoted to the subject, declaring rent control a matter of overriding statewide interest requiring uniform statewide regulation. What survives preemption matters as much as what does not: 5321.19(B) expressly preserves local housing, building, health and safety codes, any ordinance of the kind described in 5321.04(A)(9), local regulation of rent for premises the subdivision itself owns or operates, and voluntary-incentive programs such as tax abatements or bond financing.

title: Interest on Larger Deposits
bodyText: If a deposit is more than $50 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, the excess earns interest at 5% a year for any period the tenant stays in possession six months or more. Compute and pay it to the tenant every year. No interest is owed on the part at or below that threshold (R.C. 5321.16(A)).

title: Tenants' Right to Display Certain Flags
bodyText: Ohio doesn't let a lease restrict a tenant from displaying the U.S. flag, the POW/MIA flag, the Ohio flag, or a Defense-approved service flag, displayed according to federal, state and local law and patriotic custom (R.C. 5321.131). Before installing a flag pole or a permanently affixed bracket for the U.S. or POW/MIA flag, the tenant must contact you with reasonable notice to discuss placement and size, and a lease term requiring the tenant to return the property in the same condition at the end of the term still applies (R.C. 5321.131(E)). If the tenant installs a pole or bracket without that contact, you are not liable for damages, fines or costs arising from its placement (R.C. 5321.131(C)). A lease term that breaks this section is unenforceable and is an unconscionable term under R.C. 5321.14 (R.C. 5321.131(D)).

title: Your Basic Duties as an Ohio Landlord
bodyText: Ohio requires you to comply with building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is reasonably necessary to keep the property fit and habitable; keep common areas safe and sanitary; keep the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning fixtures and appliances, and elevators, you supply or must supply in good and safe working order; and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat at all times, unless the building isn't required by law to have them or the unit's heat or hot water comes from an installation under the tenant's exclusive control on a direct utility connection. If you rent four or more units in the same structure, you must also provide waste receptacles and arrange removal (R.C. 5321.04). These duties can't be waived; see the rent-escrow note for the tenant's remedy.

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Itemization
bodyText: Within 30 days after the lease ends and the tenant delivers possession, deliver or mail the deposit, less amounts properly applied, with a written itemization of the deductions and the reasons for them (R.C. 5321.16(B)). A tenant who didn't give a forwarding address in writing still gets the balance but can't recover damages or attorney's fees (5321.16(B) and (C)).

title: Termination Notice Periods
bodyText: In Ohio, either party may end a week-to-week tenancy with notice at least 7 days before the termination date, and a month-to-month tenancy with notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date (R.C. 5321.17). These minimums don't apply to a termination for breach of the lease or of a duty imposed by law, and they don't limit a shorter notice Ohio law requires where a tenant has violated R.C. 5321.05(A)(9).

title: No General Just-Cause Rule in Ohio, With Three Situational Limits
bodyText: Ohio has no general just-cause or good-cause requirement for ending a residential tenancy. Under R.C. 5321.17 either party may end a month-to-month tenancy on at least 30 days' notice before the periodic rental date, or a week-to-week tenancy on at least 7 days' notice, and the landlord needs no reason; holding over after a term ends is itself a ground for a possession action under R.C. 1923.02(A)(1). Three situations narrow that. FIRST, retaliation. R.C. 5321.02(A) bars you from raising the rent, cutting services, or bringing or even threatening a possession action because the tenant complained to a government agency about a code violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to you about an R.C. 5321.04 violation, or joined with other tenants to bargain collectively. The tenant can use that as a defence, recover possession, or terminate, plus actual damages and attorney's fees. But the bar is expressly 'subject to section 5321.03', and R.C. 5321.03(A) then lets you bring the action anyway on five enumerated grounds: the tenant is in default in rent; the violation the tenant complained of was primarily caused by the tenant, the tenant's household, or someone there with the tenant's consent; compliance would need alteration, remodelling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit; the tenant is holding over; or the premises are within one thousand feet of a school or child care premises and a tenant or occupant is on the state sex offender registry for a qualifying offence. So once a tenant has done something R.C. 5321.02 protects, those five grounds are in practice the only ones available - a for-cause rule in that situation, even though Ohio has none in general. R.C. 5321.02(C) separately lets you raise rent to reflect the cost of improvements or an increase in operating costs. SECOND, student tenants of a college or university. R.C. 5321.031 lets a college or university end a student tenant's agreement early only after a hearing at which it determined the student broke a lease term or the institution's code of conduct, preceded by written notice and a right to be heard. R.C. 5321.03 does not apply to a unit occupied by a student tenant at all. THIRD, the registered-offender ground runs the other way, adding a cause: R.C. 5321.03(A)(5) and R.C. 5321.051 let you terminate where the premises are within 1,000 feet of school, preschool, child care, children's crisis care or residential infant care premises and a tenant or occupant is on the R.C. 2950.13 registry for a qualifying offence.

title: Ohio Has No Rule on Algorithmic Rent Pricing
bodyText: Ohio has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic or revenue-management pricing software, and none on sharing rent or occupancy data with other landlords or with a pricing vendor. Federal and state antitrust law and the general law on unfair competition still apply, and Ohio's rent-control preemption (R.C. 5321.19 and 5321.20) says nothing either way.

title: No Ohio Rule on Whether Fees Count as Rent
bodyText: No Ohio statute says whether a late fee, a utility charge or any other fee counts as 'rent', so nothing in Ohio law stops a lease from calling such a charge additional rent - and nothing confirms that an eviction for nonpayment can rest on unpaid fees alone. Two things bear on it. The notice that starts an Ohio eviction is a notice to leave the premises under R.C. 1923.04, not a pay-or-quit notice, so there is no statutory text tying the amount demanded to 'rent'. And R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, which is the only real ceiling. This library's clauses do not label fees as rent, and the shared Application of Payments clause applies each payment to rent first and only then to fees, so a tenant who pays in full cannot be left owing rent because a fee absorbed the payment.

title: Ohio Has No Landlord Self-Cure Statute
bodyText: Ohio gives you no statutory right to fix a tenant's breach yourself - repairing damage, cutting the grass, hauling away rubbish - and bill the cost back as rent. Some states have one; Ohio does not. What you have instead is the ordinary route: recover the cost as damages, or apply the security deposit at the end of the tenancy under R.C. 5321.16(B), which reaches past due rent and damage from the tenant's noncompliance. The lease can give you a self-cure right by contract, but take care with two Ohio rules: R.C. 5321.13(C) means you cannot add your attorney's fees to the bill, and a self-cure clause must not become a way to charge the tenant for something R.C. 5321.04 makes your own duty, which R.C. 5321.13(A) and (E) would void.

title: No Ohio Rule Requiring Every Blank to Be Filled
bodyText: Ohio has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be completed, and no statute making a blank a breach or a ground to void the lease. Fill them in anyway. A blank leaves the term unsettled, and in Ohio the practical risk lands on you twice over: R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce a term it finds unconscionable, and several of the figures this library leaves for you to set - the holdover daily rate, the late fee, the returned-payment fee - have no statutory cap in Ohio, so an unfilled or indefensible number is the whole of your protection.

title: No Ohio Quiet-Enjoyment Statute - the Duty Comes From Elsewhere
bodyText: No Ohio statute states a covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession for a residential lease. The protection a tenant actually has in Ohio comes from two other places. R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) to (6) sets out your repair and habitability duties and R.C. 5321.13(A) makes them non-waivable, and R.C. 5321.15 bars you from excluding the tenant from the premises, cutting off utilities, or threatening either, outside a court process. Ohio courts also treat a lease as carrying an implied covenant of quiet enjoyment as a matter of common law rather than statute. So a clause promising quiet enjoyment adds little in Ohio, and leaving it out takes nothing away.

title: Ohio Prescribes One Form of Words, and It Is the Eviction Notice
bodyText: Ohio supplies no statutory residential lease form and no statutory notice-to-terminate form. It prescribes exactly one piece of wording, and it is the notice that starts an eviction. Under R.C. 1923.04(A) every notice a landlord gives to recover residential premises must contain this language, printed or written in a conspicuous manner: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." The notice must be given three or more days before the action begins, by certified mail with return receipt requested, by handing a written copy to the tenant, or by leaving it at the tenant's usual place of abode or at the premises. Serving the three-day drug-activity notice under R.C. 5321.17(C) counts as compliance with that requirement. One other provision dictates lease content rather than a form: R.C. 5321.031 requires a college or university letting to a student tenant to specify in the written agreement the conditions for termination and the institution's notice and hearing procedures.

title: No Ohio Rule on Tenant Cameras - and Ohio Is One-Party Consent
bodyText: No Ohio statute says whether a tenant may install a security camera or a video doorbell, so the lease controls, together with its rules on alterations. Audio is where Ohio differs from several other states, and it differs in the permissive direction: under R.C. 2933.52(B)(4) a person who is not a law enforcement officer may lawfully intercept a communication if that person is a party to it, or if any one party consented, provided the recording is not made to commit a crime, a tort, or another injurious act. Ohio is a one-party-consent state, so a tenant recording a conversation they are part of - a doorstep exchange with you, for instance - is generally lawful. A device left running to capture conversations between other people, where no participant consented, is not.

title: Your Ohio Lease Is the Switch for Cannabis Home Grow
bodyText: Ohio adult-use cannabis law makes your lease the deciding document on home growing, and if the lease says nothing the tenant may grow. Under R.C. 3796.04(A)(1) an adult-use consumer may cultivate up to six plants at their primary residence, and up to twelve at a single residence, inside a secured enclosed area not visible by normal unaided vision from a public space and not accessible to anyone under 21. But that authority does not apply at "a residential premises occupied pursuant to a rental agreement that prohibits the activities otherwise authorized by this section" - R.C. 3796.04(A)(1)(d)(iii). So a lease term prohibiting cultivation removes the right, and a silent lease leaves it in place. If you do not want plants grown at your property, the prohibition has to be in the lease. Use and possession work differently. R.C. 3796.221 lets an adult-use consumer use and possess cannabis and gives no lease-prohibition hook, but its protection is framed as freedom from arrest and prosecution, not as a contract right against a landlord - and R.C. 3796.04(C)(2) separately bars consuming in a public place. A lease ban on smoking or vaping cannabis therefore rests on ordinary freedom of contract under R.C. 5321.06, and the shared smoking clause in this library is lawful in Ohio. Watch the citations: this chapter was Chapter 3780 when adult use began and was amended and renumbered into Chapter 3796 by S.B. 56, effective March 20 2026. Older Ohio guidance still cites 3780.

title: Electronic Notices Work in Ohio, But Consent Is Not Something You Can Take Once
bodyText: Ohio's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, R.C. Chapter 1306, applies to landlord-tenant records. Its list of exclusions in R.C. 1306.02(B) covers only wills, codicils and testamentary trusts and specified UCC chapters - unlike some states it carves out nothing for eviction, default or cure notices. Two conditions matter to you. R.C. 1306.04(B) applies the Act only between parties who have each agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means, and whether they agreed is judged from the context, the surrounding circumstances and the parties' conduct, so a signature block is not the end of the question. And R.C. 1306.04(C) says a party who agrees to conduct one transaction electronically may refuse to conduct others that way, and that right may not be waived by agreement - so a lease term committing the tenant to accept every future notice electronically is unenforceable to that extent. Separately, R.C. 1923.04(A) sets its own service methods for the notice to leave the premises: certified mail with return receipt requested, personal delivery, or leaving it at the premises or the tenant's usual place of abode. Email is not on that list. Do not serve an eviction notice electronically.

title: A Void Term Costs You Nothing Extra in Ohio
bodyText: Ohio attaches no penalty to using a lease term the law prohibits. R.C. 5321.13 lists the terms that are not recognised - confession of judgment, attorney's fees either way, exculpation or indemnity of the landlord, and any waiver of Chapter 5321 - but it provides no damages, no civil penalty and no fee award for having used one. The term simply has no effect, and R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term or limit how it is applied. That is a real difference from some states: Kansas, for example, gives the tenant actual damages where a landlord deliberately uses an agreement containing terms it knows are prohibited. Ohio's consumer protection act does not fill the gap either, because R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a consumer transaction by reference to goods, services, a franchise or an intangible, and a residential lease of real property is none of those. None of this makes a prohibited term safe. It is unenforceable the moment you need it, a tenant can raise it as a defence, and a lease built on terms that fail is worse than one drafted to Ohio law in the first place.

title: Ohio Does Not Bless a Pre-Set Schedule of Deposit Charges
bodyText: No Ohio statute lets you fix in advance what you will charge against the deposit for a stained carpet, a repaint, a lost key or a turnover clean, and none prescribes a notice you could give to make such a schedule stick. There is no authorised cost schedule and no safe harbour. What the statute allows is narrower than a price list: at termination you may apply the deposit to past-due rent and to the amount of damages you have actually suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the statutory tenant duties or the rental agreement, and you must itemise and identify each deduction in a written notice (R.C. 5321.16(B)). 'Damages that the landlord has suffered' means loss you can show, so a flat figure above your real loss is not protected, and a flat charge for something that is not a breach at all - ordinary wear, routine turnover cleaning - sits outside the permitted uses whatever the lease says. A schedule is still worth having, as notice to the tenant of what you expect, and the lease may carry it because Ohio allows any term not inconsistent with the chapter (R.C. 5321.06), with unconscionability as the only ceiling (R.C. 5321.14). Treat your figures as estimates you must be able to document: keep receipts and dated photographs, and bill the actual cost. Searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held and the Attorney General's consumer rules; no cost-schedule provision exists. City ordinances were not checked.

title: An Unreturned Deposit Becomes State Unclaimed Funds After One Year
bodyText: If you cannot get a deposit refund to a former tenant, you do not get to keep it. Ohio's unclaimed funds act names this money precisely: any deposit made to secure payment of rents or leases, and any sum paid in advance for rents, leases, possible damage to property, unused services or performance requirements, held or owed and unclaimed for one year (R.C. 169.02(M)(1)). One year - not the three or five years other categories get. You are the holder, meaning any person with possession, custody or control of money owed to another (R.C. 169.01(D)), and the clock runs from the last point the tenant indicated any interest in the funds (R.C. 169.01(B)). Before reporting, send notice to the tenant's last known address for any item worth fifty dollars or more, enclose a stamped self-addressed envelope, and wait thirty days (R.C. 169.03(E)). File the annual report before the first of November for the year ended the preceding thirtieth of June, then remit (R.C. 169.03(D), 169.05(A)). Report in good faith and the state takes the money and holds you harmless (R.C. 169.07(A)). Not reporting is where it hurts: one hundred dollars a day for a knowing failure, plus interest and one per cent a month for up to twenty-five months (R.C. 169.12). A lease term forfeiting an unclaimed deposit to you does not help, because the landlord-tenant chapter cannot be waived by agreement (R.C. 5321.13(A)): the money stays owed, and money owed is what this act reaches.

title: No Ohio Right to Pay the Deposit in Instalments
bodyText: An Ohio tenant has no statutory right to pay the security deposit in instalments. Nothing in the landlord-tenant chapter lets a tenant demand a payment plan, sets a minimum number of monthly payments, caps what you may require at move-in, or switches an instalment right on once the deposit passes one month's rent. You may insist on the whole deposit before the tenant takes possession, and you may refuse a plan you do not want. If you do choose to allow instalments, two things follow. The money is a security deposit from the moment each payment reaches you, because the definition catches any deposit of money or property held to secure the tenant's performance (R.C. 5321.01(E)) - so the interest threshold and the thirty-day itemise-and-return duty apply to the running total, not only to the final figure. And an unpaid instalment is a lease breach rather than a deposit question: say in the lease exactly when each instalment falls due, and pursue a missed one as you would any other sum the lease makes due. An instalment arrangement is lawful because the lease may contain any term the chapter does not prohibit (R.C. 5321.06), not because any statute authorises it. Searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held, chapter 5321 read section by section, plus the Attorney General's consumer rules; no instalment right exists. City ordinances were not checked.

title: Last Month's Rent Taken Up Front Is Deposit Money in Ohio
bodyText: Ohio has no last-month's-rent statute - none appears across the 37 Revised Code chapters this library holds - and the definition is why it does not need one. A security deposit is any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under the rental agreement (R.C. 5321.01(E)). Money you take at signing and hold against the final month of the term is money held to secure performance, so the cautious and almost certainly correct treatment is to count it as part of the security deposit: add it to whatever else you hold when you test the interest threshold, which is fifty dollars or one month's periodic rent, whichever is greater - so a month's rent on any ordinary tenancy, and itemise and account for it within thirty days of the end of the tenancy and delivery of possession. Labelling it 'prepaid rent' or 'last month's rent' in the lease does not move it, because no provision of the chapter can be waived by agreement (R.C. 5321.13(A)). The one genuinely different thing is rent actually paid and applied for a stated period at the front of the term - rent for month one, paid and credited in month one. If what you want is the final month covered, the safer route is to take a larger deposit, which Ohio does not cap, and say plainly in the lease that it may be applied to past-due rent at the end of the tenancy.

title: The Only Surrender Notice in Ohio's Deposit Rule Runs From the Tenant to You
bodyText: Ohio makes you give the tenant no notice at move-out about the deposit. There is no pre-surrender letter setting out what you intend to deduct, no offer of a joint walk-through, no inspection report, and no statement of deposit rights you must hand over. The notice duty in the deposit rule runs the other way: the tenant shall provide you, in writing, with a forwarding or new address to which the written notice and the amount due may be sent, and a tenant who fails to do so is not entitled to the damages or attorney's fees the statute otherwise gives (R.C. 5321.16(B)). You still owe the money itself. Your own clock is the thirty days after the rental agreement terminates and possession is delivered, and both have to have happened - a tenant who stops paying but keeps the keys has not started it. Practical course: ask for the forwarding address in writing when notice to vacate goes out and again at key return, keep whatever you are given, and if nothing comes, send the itemisation and the balance to the last address you hold, within thirty days anyway. The lease wording for this belongs in your deposit-return clause rather than a clause of its own.

title: One Deposit Deadline in Ohio, and No Fast Track Either Way
bodyText: Ohio gives neither side a way to speed the deposit accounting up or slow it down. There is one deadline - thirty days after the rental agreement terminates and possession is delivered (R.C. 5321.16(B)) - and no shortened track for a tenancy ended by mutual agreement, for a tenant who leaves early, for a surrender mid-term, for a tenant in hardship, or on a tenant's written demand. No statutory demand letter starts a shorter clock, and there is no procedure letting a tenant get the money before the thirty days run. Nothing lengthens it either: the thirty days do not stretch because repairs are unfinished, because a contractor has not invoiced you, because an insurance claim is open, or because you and the tenant are arguing about the figure. If you cannot price a loss inside thirty days, deduct and itemise what you can document and return the rest - withholding the balance while you work it out is exactly what triggers the damages and the attorney's fees. Nor can the lease change the period, in either direction, because no provision of the chapter may be waived by agreement. Searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held, chapter 5321 read section by section; no expedited or extended disposition provision exists. City ordinances were not checked.

title: Ohio Has No Deposit-Alternative Fee Programme, and the Definition Is Why It Is Risky
bodyText: Ohio has no statute authorising a monthly fee, a deposit waiver or an insurance-backed product in place of a security deposit. There is no offer-to-all duty, no right for the tenant to switch back to a deposit, no cap on the fee, and no notice rule before you report a damage claim to a credit bureau or a collector. The absence cuts against you, and the definition is the reason. A security deposit is any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant (R.C. 5321.01(E)), and no provision of the chapter may be modified or waived by agreement (R.C. 5321.13(A)). So money you collect that stands in for the deposit and secures the tenant's performance is at serious risk of simply being a security deposit - meaning interest above the threshold, a written itemisation within thirty days, and damages equal to the amount wrongfully withheld plus the tenant's attorney's fees if you have treated it as earned income. A charge that is genuinely not security stands differently - a premium the tenant pays to a third-party insurer naming you as the insured, with no tenant money held by you - but no Ohio statute says so. If the product is insurance, only a licensed agent may sell, solicit or negotiate it, and asking or urging a tenant to apply for a particular insurer's product is soliciting (R.C. 3905.01(S), 3905.02). No exception in R.C. 3905.03 covers a landlord, so let the provider's licensed agent offer it and do not urge it yourself. Cautious course: take a deposit, which Ohio does not cap, or get Ohio-specific advice before running a fee programme here.

title: Money Taken Before the Lease Is Signed Sits in an Ohio Gap
bodyText: Ohio regulates nothing about money you take from an applicant before there is a lease. No statute limits a holding deposit, good-faith money or earnest money on a rental, requires a receipt, says how long you must hold the unit, says what happens if the applicant backs out or if you rent to someone else, or sets a deadline for giving the money back. The landlord-tenant chapter is drafted around an agreement that already exists: a tenant is a person entitled under a rental agreement to use the premises, and a security deposit is money held to secure performance by the tenant under a rental agreement (R.C. 5321.01(A), (E)). Before a rental agreement exists there is no tenant, so the deposit rules do not obviously reach the money, and no other Ohio statute picks it up - the Attorney General's deposit-receipt rule binds a supplier taking a deposit in a consumer transaction in goods or services, which a residential lease is not. What is left is ordinary contract law, meaning whatever you wrote down. So write it down before you take a dollar: the amount, what it holds and for how long, whether it is credited to first month's rent or to the deposit, and when it is refunded if no lease is signed. Once the lease is signed, treat anything you still hold as a security deposit.

title: Ohio Requires No Nonrefundable-Fee Notice, Because It Does Not Recognise the Fee
bodyText: Ohio has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant that a charge is nonrefundable - no prescribed words, no timing, no acknowledgement you must collect before taking the money. The reason is that Ohio never reaches the notice question. A security deposit is any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under the rental agreement (R.C. 5321.01(E)), and no provision of the chapter may be modified or waived by any oral or written agreement (R.C. 5321.13(A)). So if the money you collect secures the tenant's performance - a 'nonrefundable pet deposit', a 'nonrefundable cleaning deposit', a 'nonrefundable damage fee' - it is a security deposit, it must be itemised and accounted for within thirty days of the end of the tenancy, and the label does not survive. A notice would not rescue it: telling a tenant in advance that you intend to keep deposit money does not make keeping it lawful, because the tenant cannot consent to the chapter being set aside. What can be genuinely nonrefundable is a charge that buys something and secures nothing - a screening or application fee for work actually done before the tenancy, or rent itself. So say what each sum is for, price it separately from the deposit, and never call something a deposit if you mean to keep it. Searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held and the Attorney General's consumer rules; no residential nonrefundable-fee notice exists. City ordinances were not checked.

title: No Separate Signed Disclosure for a Nonrefundable Charge in Ohio
bodyText: Ohio prescribes no form at all for disclosing a nonrefundable charge to a tenant. There is no separate document, no separate signature line or initial box, no minimum type size, no bold or capitals requirement, no placement rule putting it on the first page or above the signature, and no duty to hand the tenant a copy or a receipt. Nothing about where the words sit, because Ohio does not require the words. Worth knowing what Ohio does prescribe, so you can see the contrast: the only landlord document whose wording and conspicuousness the Revised Code dictates is the notice that starts an eviction, which must carry prescribed language 'printed or written in a conspicuous manner' (R.C. 1923.04(A)). Nothing comparable exists for money. The practical consequence is the one that matters. Because no separate form is required, a separately signed rider buys you nothing: it cannot make a performance-securing charge nonrefundable, since the definition catches the money whatever document it is described in and the chapter cannot be waived by agreement. A rider is useful only as evidence of what each sum was for. Searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held and the Attorney General's consumer rules; no form, placement or separate-signature requirement for a nonrefundable charge exists. City ordinances were not checked.

title: Ohio Caps Nothing - The Figure You Have Heard Is the Interest Line
bodyText: Ohio sets no dollar cap and no multiple-of-rent cap on a residential security deposit. You choose the figure. The number people quote at you - fifty dollars or one month's periodic rent, whichever is greater - is not a ceiling. It is the interest line: whatever you hold above it earns the tenant five per cent a year, computed and paid annually, once the tenant has been in possession six months or more (R.C. 5321.16(A)). A larger deposit is lawful. It simply puts more money into the interest band and more money into the thirty-day itemise-and-refund duty. The only ceiling on your figure is unconscionability: a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term or limit how far it applies (R.C. 5321.14). Two further limits bite. Anything you hold to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever you name it (R.C. 5321.01(E)), so pet money and cleaning money sit inside the same rules. And you may not demand a deposit above the one you customarily require as the price of approving a disability modification (R.C. 4112.02(H)(18)(b)). No cap appears anywhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched - 5321, 1345, 1349, 4112 and 169 among them - or in the Attorney General's consumer rules. City ordinances were not checked.

title: Ohio Does Not Tell You Where to Keep the Deposit
bodyText: Ohio imposes no holding rules on a residential security deposit. You need no escrow account, no trust account, no separate or segregated account, no bank in this state, no surety bond in place of the money, and no written notice to the tenant of where the money sits or who holds it. You may put the deposit in your operating account. What the money never stops being is the tenant's. At termination you may apply it only to past-due rent and to damages from the tenant's statutory or lease breaches, you must itemise any deduction in writing, and you must deliver the notice and the balance within thirty days (R.C. 5321.16(B)). Interest is owed on the part above fifty dollars or one month's periodic rent, whichever is greater - a month's rent on any ordinary tenancy - once the tenant has stayed six months (R.C. 5321.16(A)) - and you owe it whether or not the money was ever anywhere that earned it. Nothing in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched, 5321, 1345, 1349 and 169 among them, requires a depository or a depository notice. Because no statutory account does the record-keeping for you, keep a ledger per tenancy showing the deposit, the date received and the interest accrued.

title: You Cannot Draft Your Way Out of Ohio's Deposit Rules
bodyText: Every deposit rule in Ohio's landlord-tenant chapter is non-waivable. No provision of the chapter may be modified or waived by any oral or written agreement (R.C. 5321.13(A)). Applied to the deposit, that means a lease term saying the deposit is nonrefundable, that you need not itemise deductions, that you have sixty days instead of thirty, that no interest accrues above the threshold, or that the tenant gives up the damages and fees the statute provides, is simply not recognised. The rest of the lease stands without it. The tenant's signature changes nothing, and neither does a separately initialled rider or an addendum signed later. The definition closes the other door: anything you hold to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever the lease calls it (R.C. 5321.01(E)), so renaming the money does not move it outside the rules you cannot waive. What you may still do is write terms the chapter does not reach - how much the deposit is, what the tenant must do to keep it intact, where the forwarding address goes - because the lease may contain any term not inconsistent with the chapter or another rule of law (R.C. 5321.06). Draft inside the statute, not around it.

title: What Missing the Deposit Deadline Costs You in Ohio
bodyText: Ohio's deposit penalty is not a flat multiple of the deposit you took. If you fail to deliver the itemised written notice of deductions together with the amount due within thirty days after the rental agreement terminates and possession is delivered, the tenant recovers the property and money due, plus damages equal to the amount wrongfully withheld, plus reasonable attorney's fees (R.C. 5321.16(C)). The measure is what you wrongfully kept, so the money comes back and the same sum comes again on top. The fees are the real exposure, and they are not something your lease can head off, because this award comes from the statute rather than from any agreement. One escape exists and it is the tenant's to lose: a tenant who never gave you a forwarding or new address in writing is not entitled to the damages or the fees, though you still owe the money itself (R.C. 5321.16(B)). Late is as bad as short - a partial refund delivered on day forty-five carries the same exposure as a refusal. Two habits remove most of the risk: diary the thirtieth day from the later of termination and delivery of possession, and send the itemisation even when you are deducting nothing.

title: No Deposit-Standards Disclosure in Ohio - Fair Housing Is What Limits the Number
bodyText: Ohio has no statute requiring you to post, publish or hand over the standards by which you work out a security deposit, and no unit-count threshold switches such a duty on. You may charge one tenant more than another, and you need not show the arithmetic. What constrains you is fair housing, not deposit law. It is an unlawful discriminatory practice to discriminate in the terms or conditions of renting housing accommodations because of race, colour, religion, sex, military status, familial status, ancestry, disability or national origin (R.C. 4112.02(H)(4)) - and the deposit figure is a term of renting. Separately, you may not require a tenant with a disability to pay a deposit above the one you customarily require of all tenants of those premises as the price of approving a modification; what you may require instead is payment into an interest-bearing restoration escrow in your name, with the interest running to the tenant (R.C. 4112.02(H)(18)(a)(iii), (b)). So the practical course is the one no statute makes you take: write down a neutral standard, apply it the same way every time, and keep the record, because the record is the defence. No deposit-standards disclosure provision appeared in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched or in the Attorney General's consumer rules. City ordinances were not checked.

title: Interest on Amounts Tenant Owes
bodyText:
Unless the lease sets a different rate, Ohio law gives a creditor interest on money that has become due at the rate R.C. 5703.47 fixes for that calendar year: the federal short-term rate for July, rounded to the nearest whole per cent, plus three per cent, set by the Tax Commissioner each October 15 for the year that follows (R.C. 1343.03(A)). That section applies to money due on a written instrument, a book account, a settlement, a verbal contract, and to judgments, and it says the contract rate governs instead 'unless a written contract provides a different rate.' A rate the lease does state keeps running after judgment at the lease's own rate (R.C. 1343.02). The ceiling on a stated rate is eight per cent a year (R.C. 1343.01(A)), subject to six exemptions in R.C. 1343.01(B) that a residential lease will usually not meet. Charging above the ceiling does not void the debt: the excess is credited against principal (R.C. 1343.04). Interest on an excess security deposit is a separate rule and the lease cannot change it (R.C. 5321.16(A); R.C. 5321.13(A)).

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review plus chapter 1343 and R.C. 5703.47 read in full. Whether a residential lease counts as an 'instrument of writing for the forbearance or payment of money at any future time' under R.C. 1343.01(A) is not settled by the statutory text, and no Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: Ohio Never Makes You House a Tenant Somewhere Else
bodyText: No Ohio provision makes a residential landlord provide or pay for alternate housing - not while a unit is being repaired, not when it becomes unfit, not after a fire, and not when the tenant asks. Ohio answers an unfit unit with money and exit rather than a bed. After serving the written repair notice and waiting out the cure window, the tenant may deposit rent with the clerk of court, ask the court to order you to remedy the condition (the court can reduce the rent until you do, or order the deposited rent spent on the repair), or terminate the rental agreement (R.C. 5321.07(B)). None of those is a relocation duty, and none of them obliges you to find the tenant anywhere to go. The same is true when the unit is emptied over your head: a court can order an agency inspection and forbid re-rental until conditions are corrected (R.C. 1923.15), and a court can put a nuisance building into receivership (R.C. 3767.41), and neither makes you house anyone. Because nothing supplies the answer, your lease has to: say what happens to rent and to the tenancy for any period the unit cannot be lived in.

title: Habitability in Ohio: What You Have and What Is Missing
bodyText: How Ohio compares on habitability features found in other states. PRESENT: six landlord duties in R.C. 5321.04(A), covering code compliance, repairs and fit and habitable condition, safe and sanitary common areas, good and safe working order for supplied fixtures and appliances, waste receptacles where you let four or more units in one structure, and running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat; non-waivability by any oral or written agreement; the tenant's written-notice and rent-escrow route, with a court able to order you to remedy, reduce the rent until you do, or spend the deposited rent on the repair, or the tenant able to terminate; the clerk's escrow account and your routes to get the money released; damages for breach of any duty imposed by law; a tenant counterclaim with a discretionary pay-in in your own eviction case; a court-ordered agency inspection with power to forbid re-renting; nuisance receivership; and unconscionability review. ABSENT - we found no provision, in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library, that gives you: a statutory implied warranty of habitability or any list of uninhabitable conditions; repair-and-deduct, rent withholding or statutory rent abatement; any minimum indoor temperature or heating season; a duty to provide or pay for alternate housing; any habitability presumption; a required habitability statement in the lease; a repair-cost termination threshold; a rule about written promises to repair; any designated-repairer or response-time rule; or a uniform-act single-family or separate-writing route for moving your duties to the tenant. Two further gaps are not absences but unread sources: the Ohio Building and Residential Codes, Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 and 4101:8, which R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes your duty, and city housing codes, which Ohio's preemption statute leaves standing - a temperature or maintenance standard may well be in one of them. Two carve-outs cut the escrow remedy only: three or fewer dwelling units where you gave written notice of that fact, and a college's own student tenant. They do not touch the damages claim, the counterclaim or the inspection order. Details are in the linked Ohio rows.

title: Ohio Makes You Name No Repairer - and Gives the Tenant None Either
bodyText: No Ohio statute makes you name a repair contact, an approved repairer or a response time, and none lets a tenant hire someone and bill you or take the cost out of the rent. Ohio has no repair-and-deduct right at all. That makes the ordinary lease arrangement safe here: under R.C. 5321.06 your lease may name the person and number repair requests go to, require your written consent before any work at your expense, and bar deductions from rent, and the term stands unless a court finds it unconscionable (R.C. 5321.14). Three limits to build in.
