The statutory notice address is fixed and your clause cannot move it: the R.C. 5321.07(A) notice goes to the person or place where rent is normally paid, so route those on immediately whatever your repair line says. Nothing in the clause may relieve you of a duty under R.C. 5321.04 or limit your liability - R.C. 5321.13(A) and (D) refuse both, however the clause is worded. And a court can go round your designation anyway: it may order the escrowed rent spent on the repair (R.C. 5321.07(B)(2)), or order an agency inspection and order the conditions corrected (R.C. 1923.15).

title: Only One of Ohio's Habitability Duties Carries a Materiality Test
bodyText: Ohio uses the phrase 'materially affect health and safety' in three places, and where it sits decides whom it helps. It qualifies your code-compliance duty and nothing else: you must comply with building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety (R.C. 5321.04(A)(1)). The other duties in that subsection carry no materiality qualifier at all - repairs and fit and habitable condition, safe and sanitary common areas, good and safe working order for the fixtures and appliances you supply, waste receptacles where you let four or more units in one structure, and running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat. So 'that defect was not material' is an argument about a code requirement, not about heat, hot water or habitability. Materiality works for you in one place: the thirty-day cure-and-terminate notice is available only where your tenant's breach of R.C. 5321.05 materially affects health and safety (R.C. 5321.11). And the tenant needs no material defect to start the rent-escrow clock - a reasonable belief that you failed any obligation under R.C. 5321.04, or an agency finding of code non-compliance, is enough (R.C. 5321.07(A)).

title: Ohio Narrows Your Habitability Duty by Statute, Never by Agreement
bodyText: Your habitability duty can be narrower than the list suggests, but only on the statute's own terms - never because the lease says so. Two limbs carry their own built-in limits. Waste receptacles and removal are owed only where you are a party to rental agreements covering four or more dwelling units in the same structure (R.C. 5321.04(A)(5)). And running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat are not owed where the building that includes the unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or where the unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection (R.C. 5321.04(A)(6)). That second escape is structural and cumulative: how the unit was built, an installation the tenant actually controls, and a direct utility connection. A submeter you read and bill is not one. The chapter also does not reach every letting - R.C. 5321.01(C) excludes ten categories, among them a farm residence let with at least two acres for agricultural production by the occupant, and an agricultural labour camp subject to chapter 3733. A manufactured-home-park lot is outside chapter 5321 too, but it is not one of the ten: R.C. 4781.01(W) makes a park's 'residential premises' the lot and the park's grounds, while R.C. 5321.01(C) requires a dwelling unit. Outside those statutory limits the duty is fixed: R.C. 5321.13(A) lets no oral or written agreement modify or waive it.

title: Ohio Creates No Habitability Presumptions - the Record Decides
bodyText: Nothing in Ohio's landlord-tenant law presumes anything about habitability. No provision deems a unit uninhabitable because a code violation was cited, none presumes that passing the cure window means your delay was unreasonable, and none presumes that your response to a complaint was retaliatory. The only presumption in the whole landlord-obligations section is about entry: twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice in the absence of evidence to the contrary (R.C. 5321.04(A)(8)). Two things do run against you, and they are triggers rather than presumptions. The tenant may serve the repair notice on a reasonable belief that you failed an obligation, without proving you did, and an agency finding of code non-compliance is an independent trigger on its own (R.C. 5321.07(A)). Bad faith sits on the tenant's side of the ledger, not yours: if the condition was the tenant's own doing, or the tenant acted in bad faith, the tenant pays your damages and costs, plus fees for intentional bad faith (R.C. 5321.09(D)). With no presumptions either way, a conditions dispute turns on evidence of what you knew and what you did, so date and keep every repair request, inspection and invoice.

title: Ohio Requires No Habitability Promise in the Lease - Only One Thing
bodyText: No Ohio statute makes you state in the lease that you will deliver or keep the unit fit to live in, and none prescribes any habitability wording. Ohio takes the opposite route: the duty is implied into every tenancy by R.C. 5321.04 whether the lease mentions it or not, and R.C. 5321.13(A) stops any agreement from modifying or waiving it, so there is nothing for a lease statement to add. R.C. 5321.18 is the only provision that says what a written Ohio lease must contain, and it is the name and address of the owner and of the owner's agent - nothing about condition. That one requirement is worth getting right, because leaving it out costs you the thirty days: under R.C. 5321.18(C) you waive your right to the tenant's repair notice and the clerk's escrow notice, so the tenant can go straight to rent escrow without warning you. Say nothing about the unit's condition in the lease that is not true. If you describe the property as code-compliant or fully repaired and it is not, you have written yourself a lease obligation the tenant can enforce through the rent-escrow route.

title: Ohio Habitability Cannot Be Waived, Traded or Discounted
bodyText: You cannot buy your way out of a habitability duty in Ohio, and you cannot get the tenant to sell it. R.C. 5321.13(A) is one sentence: no provision of the chapter may be modified or waived by any oral or written agreement, except as provided in division (F). That 'except' qualifies this sentence alone, and (F) opens only one door - you may agree to take on a tenant duty, never the reverse. So three arrangements that are lawful in other states are void here. A clause reciting that the tenant accepts the unit as is, with or without a rent reduction for the condition, modifies R.C. 5321.04 by agreement and has no effect. A separate document in which the tenant agrees to a lower heat level is still an agreement, and (A) does not care whether it sits inside the lease or beside it. And an arrangement letting you collect rent while the condition stands is barred twice over, because R.C. 5321.13(E) says the rental agreement may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with R.C. 5321.04. Price the rent for the unit as it is instead, and record accepted cosmetic items in the move-in condition report, not as a waiver.

title: Ohio Owes Reasonable Heat and Names No Number
bodyText: You must supply reasonable heat at all times, and you must keep the heating, ventilating and air-conditioning fixtures and appliances you supply in good and safe working order (R.C. 5321.04(A)(6) and (A)(4)). Ohio sets no temperature and no heating season. We found no degree figure and no heating-facilities standard anywhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Constitution or the administrative rules we hold, which include the Ohio Fire Code rules at Ohio Adm.Code 1301:7-7. Any figure sits somewhere we could not read: the state Residential and Building Codes at Ohio Adm.Code 4101:8 and 4101:1, which R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes your duty, or a city housing code, which R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves standing despite Ohio's otherwise broad preemption. Check both for the property before you rely on 'reasonable'. You cannot move heat onto the tenant by agreement. The two escapes in the statute are structural, not contractual: either the building is not required by law to be equipped for the purpose, or the unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation, within the tenant's exclusive control, supplied by a direct public utility connection - three parts that must all be true. A separate meter you read and bill is not that. R.C. 5321.13(A) voids anything less.

title: Rent Escrow Is Not the Only Thing a Tenant Can Do to You
bodyText: If you are relying on an exemption from Ohio's rent-escrow scheme, read this first. R.C. 5321.12 lets any party in an action under the chapter recover damages for breach of contract or breach of any duty imposed by law. It carries no written notice, no thirty-day cure window, and none of the exclusions attached to the escrow remedy - so a landlord who is party to agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and gave the required notice, or a college letting to its own student tenant, is outside the escrow scheme and still fully exposed to damages. Three more routes run alongside. A tenant you sue for possession on nonpayment, or for rent while still in possession, may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the chapter, and the court may order rent paid into court (R.C. 1923.061(B)). Abusing entry has its own remedies: actual damages, an injunction, reasonable attorney's fees, or termination of the agreement (R.C. 5321.04(B)) - and that fee award is the court's, so the ban on agreed attorney-fee clauses does not protect you from it. Shutting off utilities or locking the tenant out costs you all damages plus fees (R.C. 5321.15(C)). And the court can order an agency inspection of the premises and forbid re-renting until the conditions are corrected (R.C. 1923.15).

title: Ohio Does Not Police Your Promises to Fix Things - Your Own Lease Does
bodyText: No Ohio statute or rule we searched requires a promise to clean, repair or improve a rental to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. Ohio's consumer-protection machinery almost certainly does not reach it either: R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a consumer transaction as a sale or lease of an item of goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible, which does not name real property, and the Attorney General's deceptive-practices rules in Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3 contain no residential-rental repair rule. What does bite is your own lease. R.C. 5321.07(A) lets the tenant use the written-notice and rent-escrow route for a failure of any obligation imposed by the rental agreement, not only the statutory duties - so a repair you promise in the lease becomes enforceable the same way heat is, and R.C. 5321.12 lets the tenant recover damages for the breach. Promise only what you will actually do, write it with a date so there is no argument about what 'soon' meant, and do not describe the unit as repaired or code-compliant before it is.

title: Ohio Does Not Make a Tenant Pay to Defend - Ask, or You Get Nothing
bodyText: In Ohio any defence in an eviction action may be asserted at trial, with no deposit, bond or pleading precondition. So do not plan on arrears sitting safely with the clerk while the case runs. Where you sue for possession on nonpayment, or for rent while the tenant is still in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or under the landlord-tenant chapter, and only then may the court order past-due rent and rent coming due to be paid into court (R.C. 1923.061(B)). The word is 'may'. It is discretionary, it is triggered by the tenant's counterclaim rather than by your complaint, and nothing gives it to you automatically, so ask for the order expressly. The sting is in the same subsection: after judgment the party owed the net is paid first out of that money, and if no rent remains due once the counterclaim is applied, judgment on possession goes to the tenant. A counterclaim that wipes out the arrears defeats the eviction itself, not merely the money claim. Two other deposits exist and neither is about conditions: a continuance longer than eight days on the tenant's application requires a bond for accruing rent (R.C. 1923.08), and in a county court the party demanding a jury deposits the jury fee (R.C. 1923.101).

title: No Ohio Cost Threshold Lets You Walk Away From a Repair
bodyText: Ohio sets no figure at which a repair becomes someone else's problem. Nothing lets you end a residential tenancy because the work would cost more than a stated amount or a share of the property's value, and nothing caps the tenant's remedies by what the repair costs. The termination rights Ohio does give turn on conduct and condition, never on price: the tenant may terminate after serving the written repair notice and waiting out the cure window, or where you abuse the right of entry, and you may terminate for a tenant's breach of the statutory tenant duties that materially affects health and safety, on written notice fixing a date not less than thirty days out. Cost only ever appears on your side as a question for the court - when a tenant has deposited rent, the court may release part of it to you during the case for mortgage payments, insurance, taxes, utilities, repairs and the usual costs of running the property, weighing what it will cost to remedy the condition. So if you want an exit when a building is too damaged to be worth repairing, your lease has to write it, with your own trigger and your own figure, and a court can still refuse to enforce a term it finds unconscionable.

title: Your Repair Duty Does Not Wait for a Notice - the Tenant's Remedy Does
bodyText: Nothing conditions your R.C. 5321.04 duties on a request. They bind you from the start of the tenancy, and a tenant who never writes to you can still sue for damages under R.C. 5321.12 or counterclaim in your eviction case under R.C. 1923.061. Written notice matters for one thing: before the tenant can escrow rent, get a court order or terminate, the tenant must give you written notice specifying the acts, omissions or code violations, and it is sent to the person or place where rent is normally paid (R.C. 5321.07(A)). That address is the statute's, not yours, and a lease section sending repair requests elsewhere does not move it - so whoever receives rent must pass these on the day they arrive, because your cure window is the shorter of a reasonable time for the severity or thirty days. Two traps. The notice can rest on the tenant's reasonable belief that you failed a duty, or on an agency's code finding, so it proves nothing. And if you left the owner's and agent's name and address out of the written lease, R.C. 5321.18(C) waives the notice entirely and the tenant may escrow with no warning. Ask for repair requests in writing by all means, but treat that as record-keeping: a lease term making written notice a condition of your duty modifies the chapter, and R.C. 5321.13(A) refuses it.

title: Entity Landlords Need a Lawyer to Evict
bodyText:
If you own through an LLC, a corporation or any other entity, you will need a lawyer to file and run the eviction. R.C. 4705.01 says no person may 'commence, conduct, or defend any action or proceeding in which the person is not a party concerned' unless admitted to the Ohio bar - so a property manager, a managing agent, a member or an officer cannot file or argue the case, because the entity is the party and they are not. R.C. 1923.01(C)(2) does include your managing agent in the word 'landlord', but that is a definition for the eviction chapter, not permission to appear in court for someone else. Ohio's one accommodation is narrow and does not reach eviction: under R.C. 1925.17 a corporation may have a bona fide officer or salaried employee present a claim in a small claims division, and even then only on a claim the corporation is an original party to, and only if that person does not 'engage in cross-examination, argument, or other acts of advocacy'. An eviction is not a small claims case - the municipal court hears it under R.C. 1901.18(A)(8) as a forcible entry and detainer action - so the small claims route is unavailable for possession. If you own in your own name you are the party and may appear for yourself.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review plus R.C. 4705.01 and R.C. 1925.17 read in full outside it. Chapter 4705 (attorneys) and chapter 1925 (small claims divisions) are not in the reviewed corpus, and the Supreme Court of Ohio's own rules, which R.C. 4705.01 makes an exception for, were not reviewed at all. No Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: Ohio's Four Ways an Eviction Gets Delayed - None of Them Is Hardship
bodyText: Ohio gives a court no power to postpone a tenant's removal because of hardship - illness, age, children, winter weather or an inability to find another home are not grounds for a stay anywhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row, including all of R.C. Chapters 1923 and 5321 read whole. The word 'hardship' appears in nine of those chapters and in none of the landlord-tenant or eviction ones. Four things do delay you, and you should plan around them. ONE - the eight-day continuance. A continuance may not run longer than eight days unless you applied for it and the tenant consents, or the TENANT applied for it and gave you a surety bond approved by the court and conditioned on paying rent that accrues if judgment goes against them (R.C. 1923.08). So the tenant can buy more than eight days only by bonding the rent. In the expedited drug-activity track no continuance is permitted at all (R.C. 1923.051(C)). TWO - the deployment stay, which is the closest thing Ohio has to a hardship stay. Where the tenant or a member of the tenant's immediate family is deployed on active duty, the tenant entered the rental agreement on or after 2005-05-18, and the tenant's ABILITY TO PAY the agreed rent is materially affected by the deployment, the court may act on its own motion and MUST act on the tenant's motion: either stay the proceedings ninety days, unless the court thinks justice and equity require longer or shorter, or adjust the obligation under the rental agreement to preserve all parties' interests. If a stay is granted the court may give you such relief as equity requires. This does not apply to a landlord operating fewer than four residential premises (R.C. 1923.062) - one of Ohio's small-landlord thresholds; see 'edu-portfolio-thresholds-oh'. THREE - money paid into court. Where the tenant counterclaims in a nonpayment case, the court may order past-due and accruing rent paid into court during the case, and if nothing remains due after applying it, judgment on possession goes to the tenant (R.C. 1923.061(B)). That is not a stay, but it can end the case rather than delay it. FOUR - the stay on appeal. If the tenant appeals and obtains a stay of execution with any required bond filed, the court must immediately order the officer to delay all further proceedings on the execution, and if you have already been restored to possession the officer puts the tenant back in (R.C. 1923.14(A)). Ohio does not condition that stay on the tenant filing a rent affidavit. Note the timing floor on the other side: the officer has ten days from receiving the writ to restore you (R.C. 1923.14(A)), so there is no same-day removal even without a stay. The stay-and-bond machinery R.C. 1923.14(A) assumes is in R.C. Chapter 2505 (R.C. 2505.09, 2505.11, 2505.12), which was not available here, so this row does not state what bond a tenant must post or on what terms an appellate stay is granted - in a municipal court R.C. 1901.28(A) separately lets a judgment debtor stay execution by bonding the judgment, interest and costs within ten days, with no stay allowed on the five categories in (B), but that section is written for money judgments and its application to a restitution judgment was not resolved. Ask local counsel before you tell a tenant what a stay would cost them.

title: The Ohio Eviction Process, Step by Step
bodyText: Ohio calls it forcible entry and detainer, and it runs under R.C. Chapter 1923 in the municipal or county court for the area, or in common pleas (R.C. 1923.01(A); R.C. 1901.18(A)(8)). You have two years from when the cause of action accrues (R.C. 1923.01(B)). STEP 1 - ground. R.C. 1923.02(A) lists them: holding over after the term, default in rent under an ORAL tenancy, breach of an R.C. 5321.05 duty materially affecting health and safety, breach of a written rental agreement, drug activity, the registered-offender grounds, and others. STEP 2 - notice. At least three days before you file, serve the notice to leave in the words R.C. 1923.04(A) prescribes (see 'edu-three-day-notice-language-oh'). It is a notice to leave, not a pay-or-quit notice: Ohio gives a tenant no statutory right to cure nonpayment, so nothing in the statute invites the tenant to pay and stay, and nothing requires you to say the amount owed. Which cure track a non-rent breach falls on decides the notice period (see 'edu-tenant-cure-period-oh'). STEP 3 - complaint. File a written complaint describing the premises and setting out the unlawful detention; it is copied into the record (R.C. 1923.05(A)). Never name a minor tenant alongside a parent or guardian (see 'edu-minor-tenant-filing-oh'). STEP 4 - summons. Service must be at least seven days before the trial date (R.C. 1923.06(A)). The clerk mails the summons and complaint by ordinary mail and ALSO completes service by the sheriff, bailiff or a court-designated person over eighteen - personally, on a person of suitable age and discretion at the premises, or by posting conspicuously there - or by certified mail, whichever you request when you file (R.C. 1923.06(C) to (E)). The summons carries its own court-written script telling the tenant about retaliation, rent deposits, jury trial and legal aid (R.C. 1923.06(B)). The possession hearing cannot be sooner than the seventh day after service is complete, scheduled under LOCAL court rules; answer day for any money claims is twenty-eight days (R.C. 1923.06(H)). STEP 5 - trial. The tenant need file no answer and may raise any defence at trial (R.C. 1923.061(A)). A continuance may not exceed eight days unless you ask and the tenant consents, or the tenant asks and posts a surety bond for rent accruing (R.C. 1923.08). If the tenant does not appear and service was proper, the court tries the case as though the tenant were present (R.C. 1923.07). Either side may demand a jury (R.C. 1923.10; in a county court the demanding party deposits the jury fee, R.C. 1923.101). You may try your claims for past-due rent and damages at the same hearing unless the court continues them for good cause, which includes the tenant wanting to answer, counterclaim or take discovery (R.C. 1923.081). STEP 6 - counterclaim and money into court. In a nonpayment possession case, or an action for rent while the tenant is in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or R.C. Chapter 5321, and the court MAY from time to time order the tenant to pay past-due rent and rent coming due into court during the case. Whoever is owed the net judgment is paid first out of that money; if no rent remains due after applying it, judgment on possession goes to the TENANT (R.C. 1923.061(B)). There is no provision awarding you fees if the counterclaim was brought in bad faith, and R.C. 5321.13(C) would void a lease term giving you fees anyway. STEP 7 - judgment and writ. The court gives you restitution of the premises and costs, or restitution of part only (R.C. 1923.09(A); R.C. 1923.11(A)). A judgment under this chapter is not a bar to a later action by either party (R.C. 1923.03). On your request the court issues a writ of execution in the statutory form (R.C. 1923.13(A)), and WITHIN TEN DAYS of receiving it the sheriff, police officer, constable or bailiff restores you to possession and levies costs not exceeding the standard motion fee (R.C. 1923.14(A)). Only that officer carries out the writ - never you (R.C. 5321.15(A); see 'edu-self-help-eviction-ban-oh'). If the tenant appeals and obtains a stay with any required bond, the court orders all further proceedings on the execution delayed, and if the premises were already restored to you the officer puts the tenant back in (R.C. 1923.14(A)). STEP 8 - a sting in the tail. During any residential proceeding the court may order a government agency to inspect, and if it finds R.C. 5321.04 violations it may FORBID YOU RE-RENTING the unit until they are corrected, or order them corrected with the tenant still in possession; if the tenant caused them you get damages equal to the reasonable cost of correction (R.C. 1923.15). WHAT OHIO DOES NOT GIVE YOU OR THE TENANT. Within the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row - including all of Chapters 1923, 5321, 1901 and 2329 - Ohio has no for-cause protection that attaches after twelve months' tenancy (see 'edu-for-cause-eviction-oh'), no statute reserving eviction procedure to the legislature, no bar on a court requiring its own pleading or notice form (R.C. 1923.06(H)(1) sends scheduling to local court rules, so expect local forms), no rent-affidavit condition on a stay pending appeal, no ban on a private process server filming service or execution and no $25,000 damages for it, no continuance for a federal employee or contractor during a federal shutdown, no rule barring a tenant in possession from denying your title, no provision making every person in possession liable for the rent on the part they hold, and no right to appointed counsel in an eviction - the statutory substitute is the summons script telling the tenant to contact legal aid (R.C. 1923.06(B)). Three things sit OUTSIDE those chapters and this row does not resolve them: the stay-on-appeal and supersedeas machinery R.C. 1923.14(A) refers to is in R.C. Chapter 2505 (R.C. 2505.09, 2505.11, 2505.12), which was not available; wage garnishment on a lease judgment and any percentage cap is in R.C. Chapter 2716 (R.C. 2716.01 to 2716.03), which was not available; and whether the three-day notice period excludes weekends and holidays turns on Civ.R. 6(A) and R.C. 1.14, neither of which is a statute this library has read - the statute itself says only 'three or more days'. Treat all three as open, and ask local counsel. Federal law can lengthen the notice: see 'edu-cares-act-notice'.

title: Ohio Has No Way to Seal an Eviction Record - Yours or the Tenant's
bodyText: Ohio gives nobody a route to seal, expunge or de-index the record of a forcible entry and detainer case. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row - including all of R.C. Chapter 1923, read whole - there is no sealing provision, no automatic expungement of a dismissed eviction, no seven-year removal from public indexes, and consequently no landlord right to object to sealing, because there is no application for you to object to. The only sealing provisions the search turned up are about electronic-surveillance applications and nursing-home investigation findings; the Revised Code's criminal sealing machinery sits in R.C. Chapter 2953, which is about criminal records, not civil possession cases. Two practical consequences. First, your filing is permanent and public from the moment you file: R.C. 1923.05(A) requires the complaint to be 'copied into, and made a part of the record.' A case you file and then dismiss still sits in the court's index under the tenant's name, so do not use a filing as leverage you expect to be able to withdraw. Second, when you screen applicants, remember that R.C. 1923.03 says a judgment under the chapter is not a bar to a later action by either party - a filing, or even a judgment, does not tell you what actually happened. Rely on the OUTCOME of a case rather than its existence, apply the same criteria to every applicant, and keep your screening within fair housing and federal consumer-reporting law, neither of which this topic displaces. Two things sit outside the chapters searched and this row does not resolve them: which court records are public and on what terms is governed by R.C. Chapter 149 (R.C. 149.43, the Public Records Act) and by the Rules of Superintendence for the Courts of Ohio (Sup.R. 44 to 47, which include a motion to restrict public access to a case document); and R.C. 2953.25 and 2953.26, the certificate of qualification for employment and the certificate of qualification for housing, are about a criminal record a landlord may see, not about an eviction record. Neither was available here, so do not tell a tenant flatly that no court could ever restrict access to a document in their case.

title: Your Ohio Lease Cannot Decide Who Accepts Eviction Papers
bodyText: Ohio gives the lease no role in serving an eviction. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row - including all of R.C. Chapters 1923 and 5321 read whole - there is no provision letting a tenant name, or a lease appoint, a person or an address to accept the notice to leave or the court papers, and no 'if the rental agreement so provides' hook anywhere in the service sections. Both ends are prescribed by statute instead. THE PRE-SUIT NOTICE. R.C. 1923.04(A) fixes the three permitted methods: certified mail with return receipt requested, handing a written copy to the defendant in person, or leaving it at the defendant's usual place of abode OR at the premises you are evicting from. A lease term pointing you somewhere else does not make service there good. THE COURT PAPERS. R.C. 1923.06(A) says a summons 'shall be issued, be in the form specified, and be served and returned as provided in this section.' The clerk mails the summons and complaint by ordinary mail, and must also complete service either through the sheriff, bailiff or a court-designated person over eighteen - who serves at the premises by tendering the papers, leaving them with a person of suitable age and discretion found there, or posting them conspicuously there - or by certified mail, whichever you request when you file (R.C. 1923.06(C) to (E)). One address does move, and it is yours to move: the clerk mails to the address in the caption AND to 'any address set forth in any written instructions furnished to the clerk.' Those are the PLAINTIFF'S instructions, so a notice address you collected in the lease is useful only because you can hand it to the clerk - it is not a designation the tenant makes that binds anyone. Practical course: collect a current mailing address from the tenant in the lease's notices clause and update it, so you have something to furnish the clerk; do not write a term appointing anyone to accept service of court papers for the tenant, and do not rely on one if a form you inherited has it. Note the other direction: R.C. 5321.18(A) requires YOUR written lease to carry the owner's and the agent's name and address, and for an entity, the principal place of business in the county with the name of the person in charge - see 'landlord-identity-oh'. One thing is outside the chapters searched and this row does not resolve it: Ohio has an address confidentiality program at R.C. 111.41 to 111.99, cross-referenced from R.C. 1901.25(A)(2), and whether a participant in it is served through the Secretary of State rather than at the premises is answered in that chapter, which was not available here. If an applicant or tenant tells you they are in that program, get advice before you serve anything at the unit. Whether a tenant could validly appoint an agent by appointment to receive service turns on Civ.R. 4.2, a rule of procedure this library has not read.

title: Ohio's Fast Track Exists, and It Only Runs on Drugs
bodyText: Ohio has exactly one expedited eviction track, and it is for controlled-substance activity. It switches on from the face of your complaint: if the complaint states that you seek a judgment of restitution on the R.C. 1923.02(A)(6)(a) and (b) grounds, then R.C. 1923.051 takes over the timetable. FOUR THINGS CHANGE. First, service is made under the Rules of Civil Procedure rather than the ordinary eviction service section, and the clerk must cause it to happen WITHIN THREE WORKING DAYS after the complaint is filed, if possible (R.C. 1923.051(A)(1)). Second, the court must set the trial NOT LATER THAN THE THIRTIETH CALENDAR DAY after the tenant is served (R.C. 1923.051(A)(2)) - and the ordinary seven-days-before-trial service rule in R.C. 1923.06(A) is expressly displaced. Third, NO CONTINUANCES are permitted at all; the eight-day continuance and the tenant's rent bond in R.C. 1923.08 are unavailable, and if the tenant does not appear after proper service the court tries the case as though they were present (R.C. 1923.051(C)). Fourth, the tenant need file no answer and may raise any defence at trial under R.C. 1923.061 (R.C. 1923.051(B)). Everything else in Chapter 1923 that is not inconsistent still applies (R.C. 1923.051(D)). WHAT GETS YOU ONTO THE TRACK. Two things must have happened before the tenant's three days to vacate even start running: you must have actual knowledge of, or reasonable cause to believe, a Chapter 2925 or 3719 controlled-substance violation (or a substantially similar municipal ordinance) by the tenant, a household member, or anyone on the premises with the tenant's consent, connected with the premises - charge, plea and conviction are all irrelevant - and you must have given the R.C. 5321.17(C) three-day termination notice. Giving that notice also satisfies the ordinary pre-suit notice requirement, so there is no second notice (R.C. 1923.04(B)). At trial the court must find the violation by a PREPONDERANCE OF THE EVIDENCE (R.C. 1923.02(A)(6)(b)) - the track is faster, not easier. There is a shortcut to the knowledge element worth knowing: R.C. 1923.02(A)(6)(a)(i) DEEMS you to have actual knowledge or reasonable cause where a search warrant named or described the tenant and particularly described the premises, named the substances, stated the offence and the factual basis, the warrant was properly executed, a described controlled substance was found, and a law enforcement officer then told you about it. If that is your fact pattern, document every element. This is not a right you may sit on - acting is a duty, and inaction carries its own criminal exposure: see 'edu-mandatory-drug-termination-oh'. WHAT OHIO DOES NOT GIVE YOU. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row there is no expedited track for violent crime, weapons, gang or other non-drug criminal activity, no route for police, a prosecutor or a neighbour to bring your possession case, and no removal of the tenant's right to notice or to a hearing. The registered-offender grounds in R.C. 1923.02(A)(14), (A)(15) and (C) and R.C. 5321.051 add a GROUND but no acceleration - a case on that ground runs on the ordinary timetable (see 'sex-offender-occupancy-oh'). Non-drug criminal conduct is an ordinary lease breach or an R.C. 5321.05 duty breach, and which notice period applies depends on which cure track it falls on (see 'edu-tenant-cure-period-oh'). Two cautions. The fast track's service runs on Civ.R. 4, a rule of procedure this library has not read, so confirm with the clerk how service will actually be effected before you rely on three working days. And a nuisance route exists outside this chapter: see 'edu-nuisance-receivership-oh'.

title: Ohio's Only Right to Cure a Default and Keep the Home Is for Land Contracts
bodyText: If you sell on a land installment contract rather than renting, forget what you know about Ohio evictions - the occupant gets a cure right a tenant never gets, and you can lose the property if you move too fast. A land installment contract is an executory agreement, not fully performable within a year, under which you agree to convey title to improved residential real property and the buyer pays the price in installments while you keep title as security (R.C. 5313.01(A), (B)). FORTY DAYS BEFORE YOU CAN FILE. When the buyer defaults in payment, forfeiture may be enforced ONLY after thirty days from the date of the default, and during those thirty days the buyer avoids forfeiture entirely by paying all payments currently due plus any fees or charges owed under the contract - if that happens, forfeiture 'shall not be enforced' (R.C. 5313.05). After the thirty days you start forfeiture by serving a written notice that identifies the contract and describes the property, specifies the terms not complied with, tells the buyer the contract stands forfeited unless they perform within TEN DAYS of completed service, and tells them to leave the premises; serve it in person, by leaving it at the buyer's usual place of abode or at the property, or by registered or certified mail to the last known address (R.C. 5313.06). So there are two cure windows, thirty days then ten more. Serving that notice also satisfies the three-day eviction notice requirement, so you do not serve both (R.C. 5313.08; R.C. 1923.04(B)). THE FIVE-YEAR / TWENTY-PER-CENT CLIFF. If the buyer has paid in accordance with the contract for five years or more from the first payment, OR has paid toward the purchase price a total equal to or more than twenty per cent of it, you may recover possession ONLY by foreclosure and judicial sale - not by forfeiture and not through an eviction (R.C. 5313.07). Below that line, and only after both periods above have run, you may bring an action under R.C. Chapter 1923 for forfeiture of the buyer's rights and restitution of the property, and the court may declare the forfeiture and grant other claims arising out of the contract (R.C. 5313.08; R.C. 1923.02(A)(7)). Judgment cancels the contract as of a date the court specifies, and the clerk sends an authenticated copy to the county recorder to be recorded as an instrument of cancellation (R.C. 5313.09(A)). ELECTING FORFEITURE SHUTS THE DOOR. Terminating under R.C. 5313.07 or 5313.08 is an EXCLUSIVE REMEDY barring further action on the contract, unless the buyer has paid less than the fair rental value plus deterioration or destruction from their use - in which case you may recover only the difference between what they paid and that figure (R.C. 5313.10). You cannot forfeit and then sue for the balance of the price. Note R.C. 5313.02 separately dictates sixteen contract provisions, recording within twenty days, and county-engineer review of a metes-and-bounds description - a land contract is a different document from a lease and this library's lease clauses are not drafted for one. FOR AN ORDINARY TENANCY THERE IS NO EQUIVALENT. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched, nothing lets a residential TENANT cure a rent default to keep the tenancy, before or after notice, judgment or writ - see 'edu-no-redemption-oh'.

title: Nothing in Ohio Makes You Tell the Tenant Why
bodyText: Ohio has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so there is no good-cause notice or disclosure to give, in the lease or at termination. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row, 'good cause' appears in thirty-eight of them and in R.C. Chapters 1923 and 5321 it appears exactly twice - in R.C. 1923.081, where it is the standard for continuing your money claims, and in R.C. 5321.09, where it is the standard for releasing escrowed rent. Neither has anything to do with the reason for an eviction. 'Just cause' appears nowhere in either chapter. The practical point is what your notices do NOT have to say. R.C. 1923.04(A) tells you the exact words your notice to leave must contain and nothing more: there is no requirement to state a reason, name a ground, cite a lease section, or disclose that Ohio has no good-cause rule. Terminating a periodic tenancy needs no reason at all - thirty days before the periodic rental date for month-to-month, seven days for week-to-week (R.C. 5321.17(A), (B)) - and holding over after a term ends is itself a ground (R.C. 1923.02(A)(1)). The one good-cause-style statement a tenant receives in an Ohio eviction is not yours and you do not draft it: the COURT-ISSUED summons must carry, printed in a conspicuous manner, 'No person shall be evicted unless the person's right to possession has ended and no person shall be evicted in retaliation for the exercise of the person's lawful rights' (R.C. 1923.06(B)). Expect the tenant to read it, and make sure your file shows which of those two things is true. THREE QUALIFICATIONS, none of them a notice duty. First, once a tenant has done something the retaliation statute protects, your available grounds narrow sharply - that is a cause rule in that situation even though Ohio has none in general, and R.C. 5321.03's five grounds are the safe harbour, not a general list. Second, a college or university letting to its own student tenant is the exception that DOES carry a lease-content duty: the written rental agreement must specify the conditions under which it may be terminated and the institution's notice and hearing procedures (R.C. 5321.031). Third, the registered-offender ground runs the other way and adds a cause. All three are set out in 'edu-for-cause-eviction-oh'; this row does not restate them. Two outside limits remain. A city cannot fill the gap: R.C. 5321.19(A) bars a political subdivision from regulating the rights and obligations of parties to a rental agreement that Chapter 5321 regulates (see 'edu-rent-control-preemption-oh'), though municipal measures are flagged here rather than resolved. And a federal program can impose its own cause requirement regardless of state law - a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy is the common one - so check your HAP contract and tenancy addendum, which this library has not reviewed.

title: No Ohio Lease Can Buy You the Right to Change the Locks
bodyText: Some states let a landlord and tenant opt in to a lockout for unpaid rent - advance written notice, a lease clause the tenant signs, and the tenant entitled to a key on request within twenty-four hours. Ohio has nothing of the kind, and the lease cannot create it. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row, including all of R.C. Chapters 1923 and 5321 read whole, there is no opt-in lockout, no advance-notice-then-lockout procedure, no key-on-request duty and no partial or conditional version of any of them. The word 'locks' appears in only two of those chapters and both are building-code sections about deadbolts on swinging doors, not remedies. That matters more here than in most states because of HOW the ban is written. The prohibition itself - no act for the purpose of recovering possession other than through R.C. Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321, including terminating utilities and excluding the tenant from the premises, reaching even a tenant whose right to possession has already ended, with all damages and attorney's fees if you break it - is set out in 'edu-self-help-eviction-ban-oh'. What this row adds is that you cannot contract out of it. R.C. 5321.13(A) says no provision of Chapter 5321 may be modified or waived by any oral or written agreement except the one-way duty-shifting in division (F), so a signed lockout clause, a tenant's written consent at move-in, an acknowledgment in a payment plan and a hand-written agreement at the door are all equally ineffective. The tenant's consent is not yours to collect. See 'edu-one-way-delegation-oh' for how narrow (F) is. Two further points. First, a clause that purports to authorise a lockout is worse than useless: it tells a court you intended the conduct, and the R.C. 5321.15(C) remedy includes reasonable attorney's fees, which R.C. 5321.13(C)'s ban on fee agreements does not protect you from because the award is statutory. Second, Ohio's only statutory landlord self-help over a tenant's property is the self-service storage facility lien in R.C. 5322.02 and 5322.03, and that is a lien over goods with a notice-and-sale procedure, not a right to exclude - even there, removing the occupant goes through a court action under R.C. 1923.02(A)(13). WHAT TO DO. Take the lockout clause out of any form you inherited. Serve the R.C. 1923.04(A) notice to leave, file, get judgment, get the writ, and let the officer execute it (see 'edu-eviction-process-oh'). Changing the locks the day after rent is late is the exact conduct R.C. 5321.15 was written to stop, and it converts your rent claim into the tenant's damages claim.

title: Which Ohio Notices Your Lease May Change, and Which It May Not
bodyText: Ohio does not use the phrase 'notice to quit' - it appears nowhere in the Revised Code chapters searched for this row - and the answer to whether your lease may shorten or waive a termination notice depends entirely on WHICH CHAPTER the notice lives in. CHAPTER 5321 NOTICES: NO. R.C. 5321.13(A) makes every provision of Chapter 5321 non-waivable and unmodifiable by any oral or written agreement, except the one-way duty-shifting in division (F). So the periodic-termination minimums in R.C. 5321.17 - at least thirty days before the periodic rental date for month-to-month, at least seven days before the stated termination date for week-to-week - are a floor your lease may exceed but may not cut, and the tenant's signature does not change that. The same goes for R.C. 5321.11's thirty-day notice and cure for a breach of an R.C. 5321.05 duty materially affecting health and safety; compliance with it is a condition precedent to filing (R.C. 1923.02(A)(8)), so a seven-day clause in a form lease does not just fail, it defeats the case. See 'edu-one-way-delegation-oh' and 'edu-tenant-cure-period-oh'. Note too that R.C. 5321.17(A) and (B) run BOTH ways, 'the landlord or the tenant', so a clause giving the tenant less notice than it gives you is doubly exposed. The library's 'termination-notice-oh' clause is built as a floor for this reason. THE THREE-DAY NOTICE TO LEAVE: DO NOT TRY. R.C. 1923.04(A)'s three-or-more-days notice sits in Chapter 1923, not Chapter 5321, and Chapter 1923 contains no non-waiver clause of its own - so R.C. 5321.13(A) does not reach it on the face of the statutes, and the statutes alone do not say a lease may not shorten or waive it. Treat that as a trap rather than an opportunity. The notice is a condition precedent to the action, Ohio courts have treated it as jurisdictional, and parties cannot confer jurisdiction on a court by contract; the library's own 'edu-waiver-by-acceptance-oh' records that position. CAUTIOUS COURSE: never write a clause purporting to waive or shorten the three-day notice, and always serve it in the prescribed words even where a lease you inherited says you need not. If a specific deal makes the point worth money, get an Ohio opinion - this row does not resolve it. WHERE YOUR LEASE DOES CONTROL. Three places. First, a breach of an obligation your WRITTEN lease imposes with no health-and-safety dimension is its own ground under R.C. 1923.02(A)(9), which carries no statutory cure period, so the period your lease sets is the period that governs. Second, you may always give MORE notice than the statute requires, and may bind yourself to do so. Third, R.C. 5321.06 lets the lease carry any term not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or another rule of law, with R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability as the only ceiling - so longer periods, extra warnings and courtesy notices are all available. One limit you cannot contract around at all: on a federally backed property the federal 30-day notice to vacate applies whatever the lease says (see 'edu-cares-act-notice').

title: No Possession Bond in Ohio, and the Confessed-Judgment Version Is Void
bodyText: Ohio has no possession bond. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row - including all of R.C. Chapters 1923, 5321, 1901 and 2329 read whole or searched whole - there is no bond you can post to get possession faster, no bond a tenant must post to keep possession, and no end-of-term possession bond with a confessed judgment attached. The phrase does not exist in Ohio law; 'bond' appears in ninety-three of those chapters and every bond in the eviction machinery runs the other direction. Here is what the statute actually offers. ONE - the tenant's continuance bond. A continuance may not exceed eight days unless you asked for it and the tenant consents, or the TENANT asked for it and gave you a bond with good and sufficient surety, approved by the court and conditioned on paying rent that accrues if judgment goes against them (R.C. 1923.08). That is the tenant buying time, not you buying possession. TWO - the stay bond on appeal. R.C. 1923.14(A) delays execution once a stay is obtained and 'any required bond' is filed, and in a municipal court R.C. 1901.28(A) lets a judgment debtor stay execution within ten days by bonding the judgment, interest and costs with a freeholder or corporate surety, with no stay allowed in the five categories listed in (B). THREE - the jury fee deposit in a county court (R.C. 1923.101). That is the whole list. AND DO NOT REACH FOR THE CONFESSED-JUDGMENT SHORTCUT. R.C. 5321.13(B) bars any warrant of attorney to confess judgment, both in the residential rental agreement and in ANY OTHER agreement between you and the tenant for the recovery of rent or damages - so you cannot move it into a side letter, a payment plan or a move-out agreement. See 'edu-exculpation-indemnity-ban-oh', which carries that prohibition. The only other cognovit-style provision in the chapters searched is the matching ban for manufactured home parks at R.C. 4781.47. WHAT TO DO INSTEAD. Recover possession through the Chapter 1923 action (see 'edu-eviction-process-oh'), secure performance with the security deposit and, if the tenant's covenant is thin, a guarantor. One limb sits outside the chapters searched and this row does not resolve it: the appellate stay-and-bond terms R.C. 1923.14(A) refers to are in R.C. Chapter 2505 (R.C. 2505.09, 2505.11, 2505.12), which was not available here, so do not tell a tenant what a stay would cost.

title: The Writ Gets You the Unit, Not an Answer About What Is Left in It
bodyText: The officer who executes the writ restores you to possession of the premises and levies costs (R.C. 1923.14(A)) - and that is where Ohio's instructions stop for an ordinary residential rental. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row, including all of R.C. Chapters 1923 and 5321 read whole, there is no post-writ duty to store, inventory, care for or give notice about belongings left behind, no claim period, no sale procedure and no safe harbour for disposing of them. The detailed machinery that does exist - written notice to remove, the valuation affidavit, county auditor sign-off, sale, destruction and transfer of title in R.C. 1923.12 to 1923.14(B) - applies ONLY to a manufactured home, mobile home or recreational vehicle in a manufactured home park. For the disposal problem itself and R.C. 5321.15(B)'s bar on seizing a tenant's furnishings, see 'edu-no-abandoned-property-safe-harbor-oh'; this row adds the four other post-writ questions. NO PET RULE. Nothing in those chapters says anything about an animal left at the property after a writ. This is Ohio's starkest eviction-duty gap and the statutes give you no procedure at all. Ohio's animal-cruelty and dog provisions sit in R.C. Chapters 959 and 955, neither of which was available here, so do not treat the silence as permission: the cautious course is food, water and shelter, contact the former tenant in writing, and call the county dog warden or a humane agent at once, before you touch anything else. NO IMMUNITY FOR YOU. The only writ-execution immunity in the chapter is a park operator's, and it is narrow even there: R.C. 1923.14(B)(2) shields a PARK OPERATOR from liability for damage from removing a manufactured home or personal property, and for damage while it is abandoned or stored, UNLESS the damage results from acts done with malicious purpose, in bad faith, or in a wanton or reckless manner - and separately shields the officer. There is no counterpart for an ordinary landlord, and R.C. 5321.13(D) would void a lease term in which the tenant exculpated or indemnified you for your own liability (see 'edu-exculpation-indemnity-ban-oh'). So stand back and let the officer do it: you are safest when the removal is the officer's act, not yours (R.C. 5321.15(A); 'edu-self-help-eviction-ban-oh'). TWO LIMBS SIT OUTSIDE THE CHAPTERS SEARCHED AND THIS ROW DOES NOT RESOLVE THEM. First, whether a former tenant who stays or comes back after a writ commits a crime: criminal trespass is R.C. 2911.21, in a chapter that was not available, so do not tell a former tenant they are committing an offence - call the police and let them decide. Second, Ohio has a separate action for the recovery of real property in R.C. Chapter 5303, which R.C. 5321.15(A) names alongside Chapter 1923 as a permitted route to possession; that chapter was not available either, so whether it offers a different or warehouse-style storage option is open. The word 'ejectment' appears nowhere in the chapters searched, and the six 'warehouse' hits are consumer-sales, drug-exemption, refrigerator, Medicaid and self-storage provisions, none of them an eviction storage option. PRACTICAL COURSE. Get the writ, let the officer execute it, photograph and date everything that is left, write to the former tenant's last known address offering a reasonable collection window, store rather than discard, and get a court order before you dispose of anything of value.

title: An Ohio Tenant Cannot Pay to Stop the Eviction - But Watch What You Accept
bodyText: Ohio gives a tenant no statutory right to redeem a tenancy by paying. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row - including all of R.C. Chapters 1923 and 5321 read whole - there is no right to cure nonpayment within the notice period, no right to pay everything owed before trial, before judgment, or up to any number of hours before the writ is carried out, nothing that stops a writ of restitution once a money judgment is satisfied, no wording you are required to use when you accept a partial payment, and nothing requiring you to accept payment from a charity, a government rent-assistance program or any other third party, or barring you from limiting how such a payment is made. The R.C. 1923.04(A) notice is a notice to LEAVE, not a pay-or-quit notice: it does not offer the tenant the option of paying, and you are not required to state an amount. The redemption provisions the search did find are elsewhere and do not reach a lease - R.C. 2329.33 lets a judgment DEBTOR redeem REAL ESTATE sold on execution before the sale is confirmed, and R.C. 5313.05 gives a land-installment-contract vendee thirty days to avoid forfeiture (see 'edu-forfeiture-redemption-oh'). TWO THINGS YOU MUST STILL GET RIGHT. FIRST, what the tenant pays into court can end your case. Where the tenant counterclaims in a nonpayment possession action, the court may order past-due and accruing rent paid into court, and if no rent remains due after the net judgment is applied, judgment on POSSESSION is entered for the tenant (R.C. 1923.061(B)). The court-issued summons itself tells the tenant to keep depositing rent with the clerk and that failing to do so may result in eviction (R.C. 1923.06(B)). So Ohio's functional substitute for redemption is the deposit, and it is in the tenant's hands, not yours. SECOND, accepting money can destroy your notice. Ohio has no statutory reservation wording, but it has a well-settled rule about which PERIOD the money covers - and a 'no waiver' clause will not save you. Do not improvise here: see 'edu-waiver-by-acceptance-oh' before you take, hold or bank anything after serving a notice. PRACTICAL COURSE. Decide your policy before money arrives, in writing, and apply it the same way every time. If you intend to go on with the case, do not accept the payment; return it promptly and say in writing that it is not accepted. If you intend to accept it, expect the default to be treated as cured for the period it covers and plan to start over. If a rent-assistance agency offers to pay, you may decline - but think hard, because a full payment usually beats a judgment you have to execute.

title: Ohio Never Makes You Demand the Rent First
bodyText: In many states you cannot file for nonpayment until you have served a written demand for the rent, in a prescribed form, and the lease cannot shorten it. Ohio has no such requirement and no such bar. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched for this row, the word 'demand' appears in only four sections of R.C. Chapters 1923 and 5321 - three of them about demanding a JURY (R.C. 1923.09, 1923.10, 1923.101) and the fourth about repeated demands for ENTRY (R.C. 5321.04(B)). No section of either chapter contains the words 'demand' and 'rent' together, and 'demand for rent', 'demand the rent' and 'without demand' return nothing anywhere in those chapters. The only thing you must serve before filing is the R.C. 1923.04(A) notice to leave the premises, three or more days ahead, in the words the statute prescribes. That notice is not a demand: it does not ask the tenant to pay, it need not state an amount, and Ohio gives the tenant no statutory right to cure nonpayment by paying it (see 'edu-three-day-notice-language-oh' and 'edu-no-redemption-oh'). Know which ground you are on, because the chapter splits nonpayment by lease type. Under an ORAL tenancy, default in rent forfeits the right of occupancy and you may at your option terminate by giving the R.C. 1923.04 notice to leave, then sue (R.C. 1923.02(A)(2) and (B)). Under a WRITTEN lease, nonpayment is a breach of an obligation your written rental agreement imposes, which is its own ground (R.C. 1923.02(A)(9)) - so your lease has to actually impose the obligation in terms. Neither route involves a demand. The flip side is that Ohio supplies none of the rent mechanics either. There is no statutory due date, no grace period, and nothing saying rent is payable in advance or without demand - all of that is contractual, so if your lease does not say when rent is due and that it is due without demand, nothing else will. The library's 'rent-payment' clause carries exactly that language and it is doing real work in Ohio; see also 'late-fee', 'edu-no-statutory-caps-oh' and 'edu-rent-increase-notice-gap-oh'. TWO CAUTIONS. First, 'no demand required' is not 'no risk in demanding': if you accept money after serving the notice, which period it covers can cost you the notice, and a 'no waiver' clause may not save you. That rule is Ohio case law, not statute - nothing in the 37 chapters searched for this row addresses acceptance of rent - and the cases were not read here, so read 'edu-waiver-by-acceptance-oh', which carries them, before you take or hold anything. Second, if you choose to tell the tenant the amount owed, do it without disturbing the statutory wording, and do not write the notice so it reads as an offer to let them pay and stay, which is not what Ohio's notice is. Federal law can still require a 30-day notice to vacate on a federally backed property: see 'edu-cares-act-notice'.

title: Which Ohio Notices the Statute Actually Puts in Writing
bodyText: Ohio's writing requirements are specific rather than general, and the gaps surprise people. What follows is chapters 1923 and 5321 read whole, plus the individual sections named, so read it as the writing rules those chapters impose rather than as every writing rule in Ohio law - the Statute of Frauds sections below, R.C. 1335.04 and 1335.05, sit in a chapter outside this library's Ohio corpus and were fetched one section at a time. PUT THESE IN WRITING BECAUSE THE STATUTE SAYS SO. (1) The notice to leave that starts an eviction - its prescribed language must be 'printed or written in a conspicuous manner', and one of the three permitted service routes is handing the tenant a WRITTEN COPY, so there is no oral version (R.C. 1923.04(A)). (2) The thirty-day notice for a tenant's breach of an R.C. 5321.05 duty materially affecting health and safety: you 'may deliver a written notice' specifying the act or omission and a termination date not less than thirty days after receipt (R.C. 5321.11). (3) Your security-deposit accounting: every deduction must be itemized and identified in a WRITTEN notice delivered to the tenant with the amount due, within thirty days after the rental agreement ends and possession is delivered (R.C. 5321.16(B)). (4) Owner and agent identity: it must be IN the written rental agreement, and if the tenancy is oral you must deliver a written notice of it at the start of occupancy (R.C. 5321.18(A), (B)). (5) The three-or-fewer-units escrow exemption, which you lose unless you give notice of it in a written rental agreement or, for an oral tenancy, deliver written notice at the time of initial occupancy (R.C. 5321.07(C)). (6) Your eviction complaint - the summons does not issue until you file a complaint 'in writing' (R.C. 1923.05(A)). (7) If you sell on a land installment contract, the forfeiture notice (R.C. 5313.06). NOW THE GAPS, WHICH MATTER MORE. R.C. 5321.17 does NOT require writing. Ending a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy takes 'notice given the other' - thirty days or seven - and even the mandatory three-day drug-activity termination under R.C. 5321.17(C) is framed as 'giving a notice of termination' with no written form prescribed. Do not take that as licence: an unwritten notice is a notice you cannot prove, and you will have to prove it. Use writing every time and keep the proof of delivery. Nor does Ohio require the LEASE to be written at all - R.C. 5321.01(D) defines a rental agreement to include an oral one, and R.C. 5321.01(E)'s security-deposit definition reaches money OR property. But an oral Ohio tenancy costs you two things. An action on an agreement not to be performed within one year of the making cannot be brought unless there is a signed writing (R.C. 1335.05), and an assignment or grant of a leasehold needs a deed or signed writing (R.C. 1335.04) - so an oral lease beyond a year is inside Chapter 5321 but may be unenforceable. And R.C. 1923.02(A)(9), the eviction ground for breaching a lease obligation, reaches only an obligation 'imposed upon them by a WRITTEN rental agreement', so with an oral tenancy you have no (A)(9) ground at all - nonpayment runs on (A)(2), and a non-rent breach has to fit a different division. Write the lease. TWO FURTHER POINTS. The tenant has writing duties too: a repair complaint that starts the escrow clock must be given 'in writing' to the place where rent is normally paid (R.C. 5321.07(A)), and a tenant who does not give you a forwarding address IN WRITING forfeits deposit damages and attorney's fees (R.C. 5321.16(B)). And electronic delivery is not the same question as writing - Ohio's electronic transactions act applies, with conditions, but email is not one of R.C. 1923.04(A)'s service methods: see 'edu-electronic-notice-regime-oh' before you send any notice electronically.

title: Ohio Does Not Regulate Application or Screening Fees
bodyText: Ohio has no rental-application or tenant-screening statute. Nothing caps an application or screening fee, nothing makes you refund an unused one, nothing exempts a minor household member, and nothing requires a written pre-application disclosure of estimated rent, fees, availability or screening criteria. There is no consumer-protection route either: the Consumer Sales Practices Act reaches only a transfer of 'goods, a service, a franchise, or an intangible' (R.C. 1345.01(A)), which does not take in a lease of real property, and neither Chapter 1345 nor the Attorney General's rules in Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3 contain the word landlord. Two cautions remain. R.C. 5321.01(E) defines a security deposit as any deposit of money or property to secure the tenant's performance, so money you hold to reserve a unit becomes deposit money once a rental agreement exists and falls under R.C. 5321.16. And R.C. 5321.14 is the only ceiling on the figure. Keep a true screening fee separate from any deposit, set it at what screening actually costs you, and state in writing what it buys and that it is not refundable.

title: Collection Fees and What Ohio Does Not Allow
bodyText:
Ohio sets no collection fee and caps none, so a fee you charge for collecting past-due rent rides entirely on the lease (R.C. 5321.06), with unconscionability the only ceiling (R.C. 5321.14). Two limits matter more than the fee itself. First, R.C. 5321.13(C) recognises no agreement to pay the landlord's or the tenant's attorney's fees, in a rental agreement or in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant, and it runs both ways - so a collection charge is unenforceable so far as it reaches your legal fees, whatever the lease calls it. Fees can still reach a tenant by statute, for example under R.C. 5321.05(C)(1), but never by agreement. Second, do not borrow the thirty-dollars-or-ten-per-cent figure that circulates in Ohio templates: R.C. 1319.16(A) gives that charge to a collection agency designated to collect on a dishonoured check, not to a landlord and not on past-due rent, and R.C. 1319.12(A)(2) puts outside the term 'collection agency' any person 'whose collection activities are confined to and directly related to the operation of another business', which is a landlord collecting its own rent. Passing on what a genuine third-party agency actually charges you is a different thing and the lease may provide for it.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, plus R.C. 1319.12 and 1319.16 read in full outside it. Ohio has no collection-agency licensing or registration requirement to point a clause at, and R.C. 1345.01(A) excludes residential landlord-tenant transactions from the Consumer Sales Practices Act, so no consumer-protection disclosure route applies. No Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: Ohio Has No Fee-Transparency Law - Except for Manufactured-Home Parks
bodyText: Ohio has no all-in-pricing or fee-transparency law for a residential tenancy, on a search of the 37 Revised Code chapters this library holds, the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - which include the consumer sales practices rules at Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3 - rather than of the whole Revised Code. Within that bound: nothing makes rent appear as one figure including every mandatory fee, nothing puts a fee list on the lease's first page under prescribed words, nothing requires fees to be itemized, and nothing makes charging a fee that the lease never mentions an unfair or deceptive trade practice. The Consumer Sales Practices Act is not a back door: R.C. 1345.01(A) reaches only a transfer of goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible, not a lease of real property, and neither Chapter 1345 nor the Attorney General's rules in Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3 mentions a landlord. R.C. 5321.18 is the only statute that dictates what an Ohio written rental agreement must contain, and all it requires is the owner's and the agent's name and address. Ohio does have a real fee-transparency regime - R.C. 4781.40(B) and (H)(4) make a manufactured-home-park operator disclose every fee in writing before signing, bar collecting an undisclosed one, and bar evicting over a refusal to pay it - but it does not reach you, because a park lot is outside Chapter 5321 altogether: R.C. 4781.01(W) makes a park's 'residential premises' the lot and the park's grounds, while R.C. 5321.01(C) requires a dwelling unit. Listing every fee is still the safer practice, because your right to a fee rests only on the lease.

title: No Ohio Rule on Charging for a Service You Stop Providing - But One Lease Term Is Void
bodyText: No Ohio statute says you may not charge a fee for a service you do not actually provide, and there is no consumer-protection route to it either - the Consumer Sales Practices Act reaches goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible, not a lease of real property (R.C. 1345.01(A)), and the Attorney General's rules in Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3 never mention a landlord. Three Ohio provisions still reach the conduct. R.C. 5321.13(E) voids any term by which a rental agreement, or an assignment or security instrument of your interest in it, would 'permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with section 5321.04' - so you cannot write yourself the right to keep collecting while a statutory duty goes unperformed. R.C. 5321.07 lets the tenant escrow rent, ask a court to order the work done or to reduce the rent, or terminate, over a failure of either a statutory duty or a duty your own lease created - so promising a service in the lease and charging for it puts that promise inside the escrow remedy. And a reduction in services done because the tenant complained is retaliation under R.C. 5321.02(A). Charge for a service only while you provide it, and stop the charge when the service stops.

title: No Ohio Late-Fee Cap, and No Grace Period Either
bodyText: Ohio sets no late-fee cap for a residential tenancy. It also sets no grace period before a late fee may be charged, no reasonableness test for the amount, and no rule against charging the same late fee twice over one late payment. The figure and the grace period are yours to set, and R.C. 5321.14 - a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term or limit how it applies - is the only ceiling on either. Ohio does have two late-fee statutes, and neither reaches a residential landlord. R.C. 5322.05 governs self-service storage facilities: it forbids a late fee if the occupant pays in full by the third day after the due date, deems twenty dollars or twenty per cent reasonable, and bars collection outright unless the fee and the conditions for it are stated in the rental agreement. R.C. 1345.031(B)(7) bars a second late fee on one late payment, but only in a residential mortgage. Do not import either statute's figures into a lease. Interest on money that is already overdue is a different route with its own Ohio rule; see this library's Ohio interest rows rather than folding a rate into the late fee.

title: A Refundable Pet Deposit Is Deposit Money in Ohio
bodyText: Ohio has no pet statute at all: nothing caps a pet fee, pet rent or a pet deposit, and nothing requires you to allow a pet. What Ohio does have is a deliberately broad definition - a security deposit is 'any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under a rental agreement' (R.C. 5321.01(E)). A refundable pet deposit secures the tenant's performance, so it is deposit money, and three consequences follow. It counts together with every other deposit toward the R.C. 5321.16(A) threshold, so the amount above fifty dollars or one month's periodic rent, whichever is greater, earns five per cent a year once the tenant has been in possession six months or more. It must be itemized and accounted for under R.C. 5321.16(B) within thirty days after the agreement ends and possession is delivered. And R.C. 5321.13(A) means no lease term waives either rule, so calling the money nonrefundable does not move it. A fee that is genuinely earned at signing is not a deposit, but keep it separate, say what it buys, and never use it as a substitute deposit. Pet rent is rent. An assistance animal is not a pet - see the Ohio assistance-animal row before charging anything for one.

title: In Ohio the Right to the Rent Cannot Be Separated From the Repair Duty
bodyText: Ohio answers this in the exact terms the question is usually asked. R.C. 5321.13(E) says a rental agreement, or the assignment, conveyance, trust deed, or security instrument of the landlord's interest in the rental agreement, may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with R.C. 5321.04. So the right to collect rent cannot be split from the habitability duties - not by the lease, and not by any of the four instruments through which you might pass your interest to somebody else. This bites hardest when you are no longer the one collecting. Assign the rents to a lender, pledge the lease as security, convey the property subject to the lease, or put it into a trust deed, and the instrument cannot carve the duty off the money. Ohio reinforces it from the other side: R.C. 5321.01(B) defines a landlord to include any person authorized by the owner, lessor or sublessor to receive rent from a tenant, so whoever takes the right to the rent is itself a landlord with those duties. R.C. 5321.13(A) makes all of this unwaivable. Keep any rent-assignment language in a loan or sale document clear of Chapter 5321.

title: Ohio Requires No Rent Receipt, Which Makes Your Own Record the Only Proof
bodyText: No Ohio statute requires you to give a tenant a receipt for rent, in cash or in any other form. There is no cash-receipt duty, no penalty for not giving one, and no Ohio rule making a missing receipt a defence to an eviction. There is also no Ohio statute creating a presumption that earlier rent was paid because you gave a receipt for a later period. Two practical consequences. Because nothing obliges either side to document a payment, your own ledger is the only proof of what was paid and when, and that is the evidence an action for possession turns on. And because accepting rent after you have served a notice to leave can waive the notice, when you take and record a payment matters as much as whether you receipt it - date every payment, record which rental period it is applied to, and do not accept a payment you do not intend to treat as rent. Ohio does not require you to take cash at all: under R.C. 5321.06 your lease may limit payment to traceable methods, which is the simplest way to avoid the problem.

title: Reselling Electricity To Your Ohio Tenants: No Disclosure Rule, But Three Real Consequences
bodyText: If you buy electricity on a master meter and resell it to tenants, Ohio imposes no lease disclosure, no prescribed statement, no required discount off the utility's own residential rate and no cap on what you may charge. The bill that would have imposed all four - H.B. 173 of the 136th General Assembly, which would have required a lease disclosure at R.C. 5321.04(A)(11) and a bill at least three per cent below the electric utility's standard service offer - was vetoed on June 25, 2026 and is not law. What does apply comes from the electric company's side, not yours. First, under Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-18-08(H) the company provides master-metered service only to you as landlord or owner, and you must give it an accurate list of each unit's individual mailing address. Second, under (I) it may charge you a reasonable tariffed fee for the cost of notifying your tenants of a pending disconnection, and under (J) it must look to you, not them, to collect what is unpaid. Third, under R.C. 4933.121(B)(2) and R.C. 4933.12(C)(2), where you are the one responsible for paying the bill the company may not cut off a residential tenant between November 15 and April 15 without first giving that tenant five days' notice. Plan on being the account holder, the address-list keeper and the party the company bills. One question this pass could not settle: whether reselling electricity on a metered basis makes you a regulated public utility turns on R.C. 4905.02 and 4905.03 and the Commission's rules in Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1, none of which was available here. Treat it as unsettled and get Ohio counsel before you build a resale business on it.

title: No Ohio Statute Gets You A Tenant's Energy Usage Data
bodyText: Ohio has no statute that lets a lease clause authorize release of a tenant's energy usage data to you, and no building energy benchmarking or disclosure mandate that would make you want one. There is no whole-building aggregate data right, no duty on a utility to give an owner a tenant's consumption history, and no prescribed consent form. Nothing in the landlord-tenant act touches customer data at all. That does not mean you cannot get the data. It means the lease is only half of the mechanism. R.C. 5321.06 lets you include a term obliging the tenant to sign and keep in force whatever authorization the serving utility requires, and to give you the usage figures for the unit on request - and that term binds the tenant, which is the most a lease can do. Whether the utility will release on that authorization, and in what form, is decided by its own tariff and by the Public Utilities Commission's customer-information rules, which were not available in this pass and which you should confirm with the serving company before you promise a lender or a benchmarking programme anything. Two drafting limits. R.C. 5321.13(D) voids any tenant agreement limiting your liability arising under law or indemnifying you for it, so do not bolt a data indemnity onto the clause. And R.C. 5321.14 lets a court limit a term it finds unconscionable, so keep the authorization tied to the unit's own utility usage for the tenancy rather than written as a general consent to obtain the tenant's records. This absence was checked across the 37 Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters and the Constitution this pass holds.

title: Ohio Does Not Regulate What You Add To A Submetered Water Or Energy Bill
bodyText: Ohio's landlord-tenant law has no meter conservation charge and no rules about what you may add to a utility amount you pass through. There is no energy-efficiency surcharge you may levy, no duty to notify each new tenant of one, and no rent-deduction remedy if you fail to. For submetered water, nothing in the law searched for this row requires you to charge only the city or district rate, bars a surcharge for the meter itself, or requires a monthly statement showing both meter readings, and nothing in it caps a markup, an administrative fee or a billing fee on a utility pass-through - but mind how far that search went, because here it matters more than usual. It covers the 37 Revised Code chapters this library holds, the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters. It does NOT cover R.C. chapters 4905, 4909 or 4933, or the utilities commission's rule chapter 4901:1 - which is to say it does not cover the bodies of law most likely to restrict reselling utility service at a markup. So the right statement is that no landlord-tenant statute caps your figure and R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability is the only ceiling this row can see (see edu-no-statutory-caps-oh); it is not that Ohio nowhere restricts a submetered water surcharge. Read those four before you set a markup. Two cautions before you add anything. First, the supply duty does not bend, and read its exception exactly, because it is narrower than it looks. R.C. 5321.04(A)(6) requires running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat at all times, 'except where the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection'. Two alternatives, and the second needs all three of its elements: the unit so constructed, an installation the tenant actually controls, and a direct public utility connection. A direct meter alone does not get you there, and a landlord-owned furnace or water heater fails the exclusive-control element however the unit is metered. So an unpaid surcharge is never a reason to reduce service. Second, a markup changes what you are doing.
