Ohio's Consumer Sales Practices Act defines a consumer transaction at R.C. 1345.01(A) to include the transfer of a service to an individual for household purposes, and it excludes transactions between a public utility and its customers. A landlord selling a separately billed, marked-up utility service is therefore in one of two boxes - a public utility, or a supplier under the Consumer Sales Practices Act - and neither is comfortable. That fork is a lead this pass could not resolve, because the chapters that define a public utility are not available here. The safe course is to pass through the utility's own amount, show the tenant the bill, and take your money in rent instead of in a utility surcharge.

title: A Tenant's Unpaid City Water Bill Is Usually Not a Lien on You
bodyText:
A municipal water bill your tenant did not pay generally cannot become a lien on your property, and the reason is a condition most landlords have never read. R.C. 743.04(A)(1)(a) lets a city certify unpaid water rents and penalties to the county auditor to go on the real property tax list as a lien - but only 'if the auditor also receives from the director or other official or body additional certification that the unpaid rents or charges have arisen pursuant to a service contract made directly with an owner who occupies the property served.' On a rental you do not occupy, that certification cannot honestly be given, so the lien route is closed. What remains is R.C. 743.04(A)(1)(b): the city may 'collect them by actions at law, in the name of the city from an owner, tenant, or other person who is liable to pay the rents or charges' - a lawsuit against whoever is actually liable, not a charge against the land.

If a charge is placed on your tax duplicate anyway, R.C. 743.04(A)(3) gives you a direct remedy: on valid written notice from an owner of record, the county auditor 'shall promptly remove such charge from the tax duplicate', and your notice must give the parcel number, the common address, the date the transfer to you was recorded, and the charge you say was wrongly placed. Division (A)(2) also bars certification outright in three situations, including where a purchaser bought at sheriff's or auditor's sale and is not the former owner or one of that owner's insiders. Three more provisions are worth knowing: the city must read each meter at least once every three months and bill quarterly on the actual reading, and must have a procedure for resolving billing disputes (division (A)(4)); when the property is about to be sold, any party may ask for a final bill, to be rendered within ten days, and the request must be made at least fourteen days before title transfers (division (A)(5)); and before certifying, the city must accept any partial payment of ten dollars or more (division (A)(6)).

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, and every hit for 'lien' combined with 'water', 'sewer' or 'utility' checked and none a municipal utility lien - plus R.C. 743.04 read in full outside it. This covers municipal WATER only. Sewer charges run under R.C. Chapter 729, and county and regional sewer districts under R.C. Chapters 6117 and 6119, none of which was read; the owner-occupant condition above may not be repeated in them, so do not assume a sewer charge is equally safe. Electric and gas supplied by a municipal utility were not reviewed either, and note that a municipal utility sits outside the Public Utilities Commission's jurisdiction altogether under R.C. 4905.02(A)(3), so the PUCO disconnection rules do not apply to it.

title: Three Disclosures Ohio Does Not Require: Ordnance, Demolition And Shared Meters
bodyText: Ohio requires none of the three. You need not tell a tenant that the property is within any distance of a former military ordnance location - Ohio has no ordnance-location disclosure at all. You need not notify an applicant or a tenant that you have applied for or received a demolition permit, and Ohio sets no notice period before a demolition. And you need not disclose that the unit's gas or electric meter also serves areas outside the unit, which is the shared-meter disclosure several states require; Ohio has no shared-meter provision and no rule about who pays for service running through a tenant's meter to common areas. The only thing a written Ohio lease must contain is the owner's and agent's name and address under R.C. 5321.18(A). Demolition appears in the landlord-tenant act once, and not as a disclosure: R.C. 5321.03(A)(3) lets you recover possession notwithstanding the retaliation rules where compliance with a building, housing, health or safety code would require alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of the use of the unit. That is a ground for an action, not a notice you owe. Two practical points. A shared meter is still your problem even without a disclosure rule, because the service running to common areas is service you are supplying and R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) requires you to keep common areas safe and sanitary - do not leave a tenant paying for it without saying so in the lease. And if demolition is in prospect, the tenancy has to be ended by the ordinary route, with the ordinary notice. This absence was checked across the 37 Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters and the Constitution this pass holds.

title: No Ohio Recycling Notice - But A Four-Unit Receptacle Duty You Can Miss
bodyText: Ohio imposes no duty to tell tenants where or how to recycle. There is no recycling notice, no posting requirement, no recycling provision you must put in the lease, and no state duty to provide recycling collection at a rental at all. Across every chapter and rule this pass holds, 'recycling' appears once, in a licence-plate fund, and 'recycle' once, in the littering offence. Neither is a landlord duty. What Ohio does require is the waste duty either side of recycling, and the landlord half has a threshold worth knowing. Under R.C. 5321.04(A)(5), where you are a party to rental agreements covering four or more dwelling units in the same structure, you must provide and maintain appropriate receptacles for the removal of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste incidental to occupancy, and arrange for their removal. Below four units in the structure that duty does not apply, and waste removal is whatever your lease says it is - see edu-portfolio-thresholds-oh for Ohio's several unit-count thresholds and how easily they are confused. The tenant's half is R.C. 5321.05(A)(2): dispose of all rubbish, garbage and other waste in a clean, safe and sanitary manner. The real recycling rules, where they exist, are local. Ohio's solid waste management districts and individual cities set collection and separation requirements, and R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) preserves local health and safety codes from the landlord-tenant act's preemption, so a city recycling ordinance can bind you even though the state does not. Check the municipality before you promise a tenant anything about recycling, and if you do provide it, say so in the lease as a service you supply rather than a duty you owe.

title: Ohio Lets You Apportion Unmetered Utilities - But You Still Owe Heat And Water
bodyText: Ohio has no statute making it unenforceable to charge a tenant for utilities that are not separately metered to the unit. There is no allocation formula, no building-size threshold, no cut-off date for leases signed after it, and no bar on ratio billing. Under R.C. 5321.06 your lease may apportion a master-metered bill however you choose, and R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability is the only ceiling - state the method and the share as your own figures, not as something the statute sets. What Ohio does regulate is the supply itself, and that part you cannot shift. R.C. 5321.04(A)(6) requires you to supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat at all times, and the only escape is where the building is not required by law to be equipped for the purpose or the unit is built so that heat or hot water is generated by an installation in the tenant's exclusive control and fed by a direct public utility connection. On a master meter that escape does not apply. R.C. 5321.13(A) makes that duty unwaivable, and R.C. 5321.13(E) says the lease may not let you receive rent free of your R.C. 5321.04 obligations. So a tenant's failure to pay an apportioned share is a rent default you pursue like any other: it does not excuse you from supplying heat and water, and interrupting the service to collect is prohibited self-help under R.C. 5321.15(A). This absence was checked across the 37 Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters and the Constitution this pass holds.

title: A "Utility Deposit" You Collect Is A Security Deposit In Ohio
bodyText: Ohio has no separate utility-deposit statute, and it does not need one. R.C. 5321.01(E) defines a security deposit as any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under a rental agreement. A sum you collect to cover utility charges secures the tenant's performance, so whatever you call it - utility deposit, utility reserve, service deposit - it is a security deposit, and every rule in R.C. 5321.16 applies to it. That means it counts toward the total for the five per cent interest calculation in R.C. 5321.16(A); it may be applied at termination only to past due rent and to damages from the tenant's noncompliance; any deduction must be itemized and identified in a written notice delivered with the balance due within thirty days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered; and if you get that wrong the tenant recovers the amount wrongfully withheld, damages equal to that amount again, and attorney's fees. You cannot contract out of it - R.C. 5321.13(A) bars waiving any provision of the chapter. The practical consequence: do not keep a utility deposit in a separate bucket with its own rules, and do not hold one back past the thirty days while you wait for a final utility bill. Collect it as part of the deposit, account for it in the one itemization, and estimate the final utility charge within the thirty days rather than after. For the deadline and itemization mechanics see edu-security-deposit-return-oh, and for the interest threshold see edu-security-deposit-interest-oh. A deposit the utility company itself takes from a tenant-customer is a different thing, governed by the Public Utilities Commission's rules, not by your lease.

title: No Ohio Rule On How To Present A Utility Disclosure - Because There Is No Utility Disclosure
bodyText: There is nothing for Ohio to prescribe the format of. Ohio requires no utility or submetering disclosure in a residential lease, so there is no rule making it a separate attachment, no separately signed page, no initialling requirement, no type-size or boldface rule and no requirement that the disclosure be given before signing. H.B. 173 of the 136th General Assembly would have created a submetered-utility disclosure duty at R.C. 5321.04(A)(11); it was vetoed on June 25, 2026 and is not law. The only thing a written Ohio lease must contain is in R.C. 5321.18(A) - the owner's name and address and the agent's name and address (see landlord-identity-oh) - and the only wording Ohio prescribes anywhere in residential tenancy law is the conspicuous paragraph in the three-day eviction notice under R.C. 1923.04(A) (see edu-statutory-forms-oh and edu-three-day-notice-language-oh). Across every chapter and rule this pass holds, no provision applies a type-size, boldface, capital-letter or separate-signature requirement to a residential rental agreement. Compare what Ohio does do one chapter over: a manufactured home park operator must, under R.C. 4781.40(B), fully disclose in writing all fees, charges and assessments before the tenant signs, and a park operator that fails to disclose a fee cannot collect it and cannot evict for refusing to pay it. Ordinary residential landlords under R.C. Chapter 5321 have no equivalent duty and no equivalent sanction. A separate, signed utility addendum is therefore optional in Ohio - but it is still the better practice, because the evidence that the tenant saw the billing terms is worth having and because R.C. 5321.14 lets a court limit a term it finds unconscionable, which is harder to argue about a page the tenant signed.

title: Getting Notice Before a Tenant's Utility Is Shut Off
bodyText:
You have two ways to hear that a tenant's utility is about to be shut off, and one of them does not need the tenant's cooperation at all. Under Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-18-06(A)(3)(d), 'Upon the request of a property owner or the agent of a property owner, each utility company shall provide the property owner or the agent of a property owner with at least three days' advance notice when service to his/her property is to be disconnected either at the request of a residential customer who is a tenant or for nonpayment.' So ask the serving electric, gas or natural gas company once, in writing, for each property. The second route is longer notice but needs the tenant to act: division (A)(3)(a) requires every utility company to let a residential customer designate a third party to receive notice of pending disconnection and any delinquent-payment reminders, and the company must give that third party at least fourteen days' notice. Being that designee does not make you liable for the tenant's bill - division (A)(3)(b) requires the company to say so, unless you have separately agreed in writing to be a guarantor, which you should not do. A third arrangement exists and is different in kind: under division (F) a landlord may enter a landlord reversion agreement so service reverts to your name rather than shutting off, and (F)(3) makes the next resident responsible from move-in 'as indicated in the terms of the lease agreement' - so if you use one, the lease needs to say it.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review plus Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-18-06 and 4901:1-18-08 read in full outside it. These are rules binding the utility company, not duties Ohio places on you, and nothing in R.C. Chapter 5321 requires a tenant to designate anyone. The rest of Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1 and the water and sewer rules were not read, and a municipal utility is outside the Public Utilities Commission's jurisdiction under R.C. 4905.02(A)(3), so these rules do not reach a city water or sewer department.

title: Ohio Has No Shutoff Rulebook For A Landlord's Own Submeter - Which Is The Trap, Not The Permission
bodyText: If you submeter electricity yourself and a tenant does not pay, Ohio gives you no procedure to follow - and no permission either. There are no arrears thresholds, no notice periods, no winter window, no reconnection terms and no payment-plan duty for a landlord-run submeter. The regime that would have supplied them, R.C. 4933.56 under H.B. 173 of the 136th General Assembly, was vetoed on June 25, 2026. The disconnection rules that do exist - R.C. 4933.12, R.C. 4933.121 and Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-18-08 - are written as limits on the gas or electric company and give a landlord no corresponding right. Four provisions bite instead. R.C. 5321.15(A) prohibits any act, 'including termination of utilities or services,' aimed at recovering possession. R.C. 5321.04(A)(6) requires you to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat at all times - and read the exception narrowly, because it is two alternatives and the second needs all three of its elements: the building not required by law to be equipped for the purpose, OR the unit so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control AND supplied by a direct public utility connection, so a direct meter alone is not enough and a landlord-owned furnace never qualifies, and (A)(4) requires you to keep the electrical fixtures you supply in good and safe working order. R.C. 5321.13(A) makes those duties unwaivable and (E) bars a lease that lets you take rent free of them. And nothing in Ohio turns an unpaid utility charge into a self-help remedy. Note the gap honestly: R.C. 5321.15(A) is limited on its face to acts aimed at recovering possession, so a shutoff purely to collect money is not squarely inside it - but it will still breach R.C. 5321.04 and expose you to the tenant's remedies under R.C. 5321.07 (depositing rent with the court, a court order to remedy the condition, or ending the lease) and to damages under R.C. 5321.12. Collect the charge as you would rent. Do not cut the service.

title: Ohio's Utility Shutoff Rules Bind The Company, Not You - And Two Of Them Cost You Money
bodyText: Ohio's disconnection rules are written as limits on the gas or electric company, not as duties on you, but three of them decide what happens to your building. Know where this row's law comes from before you lean on it: chapter 4933 and the utilities commission's rule chapter 4901:1-18 are both outside this library's Ohio corpus, so R.C. 4933.12, R.C. 4933.121 and Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-18-08 were fetched and read on 30 October 2026 and nothing else in either chapter was read. Treat what follows as those three provisions, not as the whole of Ohio's disconnection law. All year round, where the company knows its customer is the landlord of a master-metered multi-unit building or of a single-occupancy unit with utilities in the rent, Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-18-08(A) requires it to give you fourteen days' notice before disconnection and then, if nothing is paid or arranged, a separate ten-day notice to you, to each unit, and posted conspicuously in the building. The winter rule is different and narrower: between November 15 and April 15 the company may not cut off a residential consumer unless the account is thirty days or more in arrears and, where the occupant is your tenant and you are the one responsible for the bill, it has given that occupant five days' notice first (R.C. 4933.121(B) for electric, R.C. 4933.12(C) for gas). That is not a winter moratorium - it is two extra conditions on the company's existing right. Then the two that cost you. If you ask the company to disconnect while residential tenants are living there, Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-18-08(K) requires it to give the tenants at least ten days' notice and to tell you that you remain liable for everything consumed during those ten days. And under (G), reconnection follows payment of the current month's bill plus any reconnection charge within fourteen days - except that under (G)(4) the company need not reconnect on that basis where the landlord resides on the premises. Never interrupt service yourself to get a tenant out or to collect: R.C. 5321.15(A) names termination of utilities as prohibited self-help (see edu-self-help-eviction-ban-oh).

title: Ohio Has No Submetered-Utility Disclosure Duty - The Bill That Would Have Created One Was Vetoed
bodyText: Ohio requires no submetering or utility-billing disclosure in a residential lease. R.C. 5321.04 lists your duties and stops at (A)(10): there is no duty to disclose submetered, ratio-billed or charged-back utilities, no prescribed wording, no type-size rule, no billing limit and no late-fee cap on a utility charge. H.B. 173 of the 136th General Assembly would have created all of that - a new R.C. 5321.04(A)(11) requiring you to disclose the nature of the utility service and all related charges or fees in your leases, a new (A)(12) barring you from separately billing common-area electricity, and a new R.C. 4933.51 to 4933.66 regime with a pricing discount, disconnection standards and a filed compliance plan. The General Assembly passed it on June 10, 2026 and the Governor vetoed it on June 25, 2026. It is not law, and no override is recorded, so do not follow guidance written from that bill. You may still describe your utility billing in the lease under R.C. 5321.06, and R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability is the only ceiling on what you charge (see edu-no-statutory-caps-oh). This absence was checked across the 37 Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters and the Constitution this pass holds; 'submeter', 'submetered', 'submetering', 'metered' and 'separate meter' appear nowhere in them. One question is left open: whether reselling electricity to tenants on a metered basis makes you a regulated public utility is governed by R.C. ch. 4905 (R.C. 4905.02 and 4905.03) and the Public Utilities Commission's own rules in Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1, neither of which is held here - treat it as unsettled rather than answered.

title: In Ohio You Cannot Cut Off A Tenant Who Never Transferred The Utilities
bodyText: The device some states allow - give the tenant three days to put the utilities in their own name, then have the service cut off if they do not - does not work in Ohio, and trying it costs you money. No Ohio statute requires a tenant to transfer an account or gives you a cutoff right if they fail to. What governs instead is Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-18-08(K): where you or your agent ask the utility to disconnect while residential tenants are still living there, the company must give those tenants at least ten days' notice, and it must tell you that you remain liable for all service consumed during those ten days. So the shortest route out is ten days of notice, with the bills for those ten days in your name, no matter what your lease says about three. Shutting the service off yourself is worse - R.C. 5321.15(A) names termination of utilities as prohibited self-help, and R.C. 5321.04(A)(6) obliges you to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat at all times - and read the exception narrowly, because it is two alternatives and the second needs all three of its elements: the building not required by law to be equipped for the purpose, OR the unit so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control AND supplied by a direct public utility connection, so a direct meter alone is not enough and a landlord-owned furnace never qualifies. Handle it in the lease instead and handle it before move-in. Require the transfer as a condition of receiving keys, require proof of the account in the tenant's name, and make the cost of any service left in your name a charge you bill the tenant rather than a reason to disconnect. If you choose to charge a daily or monthly amount for service the tenant left in your name, that figure is yours, not one Ohio sets, and R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability is the only ceiling on it.

title: Ohio Does Not Make You Disclose Asbestos to a Tenant
bodyText: Ohio has no asbestos disclosure for a residential tenancy. Nothing requires an asbestos statement in the lease, an asbestos management plan, or a notice to a tenant or applicant that the building contains asbestos. Chapter 5321 (Landlords and Tenants), searched whole, uses the word asbestos nowhere; across the other 36 Revised Code chapters in this project's Ohio corpus the only asbestos provision is a ban on burning an asbestos-containing building for fire-fighting practice (R.C. 3737.14(B)). Ohio's asbestos law is a contractor-licensing regime, not a disclosure regime: an asbestos hazard abatement contractor must run a respiratory-protection program, certify its workers, and notify the Ohio EPA at least ten working days before each project (R.C. 3710.07). That notice runs to the agency, not to your tenant. Two limits on this answer. Chapter 3710 as a whole and the Department of Health's asbestos rules (Ohio Adm.Code 3701-34) are not in this project's Ohio corpus, so a duty to notify occupants before abatement work is in the building cannot be ruled out - treat that as your licensed contractor's obligation and get it in writing from them before work starts. And asbestos in poor condition is still a condition of the premises: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes you comply with the building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety, and R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) makes you keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition, so deteriorating asbestos is a repair problem even though it is not a disclosure problem. The federal lead rule has no asbestos counterpart for rentals.

title: No Association Disclosure to Tenants - but the Tenant Is Bound Anyway
bodyText:
Ohio requires no association disclosure to a tenant. The one condominium disclosure statute is aimed at buyers, not renters: R.C. 5311.26 bars a developer or its agent from selling or offering to sell a condominium ownership interest unless it gives 'the prospective purchaser a condominium development disclosure statement', and its fifteen required contents - budgets, reserves, warranties, management contracts, litigation - are all purchase information. Nothing in it reaches a landlord letting a unit, and nothing requires you to hand a tenant the declaration, the bylaws or the rules. What Ohio does instead is bind your tenant directly: R.C. 5311.19(A) says 'All unit owners, their tenants, all persons lawfully in possession and control of any part of a condominium property, and the unit owners association' shall comply with the covenants, conditions and restrictions in the deed, the declaration, the bylaws or the association's rules. So the duty exists whether or not your lease mentions it - but a tenant cannot comply with rules they have never seen, so give them a copy and have the lease say you did.

The reason this matters more than a missing disclosure: when the association charges for a violation, Ohio sends the bill to you, not to the tenant. R.C. 5311.19(B)(3) makes the costs of an enforcement eviction 'charged to the unit owner' as a special assessment and a lien on the unit, and R.C. 5312.11(A) assesses the individual lot in a planned community. Recover that money from the tenant as damages for breaking the lease, not as an indemnity of what you owe the association - the difference is explained under the association-compliance clause.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, plus R.C. 5311.19, 5311.26 and 5312.11 read in full outside it. Chapters 5311 and 5312 as a whole were not read, so this is not a claim that no other section of either touches a tenant; it is a claim about the three that decide this question. A condominium's own declaration may require an owner to give its tenant the rules, which is a private obligation this review cannot resolve - read yours.

title: Ohio Has No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Ohio has nothing on defective or imported drywall. There is no disclosure, no remediation standard, no registry and no tenant termination right. This was a Gulf Coast and mid-Atlantic problem - the states that legislated it did so because imported wallboard installed during the 2001 to 2009 building boom was corroding wiring and fixtures in their housing stock - and Ohio never followed. Do not import another state's drywall clause into an Ohio lease: a clause that tells your tenant Ohio law requires a drywall disclosure is simply wrong, and the only Ohio section that prescribes what an ordinary residential lease must contain is R.C. 5321.18, which requires the owner's and any agent's name and address and nothing else. The words drywall, gypsum, wallboard, sulfur and sulfide appear nowhere in chapter 5321 or in the other 36 Revised Code chapters in this project's Ohio corpus, nor in the administrative rules it holds. If a unit actually has corroding wiring or failing fixtures, that is an ordinary habitability and code matter: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes you comply with the building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety, R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) makes you keep the premises fit and habitable, and R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) makes you keep electrical fixtures and systems in good and safe working order. Handle it as a repair, not as a disclosure.

title: Ohio Requires No Flood Disclosure to a Tenant
bodyText: Ohio requires you to tell a residential tenant nothing about flood risk. There is no flood-zone disclosure, no flood-history disclosure, no state rider or model form, and no tenant right to terminate because the unit floods or sits in a mapped flood area. The only thing an Ohio statute makes a written residential lease contain is the owner's and any agent's name and address (R.C. 5321.18). Searching the whole of chapter 5321 (Landlords and Tenants) and the other 36 Revised Code chapters in this project's Ohio corpus, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules it holds, the only Ohio flood provisions found sit outside an ordinary tenancy: a manufactured-home park operator must report a flood event to the state and the board of health within forty-eight hours (R.C. 4781.33), and park and recreational-vehicle-park development in a flood plain needs a permit (R.C. 4781.32, R.C. 3729.04). None of those is a disclosure to a tenant, and R.C. 5321.01(C)(7) excludes agricultural labour camps; manufactured-home-park lots are outside chapter 5321 because R.C. 4781.01(W) makes a park's 'residential premises' the lot rather than a dwelling unit. You may still disclose voluntarily, and R.C. 5321.06 lets your lease say what you like about flood risk, but understand what a voluntary statement does: once you say something about the condition of the premises you can be held to its accuracy, and a silent lease is safer than an inaccurate one. If flood exposure is real, the useful clauses are the ones you already have - require renter's insurance, keep the casualty-termination clause, and do not promise the unit will stay dry.

title: No Contamination Disclosure - but a Recorded Covenant Binds Your Tenant
bodyText:
Ohio requires no contamination disclosure to a tenant, but a recorded environmental covenant can bind your tenant without anyone telling them - which is why this one needs a lease sentence rather than a disclosure form. Ohio's Uniform Environmental Covenants Act, R.C. 5301.80 to 5301.92, works through the land records, not through notice to occupants. R.C. 5301.85(A) says an environmental covenant that complies with those sections 'runs with the land', and (B)(5) confirms it is valid and enforceable even though it 'imposes an affirmative obligation on a person having an interest in the real property'. A tenant holds an interest in the real property, so a covenant's activity and use limitations - no disturbing a soil cap, no using a well, no digging below a depth, no change to a particular use - can reach your tenant directly. The only notice the Act requires is recording: R.C. 5301.88(A) has the covenant filed with the county recorder of each county where the property sits and 'recorded in the same manner as a deed', with the holder indexed as a grantee, and (B) puts it on the register for registered land. That is constructive notice, which protects the agency and the holder, not your tenant's actual knowledge.

So if your property carries one: get a copy from the county recorder, give it to the tenant with the lease, and have the lease require compliance with recorded restrictions affecting the property. Nothing in Ohio law makes you do that. It is simply the only way a tenant can comply with a limitation they would otherwise never see, and a breach by your tenant is a problem for you, because the covenant burdens the land you own.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, 'environmental covenant' 2, 'contamination' 2, 'hazardous substance' 2, 'remediation' 1, 'activity and use limitation' 0, 'institutional control' 0, 'groundwater' 0, against 'landlord' 34 - plus, outside the corpus, R.C. 5301.85 and 5301.88 read in full. R.C. 5301.80 to 5301.92 as a whole was not read, nor was R.C. Chapter 3746, Ohio's voluntary action programme, which is where a covenant usually originates. Neither the federal CERCLA and RCRA regimes nor Ohio EPA practice was reviewed.

title: Ohio's Free Lead-Safe Rental Registry
bodyText:
Ohio has a lead-safe rental registry, it is free, and for most landlords it is voluntary - but check that it is actually operating before you plan around it. R.C. 3742.41(A) directs the Director of Health to establish and maintain a lead-safe residential rental unit registry and says the Director 'shall not impose a fee for registration'. Registration is optional in three situations: the owner of a unit built before January 1, 1978 who carries out the lead-safe maintenance practices in R.C. 3742.42 may then register it (divisions (B) and (C)); and the owner of a unit built after January 1, 1978, or one a licensed lead inspector or risk assessor has found lead free, may register it as well (division (D)). It is mandatory in one situation only: under division (E)(1), an owner whose unit is subject to a lead hazard control order under R.C. 3742.37 shall register it once the unit passes a clearance examination under R.C. 3742.39, and division (E)(2) exempts housing the Director designates as housing for the elderly or senior housing. A lead hazard control order is issued only after a child's lead poisoning is investigated and a risk assessment finds a lead hazard in the unit contributing to it (R.C. 3742.35 to 3742.37). The order names each hazard and a date by which the unit must pass a clearance examination (R.C. 3742.37(B)). The unit stays subject to the order until it passes (R.C. 3742.39), and the pass standards are set by Department of Health rule (Ohio Adm.Code 3701-32-12, 3701-32-19). The Department's lead rules define the registry (Ohio Adm.Code 3701-30-01(N)) but set no registration procedure, maintenance-practice training approval or dust-sampling rule, though R.C. 3742.45(A)(6), (8) and (9) call for them. So ask the Department before relying on registration. The maintenance practices themselves, in R.C. 3742.42(A), are an approved training course, an annual visual examination for deteriorated paint and underlying damage, repair to the federal work practice standards, post-maintenance dust sampling, and keeping records for at least three years. They cover interior surfaces and all common areas, outbuildings within the same lot line such as garages, play equipment and fences, and the lot itself (division (B)), and you need no abatement licence to do them, but you do need the approved training (division (C)).

The caution, and the cautious course: R.C. 3742.41(A) makes the registry run 'in accordance with rules adopted under section 3742.45', and division (B) starts the voluntary route only 'six months after the effective date of the rules'. Ohio Adm.Code 3701-32, the lead chapter, contains licensing and abatement-practice rules and no registry rule, no lead-safe maintenance practice rule and no dust-sampling rule. So the registry may not be operating. Confirm with the Ohio Department of Health before relying on registration, and in the meantime treat the R.C. 3742.42 practices as the substance worth doing and the federal lead disclosure as the duty you certainly have.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, plus R.C. 3742.41 and 3742.42 and the chapter index of Ohio Adm.Code 3701-32 read outside it. Chapter 3742 as a whole, the rest of Ohio Adm.Code 3701, and the Department of Health's own published materials were not reviewed, nor was any Ohio case law.

title: No Ohio Lead Notice - the Duty Is Federal
bodyText:
Ohio imposes no state lead disclosure on a landlord. The duty you have is federal, and the library carries it in the lead-based paint clause - do not look for an Ohio notice to add to it. Ohio's own lead legislation works on the property and the contractor rather than on the lease: R.C. 3742.41 sets up a registry of lead-safe rental units, R.C. 3742.42 sets out the maintenance practices an owner performs to qualify, and the licensing and clearance provisions run to inspectors, risk assessors and abatement contractors. None of them requires you to tell a tenant anything, at any point - not before signing, not on renewal, and not when a hazard is found. The one place a tenant-facing consequence appears is indirect: under R.C. 3742.41(E)(1) a unit under a lead hazard control order must be registered once it passes a clearance examination, and the registry is public, so the fact of an order becomes discoverable without anyone having to disclose it. Separately, deteriorated paint that materially affects health and safety is already within your R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) duty to comply with applicable housing, health and safety codes, whatever the lead rules say.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - 'lead-safe' 0 sections, 'lead hazard' 0, 'deteriorated paint' 0, 'lead-based paint' 1 (a federal cross-reference, not a notice duty), 'paint' 8, control term 0 - plus, outside the corpus, R.C. 3742.41 and 3742.42 read in full and R.C. 3742.01, 3742.03, 3742.04, 3742.07, 3742.32 and 3742.50 read from the enrolled act text the corpus does hold. That is a bounded search: chapter 3742 as a whole, the rules under R.C. 3742.45, and the rest of Ohio Adm.Code 3701 were not read, and a city lead-safe ordinance is a real possibility this review did not resolve - Cleveland's and Toledo's are the ones to ask about, because R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) preserves local health and safety codes from preemption.

title: Ohio Requires No Military Air Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Ohio requires no military-installation disclosure in a residential lease, even near Wright-Patterson, Rickenbacker or Youngstown. There is no noise-zone or accident-potential-zone disclosure, no military impact district, no distance trigger, and no thirty-day termination right of the kind some states give a tenant who learns the unit sits under a flight path. The phrases military installation, air installation, noise zone, accident potential and military impact appear nowhere in chapter 5321 or in the other 36 Revised Code chapters in this project's Ohio corpus, nor in the administrative rules it holds - and the corpus does hold Ohio's two military chapters, the National Guard and the organized militia, so the gap is the subject's and not the search's. The only Ohio section prescribing what an ordinary residential lease must contain is R.C. 5321.18, which requires the owner's and any agent's name and address. What Ohio does have in this family is different and it binds you: military status is a protected class in Ohio housing discrimination, so you may not refuse, condition or vary a tenancy because of it. Note also that if your tenant is a servicemember, the termination right that matters comes from the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which R.C. 5321.04(A)(10) expressly makes you comply with - not from any Ohio air-zone statute. Disclosing aircraft noise voluntarily is allowed under R.C. 5321.06 and is often sensible, but it is your choice, not a requirement, and once you describe the noise you can be held to the description.

title: No Ohio Duty to Test a Well or Show a Tenant the Results
bodyText: If your Ohio rental is on a private well, no landlord-tenant statute makes you test the water, test it on any schedule, or give the results to your tenant or applicant. Chapter 5321's only water duty is R.C. 5321.04(A)(6): supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat at all times, except where the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose or where the tenant has exclusive control of the installation and a direct public utility connection. Nothing in it mentions a well, a sample or a test result, and R.C. 5321.18 - the only section prescribing what an ordinary residential lease must contain - requires only the owner's and any agent's name and address. Ohio does require water testing, but it chose to require it only in licensed camps rather than in rentals: no agricultural labor camp licence issues unless water supply tests show the supply meets required standards (R.C. 3733.45), and the licensor of a recreational vehicle park or recreation camp may charge for collecting and bacteriologically examining water samples (R.C. 3729.10). That contrast is the point - the subject is squarely within Ohio's regulatory vocabulary and the legislature did not extend it to a tenancy. Two things still bind you. Water that is not potable is a habitability and code problem under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) and (A)(2), whatever its source, so a contaminated well is a repair obligation even without a testing statute. And installing or altering a private water system is separately regulated by the Department of Health, which this pass could not read - see the note on that below if you are putting in a new well. Testing annually and keeping the results is cheap, voluntary and the best answer to a tenant who asks.

title: There Is No Ohio Proposition 65 - Do Not Put a Chemical Warning in an Ohio Lease
bodyText: Proposition 65 is Californian. Ohio has no counterpart: no list of chemicals known to the state to cause cancer or reproductive harm, no duty to warn a tenant or post a sign about exposure in a building, and no private enforcement bounty. If your lease form carries a 'WARNING: This property may contain chemicals known to the State to cause cancer' block, delete it for Ohio or confine it to the California version of the form. Keeping it does you no good and does two kinds of harm: it tells your tenant that an Ohio agency has assessed this building, which is not true, and it invites a complaint about a hazard you have just announced. The words carcinogen, Proposition 65 and birth defects appear nowhere in chapter 5321 or in the other 36 Revised Code chapters in this project's Ohio corpus, nor in the Ohio Attorney General's deceptive-trade-practice rules, which the corpus holds. The only Ohio section prescribing what an ordinary residential lease must contain is R.C. 5321.18, which requires the owner's and any agent's name and address. Note too that Ohio's consumer-protection statute is a poor substitute for thinking about this: R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a consumer transaction as a transfer of goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible, which does not describe a lease of real property. Your real obligations about anything genuinely hazardous in the building run through R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) and (A)(2) - comply with the codes that materially affect health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable - and through the federal lead-based paint disclosure your lease already carries.

title: Ohio Requires No Property-Tax-Portion-of-Rent Statement
bodyText: Ohio never makes you tell a tenant how much of the rent is property tax. There is no annual statement, no July deadline, no statement on a rent change, and no certificate for the tenant to file with a tax return. The only section prescribing what an ordinary Ohio residential lease must contain is R.C. 5321.18, which requires the owner's and any agent's name and address. Ohio's choice is to let you recover a tax rise through the rent instead of accounting for it. R.C. 5321.02(C) says nothing in the retaliation prohibition stops a landlord from increasing the rent to reflect the cost of improvements or 'an increase in other costs of operation of the premises', and R.C. 5321.10(A) treats real estate taxes on the premises as one of the customary and usual costs of operating the premises as a rental unit. So the way a tax increase reaches your tenant in Ohio is a rent increase, which needs no statutory notice period - see the Ohio tax escalation and rent increase notice rows rather than inventing a statement here. It is worth knowing that Ohio does require a periodic statement to an occupant in one place, and it is not a lease: a vendor under a land installment contract must furnish the vendee a statement of principal, interest and balance at least once a year or on demand (R.C. 5313.03) - and even there, nothing about taxes. One adjacent duty that is real but runs the other way: as the owner of residential rental property you must file your name, address and telephone number, and the responsible person for any entity owner, with the county auditor of the county where the property sits (R.C. 5323.02), and what you file is a public record (R.C. 5323.04). That is a filing with the county, not a disclosure to the tenant, and failing to make it carries its own penalty.

title: You Owe No Registry Disclosure in Ohio - But You Must Let the Sheriff Post, and You Can Opt In
bodyText: Ohio puts no disclosure duty on you. Chapter 2950, the sex offender registration chapter, does not contain the words landlord, lessor, tenant or rental agreement anywhere in its thirty-three sections. You need not tell an applicant or a tenant that a registered offender lives in the building or nearby, and you need not answer a question about one, though if you do answer, answer truthfully. The duties run to the offender, who must register and verify with the sheriff, and to the sheriff, who notifies. Three things in that chapter do reach you. First, a real duty: if you manage a multi-unit building within one thousand feet of a registered offender's residence - including the building the offender lives in - the sheriff must notify the building manager, or whoever the owner or the condominium unit owners association authorises to exercise management and control, and must post the notice prominently in each common entryway, and R.C. 2950.11(A)(1)(c) says the manager 'shall permit the sheriff to post copies of the notice'. Do not take those postings down. Second, an opportunity: under R.C. 2950.11(J) any company or individual may ask the sheriff by email or through the sheriff's website to receive these notices, either for one offender or for everyone in the notification area. Doing that is worth considering, because the chapter's immunity in R.C. 2950.12(A)(8) covers a person who gets notice as a requester under R.C. 2950.11(A)(10) and does not list the building manager who receives notice under (A)(1)(c) - so opting in puts you on the protected side of the line. Third, a sword: an offender may not occupy residential premises within one thousand feet of school, preschool, child care, children's crisis care or residential infant care premises, and an owner or lessee of property inside that radius can sue for an injunction without proving irreparable harm (R.C. 2950.034). For an offender in your own unit see the Ohio occupancy clause, and for eviction see the Ohio for-cause row.

title: No Ohio Single-Family Lease Disclosure, and No Ohio Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Ohio singles out a single-family rental for nothing. There is no disclosure that the dwelling is a single-family residence, no exemption notice of the kind states with rent caps and just-cause rules require, and no occupancy statement a single-family lease must carry. There is also no Ohio rule about how a lease must look: nothing prescribes a point size, a boldface or capitalised block, or placement on the first page. Ohio does know how to prescribe those things - it does it for consumer transactions and for the eviction notice, which must be printed or written in a conspicuous manner - but it has not done it for a residential lease. Note that the reason the exemption notices exist elsewhere does not arise here: Ohio has no rent control, because R.C. 5321.19 preempts local rent control and rent stabilisation, and no general just-cause eviction rule, so there is no protection for a single-family rental to be exempt from and nothing to tell the tenant about. The only Ohio section prescribing what an ordinary residential lease must contain is R.C. 5321.18 - the owner's and any agent's name and address. The one Ohio notice that works like an exemption notice is about unit count, not house type, and your lease should already carry it: if you are party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units, the tenant's rent-escrow remedy does not apply to you, but only if you give notice of that fact in the written rental agreement, or deliver written notice of it at the time of initial occupancy for an oral tenancy (R.C. 5321.07(C)). No type size and no placement is prescribed for it - but put it where the tenant will plainly see it, because the notice is the whole condition of the exemption.

title: No Shoreline or Coastal Disclosure in Ohio
bodyText:
Ohio has no shoreline or coastal disclosure for a lease, and its one coastal regime is a building-permit rule rather than anything a tenant is told. Under R.C. 1506.06 the Director of Natural Resources identifies Lake Erie coastal erosion areas and notifies each municipal corporation, county and township of the final identification; under R.C. 1506.07(B) no person may 'erect, construct, or redevelop a permanent structure on land within a Lake Erie coastal erosion area without a permit'. That duty falls on whoever builds, at the moment of building. Nothing in it requires an owner to tell a tenant that a property sits in such an area, and nothing in Ohio law requires you to disclose shoreline access, beach rights, lake frontage or erosion risk in a residential lease. Two practical consequences. First, if you are letting Lake Erie frontage, the erosion-area status is public information your tenant can look up, and giving it to them costs you nothing and avoids an argument about a shoreline they thought came with the unit - say in the lease what the tenant may and may not use. Second, R.C. 1506.07(D) lets a county or municipal corporation run its own coastal erosion ordinance in place of the state permit once the Director approves it, so on the lake shore the operative rules are frequently local; this review does not resolve city ordinances.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, 'shoreline' 0, 'coastal erosion' 0, 'littoral' 0, 'beach' 1, 'public access' 1, 'navigable' 2, 'Lake Erie' 5, against 'landlord' 34, and none of those hits is a disclosure to a tenant - plus R.C. 1506.07 read in full outside it. R.C. Chapter 1506 as a whole was not read, nor were the Director's rules under R.C. 1506.07(A), nor R.C. 1506.10 and 1506.11, which govern the state's own territory and submerged lands.

title: Ohio Has No Sprinkler Disclosure - and No Sprinkler Duty Below Seventy-Five Feet
bodyText: Ohio requires no statement in a lease about whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, whether it is maintained, or what happens if it is taken out of service. The only Ohio section prescribing what an ordinary residential lease must contain is R.C. 5321.18, which requires the owner's and any agent's name and address. Do not read Ohio's one apartment sprinkler section as more than it is. R.C. 3781.104 is titled as though it covered apartment buildings generally, but it reaches only an existing apartment or condominium building that exceeds seventy-five feet in height measured from ground level and that lacked an automatic smoke detection or sprinkler system conforming to the board of building standards' rules. For a house, a duplex, a walk-up or anything else at or under seventy-five feet, that section requires nothing - and it requires nothing to be disclosed even where it does apply. Where a sprinkler system is actually required, the requirement comes from the codes R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes you follow, principally the Ohio Fire Code and the building codes, and keeping an installed system in working order falls under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) and (A)(2) as a code and habitability duty rather than a disclosure one. No Ohio grant or loan programme for sprinkler retrofits was found in the acts of the 135th or 136th General Assembly. Two practical points. If you take a system out of service for work, tell your tenants in writing and tell the fire code official - not because a disclosure statute says so but because an impairment is a code matter and a silent impairment is the one that hurts you. And if your form carries another state's sprinkler notice, delete it rather than leave a promise Ohio does not require and you may not be able to keep.

title: Ohio Makes You Disclose No Death, Crime or Illness in the Unit - and Bars You From Asking About One
bodyText: Ohio has no stigmatized-property or psychologically-impacted-property rule for a rental. Nothing requires you to tell an applicant or tenant that someone died, was killed or took their own life in the unit, that a crime happened there, or that a former occupant was ill. There is also no Ohio statute that immunises you for staying silent - Ohio simply does not legislate the subject for a tenancy, and R.C. 5321.18, the only section that prescribes what an ordinary Ohio residential lease must contain, requires only the owner's and any agent's name and address. The illness side of this topic runs the other way in Ohio, and it binds you. HIV infection is a 'physical or mental impairment' under R.C. 4112.01(A)(16)(a)(iii), so it is a disability, and R.C. 4112.02(H) makes it unlawful to refuse or condition a rental because of disability, to discriminate in the terms of a tenancy because of one, to make any inquiry or keep any record concerning disability in connection with a lease (R.C. 4112.02(H)(8)), or to ask whether an applicant or intended occupant has a disability or how severe it is (R.C. 4112.02(H)(17)). Discussing a former tenant's diagnosis with a prospect, or asking a prospect about one, is the exposure here - not silence. Two practical limits. Volunteering a half-accurate story is riskier than saying nothing: once you describe the unit's history you can be held to what you said. And if a prospect asks you a direct question, answer it truthfully or decline to answer; do not answer it falsely. For sex-offender registry information specifically, see the separate Ohio row on that subject.

title: Familial Status Is Protected In Ohio - And You Set Your Own Occupancy Number
bodyText: Familial status is a protected class in Ohio housing. R.C. 4112.01(A)(15) defines it as one or more individuals under eighteen domiciled with a parent or guardian with legal custody, or with that parent's written designee, and also covers anyone who is pregnant or in the process of securing legal custody of a child. R.C. 4112.02(H) then runs that class through every housing limb: refusing to rent, representing a unit unavailable, discriminating in terms or conditions, advertising a preference, and asking about it or recording it. Ohio protects it in one place only. Chapter 5321 never uses the words familial status and does not restrict ending a tenancy because a family grew during it, so there is no second, landlord-tenant-side prohibition and no notice period attached to one. You may still limit how many people live in a unit. R.C. 4112.024(C) preserves reasonable local, state and federal maximum-occupancy restrictions and expressly permits you to implement reasonable occupancy standards based on the number and size of sleeping areas or bedrooms and the overall size of the unit, so long as they are not used to circumvent the chapter. Ohio sets no number, so the number in your lease is yours - make it defensible on bedrooms and square footage, apply it to every household alike, and expect it to be read against your actual units. Nothing in Ohio law requires your lease to address children at all: the only content R.C. 5321.18 mandates is the owner's and agent's name and address. The familial-status rule also yields for genuine older-persons housing.

title: Ohio's Disability Duties, And The Escrow Account You Have To Ask For
bodyText: Ohio imposes a reasonable-accommodation duty directly: under R.C. 4112.02(H)(19) refusing to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services, when necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling unit and its common and public areas, is an unlawful discriminatory practice. Modifications are a separate regime at R.C. 4112.02(H)(18). The tenant pays for a physical modification, and you may not refuse a reasonable one - but you may condition permission on three things, and this is where Ohio gives you something to use. You may require a reasonable description plus assurances of workerlike execution and permits; you may require an agreement to restore the interior at the end of the tenancy, subject to reasonable wear and tear; and where you reasonably find it necessary to secure the funds, you may require payments over a reasonable period into an interest-bearing escrow account in your name, capped at the projected restoration cost, with the interest accruing to the tenant. What you may not do is take a larger security deposit than you customarily take from every tenant of that property. Ask for these conditions in writing when you approve the modification: Ohio Adm.Code 4112-5-07(D) makes the restoration obligation depend on an agreement having actually been obtained. Ohio does not require any of this to appear in the lease. Two more duties: the burden of justifying a refusal is yours, and a direct-threat defence is closely scrutinised, so speculation will not carry it. And if your property has designated accessible parking, R.C. 3781.111(E) makes you mark and maintain it, which R.C. 4112.02(H)(20) turns into a fair housing violation if you do not.

title: Ohio Requires No Drug-Free Addendum - Your Duty Runs Without One, And You Cannot Contract Out Of It
bodyText: Ohio requires no drug-free housing addendum and prescribes no words for one, on a search of the 37 Revised Code chapters this library holds plus the held Administrative Code chapters, and the statutory drug regime conditions nothing on what your lease says. The tenant's duty not to permit controlled-substance offences on the premises is imposed by statute on every Ohio tenant, written lease or not, and your own duty to serve the three-day notice and promptly bring the eviction is likewise statutory - but read its trigger closely, because it is conjunctive. R.C. 5321.05(C)(2) fires only where the tenant's violation is coupled with the actual knowledge or reasonable cause to believe that R.C. 1923.02(A)(6)(a)(i) defines: a properly executed search warrant naming the tenant and particularly describing the premises and the substances, a controlled substance actually found on execution, and a law enforcement officer then telling you of the violation. Nothing you write in a lease or an addendum can supply that. Whether anything short of that chain can put you under the duty is not settled: the definition reads as a deeming rule ('a landlord has ... if'), and no case law was read. So if credible information reaches you another way, take advice before deciding not to act. An addendum therefore adds nothing to the mandatory track. Two things it can genuinely do. It can give you a second, simpler eviction ground, because R.C. 1923.02(A)(9) allows a possession action against a tenant who breached an obligation imposed by a written rental agreement - a path that does not require the statutory ground's proof structure. And it can reach conduct the statute does not, such as activity away from the premises or a person present without the tenant's consent. Three limits. Under R.C. 5321.13(A) no provision of the landlord-tenant chapter may be modified or waived by any agreement, so an addendum must not purport to soften or rewrite the statutory duty. Under R.C. 5321.13(F) you may assume any tenant duty except the drug duty, so an addendum cannot shift policing of drug activity onto you. And mind which register you write in: where the R.C. 5321.05(C)(2) conditions are met the statute says you shall act, so do not write that track as optional; but do not write the reverse error either, promising a mandatory three-day notice on a bare clause breach, because the statute attaches no duty to that. Keep the policy aimed at current conduct. Ohio's civil rights law lists drug addiction and alcoholism among protected impairments and carves out only a disorder resulting from current illegal use or current alcohol use, and the rehabilitation safe harbour for someone in recovery sits in the employment divisions, not the housing one.

title: Ohio's Address Confidentiality Program Does Not Bind You - But It Changes Your Deposit Notice
bodyText:
Ohio runs an address confidentiality program, and it reaches you indirectly rather than directly. Under R.C. 111.42 a victim of domestic violence, menacing by stalking, human trafficking, rape or sexual battery may be certified by the Secretary of State, who designates a confidential address and issues an authorization card; certification lasts four years. R.C. 111.43(A) obliges a governmental entity to accept that designated address, and division (C) lets the participant make the same request of an employer, school or institution of higher education. A landlord is on neither list. So nothing in the law searched for this row requires you to accept a designated address, to keep a tenant's domestic-violence information confidential, or to restrict your records - and nothing stops you agreeing to. One qualification you must carry through the rest of this row: that is true only until you take the authorised route. If you ask for and receive the tenant's real address from the Secretary of State under R.C. 111.43(E), a criminal confidentiality duty attaches to you at once - see the correction below. The accurate statement is not 'no landlord duty' but 'no duty unless you ask, and then a criminal one'. That absence is proved over chapters 5321 and 1923, read whole, in which the word confidential does not appear, plus R.C. 111.42, 111.43 and 111.99, read section by section; the rest of chapter 111 and the chapter's administrative rules were not read. R.C. 111.43(E)(1)(c) lets the tenant name you on the authorization form, which is the route in. Where this bites is the deposit. R.C. 5321.16(B) makes the tenant give you a forwarding address in writing, and a tenant who does not forfeits damages and fees. For a program participant that address is the Secretary of State's, and because R.C. 111.43(D)(1)(a) makes the Secretary forward first-class and certified mail, mailing your thirty-day itemised deposit notice there does what R.C. 5321.16(B) asks. Do not insist on a street address as a condition, and do not treat a designated address as no address. Until the rest of chapter 111 is checked, treat a tenant's participation and designated address as confidential and disclose neither. Chapters 5321 and 1923 impose no confidentiality duty of any kind: the word confidential appears in neither chapter.

One correction, and it matters: there IS a criminal disclosure offence, and it can reach you. R.C. 111.99(D) says 'No person who obtains a confidential address or telephone number from the secretary of state under division (E) of section 111.43 of the Revised Code shall knowingly disclose that information to any person, except for the purpose for which the disclosure was authorized under that division', and R.C. 111.99(F) makes a violation a misdemeanor of the first degree. You are not a 'public official' under R.C. 111.99(B) and you have no access to the law enforcement gateway under (C), so none of that reaches you. But if the tenant authorizes disclosure to you under R.C. 111.43(E)(1)(c), you become a person who obtained the address from the Secretary of State under division (E), and from that moment knowingly passing it on is a crime. That is why the Secretary's disclosure carries the warning R.C. 111.43(E)(3) requires: 'You are not permitted to redisclose the following information for any reason. Failure to protect the confidentiality of this information is a violation of state law.' So the rule of thumb is simple - you need not accept the designated address, but if you ask for and receive the real one, keep it to yourself and out of anything you file or forward.

title: No Domestic Violence Deposit Clock in Ohio - And A Protection Order Does Not Start One
bodyText: Ohio has no domestic-violence deposit rule. There is no statutory DV termination to trigger a deposit accounting in the first place, no rule making the deposit clock wait until every occupant has delivered possession, and no rule splitting a deposit between a departing survivor and a remaining co-tenant. Ohio's landlord-tenant chapter does not use the words co-tenant, joint tenant or remaining tenant at all. What governs instead is the ordinary clock in R.C. 5321.16(B), which runs thirty days from two conjunctive events: termination of the rental agreement and delivery of possession. Read that literally in a domestic-violence situation. If a court order under R.C. 3113.31(E)(1)(b) or (c) removes one party and the other stays on, the rental agreement has not terminated and possession has not been delivered, so no deposit duty arises and you should not disburse the deposit to the person who left. If every tenant goes, the clock runs from the later of the two events as it always does, and the protection order changes nothing about it. Searched Revised Code chapters 5321 and 1923 and the 35 other chapters held in this corpus, plus R.C. 3113.31 read whole.

title: Ohio Gives A Domestic Violence Victim No Eviction Defence - But Read 'With The Consent Of The Tenant'
bodyText: Ohio has no domestic-violence eviction protection. R.C. 1923.02 lists fifteen grounds for a possession action and none of them carves out a victim; R.C. 1923.061(A) lets a tenant assert any defence at trial but creates no DV defence; and Ohio's retaliation bar protects only three things, none of which is calling the police or obtaining a protection order. So being a victim is not, by itself, a shield. One textual limit is worth knowing and it cuts your way less than you might think. The grounds that reach a third party's conduct are written as the tenant, a person in the tenant's household, or a person on the premises 'with the consent of the tenant'. An abuser who forces entry or returns in breach of a protection order is arguably not there with the tenant's consent, which weakens an eviction built on his conduct. The same phrase runs through the tenant's own duty to keep order on the premises. Two cautions. The drug-activity track is mandatory once triggered and has no victim exception, so if the facts fit it you must still act. And a nuisance or disturbance eviction aimed at a victim is the exposure a court is most likely to look at hard, even without a statute. Searched Revised Code chapters 1923 and 5321 and the 35 other chapters held in this corpus, plus R.C. 3113.31 read whole.

title: Ohio Gives You No Lock-Change Duty - But A Court Can Move Possession
bodyText: Ohio imposes no lock-change duty on you for a domestic violence victim, gives the tenant no lock-change right, voids no contrary lease term, and attaches no statutory damages. Chapter 5321 has no domestic-violence provision at all: the chapter says 'domestic violence' only twice, at R.C. 5321.01(C)(9)(b)(ii) and (C)(10), and both push shelters outside the definition of residential premises. R.C. 3113.31, the civil protection order statute, never uses the word lock, and never says landlord, lessor or rental agreement. What it does is move possession. Under R.C. 3113.31(E)(1)(b) and (c) a court may evict the respondent where the petitioner is the sole lessee, order the respondent to vacate a jointly leased unit, or order the respondent out even where the respondent is the sole lessee. Honour that order when you are served with one: it changes who may lawfully be present, not who holds a key, and it is the court's act, not yours. Never change locks on a victim's request alone - R.C. 5321.15(A) bars you from excluding any tenant to recover possession. If you want a lock-change protocol, put it in the lease; R.C. 5321.06 allows it. This was searched across Revised Code chapters 5321 and 1923 and the 35 other chapters held in this corpus, plus R.C. 3113.31 read whole. Chapters 2919, 2903 and 2151, which carry Ohio's other protection-order sections, were not available to read.

title: Ohio's Civil Protection Order Statute Has Not Moved - It Is Still R.C. 3113.31
bodyText: Cite Ohio's domestic violence civil protection order as R.C. 3113.31. It has not been renumbered and it has not moved chapters. Here is exactly how far that is proved, because chapter 3113 is outside this library's Ohio corpus and the section itself was fetched and read on 30 October 2026 rather than held. Its current version took effect 23 March 2023 under S.B. 210 of the 134th General Assembly, and no act of the 135th or 136th General Assembly has amended it, re-enacted it or moved it - a scan of all 215 enrolled acts of both General Assemblies and the 2024 special session turns up no act printing it as an amended section, while thirteen of those acts cross-reference it by that same number, two of them in the 136th General Assembly. Chapter 3113 is intact around it: 136th General Assembly acts still cite R.C. 3113.33 and 3113.34 and the range 3113.35 to 3113.39 by those numbers. Four other protection-order section numbers are live, and the numbers are all this row can give you: R.C. 2919.26, 2151.34, 2903.213 and 2903.214. All four appear by those numbers in S.B. 315 of the 136th General Assembly, which is how their currency was checked - but chapters 2919, 2151 and 2903 are outside this library's Ohio corpus and none of the four sections was read for this row, so what each one covers, and which of them a tenant's order was issued under, are questions you must answer from the sections themselves. Ohio does renumber - cannabis moved from chapter 3780 into chapter 3796 effective 20 March 2026, and the dog statute R.C. 955.011 became 955.021 - so check a citation rather than assume, and look at the section's catchline, which is where a renumbering note appears.

title: Ohio Sets No Proof Standard For A Domestic Violence Claim - Because It Gives No Right To Prove
bodyText: Ohio tells you nothing about what proof of domestic violence you must accept, and the reason is structural: Ohio gives a survivor no statutory lease right, so there is no statutory claim for a document to support. There is no list of qualifying documents, no rule that a police report, a protection order, or a letter from an advocate or a health professional must be accepted, no bar on asking for more, and no confidentiality rule governing what you do with what you are given. Two real Ohio documents exist in this area, and neither is addressed to you. A civil protection order under R.C. 3113.31 is a court order you must honour on its own terms. And the Secretary of State's address confidentiality program under R.C. 111.42 has its own proof regime - an application assistant's recommendation and a notarised statement go in, and a participant identification number and an authorization card come out, with certification lasting four years - but that is proof to the Secretary of State, not to a landlord. If you want a documentation standard, you have to write it into the lease; R.C. 5321.06 allows it and R.C. 5321.14 is the only ceiling. Keep whatever you ask for proportionate, and keep it confidential as a matter of practice rather than of statute. Searched Revised Code chapters 5321 and 1923 and the 35 other chapters held in this corpus, plus R.C. 3113.31, 111.42 and 111.43.

title: Ohio Requires No Background Check On Your Staff - And Screening Them Is Its Own Legal Risk
bodyText: Ohio requires no background check, criminal records check or registry check on the people you employ to manage, lease or maintain residential rental property, and it sets no disqualifying offences, no look-back period and no conditional-offer sequence. The one housing-sector mandate in Ohio law is narrow and is not about you: R.C. 3735.311 bars a metropolitan housing authority from employing anyone with a felony conviction or guilty plea as a member of its police force, and requires termination or suspension on a later felony. Nothing extends that to a private apartment employee. Screening staff is therefore your choice, and it carries its own exposure in both directions. FEDERAL: the Fair Credit Reporting Act governs the report, the disclosure and authorisation you must get, and the pre-adverse-action and adverse-action notices you must send if you use a screening company. On the Ohio side, if you employ four or more people you are an employer under R.C. 4112.01(A)(2), and R.C. 4112.02(A) then bars discharging without just cause, refusing to hire, or otherwise discriminating on race, colour, religion, sex, military status, national origin, disability, age or ancestry - a class list that includes age, meaning forty or older, which the housing division does not. Note two asymmetries with the housing side. Division (H) reaches any person, so staff size is irrelevant to your fair housing exposure. And under R.C. 4112.08 a supervisor, manager or other employee is not personally liable for employment discrimination unless they are the employer, whereas in housing your leasing agent is exposed in their own right.

title: Ohio Hands You No Pet Fact Sheet To Deliver
bodyText: Ohio publishes no pet-and-eviction fact sheet, requires no notice or disclosure about pets, and attaches nothing to knowing that your tenant has a dog or a cat. There is no Ohio equivalent of the Maryland delivery duty. The point is structural rather than an oversight: Ohio mandates almost no lease content at all. The only thing R.C. 5321.18 requires a written rental agreement to contain is the name and address of the owner and of the owner's agent, and the only form of words Ohio prescribes for a landlord is the warning paragraph that must appear on a notice to leave before an eviction. Nothing about animals is in either. So your pet terms are yours to write, subject only to the general limits: the lease may say what you choose, a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, and nothing in the lease may modify or waive the landlord-tenant chapter. Two things do constrain you, and neither is a fact sheet. An animal a tenant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not a pet and cannot carry a pet fee or deposit. And the one Ohio statute that mentions a service dog is a criminal offence for assaulting or harassing one - it says nothing to a landlord and gives you no notice duty.

title: Ohio Bans The Question, Not Just The Decision
bodyText: Ohio's fair housing law reaches your application form, not only your decision. Under R.C. 4112.02(H)(8) it is an unlawful discriminatory practice, in connection with the sale or lease of housing, to make any inquiry, elicit any information, make or keep any record, or use any application form containing questions or entries concerning race, colour, religion, sex, military status, familial status, ancestry, disability or national origin. All four verbs matter: an unasked question you record anyway, and a blank on a form you never score, each breach the division on its own terms. The division's own exception is narrow - any person may make inquiries and keep records on those characteristics for the purpose of monitoring compliance with the chapter - and Ohio Adm.Code 4112-5-04(B) adds a second, for records kept to the requirements of a government agency or court administering an anti-discrimination programme, gathered so they cannot be misused or misread. Disability has its own regime at R.C. 4112.02(H)(17), which bars asking whether someone has a disability or how severe it is while expressly allowing five inquiries of every applicant alike: ability to meet the requirements of tenancy, qualification for disability-restricted housing or a disability priority, current illegal controlled-substance use, and any conviction or guilty plea for distributing a controlled substance. Be careful with the two of those five that ask about disability itself, because the Civil Rights Commission's own rule, Ohio Adm.Code 4112-5-07(B), bans disability inquiries with a much narrower exception than the statute allows. Note what the statute does not list. Age is not a protected class in the housing division at all, and neither sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status nor source of income appears anywhere in it. Many Ohio cities protect classes the state does not, by ordinance.

title: Denying An Assistance Animal Is Not A Crime In Ohio - It Is Worse Than That
bodyText: Ohio attaches no criminal penalty to refusing an assistance animal. Chapter 4112, the whole of Ohio's civil rights law, creates no offence at all - the word misdemeanour appears nowhere in its thirty-one sections - and Ohio has no dog-guide or hearing-dog statute that makes a landlord waive a lease restriction on pain of prosecution. Do not read that as a lighter exposure. A refusal is an unlawful discriminatory practice in housing, and R.C. 4112.99(A) makes whoever violates the chapter subject to a civil action for damages, injunctive relief or any other appropriate relief, in addition to the Civil Rights Commission track and its civil penalties. Two features make it personal. R.C. 4112.01(A)(1) defines 'person' to include any owner, lessor, manager, agent or employee, so the leasing agent who says no is exposed in their own right. And R.C. 4112.02(J) separately prohibits aiding, abetting, inciting, compelling or coercing the practice. One trap to avoid: Ohio's public-accommodation rule at R.C. 4112.02(G) is not a back door into your building. The definition at R.C. 4112.01(A)(9) is a list of trades - an inn, a restaurant, an eating house, a barbershop, a public conveyance, a theatre, a store or another place for the sale of merchandise - closing with any other place of public accommodation or amusement whose facilities are available to the public. It does not name the common halls of buildings or lodging for permanent guests, and a dwelling let to a tenant is not available to the public. Housing is governed by division (H), not division (G).

title: Ohio Has No Fake-Service-Animal Offence, And Its Definition Gives You Little To Argue With
bodyText: Ohio has no statute penalising a tenant who misrepresents an animal as an assistance animal, so there is no offence to warn a tenant about and nothing to cite in a lease. Ohio's definition also runs against you. The Civil Rights Commission's rule, Ohio Adm.Code 4112-5-02(C), defines an animal assistant as any animal which aids a person with a disability, and its own examples include a monkey - it is species-neutral and it does not require formal training or certification, so breed, size and training objections get you nowhere. Combine that with the rule that you may charge no extra fee for the animal and you have a right with almost no gatekeeping attached. What you do have is ordinary tools. You may ask for reliable documentation where neither the disability nor the disability-related need is readily apparent. A false written statement on an application breaches an application-accuracy clause, and under R.C. 1923.02(A)(9) a breach of a written rental agreement obligation is a ground for a possession action. And R.C. 2921.13(A)(8) makes it falsification, a first-degree misdemeanour, to make a written statement intended to induce another to bestow a valuable benefit where that person relies on it to their detriment - a general offence that could textually cover a fabricated animal claim, though no Ohio case applies it that way and only a prosecutor can bring it. Do not threaten a tenant with it.

title: A Late Benefit Cheque Is No Defence In Ohio - And The Continuance Costs A Bond
bodyText: Ohio gives a tenant no continuance, no stay and no reinstatement because a government benefit or a housing voucher payment arrived late.
