Nothing in the eviction chapter mentions social security, public assistance, a housing voucher or housing assistance at all. The continuance rule cuts the other way. Under R.C. 1923.08 no continuance in an eviction may run longer than eight days unless you apply for it and the tenant consents, or the tenant applies for it and posts a bond with good and sufficient surety, approved by the court and conditioned on paying rent that accrues if judgment goes against them. So a tenant waiting on a payment gets eight days at most without putting up security. Ohio does have one stay of exactly the shape other states give for benefits, and it is military, not financial: R.C. 1923.062 requires the court, on motion, to stay the proceedings ninety days or adjust the rental obligation where a tenant or an immediate family member is deployed on active duty and that deployment materially affects the ability to pay - and that section does not apply to a landlord operating fewer than four residential premises. Two cautions. Ohio gives no statutory right to cure nonpayment at all, so a late payment does not reset the notice. And although Ohio has no general source-of-income protection, refusing to consider a disabled applicant's income is separately unlawful, so a blanket rule about benefit income is a different risk.

title: Ohio Barely Regulates Screening - But It Hands You Two Liability Shields
bodyText:
Ohio has no tenant-screening statute, on a search of this library's 37-chapter Ohio corpus together with every enrolled act of the 135th and 136th General Assemblies: no conditional-offer sequencing, no criminal-history look-back period, no limit tying a minimum-income test to the tenant's share of the rent, no cap on application or screening fees, and no bar on relying on a sealed or expunged record. The phrase tenant screening appears once in all 37 chapters, at R.C. 1349.52(L)(3)(e), and that is the quirk below. FEDERAL: the Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. 1681, is the regime that actually governs your screening report, your adverse-action notice and your use of a consumer reporting agency, and Ohio's own consumer statutes do little more than point at it. One Ohio quirk is worth knowing: a credit security freeze does not block you. Under R.C. 1349.52(L)(3)(e) a reporting agency need not place a freeze on a database used solely for tenant screening, so a frozen credit file and an available tenant-screening report are different things. Ohio also gives you two liability shields for renting to, or keeping, someone with a record, and both are now settled law. The first: under R.C. 1923.02(C)(2), if you are entitled to terminate a tenancy because a registered offender lives within a thousand feet of school premises, children's crisis care facility premises or residential infant care center premises and you choose not to, you are not liable in tort for injury, death or loss said to result from that decision. The second is a certificate of qualification for housing. A court may issue one to a person whose conviction carries a housing bar; it lifts the automatic bar, creates a rebuttable presumption that the convictions do not make the person unfit, and requires you to decide case by case - and it gives you immunity in a negligent-leasing action if you knew of the certificate when you leased. Treat a certificate as a sound reason to rent, ask whether an applicant holds one, and record that you knew of it - that last step is what buys you the immunity described below. Three limits remain. It does not relieve anyone of sex-offender registry requirements, it is revoked on a later felony or violent misdemeanour, and if the tenant later shows dangerousness you can still be liable for keeping them, on actual knowledge plus wilfulness.

One Ohio provision here is a shield rather than a burden, and landlords routinely read it backwards. A certificate of qualification for housing under R.C. 2953.26 (in force since September 20, 2024) does not force you to rent to anyone. It lifts the automatic legal bar that a conviction created, and you 'shall consider on a case-by-case basis whether to provide or deny housing' (division (D)(1)); the certificate is only a rebuttable presumption that the convictions are insufficient evidence of unfitness, and you 'may deny the housing to the person if it determines that the person is unfit' (division (D)(2)). What you get in return is substantial: in a tort action for negligent leasing the certificate 'provides immunity for the decision-maker as to the claim if the decision-maker knew of the certificate at the time of the alleged negligence' (division (F)(2)), and it is evidence of your due care generally (division (F)(1)). The section names you directly - 'decision-maker' includes 'a landlord as defined in section 1923.01' (division (A)(2)). So ask whether an applicant holds one and write down that you knew. The one trap is division (F)(3): if the tenant later turns out dangerous or is convicted of a felony or a violent misdemeanor and you keep them on, you can be liable - but only on proof that you had actual knowledge and were willful in retaining them.

One more thing, and it depends on how you take the rent. R.C. 4112.021 makes it an unlawful discriminatory practice for a 'creditor' to do various things, and two of them would reach your application form: division (B)(1)(g) requires a creditor to print on or firmly attach to every credit application, in a type size no smaller than the rest of the form, a notice beginning 'The Ohio laws against discrimination require that all creditors make credit equally available to all credit worthy customers'; and division (B)(1)(f) requires a written statement of the specific reasons for rejecting an application, within thirty days, if the applicant asks in writing within sixty days. Division (D) lets an aggrieved person sue in common pleas within one hundred eighty days and recover compensatory and punitive damages of not less than one hundred dollars plus attorney's fees and costs.

Whether that reaches you turns on the definitions. 'Credit' is the right 'to defer payment of a debt, to incur debt and defer its payment, or to purchase property or services and defer payment', and a 'creditor' is a person who regularly extends it. **Rent payable in advance is not credit** - the tenant pays before the month rather than after it, so nothing is deferred, and on that footing the section does not reach an ordinary Ohio tenancy. But if you regularly let rent be paid in arrears, take a security deposit by installments, or put a tenant in arrears on a payment plan, you are arguably granting the right to defer payment of a debt - and if you do it regularly you may be a creditor, with that notice due on every application and written reasons due on every rejection. No Ohio case law decides it. The cautious course costs almost nothing: keep rent payable in advance, and if you do offer deferred terms, put the notice on the form and give written reasons when asked.

title: Ohio Has No Balcony or Deck Inspection Requirement
bodyText: Ohio imposes no periodic balcony, deck or exterior elevated element inspection on a residential landlord. There is no Ohio equivalent of the California or Washington balcony inspection statutes, no inspection interval, no qualified-inspector requirement and no filing or certification duty. We searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in our Ohio corpus, which include ch. 5321, ch. 3781 building standards, ch. 3737 fire marshal and ch. 3767 nuisances, and the Ohio Fire Code rules in Ohio Adm.Code 1301:7-7. The word balcony appears once in the Revised Code chapters we hold, inside R.C. 3767.41's list of habitability conditions used to decide whether a building is a public nuisance in a receivership action, and once in the Fire Code rules, in a sprinkler provision. Neither creates an inspection duty. What does apply is general. R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) requires you to make all repairs and do whatever is reasonably necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition, and R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) requires you to keep all common areas in a safe and sanitary condition. R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes you comply with applicable building, housing, health and safety codes. Those are duties to maintain, not a schedule, so the cautious course is to inspect elevated walkways, stairs, landings and balconies on a regular cycle you set and document, because a failure shows up as a habitability or negligence claim rather than as a missed inspection. Note two limits on this answer. We could not read the Ohio Building Code or Ohio Residential Code, so a construction-phase or alteration-phase requirement that lives only there is not covered here. And R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves local building and housing codes in force, so a city may have an inspection program of its own.

title: Ohio Gives You a Common-Area Duty With No Number Attached
bodyText: Ohio puts common areas squarely on you but never says how bright they have to be. R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) requires you to keep all common areas of the premises in a safe and sanitary condition, and R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) requires you to maintain in good and safe working order all electrical fixtures you supply or are required to supply. Together those cover hallway, stairwell, entry and parking-area lighting. What Ohio does not give you is a standard: no footcandle level, no dusk-to-dawn requirement, no fixture count, no emergency-lighting duty for ordinary rentals in the Revised Code. Searching the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters we hold turns up no landlord lighting figure at all, and the word illumination appears only in a motor-vehicle section. So the level is your judgment call. Pick something defensible, write it into your maintenance routine, and replace failed lamps promptly, because the claim you will face is that an unlit stairwell was not safe, not that you missed a number. Two cautions. First, you cannot shift this duty to the tenant. R.C. 5321.13(A) bars modifying or waiving any provision of ch. 5321 by agreement, and R.C. 5321.13(F) lets the landlord assume a tenant duty but gives no route the other way, so a clause making the tenant responsible for keeping common-area lights working will not hold. Allocating who pays the electric bill for a common-area fixture is a different question, and Ohio has no rule on it either way; Ohio has no counterpart to the Massachusetts rule that lets a lease shift common-area light costs to a tenant only at the start of a new tenancy. If you want to try it, R.C. 5321.06 lets a lease carry terms not inconsistent with ch. 5321, but keep the duty to keep the lights working with you. Second, we could not read the Ohio Building Code or Ohio Residential Code, and emergency egress illumination for existing buildings sits in Ohio Fire Code chapter 11, whose base text is the ICC's and is not published by the state, so check your local building and housing code.

title: Ohio Has Two Separate Code Systems, and Only One of Them Is Readable
bodyText: Ohio does not write its fire and building requirements into statute. It writes two code systems and then makes you follow them: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires you to comply with all applicable building, housing, health, and safety codes that materially affect health and safety. The first system is the Ohio Fire Code, which the state fire marshal adopts under R.C. 3737.82 as Ohio Adm.Code 1301:7-7. Its own scope provision says it applies to all residential occupancies and premises, naming one-, two- and three-family dwellings and R occupancies, but it does not reach structural building requirements covered by the Ohio Building Code. The second system is the building codes the board of building standards adopts under R.C. 3781.10. Which one covers your property turns on size: R.C. 3781.06(C)(9) defines a residential building as a one-, two- or three-family dwelling house, so a four-unit-or-larger apartment building is a nonresidential building under R.C. 3781.06(C)(10) and sits under the Ohio Building Code, not the Residential Code. For this entry we read the Ohio Fire Code rules in Ohio Adm.Code 1301:7-7 directly. We could not read the Ohio Building Code (Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1) or the Ohio Residential Code (Ohio Adm.Code 4101:8) at all, so no requirement that lives only in those codes is stated here. Two things also keep the state codes narrower than they look. Under R.C. 3781.10(A)(2)(b) the residential code is uniform only for building new residential buildings and for repairing and altering existing ones, so a day-to-day maintenance duty on a sitting landlord may not be in the state code at all. And R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves local housing, building, health and safety codes untouched by the landlord-tenant chapter, so for an existing rental the requirement that actually bites is often a city housing code. Get the code list for your own municipality before you rely on anything here.

title: Ohio's Sprinkler Rules Are Height Rules, Not Landlord Rules
bodyText: Ohio has no sprinkler retrofit duty for an ordinary rental. The two Revised Code sprinkler provisions are both keyed to building height, not to being a landlord. R.C. 3781.108 requires a fire suppression system in a building constructed on or after September 15, 1989 with floors used for human occupancy more than seventy-five feet above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access. R.C. 3781.104 reaches only an existing apartment or condominium building that exceeds seventy-five feet in height, and what it requires there is smoke detection, not sprinklers; a sprinkler system already in place is simply one way out of that obligation. Below seventy-five feet neither section imposes anything. Do not read R.C. 3781.104's catchline, which mentions a sprinkler system, as a general duty to sprinkler a rental. The Ohio Fire Code does carry a sprinkler chapter, and we read Ohio's changes to it. Two of them matter to you. Ohio amended the where-required provision so that sprinklers are required in the locations where the building code official requires them, which pushes the question into the building code rather than answering it in the fire code. And Ohio added an exception for a Group R-2 building permitted a single exit, which can take a small walk-up out of the sprinkler requirement if it meets seven conditions including two-hour fire barriers, no more than two dwelling units per floor per fire area, no more than six units per fire area, a basement plus two stories at most, and no more than twelve units in the building. For an existing building, Ohio also wrote a real brake into the fire code: the code does not apply to an existing building or condition unless a fire official proves a distinct hazard to life or property by a preponderance of the evidence. The sprinkler requirements that would actually apply to your building sit in the Ohio Building Code or Ohio Residential Code, which we could not read, and the underlying International Fire Code text, which is the ICC's and is not published by the state. If you have a sprinkler system, R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) and (A)(4) make maintaining it your problem, and a variance is available from the board of building appeals under R.C. 3781.19 where literal enforcement would cause unnecessary hardship.

title: Ohio Cites Outside Standards by Frozen Date - Read the Citation, Not the Current Edition
bodyText: Ohio law routinely borrows outside standards, and it usually borrows a particular edition, frozen at the moment of enactment. That matters to you because the current published version of a standard is not necessarily the version Ohio made you follow, and the version Ohio made you follow may no longer exist under that name. Four examples show the pattern, and all four touch rentals. The Ohio Fire Code adopts specific editions of the International Fire Code: chapters 1 through 11 and 20 through 80 of the 2021 edition and chapter 12 of the 2024 edition, published by the International Code Council and incorporated by reference. Those are fixed editions, not whatever the ICC publishes next, and the base text is the ICC's copyrighted work, which the state does not reprint, so the Ohio rules you can read online show only Ohio's own changes. R.C. 3781.104, the high-rise smoke detection section, adopts by name national fire prevention association standard No. 74, the household fire warning system standard, and does so for the purpose of installation and maintenance only. That standard number has since been reorganised in NFPA's own numbering. R.C. 5321.04(A)(10) requires you to comply with tenants' rights under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which it cites as 117 Stat. 2835, 50 U.S.C. App. 501 - an appendix that has since been editorially reclassified, so the citation in the statute no longer matches where you will find the Act. And R.C. 3767.41, the nuisance receivership section, imports the federal habitability standards at 24 C.F.R. 5.703 subsection by subsection and pins certain Section 8 programs to the program as in effect immediately before October 1, 1983. By contrast, R.C. 3737.82 lets the fire marshal incorporate published standards and later amendments published by the same authority, so that one authority rolls forward. A related trap is a section whose printed text is not a single enactment at all. R.C. 3749.01, the swimming pool definitions, is presented by the Legislative Service Commission as a composite of amendments made by two different acts, reconciled under R.C. 1.52(B); its effective date and its Latest Legislation line both list more than one source. When you see that, you are reading a harmonised text rather than something one legislature voted on word for word. The practical rule: when an Ohio provision points you at an outside standard, note the edition, date or Stat. and U.S.C. numbers in the citation, and work from that version. If the citation is stale, do not assume the newest edition governs, and do not assume the old one does either - ask before you spend money on the difference.

title: No Ohio Duty to Hand a Tenant Your Health District's Rental Rules
bodyText: Ohio puts no health-district paperwork duty on you. Nothing requires you to give a tenant a copy of a health district's rental regulations on request, to post them, to attach them to the lease, or to refer a complaining tenant to the health district. Ohio also has no statewide health-district rental licensing scheme for ordinary residential rentals. The health-district licensing regimes we found in the Revised Code reach only places that are not ordinary rentals: recreational vehicle parks, recreation camps and combined park-camps under ch. 3729, where the board of health is the licensor; agricultural labor camps under ch. 3733; and manufactured home parks under ch. 4781. Each of those is outside the landlord-tenant chapter anyway. R.C. 5321.01(C)(3) takes transient occupancy in a recreation camp or RV park out of residential premises, R.C. 5321.01(C)(6) takes out a farm residence let with at least two acres for agricultural production, and R.C. 5321.01(C)(7) takes out agricultural labour camps; park lots are outside chapter 5321 because R.C. 4781.01(W) makes a park's 'residential premises' the lot rather than a dwelling unit. So for an ordinary house, duplex or apartment, there is no state health-district rental rule to hand over. Two things remain true and matter. R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires you to comply with all applicable building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety, which is the hook that pulls a local health regulation onto you if one exists. And R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) keeps housing, building, health and safety codes of a political subdivision outside the landlord-tenant chapter's preemption, so your county or city health district may have regulations that apply even though no statute makes you circulate them. We do not resolve any particular health district's rules here. Find out whether your district regulates rental housing, keep a copy if it does, and treat a health-district order as a code obligation under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1). Giving a tenant a copy on request costs you nothing and heads off a complaint, but it is your choice, not Ohio's requirement.

title: Ohio Mandates No Key-Control Policy and No Employee Background Checks
bodyText: Ohio requires no key-control policy. There is no duty to keep a key log, no rule on who may hold a master key, no limit on duplicates, no required procedure when a key goes missing, and no threshold at which a larger complex has to adopt a written policy. Ohio also imposes no background-check requirement on the maintenance staff, leasing agents or contractors who carry your keys. We searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in our Ohio corpus, which include ch. 5321 landlord and tenant, ch. 3781 building standards and ch. 3737 fire marshal, and the Ohio Fire Code rules in Ohio Adm.Code 1301:7-7; the phrases key control, master key, duplicate key and rekey appear in none of them. That makes a written key-control policy a management choice, and a worthwhile one, because Ohio's entry rules assume you hold a key and will use it. R.C. 5321.05(B) says the tenant must not unreasonably withhold consent for you to enter to inspect, make repairs, supply services or show the unit. R.C. 5321.04(A)(7) and (A)(8) bound that: do not abuse the right of access, give reasonable notice of intent to enter, enter only at reasonable times, and twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable unless the evidence says otherwise. If a key in the wrong hands produces an unannounced entry, the exposure is R.C. 5321.04(B), which lets the tenant recover actual damages, get an injunction and recover reasonable attorney's fees, or terminate the rental agreement. Keep a policy that tracks every key issued and returned, limits master keys to named people, and rekeys at turnover and whenever a key is unaccounted for. Under R.C. 5321.06 the lease may also require the tenant to return all keys at move-out and bar locks you have no key to, since a lock you cannot open defeats your access and your emergency response. Any key or lock-change charge you set is your figure, not Ohio's, and R.C. 5321.14 is the only ceiling on it.

title: Four Families Turns Your Pool Into a Public Pool, Fee or No Fee
bodyText: Whether your rental pool is regulated in Ohio turns on one number: how many families the dwelling houses. R.C. 3749.01(F) defines a private residential swimming pool as one located at a dwelling housing no more than three families and used exclusively by the dwelling's residents, their nonpaying guests, or a paying guest in a one-on-one certified swimming class with no more than four people in the pool. A pool that fits that description falls outside Ohio's public pool regime entirely. R.C. 3749.01(G) then defines a public swimming pool as one intended to be used collectively and operated by any person as owner, lessee, operator, licensee or concessionaire, regardless of whether or not a fee is charged for use. That last phrase is the trap. A shared pool at a four-unit building or a larger apartment community is a public swimming pool under Ohio law even though no resident pays a cent to swim, and even though the pool is only for residents. Your landlord status does not exempt you; the definition names owners and lessees. The licensor is local, not the state: under R.C. 3749.01(D) it is the city board of health or the general health district, or the Director of Health 'when acting under section 3749.07'. Under R.C. 3749.07(B), the Director steps in only where a health district is not on the Director's approved licensing list. So if your property houses four or more families and has a shared pool, your obligations run to the local board of health, and you should contact it before the pool opens. If it houses three or fewer, keep it genuinely residents-only and nonpaying, because letting the pool be used collectively or charging for it is what moves you across the line. No person may operate or maintain a public swimming pool without a licence from the licensor (R.C. 3749.04(A)). Apply each April for an existing pool, and at least thirty days before opening a new or unlicensed one (R.C. 3749.04(B)). The safety standards are the Director of Health's rules (R.C. 3749.02; Ohio Adm.Code chapter 3701-31). The perimeter barrier must stay in good repair, with self-closing, lockable gates or doors (Ohio Adm.Code 3701-31-04(B)(6)(s)). A new or substantially altered pool needs a barrier at least forty-eight inches high, self-closing and self-latching patron gates with the latch at least thirty-eight inches up, and no gap of four inches or more (Ohio Adm.Code 3701-31-05.1(O)). The rules also set water quality, safety equipment, signs and, by pool size and bather numbers, lifeguards (Ohio Adm.Code 3701-31-04(C) to (E)). A pool that needs no lifeguard must post 'Warning, No Lifeguard' (Ohio Adm.Code 3701-31-04(E)(3)(a)). Underneath all of this, R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires you to comply with all applicable health and safety codes, which is what makes a board of health order your problem, and R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) requires you to keep common areas safe and sanitary, which covers the pool deck, gate and enclosure whichever side of the line you are on. R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves local health and safety codes outside the landlord-tenant chapter's preemption, so the detail is genuinely local here.

title: Ohio Has No State Rental Inspection Program - But Three Other Doors Open
bodyText: Ohio runs no statewide rental inspection or rental licensing program. There is no state periodic inspection, no certificate of compliance you have to obtain before renting, no state rental licence, and no state inspection fee. The one statewide filing Ohio does require is not an inspection: R.C. 5323.02 requires an owner of residential rental property to file the owner's name, address and telephone number, the responsible person for an entity owner, and the street address and parcel number with the county auditor, and to update it within sixty days of a change. An out-of-state owner must also designate an in-state agent for service of process under R.C. 5323.03. That is a registry of who you are, not a check on the property's condition. Three other doors do open. First, a court. In an eviction or other proceeding involving residential premises, R.C. 1923.15 lets the court order a government agency to inspect, and if the agency finds and the court confirms conditions violating R.C. 5321.04, the court may forbid re-rental until they are corrected, or order them corrected while the tenant stays. Second, receivership. R.C. 3767.41 lets a tenant or neighbour move a building into receivership as a public nuisance. Third, and most often, your city. R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) expressly leaves housing, building, health and safety codes and ordinances of a political subdivision outside the landlord-tenant chapter's preemption, so municipal rental registration and interior inspection programs are lawful in Ohio and many larger cities run them. We do not resolve any particular ordinance here; find out what your municipality requires. On whether your lease can let a housing inspector in: not on its own. R.C. 5321.05(B) says the tenant must not unreasonably withhold consent for the landlord to enter to inspect, so you can bring an inspector along as part of your own entry, with the reasonable notice R.C. 5321.04(A)(8) requires. But the inspector's own authority to enter comes from the ordinance or a warrant, not from your lease, and R.C. 5321.13(A) stops a lease from waiving anything in ch. 5321, so a clause purporting to make the tenant consent in advance to an inspector's independent entry is not something to rely on.

title: Ohio Grants Code Variances - But Nobody Has to Tell Your Tenant
bodyText: Ohio has a variance route, in fact two, and neither of them touches your lease. On the building side, R.C. 3781.19 lets the state board of building appeals, or a certified municipal or county board of appeals, reverse or modify an enforcing agency's order, and grant a variance from the building standards where literal enforcement would result in unnecessary hardship and the variance would not be contrary to the public interest. You get there by appealing the order; the board must decide within thirty days of the adjudication hearing outside the expedited track, and a party may then seek a de novo hearing before the state board or appeal to the court of common pleas. Filing fees are capped at two hundred dollars plus any expedited fee. On the fire side, the state fire marshal may grant a variance from the Ohio Fire Code where there are practical difficulties, on written application by an affected party, if the party shows the variance will not threaten public health, safety or welfare and will provide substantially equivalent protective measures. A granted fire variance must be in writing, entered on the marshal's records and furnished to the applicant and to the local authority having jurisdiction. It terminates automatically one year after issuance unless the marshal says otherwise, and there are no automatic renewals; each year you have to apply again. What Ohio does not do is make the variance part of the tenancy. Nothing requires you to give a tenant a copy of a variance, to post it, to attach it to the rental agreement, or to disclose that one is in effect. Massachusetts requires exactly that; Ohio has no equivalent. Two practical points. R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) still requires you to comply with all applicable codes, so a variance narrows what you owe only as far as its own terms go, and only while it lasts. And because a one-year fire variance lapses on its own, diary the expiry; an expired variance puts you back in violation with no notice from anyone. Telling the tenant is optional, and often sensible if the variance is the reason something in the unit looks wrong.

title: Ohio Has One Security-Device Statute, and It Is a Construction Rule
bodyText: Ohio has exactly one security-device statute and it is easy to over-read. R.C. 3781.103 directs the board of building standards to adopt a rule requiring that the swinging exit door of each unit in an apartment building or other multi-unit dwelling be equipped with a deadbolt or equivalent security locking device meeting the board's standards. Two things bound it. It is addressed to the board, not to you, so the operative requirement is the board's rule and not the statute's own words. And the statute says the rule applies to apartment buildings and multi-unit dwellings for which plans are approved under R.C. 3791.04 - and R.C. 3791.04 itself was NOT read for this row, chapter 3791 being outside this library's Ohio corpus, so read it before relying on what follows. On its face the cross-reference makes this a plan-approval requirement attaching when a building is built or altered rather than a retrofit duty on a landlord who already owns the building, but that reading rests on the referring section alone. So if your building was permitted with deadbolts, you have them; R.C. 3781.103 does not order you to add them to an older building. Beyond that, Ohio requires nothing. There is no peephole or door-viewer requirement, no window-latch or sliding-door-pin requirement, no keyless deadbolt, no security-bar or chain requirement, and no duty to rekey or change locks between tenants. Texas-style security-device and rekey-at-turnover duties have no Ohio counterpart. Rekeying at turnover is nonetheless worth doing and worth saying in the lease, because once a lock exists R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) and (A)(4) make keeping it in good and safe working order yours, and because you cannot contract out of either duty: R.C. 5321.13(A) bars waiving any provision of ch. 5321 and R.C. 5321.13(F) lets you assume a tenant duty but gives the tenant no route to assume yours. Under R.C. 5321.06 you may add security terms the chapter does not prohibit, such as requiring the tenant to report a broken lock promptly and barring added locks you have no key to. Finally, note what we could not check: the board's own deadbolt rule lives in the Ohio Building Code or Ohio Residential Code, which we could not read, and R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves local housing codes in force, so a city may require more.

title: Ohio Does Not Regulate Smart Locks - the Old Entry Rules Still Govern
bodyText: Ohio has no smart-access statute. Nothing regulates smart locks, app-based or code-based entry, electronic access logs, or a tenant's right to opt out of a keyless system and get a physical key. Washington has such a regime taking effect January 1, 2027; Ohio has nothing comparable and nothing pending that we found. We searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in our Ohio corpus, including ch. 5321 landlord and tenant and ch. 3781 building standards, and the Ohio Fire Code rules in Ohio Adm.Code 1301:7-7; the phrases smart lock, electronic lock, keyless, access control and electronic access appear in none of them. Because the subject is unregulated, R.C. 5321.06 lets your lease install the system and set the terms, so long as nothing in it conflicts with ch. 5321 or another rule of law. Four existing rules do the real work, and a smart lock does not soften any of them. First, access. R.C. 5321.04(A)(7) and (A)(8) require reasonable notice of your intent to enter and entry only at reasonable times, with twenty-four hours presumed reasonable; remote-unlocking capability is not notice, and an entry you could do from your phone is still an entry. Second, no self-help. Never use the system to lock a tenant out or to disable a credential as leverage, which Ohio's self-help prohibition reaches. Third, you cannot waive your way out. R.C. 5321.13(A) bars modifying or waiving any provision of ch. 5321 by agreement, and R.C. 5321.13(D) voids any tenant agreement exculpating you from liability arising under law or indemnifying you for it, so a clause disclaiming responsibility for a lock failure or a data breach will not hold. Fourth, the lock has to work. R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) and (A)(4) make maintaining it yours, which for an electronic lock means power, batteries, connectivity and a way in when all three fail. The cautious course is to keep a mechanical override, give the tenant a physical key or an offline code, and say in the lease who may hold credentials, how a lost credential is cancelled, that entry logs exist and what you use them for.

title: No Ohio Radiator Cover Duty and No Radiator Lease Rider
bodyText: Ohio has nothing on steam radiator covers. There is no duty to install a cover on request, no tenant request procedure, no deadline to respond and no mandatory lease rider. New York City's regime, where a landlord must provide a cover for a steam radiator when a child under six lives in the unit and must attach a rider saying so, has no Ohio counterpart. We searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in our Ohio corpus, which include ch. 5321 landlord and tenant, ch. 3781 building standards and ch. 3737 fire marshal, and the Ohio Fire Code rules in Ohio Adm.Code 1301:7-7. The word radiator appears in none of them, and neither does scald. Do not carry a radiator rider into an Ohio lease from another state's form. What Ohio does require is the heat itself and the equipment behind it. R.C. 5321.04(A)(6) requires you to supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat at all times, with narrow exceptions where the building is not required by law to be equipped for the purpose or the tenant's own installation generates it. R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) requires you to maintain in good and safe working order all heating fixtures and appliances you supply. R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) requires you to keep the premises fit and habitable. An uncovered radiator that burns a child is a habitability and negligence question under those provisions, not a missed-rider question, so if you have exposed steam radiators the cautious course is to cover or guard them and record that you did. If you install covers, R.C. 5321.06 lets the lease treat them as part of the premises, and R.C. 5321.05(A)(6) already forbids the tenant from removing a fixture or other part of the premises. Note also that R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves local housing codes in force, and that we could not read the Ohio Building, Residential or Mechanical Codes.

title: Ohio Sets No Water Heater Temperature - Reasonable Hot Water Is the Whole Standard
bodyText: Ohio gives you no water heater temperature to hit. There is no maximum setting, no minimum setting, and no duty to check or reset the thermostat before a new tenant moves in. Wisconsin has a statute requiring an owner to set a unit-only water heater to a stated maximum at each new tenancy, and Washington has one in its energy chapter; Ohio has neither. We searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in our Ohio corpus, which include ch. 5321 landlord and tenant, ch. 3781 building standards and ch. 3737 fire marshal, and the Ohio Fire Code rules in Ohio Adm.Code 1301:7-7. The phrase water heater appears in none of them, and the words temperature and degrees Fahrenheit appear only in an underground storage tank definition. What Ohio requires instead is a standard without a number. R.C. 5321.04(A)(6) requires you to supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat at all times, unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for the purpose or the unit is built so the tenant's own installation generates it on a direct utility connection. R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) requires you to maintain in good and safe working order all plumbing and heating fixtures and appliances you supply, which covers the water heater itself. So reasonable amounts is the test, and it cuts both ways: water too cold is a habitability problem and water hot enough to scald is a safety problem. If you pick a setting, it is your figure and not Ohio's, and the only ceiling on a lease term stating it is R.C. 5321.14, which lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. Where the heater is inside the unit and the tenant can reach the dial, say in the lease who may adjust it and record the setting at move-in so a later complaint has a baseline. Two limits: we could not read the Ohio Plumbing, Building or Residential Codes, where a temperature-limiting or mixing-valve requirement would sit if Ohio has one, and R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves local housing codes in force.

title: Ohio Requires No Window Guards and No Window-Guard Notice
bodyText: Ohio has no window guard requirement and no window-guard notice. There is nothing like the New York City regime: no duty to install guards where a young child lives, no annual survey of your tenants, no model notice text, no bold-type lease rider and no registration or reporting. We searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in our Ohio corpus, which include ch. 5321 landlord and tenant, ch. 3781 building standards, ch. 3737 fire marshal and ch. 3767 nuisances, and the Ohio Fire Code rules in Ohio Adm.Code 1301:7-7. The phrase window guard appears in none of them. Do not put a window-guard notice in an Ohio lease on the theory that another state requires one; a notice you are not required to give can read as a promise you did not mean to make. If you choose to install guards anyway, R.C. 5321.06 lets a lease carry terms not inconsistent with ch. 5321, so you can make the guards part of the premises the tenant must not remove or defeat, and R.C. 5321.05(A)(6) already forbids the tenant from intentionally or negligently removing any fixture or other part of the premises. Keep in mind that once a guard is installed, R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) and (A)(4) make keeping it in working order your problem. Two limits on this answer. We could not read the Ohio Residential Code or Ohio Building Code, where a window fall-protection or sill-height requirement for new construction would live if Ohio has one. And R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves local housing codes in force, so check your city's code before concluding there is no requirement where your property is.

title: Abandonment Is Not A Legal Event In Ohio - The Lease Just Keeps Running
bodyText: Ohio's landlord-tenant chapter never uses the word 'abandon'. There is no statutory definition of abandonment, no statutory moment at which the tenancy ends because the tenant has gone, no statutory acceleration of the remaining rent, and no statutory duty to re-rent - in the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review 'relet', 'reasonable efforts to rent' and any acceleration provision touching a lease all return nothing, and the one hit for 're-rent' is the court's power to forbid you from re-renting a unit with uncorrected code violations. So when a tenant walks out mid-term, nothing happens automatically. The term keeps running, rent keeps accruing under the contract, and your claim is an ordinary contract claim: Ohio lets any party to a chapter 5321 action recover damages for breach of contract or breach of a duty imposed by law, and your claims for past due rent and other damages under the rental agreement can be tried with the possession case. What you should not do is treat the absence as a surrender and simply take the unit back and sell what is inside: seizing a tenant's furnishings or possessions for rent without a court order exposes you to actual damages and the tenant's attorney's fees. Two things to do instead. Re-rent promptly and keep records of the advertising, the showings and the rent you achieved - Ohio's duty to make reasonable efforts to re-let is not in any statute, it comes from case law, and the cautious course is to assume it applies to you and to be able to prove you met it. And end the tenancy properly: serve the notice, get possession through the court, then sue for the shortfall.

title: Ohio Puts No Conditions On An Automatic Renewal Clause
bodyText: Ohio has no automatic-renewal statute for leases and no general consumer auto-renewal statute: across the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, plus the Ohio Constitution and the Administrative Code chapters held, 'automatic renewal', 'automatically renew', 'renewal term', 'self-renewing', 'negative option' and 'affirmative consent' return nothing. So Ohio requires no bold-face warning, no separate opt-in, no pre-renewal reminder notice in a set window, and no limit on how early you may ask a tenant to commit to a new term. Your renewal clause is simply a lease term, good because the lease may carry any term not barred by chapter 5321 or another rule of law, and the only ceiling is that a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. Two Ohio traps. First, a periodic tenancy already renews itself: a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy continues until one side gives notice - seven days, or thirty days before the periodic rental date - so you do not need a renewal clause to keep one alive. Second, Ohio counts any agreement that modifies the terms, conditions, rules or rent as a rental agreement, and an oral one counts, so a conversation can renew or vary a term you drafted carefully. Put every renewal in writing, signed, and make your clause say that nothing modifies it except a signed writing.

title: Ohio Has No Winter Vacate Notice - And The Heat Duty Stays Yours
bodyText: Ohio requires no cold-weather notice before a tenant leaves, sets no heating season, and names no date range in the landlord-tenant chapter. Searching the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review for 'freezing' and 'heating season' returns nothing, and the hits for 'freeze', 'frozen' and 'pipes' are all about credit-report security freezes and underground storage tanks. What Ohio does say is that you must supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat at all times. There are only two exceptions on the face of the statute: a building not required by law to be equipped for the purpose, and a unit built so that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection. Outside those, the heat duty is yours whether or not the tenant is in residence, and you cannot contract out of it: no provision of the chapter may be modified or waived by any agreement, and Ohio's duty-shifting runs one way only - you may take on a tenant duty, but the tenant can never take on yours. So a clause making the tenant responsible for keeping the heat on will not discharge your duty, and a vacant unit in January is still your exposure. What the lease can usefully do is create a notice-and-care obligation of its own: require the tenant to tell you before any absence over a period you name, to leave the heat set at a minimum you state, and to let you enter to check. If the tenant damages the premises by negligence - a burst pipe after shutting the heat off - Ohio already lets you recover your actual damages plus reasonable attorney's fees for breach of the tenant's statutory duties, which is one of the few places an Ohio landlord gets fees at all.

title: No Ohio Exit For A Flood, A Contamination Or A Condemnation
bodyText: Ohio gives neither party a statutory right to end a lease because of an environmental event short of the building being destroyed or made unfit. Across the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 'force majeure', 'uninhabitable', 'unfit for human habitation', 'order to vacate' and 'evacuation' return nothing, and the handful of hits for 'natural disaster', 'act of God' and 'condemnation' are about credit freezes and underground storage tanks, not tenancies. So a flood that leaves the home standing, a contamination finding, a public-health order or a declared disaster gives you no statutory termination right - and gives the tenant none either, except through the ordinary habitability route: written notice to you specifying the problem, and if you do not remedy it within a reasonable time or thirty days, whichever is sooner, the tenant may end the lease, deposit rent with the court clerk or ask the court for an order - and even that route is not always open to the tenant. R.C. 5321.07(C) takes the whole section away from a landlord who is party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units AND who gives notice of that fact in the written lease, or, for an oral tenancy, in writing at the time of initial occupancy; R.C. 5321.07(D) takes it away for a unit occupied by a student tenant. Note the condition in (C): the exemption depends on your having given the notice, so a small landlord who never says so in the lease does not have it. And note what the exemption does not do - it withdraws that SECTION only, so the tenant still has damages under R.C. 5321.12, the counterclaim under R.C. 1923.061(B), the entry remedies under R.C. 5321.04(B), self-help damages under R.C. 5321.15(C) and the inspection and no-re-rental order under R.C. 1923.15. Separately, and this is the Ohio risk most landlords miss: in any eviction proceeding over residential premises the court may order a government agency to inspect, and if the agency finds and the court finds a violation of your statutory duties, and the premises have been vacated or are coming back to you, the court may forbid you from re-renting the property until the conditions are corrected. An environmental problem discovered during an eviction can therefore cost you the unit, not just the case. If you want a contractual exit, the library's optional Ohio casualty-termination clause covers destruction or injury that cannot reasonably be repaired in a period you set; nothing in Ohio law stops you widening it to a named environmental event, but that is your own drafting, not a statutory right, and a court may still refuse to enforce a term it finds unconscionable.

title: No Ohio Absence Notice - And No Entry Right While The Tenant Is Away
bodyText: No Ohio statute requires a tenant to tell you about an extended absence, requires the lease to carry such a term, or gives you any extra right to enter while the tenant is away. Ohio's list of tenant obligations has no absence-notice duty and, unlike the URLTA states, no sentence requiring the tenant to occupy the home only as a dwelling unit - across the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review 'extended absence' and 'only as a dwelling unit' return nothing at all. Absence alone is also not a legal event: there is exactly one absence-based ground for recovering possession in Ohio and it reaches only a manufactured home park, where a resident absent thirty consecutive days with the home left unoccupied, without notice and without paying rent, may be proceeded against. That ground does not exist for an ordinary rental. You may still create the duty by contract, and the library's shared absence-notice clause works in Ohio as a lease term: the notice obligation and the actual-damages remedy for a willful failure are ordinary contract terms, not a statutory right, so claim them in a civil action or with your possession case rather than treating a missed notice as a default you can act on alone. Your entry rights do not change while the tenant is away. You still need the tenant's non-unreasonable consent to enter to inspect or repair, you must give reasonable notice of your intent to enter - twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable - and enter only at reasonable times, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable. Abusing that right lets the tenant recover damages, get an injunction, recover attorney's fees, or end the lease.

title: Ohio Prices No Holdover - The Daily Figure Is Yours To Justify
bodyText: Ohio sets no holdover formula - no double rent, no multiple of the daily rent, no statutory cap on one. Across the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review the word 'holdover' does not appear at all, 'double rent', 'daily rate', 'reasonable rental value' and 'one hundred fifty per cent' return nothing, and the only 'rental value' provision belongs to land installment contracts. What Ohio gives you is the procedure, not the price: holding over past the term is a ground for a possession action, and the trial on possession may also include your claims for past due rent and other damages under the rental agreement. So the daily holdover figure in your lease is entirely your own, not a statutory limit, and it is only worth what you can justify. Set it at a defensible multiple of the actual daily rent, state that it is a reasonable estimate of your loss and not a penalty, and keep a note of how you arrived at it - the only ceiling Ohio supplies is that a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term or limit its application, and never import another state's 150 percent or double-rent figure as though Ohio had adopted it. Two traps. Accepting rent for a period after you have served your notice to leave can cost you the notice and send you back to the start - Ohio has no statute on the point, and the rule comes from the appellate decisions collected in 'edu-waiver-by-acceptance-oh', which were not read for this row. Read that row before you take or hold money, and in the meantime decide whether you are charging for holdover or collecting rent, and do not do both for the same day. And a termination right is never a self-help right: you recover possession only through the court, and the money claim rides along with the possession case or follows in a civil action.

title: Ohio Gives No Health-Or-Infirmity Way Out Of A Lease
bodyText: A tenant who becomes ill, frail or disabled has no Ohio statutory right to end a lease early, and no right to end it by producing a doctor's letter or proof of a move into care. Across the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 'infirmity', 'physician's statement' and 'unable to live independently' return nothing, and no section pairs 'nursing home' with 'rental agreement'. The tenant's only statutory exits in Ohio are for your failure to keep the premises habitable and for abuse of the right of entry; neither turns on the tenant's health. Do not be misled by Ohio's nursing-home chapter. Its thirty-day transfer-and-discharge notice runs the other way - it binds the home that wants to move a resident out - and a home licensed under that chapter, like a hospital, is carved out of 'residential premises' altogether, so those rules are not a tenancy analogue. One real constraint does bear on this: it is an unlawful discriminatory practice in Ohio to refuse to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when necessary to afford a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling unit. That is not a termination right, and whether releasing a tenant early is ever a required accommodation is not settled by the statute's words, but it means you should answer a documented request in writing and take advice before refusing flatly. You are also free to agree an early release and to set your own buyout figure - nothing in Ohio law stops you, and the only ceiling is that a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term.

title: Possession And Money Are Two Different Cases In Ohio
bodyText: In Ohio possession and money travel on separate tracks, and the statute lets you combine them only up to a point. The eviction case gives you the unit. A judgment in it is not a bar to a later action by either party, so you can take possession now and sue for the money afterwards. You may also ask for both at once: the eviction trial may include your claims for past due rent and other damages under the rental agreement, unless the court continues those claims for good cause - and good cause expressly includes the tenant asking to file an answer or a counterclaim or to take discovery, at which point the money half proceeds like any other civil case and your possession case waits for nothing. Know the counterclaim risk before you join them. In a possession action based on nonpayment, or an action for rent while the tenant is still in, the tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or under the landlord-tenant chapter, the court may order rent paid into court, and if nothing is left owing after the set-off, judgment on possession goes to the tenant. Where to file: a municipal court has original jurisdiction in any forcible entry and detainer action, and that grant is separate from its money limit of fifteen thousand dollars - so a large rent claim may have to go to the common pleas court even though the eviction does not. If the municipal court for your area has a housing or environmental division, that division has exclusive jurisdiction over eviction and landlord-tenant cases in its territory and the fifteen-thousand-dollar limit does not bind it, so file there. There is no small-claims route for possession. And if you own through a company, plan on hiring a lawyer: the statutory allowance for an officer or salaried employee to present a claim is confined to a small claims division, which cannot hear an eviction. You never take possession yourself - no shutting off utilities, no locks, no removing the tenant's possessions for rent without a court order.

title: No Maximum Lease Term - but Notarise Anything Over Three Years
bodyText:
Ohio sets no maximum length for a residential lease - R.C. 5321.06 lets a lease carry any term the parties agree, and nothing in Chapter 5321 caps duration - but there is a formalities threshold at three years that is invisible from the landlord-tenant chapter and easy to miss. R.C. 5301.01(A) says a 'lease of any interest in real property' must be signed by the lessor and the signing 'acknowledged' before a judge, a clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor, who certifies it. Read alone that would require every apartment lease to be notarised. R.C. 5301.08 is the limit: those sections 'do not affect the validity of any lease ... of any other lands for any term not exceeding three years or require that lease to be acknowledged or recorded.'

So the practical rule has three steps. A term of three years or less needs no notarisation and no recording - sign it and you are done. A term longer than three years should be signed by you and acknowledged before a notary, and recorded; skipping that puts you outside the protection those sections give. And separately from either, R.C. 1335.05 bars an action on an agreement 'not to be performed within one year' unless there is a writing signed by the party to be charged, so a purely oral tenancy longer than a year is a tenancy Chapter 5321 recognises (R.C. 5321.01(D) includes oral agreements) but that you may be unable to enforce. Three thresholds, then: one year for enforceability, three years for acknowledgment and recording, and no ceiling on the term itself.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, and 'acknowledged' 7, 'notary public' 8, 'term not exceeding' 2, 'maximum term' 10 and 'ninety-nine' 1, every hit checked and none a residential lease-term cap, against 'landlord' 34 - plus R.C. 5301.01, 5301.08, 1335.04 and 1335.05 read in full outside it. R.C. 5301.02 to 5301.07, R.C. 5301.25 (recording and its effect on a later purchaser) and R.C. 4735.55 were not read, and no Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: How Long You Have To Sue An Ohio Tenant - And The Trap If They Die
bodyText: Ohio's eviction chapter sets one deadline and the landlord-tenant chapter sets none, so almost all of your periods come from the general limitations chapter, R.C. chapter 2305. Start with the exception, because it is the shortest period in this row and the one that governs possession. **R.C. 1923.01(B): 'An action shall be brought under this chapter within two years after the cause of action accrues.'** That is a two-year limit on any Chapter 1923 action - your eviction - and it is recent law, effective 9 April 2025 under S.B. 237 of the 135th General Assembly, so a form or a guide written before then will not mention it. See 'edu-eviction-process-oh', which carries the procedure. Chapter 5321 was read whole and carries no limitation period of its own, so for everything other than the possession action the periods come from chapter 2305. That chapter is not in this library's Ohio corpus; R.C. 2305.06 and 2305.07 were fetched and read section by section on 30 October 2026, and nothing else in the chapter was read, so treat the figures below as those two sections' and check the chapter yourself before you rely on a period they do not cover. One of them is newly amended: R.C. 2305.06's six-year written-contract period is the version effective 23 September 2026 under S.B. 219 of the 136th General Assembly. An action on a written agreement must be brought within six years after the cause of action accrued. An action on a contract not in writing, express or implied, must be brought within four years. An action on a liability created by statute, other than a forfeiture or penalty, must be brought within six years - that is the route for a claim that rests on the landlord-tenant chapter itself rather than on your lease, such as your statutory damages and fees for a breach of the tenant's duties, or the tenant's claim over a security deposit. A separate six-year period applies to an action arising out of a consumer transaction incurred primarily for personal, family or household purposes, and it accrues thirty days after the last charge or payment; but Ohio's consumer definition reaches goods, services, franchises and intangibles rather than a lease of real property, so do not plan on that period applying to a lease and do not assume a part payment restarts your clock. The safe practice is to work to the shortest period that could apply: file for possession within two years of the accrual under R.C. 1923.01(B), keep the lease signed and in writing, and sue on the money within four years of the default if any part of the deal was oral. One hard trap. If the tenant dies, probate overrides all of this: claims against the estate must be presented within six months of the death, an executor can cut that to thirty days from the notice you receive, and a claim not presented in time recovers nothing from estate assets however much of your six years is left.

title: Moving In Yourself Is A Lease Term In Ohio, Not A Statutory Right
bodyText: Ohio has no just-cause eviction law and no owner-move-in rule in either direction. Across the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 'owner occupancy', 'intends to occupy' and 'occupy the premises' return nothing, and the six hits for 'just cause' are all employment or criminal provisions. So there is no statutory owner-use ground you can invoke and, equally, no minimum holding period, relocation payment or duty to re-offer the unit if your plans change. Which means two different things depending on the tenancy. For a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy you need no reservation at all: you may end it on seven or thirty days' notice without giving any reason, so wanting the home for yourself is already enough. For a fixed term you have nothing unless the lease reserved it - the term runs, and the only statutory reason that touches remodelling is a narrow protection against a retaliation defence, not a ground for possession. If you may want the home back mid-term, use the library's optional owner-occupancy clause and fill in both blanks. Three cautions. Serve the reservation notice well clear of any complaint the tenant has made about conditions or of any tenants' group they joined: bringing or threatening a possession action after one of those lets the tenant raise retaliation as a defence, recover possession or end the lease, and in addition recover damages and attorney's fees. Do not take rent for a period after your stated termination date. And a reserved right is not a right to act: if the tenant stays, you serve the statutory notice to leave and recover possession through the court, never by changing locks or cutting utilities.

title: Ohio Has No Seasonal Tenancy - A Summer Let Is Usually A Full Tenancy
bodyText: Ohio's landlord-tenant chapter creates no seasonal, vacation or academic-year tenancy. Searching the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review for 'seasonal occupancy', 'short-term rental', 'academic year' and 'camping season' returns nothing, and the four hits for 'seasonal' are about park trailers, vehicle registration and military leave. What Ohio has instead is a scope test. Chapter 5321 does not reach 'tourist homes, hotels, motels, recreational vehicle parks, recreation camps, combined park-camps, temporary park-camps, and other similar facilities where circumstances indicate a transient occupancy'. That turns on the kind of facility and the circumstances, not on how many weeks the stay lasts. The only place Ohio puts a number on transience is the hotel chapter, where 'transient' means not more than thirty days - but every hotel category there needs more than five rooms, and the chapter expressly does not apply to apartment buildings or other structures in which all the units are residential premises. So renting out a single cottage, lake house or spare unit for a season is almost certainly an ordinary Ohio tenancy: full landlord duties, the security-deposit rules, and the seven-day or thirty-day notice to end a periodic tenancy. Do not assume a short term buys you out of chapter 5321. If the premises is a campsite in an RV park or recreation camp, a different regime applies and the campsite use agreement statute, not chapter 5321, governs the end of the stay.

title: The Three Ways An Ohio Tenant Can Walk Out On You Mid-Term
bodyText: Across the 37 Revised Code chapters this library holds, Ohio gives a tenant three statutory rights to end a lease before its term runs, and every one of them is triggered by something you did. The first is habitability. If you fail a duty under the landlord-obligations section or a duty the lease imposes, or a government agency finds a code violation that could materially affect health and safety, the tenant may send you written notice specifying the acts, omissions or violations, to the place where rent is normally paid. If you then do not remedy the condition within a reasonable time considering its severity or within thirty days, whichever is sooner, and the tenant is current in rent, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement outright - that is one of three options, alongside depositing rent with the court clerk and applying for a court order. Two escapes apply: this section does not reach a landlord who is party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and who says so in the written lease (or delivers written notice of it at the start of an oral tenancy), and it does not reach a student tenant in a unit owned or operated by their own college. The second right is entry. If you enter unlawfully, enter lawfully but in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated otherwise-lawful demands for entry that have the effect of harassing the tenant, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement - or instead recover actual damages, get an injunction and recover reasonable attorney's fees. The third is retaliation. If you raise the rent, cut services, or bring or threaten a possession action because the tenant complained to a government agency about a code violation that materially affects health and safety, complained to you about one of your statutory duties, or joined with other tenants to deal with you collectively, the tenant has a choice of three remedies under R.C. 5321.02(B) and may take one of them, not all: use your conduct as a defence to your possession action, recover possession of the premises, OR terminate the rental agreement. The damages limb is the one thing that is additive - 'In addition, the tenant may recover from the landlord any actual damages together with reasonable attorneys' fees.' Nothing in those 37 chapters gives a statutory exit for a job transfer, a relocation, a landlord's misrepresentation, domestic violence, or state military service. FEDERAL: the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act termination right is federal, and Ohio makes complying with it one of your statutory duties, so treat an SCRA notice as binding on you in Ohio whatever your lease says.

title: Ohio's Notice Ladder Has Only Two Rungs - Name One In Your Lease
bodyText: Ohio's termination statute recognises exactly two periodic tenancies: week-to-week, which either side ends on at least seven days' notice, and month-to-month, which either side ends on at least thirty days' notice given before the periodic rental date (R.C. 5321.17(A), (B)). Ohio has no tenancy at will, no tenancy at sufferance, no year-to-year tenancy and no catch-all notice period - searching the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review for those terms returned nothing at all. So if you let someone occupy with no stated term and no stated rent period, there is no statutory notice period you can point to. Always state the term in writing, and if the tenancy is periodic say whether it runs weekly or monthly, so R.C. 5321.17 supplies the notice period. A rental agreement in Ohio can be oral (R.C. 5321.01(D)) and an oral tenant is still inside chapter 5321, but an oral arrangement meant to run past a year may be unenforceable under the statute of frauds (R.C. 1335.05), and an assignment or grant of a leasehold needs a signed writing (R.C. 1335.04). None of this is a right to cure or a reason to skip the eviction notice: whatever the tenancy, you still serve the R.C. 1923.04(A) three-day notice with its prescribed wording before filing.

title: A Tenant's Death Starts A Six-Month Clock You Can Easily Miss
bodyText: A tenant's death does not end an Ohio lease. No Ohio statute terminates a tenancy on death, so the obligation passes to the estate and your claim for unpaid rent and damages becomes a creditor's claim in probate - which puts you on a deadline most landlords never hear about. All claims against an estate must be presented within six months after the date of death, and the six months runs whether or not an estate is ever opened, whether or not an executor is appointed in that window, and even if the estate is released from administration as a small estate. A claim not presented in time is forever barred: no payment may be made on it and no action may be maintained on it. Worse, an executor can shorten your window by sending you written notice, after which you have the earlier of thirty days from receiving it or six months from the death. Present the claim in writing to the executor or administrator, or to the attorney named as their counsel in the probate records, or to the probate court quoting the estate's case number - and put your address in it. The executor then allows or rejects it, normally within thirty days. Expect to be paid last if at all: rent is an ordinary debt, behind administration costs, funeral and burial, the family support allowance, federal preferences, last illness, nursing-home charges, taxes and Medicaid recovery. Three practical points. Do not clear the unit on your own - Ohio gives you no procedure for a dead tenant's belongings and seizing possessions for rent without a court order exposes you to damages and fees. Recover possession only through the court, against the estate or whoever is in possession. And although you may ask for an emergency contact in the lease, naming one gives that person no authority at all; deal with the personal representative or the heirs.

title: Changing A Term Mid-Tenancy Needs The Tenant's Agreement, Not A Notice
bodyText: Ohio sets no notice period for changing a lease term, a house rule or a fee. Across the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review there is no 'change in terms' notice, no rule-change notice and no longer period for a fee than for rent. What Ohio does instead is treat the change itself as a rental agreement: any agreement that modifies the terms, conditions, rules or amount of rent is a rental agreement, and it may be oral. Two consequences you have to work with. During a fixed term you cannot impose a new term by notice at all - you need the tenant's agreement, and because an oral one counts, a casual conversation can bind you. For a periodic tenancy your only lever is the termination notice: end the week-to-week tenancy on at least seven days' notice, or the month-to-month tenancy on at least thirty days' notice given before the periodic rental date, and offer a new tenancy on the terms you want. Nothing in chapter 5321 may be waived by agreement, so no clause can give you a unilateral right to rewrite a duty the statute imposes. Put every change in a signed writing before it takes effect and keep proof of delivery. One contrast worth knowing: if you operate a manufactured home park, a different chapter does require at least thirty days' written notice of any fee, charge, assessment, rent or rule change, and bars any increase during the term of a rental agreement. That rule is park-only and does not reach an ordinary rental.

title: In Ohio You May Arbitrate the Money, Not the Possession
bodyText: Ohio's Arbitration Act splits a lease in two. R.C. 2711.01(A) makes a written contract's arbitration provision valid, irrevocable and enforceable except on grounds existing at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract. But R.C. 2711.01(B)(1) provides that R.C. 2711.01 to 2711.16 do not apply to controversies involving the title to or the possession of real estate, subject to five exceptions - and the one that matters to you is (b), 'Controversies involving the amount of rentals due under any lease'. So a dispute about how much rent is owed is expressly inside the Act, while an eviction is a controversy about possession and is outside it. Possession goes where Ohio puts it: the municipal court has jurisdiction 'In any action of forcible entry and detainer' under R.C. 1901.18(A)(8), on the summary track in Chapter 1923. An arbitration clause in an Ohio residential lease therefore has to carve out any action for possession expressly. If it does not, it promises a forum the Act will not support, and the clause can end up tangling your own eviction case. CAUTIOUS COURSE, because two points are genuinely unsettled and this row does not decide them. First, (B)(1) says the sections 'do not apply', which withdraws the Act's machinery - compelling arbitration, staying an action, confirming an award - rather than plainly declaring such an agreement void; no Ohio case law was read for this pass, so do not assume either that the clause is void or that it binds. Second, FEDERAL: the Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. 1 et seq., may reach a lease affecting interstate commerce and may preempt a state carve-out. It makes enforceable an arbitration provision in 'a contract evidencing a transaction involving commerce' (9 U.S.C. 2), and whether a residential lease is one is a question only case law settles. If you use an arbitration clause, carve out possession and emergency relief, make sure it allocates no attorney's fees to either side because R.C. 5321.13(C) will not recognise that, and take advice before you rely on it. Two things Ohio does not give you, on the law searched here: there is no lease-arbitration statute authorising arbitration of tenancy disputes and preserving the right to counsel, and no statutory exclusion of tort or personal-injury claims from an arbitration clause. Mind that bound - chapter 2711 was read whole on 30 October 2026, and R.C. 2711.02 to 2711.16 are the stay, order-to-arbitrate, award and appeal machinery, with nothing specific to leases; elsewhere the absence is proved only across the corpus's 37 Revised Code chapters and every enrolled act of the 135th and 136th General Assemblies. Ohio's only statutory control on an arbitration clause is R.C. 1345.031(C)(1), elaborated by Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3-28, and it is confined to a home mortgage loan contract - it does not reach your lease, because R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a consumer transaction by reference to goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible, which a lease of real property is not. The library now offers an optional clause, `arbitration-agreement`, built on these limits: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury and emergency claims kept in court, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

title: Charging an Ohio Tenant for Being Evicted Splits in Two
bodyText: A clause that charges the tenant for being evicted, or for your having to bring the action, splits in two in Ohio. Anything that is really your attorney's fees is dead on arrival. R.C. 5321.13(C) provides that no agreement to pay the landlord's or the tenant's attorney's fees shall be recognised in a residential rental agreement or in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant, so an 'eviction fee', 'legal fee', 'court fee' or 'collection cost' that is in substance fees is unrecognised however it is labelled, and making it mutual or hedging it with 'to the extent permitted by law' does not rescue it. You do not need a clause for court costs anyway: under R.C. 1923.09(A) the court, finding the complaint true, renders judgment against the defendant for restitution of the premises 'and costs of suit', and taxes costs as it considers just on a partial finding. A flat non-fee penalty for having been evicted - an eviction charge, a liquidated sum, a clawed-back move-in concession - is a separate question, and nothing in the 37 Revised Code chapters, the Constitution and the Administrative Code chapters searched for this pass prohibits one. Ohio has no counterpart to the states that void a penalty imposed for an eviction notice or action. Your only two ceilings are R.C. 5321.14, which lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause or limit its application, and R.C. 5321.13(A), which voids anything that in effect waives Chapter 5321. So set your own figure, keep it tied to a real cost you could evidence, and never describe it as legal fees.

title: An Ohio Lease Cannot Waive an Exemption, and the Deposit Is Exempt Money
bodyText: Delete the exemption waiver from your Ohio lease. R.C. 2329.661(B) provides that no promise, agreement or contract shall be made or entered into that would waive the exemption laws of this state, and that every promise, agreement or contract, insofar as it seeks to waive them, is void. It is not confined to leases, so the familiar sentence waiving homestead and exemption rights is void wherever you put it, and a narrower waiver of just the household-goods exemption fails for the same reason. Ohio's exemption statute is R.C. 2329.66 and it never uses the word homestead: (A)(1)(b) exempts the person's interest up to $125,000 in one parcel or item of real or personal property that the person or a dependent uses as a residence, and (A)(4)(a) exempts $525 in any particular item and $10,775 in aggregate of household furnishings, goods, apparel, appliances and similar property. One limb is squarely about you: (A)(3) exempts $400 in money on deposit with a bank, savings and loan association, credit union, public utility, landlord or other person, so the deposit sitting in your hands is exempt money and a money judgment does not simply swallow it. Those are the statute's figures. R.C. 2329.66(B) has the Ohio Judicial Conference adjust every dollar amount in the section every three years on the first of April and publish the adjustment in the Register of Ohio, so check the current memorandum before you rely on a number. Two things not to confuse this with. R.C. 2329.661(A) does cut back the (A)(1) residence exemption for mortgages, vendor's and mechanic's liens, debts owed to the state and some uninsured-motorist judgments, but none of those is a lease. And Ohio's property-tax 'homestead exemption' in R.C. 4503.064 and 4503.065 is a reduction in assessed value for older and disabled owners - a different thing entirely, with nothing to do with collecting from a tenant.

title: Ohio Has No Jury-Waiver Rule, and No Jury in an Eviction Unless Someone Asks
bodyText: Start with what the default already gives you, because in an Ohio eviction a jury is not it. R.C. 1923.09(A) has a judge try the cause where the case is not continued, the place of trial is unchanged and 'neither party demands a jury on the return day of the summons', and R.C. 1923.10 brings a jury in only 'if a jury is demanded by either party'. Before a county court the demanding party must first deposit money sufficient to pay the jury fee (R.C. 1923.101). So a lease jury-waiver clause does almost nothing for you except try to stop the tenant demanding one. Ohio Const. art. I, § 5 says 'The right of trial by jury shall be inviolate', which restrains the legislature rather than the parties, and R.C. 1901.24(B) expressly contemplates that the right 'is waived under the circumstances prescribed in the Rules of Civil Procedure' - so the right is waivable in Ohio, and most evictions are municipal-court cases. The Civil Rules name the ways it is waived: no timely written demand, or a written stipulation filed with the court or an oral one made in open court once the case exists (Civ.R. 38(D), 39(A)). Neither mentions a waiver signed in advance in a lease. Nothing in the 37 Revised Code chapters, the Constitution and the Administrative Code chapters searched for this pass either voids a contractual jury waiver in a lease or makes one presumptively unconscionable; Ohio has no standard-form-contract statute of the Vermont kind and no signed-writing requirement for waiving a constitutional right.
