CAUTIOUS COURSE, because one point is unsettled: whether an Ohio court will enforce a pre-dispute jury waiver in a residential lease turns on case law, which was not read for this pass. Do not build your strategy on the clause. Rely on the R.C. 1923.09(A) default, keep any waiver conspicuous, separately initialled and mutual, and expect R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability to be the attack. Note also that this is not the same thing as R.C. 5321.13(B): a warrant of attorney to confess judgment is flatly unrecognised in Ohio, while a jury waiver is simply unregulated.

title: Ohio Sets No Parity Rule Between Lease Types - But the Eviction Grounds Split
bodyText: Nothing in the 37 Revised Code chapters, the Constitution and the Administrative Code chapters searched for this pass bars you from writing harsher terms for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term one, or the reverse, and nothing caps the rent difference between lease types. Ohio has no parity statute. Chapter 5321 itself is type-blind: R.C. 5321.01(D) defines a rental agreement as 'any agreement or lease, written or oral', so an oral Ohio tenancy sits squarely inside the chapter and carries the same landlord duties and tenant duties as a signed lease. Where the difference actually bites is the eviction chapter, and this is the asymmetry to plan around. R.C. 1923.02(A)(2) reaches tenants 'in possession under an oral tenancy, who are in default in the payment of rent as provided in division (B)' - the plain nonpayment ground is written for an ORAL tenancy, and division (B) is its mechanism: the tenant forfeits the right of occupancy and you may terminate by notifying the tenant under R.C. 1923.04 to leave. R.C. 1923.02(A)(9), by contrast, reaches only tenants 'who have breached an obligation imposed upon them by a written rental agreement' - that ground exists only if there is a written lease carrying the obligation. So with a written lease your route for nonpayment runs through (A)(9) on the lease's own rent covenant, or through (A)(1) holding over once the term has ended; with an oral tenancy it runs through (A)(2) and (B). Either way the R.C. 1923.04(A) notice comes first. Three more places the type matters, none of them a parity rule: the tenant's duty to maintain a landlord-supplied appliance under R.C. 5321.05(A)(7) exists only where a WRITTEN agreement imposes it; the three-or-fewer-units escrow exemption in R.C. 5321.07(C) needs notice in a written agreement, or written notice delivered at initial occupancy for an oral tenancy; and R.C. 5321.18 requires the owner's and agent's name and address in every written agreement, with (B) requiring a written notice of the same information at the start of an oral tenancy. Termination notice periods turn on periodicity rather than lease type - seven days for week-to-week, thirty days for month-to-month under R.C. 5321.17(A) and (B). Finally, an oral tenancy of more than a year runs into the statute of frauds in R.C. 1335.05, which bars the action on an agreement not to be performed within one year. Put the deal in writing.

title: Ohio Gives You No Liquidated-Damages Test for a Lease
bodyText: Ohio sets no liquidated-damages rule for a residential lease. Nothing in Chapter 5321, Chapter 1923, the other 35 Revised Code chapters, the Constitution or the Administrative Code chapters searched for this pass tells you when an agreed sum is a valid pre-estimate of loss and when it is an unenforceable penalty. In Ohio that test is common law, and no case law was read for this pass, so do not treat anything here as a statutory formula. What you do have is R.C. 5321.14: a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause, enforce the rest of the lease without it, or limit its application to avoid an unconscionable result, and under (B) both sides get a reasonable opportunity to put in evidence of the clause's setting, purpose and effect. Two traps. Substance beats label: a sum called liquidated damages that is really your attorney's fees is unrecognised under R.C. 5321.13(C) whatever you name it. And Ohio does have a liquidated-damages test on the books - R.C. 1345.031(C)(1), elaborated by Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3-28, which treats such a clause as unconscionable unless fixing actual damages is impracticable, the amount is a reasonable joint estimate of fair compensation, and it is not a penalty - but it reaches only a home mortgage loan contract. It does not reach your lease: R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a consumer transaction by reference to goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible, and a lease of real property is none of those. So treat that three-part test as useful drafting discipline rather than law that binds you. Set your own figure as a genuine estimate of a loss you could evidence, keep it separate from the security-deposit rules in R.C. 5321.16, and expect R.C. 5321.14 to be the only place it gets tested.

title: Ohio Grants Lease Freedom in Bulk and Hooks Almost Nothing to It
bodyText: Ohio gives you lease freedom in one sentence rather than clause by clause. R.C. 5321.06 lets a landlord and tenant include any terms and conditions, including rent, duration and any other provisions governing the parties' rights and obligations, that are not inconsistent with or prohibited by Chapter 5321 or any other rule of law. So the answer to 'may my Ohio lease say this?' is normally yes, and the authority is R.C. 5321.06 rather than a statute authorising the particular term. What Ohio almost never does is condition a right on what the lease says - the phrase 'unless otherwise agreed' that fills other states' landlord-tenant acts appears in only two sections of this library's whole 37-chapter Ohio corpus, and in neither of them is it a landlord-tenant provision. That makes the handful of real hooks worth knowing, because each is something you lose by silence. R.C. 5321.05(A)(7) gives the tenant a duty to keep a range, refrigerator, washer, dryer, dishwasher or other landlord-supplied appliance in good working order only where a WRITTEN rental agreement requires it - say nothing and the duty does not exist. R.C. 5321.07(C) takes you outside the rent-escrow regime if you are a party to agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units AND you give notice of that fact in a written rental agreement, or deliver written notice at initial occupancy for an oral tenancy. R.C. 1923.02(A)(9) lets you evict for breach of 'an obligation imposed upon them by a written rental agreement', so any house rule you want that route for has to be in a written lease. R.C. 5321.13(F) lets you assume any tenant duty under R.C. 5321.05 except the drug-activity duty in (A)(9). Ohio's cannabis home-grow right is withheld only where the rental agreement prohibits the activity, so your lease is the switch. And under R.C. 1343.03(A) interest on money that becomes due runs at the R.C. 5703.47 rate 'unless a written contract provides a different rate'. The floor and ceiling are fixed. R.C. 5321.18 requires every written agreement to carry the owner's and the owner's agent's name and address; R.C. 5321.031 adds required content for a college or university letting to its own student tenant; R.C. 5321.13 is the prohibited-terms list; and R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability is the only general limit on any figure you choose.

title: Ohio Voids the Lease for Some Prohibited Uses - But Never Let You Self-Help
bodyText: You may limit the premises to residential use. R.C. 5321.06 lets you include any term not inconsistent with or prohibited by Chapter 5321 or another rule of law, and nothing in Ohio overrides a residential-use-only clause. One trap to know before you read a statute as defeating yours: R.C. 5104.054 makes a type B family child care home 'a residential use of property for purposes of municipal, county, and township zoning'. Read the words 'for purposes of ... zoning' - the section binds zoning authorities and nobody else, so it does not override a lease term prohibiting home child care, and no provision of the kind that voids such a restriction appears anywhere in the law searched for this row - this library's 37-chapter Ohio corpus plus chapter 5104, read whole on 30 October 2026. Ohio then answers the prohibited-use question by statute, and unusually strongly. R.C. 3767.10 provides that where a tenant or occupant under a lawful title uses the place for lewdness, assignation or prostitution, that use makes void the lease at the option of the owner and, without any act of the owner, causes the right of possession to revert and vest in the owner. Separately, R.C. 3767.01(C) and 3767.02 make such a place - and a liquor-law place, and a building a criminal gang uses on more than two occasions in a year for a pattern of gang activity - a nuisance to be enjoined, and under R.C. 3767.06(A) the abatement order can close the place against its use for any purpose for a year and sell the contents used in it, with the tax under R.C. 3767.08 falling on the owner under R.C. 3767.09. So a prohibited use is your exposure, not only your tenant's. CAUTIOUS COURSE, and this is the part to get right. R.C. 3767.10 ends by saying the owner 'may without process of law make immediate entry upon the premises'. Do not do that in a residential tenancy. R.C. 5321.15(A) bars a landlord from initiating ANY act for the purpose of recovering possession other than as provided in Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321 - Chapter 3767 is not on that list - and R.C. 5321.15(C) makes you liable for all damages caused plus reasonable attorney's fees. R.C. 5321.15 is the later and residence-specific provision and cannot be waived (R.C. 5321.13(A)). Treat R.C. 3767.10 as a ground to terminate and then file under Chapter 1923, never as a licence to change the locks. Drug activity runs on its own mandatory track - see your drug-termination row.

title: You Cannot Get an Ohio Tenant to Accept Drifting Smoke
bodyText: Ohio will not let you take a tenant's agreement to put up with smoke drifting in from another unit. R.C. 5321.13(D) refuses to recognise any tenant agreement to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law, or to indemnify you for it, and Ohio has no common-areas exception - so a sentence saying the tenant accepts that smoke may enter from elsewhere and releases you is inoperative, whether it sits in the lease or in a separate smoking addendum. What you may do is the opposite: ban smoking outright under R.C. 5321.06, which is what your smoking clause does. Your own exposure runs through R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) codes, (A)(2) fit and habitable condition, (A)(3) safe and sanitary common areas and (A)(4) working ventilation equipment, so deal with the drift rather than disclaim it. Two limits on what this row proves. Nothing in the 37 Revised Code chapters, the Constitution and the Administrative Code chapters searched for this pass creates a secondhand-smoke or smoke-drift right, duty or disclosure. And Ohio's smoke-free regime, R.C. Chapter 3794 (the Smoke Free Workplace Act), could NOT be read: it is not in the corpus and could not be fetched. R.C. 3794.01's definitions of 'public place' and 'place of employment' and R.C. 3794.03's exemptions are what would decide whether an enclosed apartment hallway where your staff work is covered, so confirm that chapter before you tell anyone a hallway may be smoked in. For cannabis smoke, your lease is the switch - see your cannabis rows.

title: Your Ohio Tenant's Nine Statutory Duties, and the Fee Award That Comes With Them
bodyText: R.C. 5321.05 imposes nine duties on an Ohio tenant whether or not your lease repeats them. The tenant must keep the part of the premises they occupy and use safe and sanitary; dispose of rubbish, garbage and other waste in a clean, safe and sanitary manner; keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits; use and operate all electrical and plumbing fixtures properly; comply with the requirements all applicable state and local housing, health and safety codes impose on tenants; personally refrain, and forbid anyone on the premises with their permission, from intentionally or negligently destroying, defacing, damaging or removing any fixture, appliance or other part of the premises; maintain in good working order any range, refrigerator, washer, dryer, dishwasher or other appliance you supply that a WRITTEN rental agreement requires the tenant to maintain; conduct themselves and require their guests to conduct themselves so as not to disturb neighbours' peaceful enjoyment; and keep themselves, their household and their guests from violating Chapters 2925 and 3719 or substantially similar municipal ordinances on controlled substances. Division (B) adds that the tenant must not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, make ordinary, necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, deliver oversized parcels, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the unit to purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen or contractors. Three practical points. First, R.C. 5321.05(C)(1) gives you, on any violation except the drug-activity duty, actual damages resulting from the violation TOGETHER WITH REASONABLE ATTORNEY'S FEES, as well as termination, a possession action, or injunctive relief to compel access. That fee award is statutory, which is exactly why it works where an agreed fee clause does not - R.C. 5321.13(C) refuses to recognise any agreement to pay the landlord's or tenant's fees, so rely on the statute and keep the fee out of your lease. Second, the (A)(7) appliance duty is the one duty that exists only if a written agreement says so, so write it down. Third, these are duties you may take ON but never hand over: R.C. 5321.13(F) lets you assume any of the tenant's R.C. 5321.05 duties except the (A)(9) drug duty, and there is no route in the other direction. Before evicting for a breach that materially affects health and safety, R.C. 1923.02(A)(8) sends you through R.C. 5321.11 - a written notice specifying the act or omission and a termination date at least thirty days after receipt, with a chance to remedy.

title: R.C. 5321.14 Is the Only General Ceiling on an Ohio Lease Term
bodyText: Ohio's unconscionability rule is R.C. 5321.14, and because Ohio sets almost no figures it is the only general ceiling this row found anywhere in the 37 Revised Code chapters searched, the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - the whole Revised Code was not searched. If the court, as a matter of law, finds the rental agreement or any clause of it to have been unconscionable at the time it was made, it may refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the remainder without the unconscionable clause, or so limit the clause's application as to avoid an unconscionable result. Three features of that sentence decide how you draft. The test runs at the time the agreement was made, so a term that merely turns out badly later is not caught, and a term that was lopsided on day one is not rescued by your restraint in using it. The finding is made by the court as a matter of law. And division (B) requires that both parties be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present evidence of the clause's setting, purpose and effect - which is exactly why a figure you can explain and document survives and a round number you cannot does not. Ohio's legislature has deemed one clause unconscionable per se: R.C. 5321.131(D) makes any provision of a rental agreement that violates the flag-display rules 'an unconscionable term under section 5321.14'. Expect no help from Ohio's consumer statute. R.C. 1345.03 reaches only a consumer transaction, which R.C. 1345.01(A) defines by reference to goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible, and a lease of real property is none of those; R.C. 1345.031 and Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3-28 are confined to home mortgage loan contracts. R.C. 4781.48 is R.C. 5321.14's counterpart, substantively identical and differing only in one phrase - it reads 'any clause of it' where R.C. 5321.14 reads 'any clause thereof' - for manufactured-home parks, whose lots are outside Chapter 5321 under R.C. 4781.01(W) with R.C. 5321.01(C) - a park's 'residential premises' is the LOT and the park's grounds, not a dwelling unit - cite 5321.14 for an ordinary rental, never 4781.48. What counts as unconscionable beyond the statute's own words is common law, and no case law was read for this pass.

title: Ohio Does Not Forbid Double Letting - Its Definitions Make It Impossible Instead
bodyText: No Ohio provision forbids letting the same room or unit to two tenants for the same period, and none gives a rent abatement or any other fixed remedy when it happens. Searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, the Ohio Constitution and the held administrative rules; that is the bound. Ohio answers the question through its definitions instead, and the answer is stronger than a prohibition. R.C. 5321.01(A) makes a tenant the person entitled under the rental agreement 'to the use and occupancy of residential premises to the exclusion of others' - so you cannot give two tenants that entitlement in the same space, and promising it twice breaches what each of them is statutorily entitled to. R.C. 5321.01(F) then defines a dwelling unit as a structure or part of a structure used as a home, residence or sleeping place 'by one person who maintains a household or by two or more persons who maintain a common household' - one household per unit. Letting separate parts of one unit to separate households does not fit that definition, and whether each letting is then its own residential premises inside Chapter 5321 is not settled by the text; no case law is in this library's Ohio corpus. Your exposure is ordinary and open-ended rather than capped: R.C. 5321.12 lets any party in a Chapter 5321 action recover damages for breach of contract or breach of any duty imposed by law, and the tenant you cannot put in possession also has whatever the lease gives them, so use the library's 'Possession Delay' clause and keep one booking record per unit. Do not reach for Ohio's hotel chapter for a standard. It does set one occupant per room for single room occupancy and a bed for each guest, but R.C. 3731.01(B) says the chapter 'does not apply to apartment buildings and other structures in which all of the units are residential premises', and the definition of hotel excludes apartment houses, lodging houses and rooming houses - so none of it reaches your rental. Two things do change the picture. Letting rooms on a short or transient footing can take the letting out of Chapter 5321 altogether under R.C. 5321.01(C)(3), and into the hotel or recreation-camp regimes with their own licensing; and a city housing code may set a maximum occupancy per room, which this library flags and does not resolve.

title: You May Prohibit Home Child Care in Ohio - Read Past the Words 'Residential Use'
bodyText: No provision in the law searched for this row makes you allow a tenant to run a family child care home, and none voids a lease term prohibiting one: nothing of the kind appears across this library's 37-chapter Ohio corpus or in R.C. 5104.054, the one section of chapter 5104 fetched and read whole on 30 October 2026. Chapter 5104 is otherwise unread, so that is where to look before you treat the point as settled. Ohio has no counterpart, within that bound, to the statutes in other states that override a lease restriction on family day care. Under R.C. 5321.06 you may prohibit it, allow it, or allow it on conditions. Read the section a tenant will quote you carefully, because it is easy to get backwards. R.C. 5104.054 says a type B family child care home, licensed or not, 'shall be considered to be a residential use of property for purposes of municipal, county, and township zoning' and shall be a permitted use in every district where residential uses are permitted, and bars a conditional use permit or special exception. Those words 'for purposes of ... zoning' are the whole of it: the section binds zoning authorities and nobody else. It says nothing about a landlord, a lease, a rental agreement or a residential-use covenant, so it does not defeat your residential-use-only clause. If you do allow it, know what it does to your building. Ohio's child-care rules reach the premises themselves, and which rules apply turns on whether the home is type A or type B. For a licensed type B home, R.C. 5104.052 carries fire prevention and fire safety rules - but be careful about who inspects against them, because R.C. 3737.22 imposes less than it looks. Division (F) only has the fire marshal 'cooperate with' the director of children and youth on those rules, 'recommend procedures for inspecting' type B homes, and provide training. The one inspection DUTY in the section is in division (G), and it reaches only a type B home that is NOT licensed, on the provider's own request, as a precondition of approval under R.C. 3313.813 for federal child and adult care food program funds; in a municipal corporation or township with a certified fire safety inspector, that inspector makes it under the fire marshal's supervision. Whether the R.C. 5104.052 rules themselves provide for inspecting a licensed type B home is a question this row cannot answer, because those rules were not read. For a type A home, R.C. 3737.83(E) puts minimum fire-safety standards into the state fire code and R.C. 3781.10(J) brings the board of building standards in on safety and sanitation, while R.C. 3781.06(B)(2) takes an existing one-, two- or three-family detached house out of R.C. 3781.06 to 3781.18 once a type A application is filed. And if you supply the furniture, a type A home is a 'public occupancy' under R.C. 3737.841(A)(4), so its seating furniture must meet the flammability standard and carry the label R.C. 3737.842 requires, and using non-conforming seating furniture there is prohibited. The content of the R.C. 5104.052 and 5104.05 rules, and the child counts that divide type A from type B in R.C. 5104.01, are not in this library's Ohio corpus and could not be read - so if you consent, make consent conditional on the tenant obtaining and keeping the licence, passing the fire inspection, and carrying liability insurance that names you, and ask the Department of Children and Youth what the premises must have before you sign anything.

title: Ohio Has No Furnished-Rental Rules - Three Other Provisions Catch You Instead
bodyText: Ohio has no furnished-rental regime. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, the Ohio Constitution and the held administrative rules, nothing requires an inventory, allows a separate furniture deposit, sets a different refund deadline for a furnished letting, or tells you what furniture to supply. Nor does any Ohio statute make the tenant look after your furniture: R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) reaches electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air conditioning fixtures and appliances, and R.C. 5321.05(A)(7)'s written-lease route reaches appliances - a sofa is neither. So list every item and its condition in the lease, or attach a signed inventory with photographs, because nothing else will record it. Three Ohio provisions then decide how a furnished letting actually works. First, there is no such thing as a separate furniture deposit here: R.C. 5321.01(E) makes a security deposit 'any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant', so extra money you take for the furniture is part of the security deposit, it counts toward the total that R.C. 5321.16(A) measures - that section makes a deposit bear five per cent a year, computed and paid annually, on the amount by which it EXCEEDS fifty dollars or one month's periodic rent, WHICHEVER IS GREATER, once the tenant has been in possession six months or more, so on any ordinary rent the threshold is a month's rent and not fifty dollars, and it must be itemised in your written notice within thirty days of termination and delivery of possession under R.C. 5321.16(B). The words 'or property' also mean that holding something of the tenant's as security is a deposit. None of this can be waived (R.C. 5321.13(A)). Second, keep your furniture and the tenant's belongings clearly apart, in the inventory and in your head: R.C. 5321.15(B) forbids you to seize a tenant's furnishings or possessions to recover rent except under a court order, and (C) makes you liable for all damages caused plus reasonable attorney's fees - so a furnished-letting clause must never give you a lien or a right to hold what is theirs. Third, a flammability rule you would never look for. R.C. 3737.841(A) lists places that are a 'public occupancy', among them any type A family child care home and the public assembly areas of a hotel or motel with more than ten articles of seating furniture, and R.C. 3737.842 requires seating furniture made for use in a public occupancy to meet the California Technical Bulletin 133 standard and carry a prescribed label, and prohibits using non-conforming seating furniture there. An ordinary furnished apartment is not on that list. But if you let a tenant run a type A family child care home in your furnished unit, your sofas and chairs come inside the rule. R.C. 3737.841(A)(4) reaches 'any child care center and any type A family child care home as defined in section 5104.01 of the Revised Code' with no licensing qualifier of its own - and R.C. 5104.01, which supplies the definition, was not read for this row, so do not assume an unlicensed one falls outside it.

title: Ohio Gives Guests No Rights - It Makes Your Tenant Answer For Them
bodyText: No Ohio statute gives a tenant, a tenant's guest, or a tenant's supplier, caregiver or delivery or repair worker a right of access to a rental building, bars a charge for guests, or makes guest access unwaivable - and nothing turns on the number of households in the building. Searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, the Ohio Constitution and the held administrative rules; that is the bound on this statement. A guest's right to be there comes from your tenant, not from the code: R.C. 5321.01(A) defines a tenant as the person entitled under the rental agreement to use and occupy the premises 'to the exclusion of others', so a visitor is present on the tenant's permission. Every Ohio provision that mentions a person on the premises with the tenant's consent runs the other way, making the tenant answerable - the tenant must forbid them from damaging the premises (R.C. 5321.05(A)(6)), must require them not to disturb the neighbours' peaceful enjoyment (R.C. 5321.05(A)(8)), and must keep them from violating the controlled-substance chapters (R.C. 5321.05(A)(9)). The last of those turns a guest's conduct into a duty on you: R.C. 5321.04(A)(9) makes you commence an eviction. One Ohio provision does limit who may be there, and it is about occupancy rather than a visit: R.C. 5321.051(A) forbids a tenant to allow a registered sex or child-victim offender to occupy premises within one thousand feet of school, preschool or child care center, children's crisis care facility or residential infant care center premises, and lets you terminate the tenancy of the tenant and all other occupants. So guest limits and any guest charge are lease terms, allowed under R.C. 5321.06 with unconscionability (R.C. 5321.14) the only ceiling. Two live limits: a tenant with a disability may need a caregiver's or live-in aide's access as a reasonable accommodation, and a guest rule enforced unevenly against families with children is a familial-status problem.

title: Ohio Has No Home-Occupation Statute - Zoning Permission Is Not Lease Permission
bodyText: Ohio has nothing like West Virginia's home-occupation statute. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, the Ohio Constitution and the held administrative rules, no provision makes a home-based business a permitted use of a rented dwelling, bars a lease from restricting one, or sets conditions you must accept if a tenant asks. So your restriction holds under R.C. 5321.06, and the library's 'Residential Use Only' clause carries Ohio. The trap is the argument a tenant will actually make. Ohio puts home occupations in local zoning, and zoning permission is not lease permission: nothing in Ohio makes a zoning classification override a term of a rental agreement, and the one Ohio provision that does declare a home use to be residential, R.C. 5104.054 for family child care, binds municipal, county and township zoning authorities and nobody else. A tenant who shows you the zoning code has shown you only that the city will not stop them. What should move you is the other direction - a business use can shift your own duty. R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes you comply with all applicable building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety, and R.C. 3781.06(A)(1) pitches that standard at a building's 'intended use and occupancy', naming trade, manufacture, repair, storage and occupancy by the public alongside dwelling. A tenant who brings customers, stock, equipment or employees into your building can therefore change what the code asks of you, and the rules that would say how - the Ohio Building and Residential Codes, Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 and 4101:8 - are not in this library's Ohio corpus and were not read, so neither the trigger nor the cost of a change of use can be stated here. One further question to put to a lawyer before you agree to a substantial business use: Chapter 5321 reaches 'a dwelling unit for residential use and occupancy' (R.C. 5321.01(C)), and whether a unit let for a mixed or mainly commercial use stays inside the chapter is not settled by the text. If it falls outside, you lose the chapter's machinery too. If you do allow a home business, say which kinds, require the tenant to hold any licence, permit and zoning approval, require liability insurance naming you, and keep customers, signage, deliveries and employees out of common areas.

title: The Only Building Facilities Ohio Names - And Why Its Consumer Chapter Will Not Reach You
bodyText: Ohio's list of facilities you must supply is R.C. 5321.04(A) and it is short. Three limbs name something physical. (A)(3) makes you keep all common areas of the premises in a safe and sanitary condition. (A)(4) makes you maintain in good and safe working order every electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air conditioning fixture and appliance, and every elevator, that you supply or are required to supply - an elevator is the one building facility Ohio names outright. (A)(5) makes you provide and maintain appropriate receptacles for ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste and arrange for their removal, but only where you are a party to rental agreements covering four or more dwelling units in the same structure; below that threshold Ohio requires nothing. (A)(6) adds running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat, subject to its own two escapes. That is all. No Ohio statute requires you to supply a mailbox, window screens, a laundry, a garage, a garage door opener, a playground or a pool, and the words garage door, mailbox and screens do not appear in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, the Ohio Constitution or the held administrative rules. Two things follow. First, everything else you provide is defined by your lease, so list every facility, appliance and shared amenity in it, and remember that anything you do supply inside the (A)(4) categories brings a repair duty you cannot waive (R.C. 5321.13(A)). Second, and this is the question to put to rest: Ohio's consumer chapter will not make you responsible for a building facility the way Minnesota's product-safety chapter can. R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a consumer transaction as the sale, lease, assignment, award by chance or other transfer of an item of goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible, and a lease of real property is none of those, so the Consumer Sales Practices Act does not reach your tenancy and no Ohio product-safety provision in the held chapters puts a facility duty on a landlord. What does reach you is the code route. R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes you comply with all applicable building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety, and R.C. 3781.06(A)(1) requires a building to be safe and sanitary for its intended use and occupancy. The codes that would actually name a facility - the Ohio Building and Residential Codes, Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 and 4101:8 - are not in this library's Ohio corpus and were not read, and a city housing code, which Ohio's preemption statute leaves standing, may well require a mailbox or screens. If you have an elevator, ask who inspects and certifies it: R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) makes you maintain it, but no inspection regime appears in the held chapters.

title: Ohio Sets No Pest-Control Notice Period - Your Entry Notice Is the Only One
bodyText: Ohio imposes no pest-control notice duty on a landlord. There is no period you must give before a treatment, no pesticide notice to post or hand out, no lease disclosure, and no integrated-pest-management requirement. The words pest, pesticide, applicator and rodent do not appear anywhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, the Ohio Constitution or the held administrative rules; that is the bound on this statement, and one piece sits outside it - whether the licensed applicator you hire owes your tenants notice is governed by Ohio's pesticide licensing statutes and the Department of Agriculture's rules, which are not in this library's corpus and were not read. Ask the applicator what notice they must give, and build your scheduling around their answer. What does govern you is the entry rule, and it is the only notice period in play. R.C. 5321.04(A)(8) requires you, except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, to give the tenant reasonable notice of your intent to enter and to enter only at reasonable times, and it says twenty-four hours 'is presumed to be a reasonable notice in the absence of evidence to the contrary'. That twenty-four hours is the statute's presumption about entry, not a pest-control notice period - do not quote it to a tenant as one. R.C. 5321.04(A)(7) also forbids you to abuse the right of access, and R.C. 5321.04(B) lets a tenant recover actual damages, obtain an injunction and recover reasonable attorney's fees, or terminate the tenancy, for an entry in breach of (A)(8), a lawful entry made unreasonably, or repeated harassing demands for entry. On the other side, R.C. 5321.05(B) says the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to make ordinary, necessary or agreed repairs or to supply necessary or agreed services, which is how the exterminator gets in. The infestation itself is substantially your problem: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) and (A)(2) make you follow applicable codes and keep the premises fit and habitable, while R.C. 5321.05(A)(1) and (A)(2) give the tenant the sanitation duties. And an infestation is one of the conditions that can put a building into receivership as a public nuisance - see the nuisance row. Practical course: give the twenty-four hours' written entry notice as a matter of routine, tell the tenant what is being applied and how to prepare, get the preparation instructions from the applicator in writing, and keep the treatment records.

title: No Ohio Right to a Window Unit - But Supplying One Buys You a Duty You Cannot Waive
bodyText: Ohio gives a tenant no right to install a portable, window or through-wall cooling device, sets no notice procedure for asking, and does not require a lease that restricts window units to say so. It also imposes no duty on you to provide cooling at all: R.C. 5321.04(A)(6) obliges you to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat, and says nothing about cooling. Searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, the Ohio Constitution and the held administrative rules; that is the bound. So whether cooling devices are allowed is a lease and house-rules question, and the library's 'No Alterations' and 'Use of Property & Common Areas' clauses already carry Ohio and cover fastening a unit to a window, wall or fixture. Here is the part landlords get backwards, and it is the reason this row exists. Although you need not supply cooling, R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) makes you 'maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, and air conditioning fixtures and appliances' that you supply or are required to supply - and R.C. 5321.13(A) lets no oral or written agreement modify or waive it. An old window unit you leave in a unit as a courtesy is air conditioning you supplied, so you have bought a non-waivable repair duty, and a lease term saying the tenant looks after it does not remove it. Either take the unit out before the tenancy or accept that you now maintain it. A unit the tenant brings and installs is not supplied by you, so R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) does not reach it - but your duties under (A)(1) to follow applicable building, housing, health and safety codes and under (A)(2) to keep the premises fit and habitable still reach your building, so set written conditions on how a unit is mounted, sealed, drained and supported, and on keeping it clear of a window needed for escape. Whether the Ohio Fire Code or the building codes say anything about a window unit obstructing an emergency escape opening was not determined for this row: the Fire Code rules in this library print only Ohio's changes to the International Fire Code, whose base text is not on any state site, and the Ohio Building and Residential Codes are not held. Two last points: a tenant with a disability may need a cooling device as a reasonable accommodation, so handle that request under the fair housing rules and not under your window-unit policy; and if the electricity is in your name, the running cost is yours unless the lease says otherwise.

title: No Ohio Solar Rights - Your Lease Decides
bodyText:
Ohio has no solar-rights statute, so your lease decides. You may prohibit a tenant from installing a solar device, and nothing in Ohio law overrides that - R.C. 5321.06 lets a lease carry any term not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or another rule of law, and R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability is the only ceiling. The one Ohio provision in this area is easy to mistake for more than it is. R.C. 5301.63 says that 'For the purpose of ensuring adequate access of solar energy collection devices to sunlight, any person may grant a solar access easement', in writing and subject to the same conveyance and recording requirements as other easements, and it sets out what the instrument must contain. That is an enabling provision for a voluntary easement between landowners about sunlight reaching a panel. It is not a tenant right, it voids nothing, and a tenant cannot grant one over your land. Unlike California and Arizona, Ohio has no provision that strikes down a lease term, a deed restriction or an association rule forbidding a solar installation.

If you do permit one, the things worth putting in writing are yours to choose, not Ohio's: who owns the equipment, who insures it, whether it may be roof-mounted or must be free-standing, who repairs the roof penetration, and what happens at the end of the tenancy. Ohio sets no standard for any of that.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, and 'solar' 0, 'photovoltaic' 0, 'net metering' 0, 'solar easement' 0, 'generation equipment' 0 and 'renewable' 4 - every one of those four checked and none a tenant right or a lease override - against 'landlord' 34 and 'easement' 6 - plus R.C. 5301.63 read in full outside it. R.C. Chapter 4928, which governs net metering and interconnection with the utility, was not read; it is a utility-customer question rather than a lease question, but it is the limb that would answer whether a tenant could sell power back. No Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: Ohio Never Makes You Supply a Stove or Fridge - But It Does Say How to Get Rid of One
bodyText: No Ohio provision requires a residential landlord to supply a stove, range, oven or refrigerator. R.C. 5321.04(A)(6) obliges you to supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat, and nothing more on this subject - cooking and refrigeration are absent from the landlord-duty list. Searched the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, the Ohio Constitution and the held administrative rules; that is the bound, and it leaves two gaps you should know about rather than assume away. Whether a dwelling with no cooking facility is 'fit and habitable' under R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) is not settled by the statute's words, and no Ohio case law is in this library's corpus; and any rule that did require cooking or refrigeration would sit in the Ohio Building and Residential Codes, Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 and 4101:8, which are not held and were not read, or in a city housing code, which R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves standing. So what you supply is a lease term - list it in the 'Appliances & Equipment Included' clause and keep the list accurate, because Ohio has no presumption that an appliance found at the property is yours. A curiosity worth noticing: the only place the Revised Code names a refrigerator in a tenancy at all is R.C. 5321.05(A)(7), where it is misspelled 'regrigerator', and that provision is about the tenant maintaining an appliance you supplied under a written lease, not about whether you must supply one. Who maintains a range or a dishwasher you do supply is a genuinely unresolved question in Ohio - see the appliance-maintenance row - because the same items appear in both the landlord's non-waivable duty and the tenant's written-lease duty. The one hard Ohio rule in this family is about disposal. R.C. 3767.29 forbids any person to abandon or discard, or knowingly permit to remain on premises under their control in a place accessible to children, a discarded icebox, refrigerator or other airtight or semi-airtight container of one and one-half cubic feet or more with an opening of fifty square inches or more whose door or lid has a hinge, latch or other fastening device, unless the hinges, latches or other hardware that could confine a person have been removed. Those figures are the statute's. When you replace a fridge, strip the latch and hinges before it sits in the yard, the basement or the alley.

title: Ohio Has No Squatter Shortcut - But It Does Have a Second Court Route
bodyText: Ohio gives you nothing fast and nothing out of court. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library there is no squatter-removal statute, no sheriff or police affidavit procedure, no ex parte removal order with a twenty-four-hour hearing, no squatting offence and no multiple-damages penalty for misusing such a procedure. R.C. 5321.15(A) bars you from initiating any act - terminating utilities or services, excluding the occupant, or threatening any unlawful act - to recover possession 'other than as provided in Chapters 1923., 5303., and 5321.', and (C) makes you liable for all damages caused plus reasonable attorney's fees. What Ohio gives instead is two court routes, and the second is the one landlords miss. The summary action in Chapter 1923 does reach a person who never was your tenant: R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) covers a defendant who is 'an occupier of lands or tenements, without color of title' where you have the right of possession, and (A)(6) covers any other unlawful and forcible detention. You still serve the R.C. 1923.04(A) notice to leave three or more days before filing, by certified mail return receipt requested, by handing it to the person, or by leaving it at the premises or their usual place of abode, and if you are a landlord recovering residential premises it must carry the conspicuous statutory wording. For an occupant who does claim under colour of title - a failed purchaser, a disputed heir, someone holding under a tenancy you say never existed - Chapter 1923 may give you no ground at all, and the route is ejectment: R.C. 5303.03 requires you only to state that you have a legal estate and are entitled to possession, to describe the property, and to say the defendant unlawfully keeps you out, and 'It is not necessary to state how the plaintiff's estate or ownership is derived.' Two bounds you must respect. First, R.C. 5303.07 lets the parties avail themselves of R.C. 5303.08 to 5303.17, an occupying-claimant regime that can require a successful plaintiff to pay an occupant for improvements made in good faith under colour of title before taking possession, with R.C. 5303.15 the writ and R.C. 5303.16 an election to take the value of the land instead. Those sections are not in this library's Ohio corpus and have not been read, so the regime is an unpriced risk: get advice before suing an occupant who has spent money on your property. Second, where to file is not obvious - R.C. 1901.181(A)(1) gives a municipal court's housing or environmental division exclusive jurisdiction within its territory over any civil action under Chapter 1923 or 5321 or sections 5303.03 to 5303.07, except the Franklin county environmental division. Check whether your municipal court has such a division before you file anywhere else.

title: Ohio Says Nothing About Waterbeds - But Its Deposit Definition Still Catches You
bodyText: Ohio has no waterbed law of any kind. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, the Ohio Constitution and the held administrative rules, nothing gives a tenant a right to keep a waterbed or other water-filled furniture, nothing entitles you to demand insurance or an added deposit as the price of allowing one, and nothing sets an installation, liner or floor-loading standard. Do not assume Ohio has the waterbed regime other states wrote in the 1980s - it does not, in either direction. So this is a lease matter, and the library's 'Use of Property & Common Areas' clause already carries Ohio and bars a waterbed or other water-filled furniture without your prior written consent. Three Ohio rules bite on how you handle a consent. First, if you take extra money or property for the waterbed, it is a security deposit whatever you call it: R.C. 5321.01(E) defines a security deposit as any deposit of money or property to secure the tenant's performance. So it counts toward the total that R.C. 5321.16(A) measures: five per cent a year, computed and paid annually, on the amount by which the deposit EXCEEDS fifty dollars or one month's periodic rent, WHICHEVER IS GREATER, once the tenant has been in possession six months or more - so on any ordinary rent the threshold is a month's rent, not fifty dollars, and it has to be itemised in your written notice within thirty days of termination and delivery of possession under R.C. 5321.16(B). None of that can be contracted away - R.C. 5321.13(A). Second, require insurance, never an indemnity: R.C. 5321.13(D) refuses to recognise any tenant agreement to exculpate or limit your liability arising under law, or to indemnify you for it, so ask for a policy with you named rather than a promise to hold you harmless. Third, the structural question is a code question you cannot answer from the statutes - the floor-loading rules are in the Ohio Building and Residential Codes, Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 and 4101:8, which are not in this library's Ohio corpus and were not read, and R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes those codes your duty, not the tenant's. If you consent, put the conditions in writing: a liner, a professional installation, proof of insurance, and the tenant's responsibility for damage, which the deposit may cover as noncompliance with the lease under R.C. 5321.16(B).

title: A Disaster Does Not Suspend Your Occupancy Limits in Ohio
bodyText: Nothing in Ohio law lets a tenant house people displaced by a fire, flood, storm or declared disaster in defiance of the lease's guest and occupancy terms, stops you enforcing those terms after a disaster, or lets any public body place evacuees in your rental. 'Evacuee', 'evacuation', 'displaced' and 'moratorium' appear nowhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters or the Constitution searched for this entry, and the handful of disaster and state-of-emergency hits are about consumer-sales presumptions, credit freezes, temporarily relocating a court, licence plates, nursing homes and the militia. So your guest limit, your permitted-occupants clause and your subletting restriction all continue to run, and Ohio adds something helpful: discrimination law expressly preserves 'reasonable occupancy standards based on the number and size of sleeping areas or bedrooms and the overall size of a dwelling unit', and preserves reasonable local, state and federal maximum-occupant restrictions, provided your standards are not used to get round fair housing (R.C. 4112.024(C)). That is the firmest ground to stand your limit on, and it is better ground than the lease alone. Three practical points. First, agree any temporary extra occupancy in writing, with an end date, and say whether rent changes - R.C. 5321.06 lets you put almost any term in a rental agreement, and a written variation is far safer than silence that later looks like consent. Second, remember the limits still bite on you: whoever is in the unit with the tenant's consent is the tenant's responsibility under the statutory tenant duties, so extra occupants do not shift your obligations, and a crowded unit can put you on the wrong side of a local housing code, which Ohio expressly preserves from preemption (R.C. 5321.19(B)(1)). Third, a genuine Ohio trap if you are tempted to open a vacant building to evacuees: an emergency shelter operated by a 501(c)(3) organisation for people whose circumstances indicate a transient occupancy is excluded from the definition of residential premises altogether (R.C. 5321.01(C)(10)), so the landlord-tenant chapter and its protections and procedures would not govern that use - a different legal position from the one you are in, and not one to drift into by accident. What happens to the tenancy and the rent after a disaster is a separate question; see the Ohio rows on casualty termination and on environmental events. One limb was not resolved: if Ohio gave any authority the power to requisition or place people in private housing during a declared emergency, it would sit in the emergency-management chapter, R.C. Chapter 5502, which this review does not hold and could not fetch.

title: After a Disaster Ohio Keeps the Rent Running and Keeps Your Duties Running Too
bodyText: Ohio has no disaster statute for tenancies, and the gap cuts both ways. There is no rent abatement rule: 'rent abatement', 'abatement of rent', 'uninhabitable', 'force majeure' and 'moratorium' appear nowhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters or the Constitution searched for this entry, and the disaster and state-of-emergency hits are consumer presumptions, credit freezes, court relocations, licence plates, nursing homes and the militia. So rent keeps falling due while a storm-damaged home is unusable unless your lease says otherwise, and the only statutory reduction is one a court orders: after written notice specifying the problem, and after you fail to remedy it within a reasonable time considering the severity of the condition and the time needed, or within thirty days, whichever is SOONER, a tenant who is current in rent may deposit rent with the clerk, ask the court to order the repair, ask for an order reducing the periodic rent until you remedy it, or terminate (R.C. 5321.07(A), (B)). Read 'whichever is sooner': in a region-wide disaster the reasonable-time limb protects you, but it is capped at thirty days. Now the part almost nobody checks. That remedy does not exist for every tenancy. It does not apply to a landlord party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units who gave notice of that fact in a written rental agreement, or written notice of it at the start of an oral tenancy (R.C. 5321.07(C)); and it does not apply to a unit occupied by a student tenant (R.C. 5321.07(D)). For those tenancies there is no escrow and no statutory rent reduction after a disaster at all - the tenant is left to ordinary damages for breach (R.C. 5321.12). That is a strong reason to give the three-or-fewer-units notice, and a reason not to assume a tenant has a remedy they may not have. Your own duties do not abate. You must still keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas safe and sanitary, maintain the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning fixtures in good and safe working order, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat at all times, with only two narrow exceptions - where the building is not required by law to be equipped for it, or where heat or hot water comes from an installation within the tenant's exclusive control on a direct public utility connection (R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) to (A)(6)). A storm outage fits neither. And you cannot draft around it: a rental agreement may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with R.C. 5321.04 (R.C. 5321.13(E)), so a force-majeure clause suspending your duties while you keep collecting rent is not recognised. What you may do is agree a rent credit, an abatement or a temporary relocation in writing under R.C. 5321.06, because a concession is not a waiver of a duty. Whether the tenancy ends at all is the casualty question, covered in Ohio's casualty and environmental-event rows. One limb was not resolved: an eviction moratorium or rent freeze during a declared emergency, if Ohio had one, would sit in R.C. Chapter 5502, which this review does not hold.

title: Ohio Puts No Number on a Bad Entry - But It Does Put Your Lease and Your Fees at Risk
bodyText: Ohio attaches no fixed penalty to an entry-notice breach. There is no multiple of rent, no per-day figure, no civil penalty and no statutory-damages number anywhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters or the Constitution searched for this entry. What there is instead is an open-ended remedy that can cost more than a fixed figure would. If you enter without the reasonable notice R.C. 5321.04(A)(8) requires, or make a lawful entry in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that are otherwise lawful but have the effect of harassing the tenant, the tenant may recover actual damages from the entry or the demands, obtain an injunction against the conduct recurring, and obtain a judgment for reasonable attorney's fees - or may simply terminate the lease (R.C. 5321.04(B)). Read those together: the exposure is the tenant's proven loss plus your opponent's legal bill, with no ceiling, and the tenancy itself is at risk. The fee award is statutory, so the Ohio rule voiding attorney-fee agreements does not shield you from it. You also have a separate standing duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(7) not to abuse the right of access, which is what turns a pattern of lawful-looking visits into a violation. The mirror image protects you. A tenant who unreasonably withholds consent to an entry R.C. 5321.05(B) covers exposes themselves to your actual damages plus reasonable attorney's fees, and you may ask the court for an injunction compelling access, terminate, or sue for possession (R.C. 5321.05(C)(1)). The practical course, since no number is prescribed either way: paper every entry - what notice you gave, when, how, and why you entered - because both sides' remedies turn on reasonableness, and reasonableness is proved from records.

title: Ohio Does Make You Help the Police - In Three Places You Would Not Look
bodyText: Ohio has no general landlord-police cooperation statute, no tenant-information reporting duty and no crime-free-addendum regime. But three real duties do reach you, and none of them is in the landlord-tenant chapter. First, a mandatory one. Where a court order authorising a pen register or a trap and trace device directs a landlord to furnish information, facilities and technical assistance, R.C. 2933.77(A) says you SHALL furnish the officer with all of it, done unobtrusively and with a minimum of interference with the service you provide. The investigating agency must pay you reasonable compensation for your reasonable expenses, and you are immune from civil and criminal liability for complying. Second, a permissive one with a gag attached: on an interception warrant, or a judge's or prosecutor's written representation that an oral interception order was granted, you are authorised - not required - to provide assistance, you are immune if you do, and you must not disclose the existence of the interception or the device used, on pain of civil damages (R.C. 2933.581). Third, and this one applies to you as a person rather than as a landlord: knowing that a felony has been or is being committed, you may not knowingly fail to report it to law enforcement authorities, a fourth-degree misdemeanour; and whoever discovers a body must report the death immediately, and must give an investigating officer any facts within their knowledge bearing on the death (R.C. 2921.22(A)(1), (C), (D)). None of the privilege exemptions in that section covers a landlord. Ohio's child-abuse and elder-abuse reporting duties bind listed professions only, so as a landlord you may report but need not (R.C. 2151.421(A)(1)(b), (B); 5101.63(A)(2), (B)); but a licensed real estate broker or salesperson, such as a manager you hire, is on the elder-abuse list and must report immediately to the county department of job and family services, a fourth-degree misdemeanour if knowingly not done (R.C. 5101.63(A)(1), (A)(2)(aa); 5101.99(B)). Two limits to hold in mind. Ohio imposes no duty to let police into an occupied unit and gives you no power to consent on the tenant's behalf: the entry purposes in R.C. 5321.05(B) do not include a police search, the tenant's home is secure against unreasonable searches under Ohio Const. art. I, Section 14, and R.C. 2933.31 shows the lawful shape - a warrant to an officer. Whether a landlord's consent can ever substitute for the tenant's is a question only case law could settle, and no case law was searched here. And Ohio's retaliation grounds are closed and do not include a tenant calling the police, so no statute stops you penalising that - but see the separate Ohio rows on retaliation and on the absence of a right-to-call-emergency-services statute before you draft such a term. Cautious course: comply with a court order in writing, insist on a warrant for anything else, and never tell the tenant about an interception you have been asked to assist.

title: Ohio Protected Flags and Stopped - Political Signs and Canvassers Are Your Call
bodyText: Ohio gives a tenant no right to display a political sign, poster or banner, and gives no candidate, campaign worker, petition circulator or voter-registration canvasser any right to come into your building to reach tenants' doors. Nothing on either point appeared in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters or the Constitution searched for this entry: 'political sign', 'yard sign', 'canvass' and 'petition circulator' return nothing, and the hits for 'candidate' and 'campaign' are election administration, not tenancies. The contrast is the finding. Ohio did legislate on display - once, for flags - and the way it did so shows how deliberate the gap is. R.C. 5321.131 forbids restricting the United States flag, the POW/MIA flag, the Ohio flag and a Defense-approved service flag, and then goes further than any other Ohio lease rule: division (D) says a violation is against public policy and unenforceable and that any lease provision violating the section is an unconscionable term under R.C. 5321.14. That is the only place in Ohio law where a named lease clause is unconscionable by statute. The legislature wrote that protection for flags and wrote nothing for political signs, so a sign restriction stands on the ordinary footing - your lease may include any term not inconsistent with the chapter or another rule of law (R.C. 5321.06), with unconscionability under R.C. 5321.14 the only ceiling. Access by outsiders is likewise yours to decide as owner, subject to the tenant's own right to invite guests. Three cautions. Keep the flag line clean: a blanket no-signs-or-banners rule that catches a service flag or the national flag is caught by R.C. 5321.131, and a service flag is bound up with military status, which is a protected class in Ohio housing discrimination law (R.C. 4112.02(H)(4)). Apply any no-soliciting or common-area access rule the same way to every campaign, cause and faith, because uneven enforcement is where a discrimination claim starts. And the Ohio Constitution's speech and assembly guarantees (art. I, Sections 11 and 3) restrain lawmaking, not a private landlord - do not rely on them either way. One limb was not resolved: a canvasser-access right, if Ohio had one, would sit in the election statutes in Title 35 (for example R.C. ch. 3501), which this review does not hold and could not fetch, so treat the no-access conclusion as proved for the landlord-tenant, civil-rights and consumer chapters searched and unverified for election law.

title: Ohio Gives No Religious-Display Right - Fair Housing Is What Limits Your Rule
bodyText: Ohio gives a tenant no right to display a religious or cultural item - a doorpost scroll, a crucifix, a household shrine, a holiday or festival decoration - and imposes no duty on you to accommodate one. 'Crucifix', 'mezuzah' and 'altar' appear nowhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters or the Constitution searched for this entry, and the religion hits are all protected-class lists. Ohio's only display statute is R.C. 5321.131, and it is flags only: the United States flag, the POW/MIA flag, the Ohio flag and a Defense-approved service flag. Note how far that one section goes, because it shows the gap is deliberate - its division (D) makes a violation against public policy and unenforceable and makes any lease provision violating it an unconscionable term under R.C. 5321.14, which is the only statutory per-se unconscionable lease clause in Ohio. The legislature did that for flags and did not do it for anything else. So your display rule stands on R.C. 5321.06, which lets a lease carry any term not inconsistent with the chapter or another rule of law, with unconscionability the only ceiling. What limits you is discrimination law, not display law. It is an unlawful discriminatory practice to discriminate against any person in the terms or conditions of renting, or in furnishing facilities, services or privileges in connection with the occupancy or use of housing, because of religion, ancestry or national origin (R.C. 4112.02(H)(4)) - and a display rule is a condition of renting. It is separately unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone exercising a right that division protects, or aiding another to (R.C. 4112.02(H)(12)). Watch the asymmetry: Ohio's statutory duty to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services runs to disability only (R.C. 4112.02(H)(19)); there is no parallel religious-accommodation duty on a landlord, so a neutral rule you apply evenly is defensible while a rule aimed at, or enforced against, one faith or culture is not. The Ohio Constitution's rights of conscience clause (art. I, Section 7) restrains lawmaking and directs the General Assembly; it does not bind a private landlord. What to do: write any rule in neutral terms - size, placement, no penetration of doors and walls, no open flame - rest the fire-safety part on your duty to comply with applicable building, housing, health and safety codes (R.C. 5321.04(A)(1)), apply it to every tenant and every occasion, and consider allowing a small door-frame or doorpost item that causes no damage.

title: You Cannot Buy Back Ohio's Entry Notice in the Lease
bodyText: Ohio does set an entry-notice rule, which is the first thing to settle - a waiver of nothing is empty rather than lawful. Except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, you must give the tenant reasonable notice of your intent to enter and must enter only at reasonable times, and twenty-four hours is presumed to be reasonable notice in the absence of evidence to the contrary (R.C. 5321.04(A)(8)). Showings are squarely inside the permitted purposes: the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry to exhibit the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen or contractors (R.C. 5321.05(B)). What you cannot do is contract that notice away. No provision of the landlord-tenant chapter may be modified or waived by any oral or written agreement, and the one exception lets you take on a tenant's duty, not shorten your own (R.C. 5321.13(A) and (F)). So a lease clause cutting the showing notice, and a tenant's signature waiving it, are not recognised, and Ohio has no separate-signed-document route that would rescue one - nothing in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters or the Constitution searched for this entry permits an entry-notice waiver or prescribes a form for it. Two things you may still do. The twenty-four hours is a rebuttable presumption, not a statutory floor, so shorter notice is not automatically unlawful; it simply forfeits the presumption and leaves you proving the notice was reasonable, with the tenant's remedies in R.C. 5321.04(B) if a court disagrees. And nothing stops the tenant from agreeing to a particular showing on short notice when you ask, because R.C. 5321.05(B) works consent by consent. Cautious course: keep twenty-four hours in the lease, ask for short-notice showings one at a time, and confirm each agreement in writing.

title: Ohio Says Nothing About Cable, Satellite or Internet - Federal Law Does
bodyText: No Ohio landlord-tenant duty touches telecommunications. Your statutory obligations are listed in R.C. 5321.04, and the maintenance limb in R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) reaches 'all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, and air conditioning fixtures and appliances, and elevators' - telephone, cable, satellite and internet service are not on that list, so you need not supply them, maintain them or restore them. Nothing in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters or the Constitution searched for this entry makes you admit a cable or telecom company to the building, bars a rent difference between subscribers and non-subscribers, or regulates an exclusive deal with a provider: 'cable operator' and 'telephone service' return nothing, 'antenna' appears once and only inside a high-rise smoke-detection section, and the cable and satellite hits are a consumer-sales definition, a utility-switching consent rule and underground-utility marking. FEDERAL: the real constraint is the Federal Communications Commission's over-the-air reception devices rule, which prohibits any restriction - expressly including a lease provision - that impairs a tenant's installation, maintenance or use of a satellite dish one meter or less in diameter, a television broadcast antenna, or a fixed wireless antenna, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a leased balcony, patio or fenced yard. It does not give the tenant any right to install on a roof, an exterior wall, or common areas you control, and it does not stop you requiring that nothing be bolted into the structure outside the tenant's exclusive area. FEDERAL: separate FCC rules govern who owns and may use the inside wiring in a building after a provider leaves, and the FCC also restricts exclusive access arrangements in multiple-dwelling buildings. Those rules are 47 C.F.R. 1.4000 (antennas), 76.800 to 76.806 (inside wiring) and 76.2000, which makes a video provider's exclusive-access clause for a multiple dwelling unit void. The antenna rule still allows a restriction needed for a clearly defined safety objective or historic preservation, if it is no more burdensome than necessary (47 C.F.R. 1.4000(b)). What to do: drop any blanket no-dish or no-antenna clause and replace it with a term limited to the areas you control plus a no-penetration and safe-mounting requirement for the tenant's own exclusive area, and say in the lease which services, if any, you provide. Ohio's cable and video-service statutes, R.C. Chapter 1332, regulate providers and local governments; they give no provider a right of access to your building and set no inside-wiring rule.

title: Ohio Does Protect Tenants Who Organise - And the Protection Is Narrower Than It Sounds
bodyText: Tenant organising is protected conduct in Ohio, and it sits where most landlords never look: it is the third of the three retaliation triggers. A landlord may not retaliate because 'the tenant joined with other tenants for the purpose of negotiating or dealing collectively with the landlord on any of the terms and conditions of a rental agreement' (R.C. 5321.02(A)(3)). Those words bound the protection three ways. The tenant must have joined WITH OTHER TENANTS, so one tenant alone is outside this trigger - though a complaint to you about your statutory duties is protected under (A)(2). The purpose must be negotiating or dealing collectively WITH THE LANDLORD, so a tenants' group campaigning at city hall, backing a candidate or pressing a neighbouring owner is not within (A)(3). And the subject must be the terms and conditions of a rental agreement. Only three acts count as retaliation: increasing the rent, decreasing services due to the tenant, and bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession. Refusing to renew is NOT on that list - and that is deliberate, because the legislature wrote 'refusing to renew or threatening to refuse to renew the rental agreement' into the otherwise identical protection for manufactured home park residents (R.C. 4781.36(A)) and left it out of the landlord-tenant chapter. Do not read that as a safe harbour: a non-renewal announced in the middle of an organising dispute invites the argument that it was a threatened possession action, so be able to show an independent reason, in writing, before you give the notice. If you do retaliate, the tenant may raise it as a defence to your possession action, recover possession, or terminate the lease, and may recover actual damages together with reasonable attorney's fees (R.C. 5321.02(B)) - statutory fees, so the Ohio rule voiding fee agreements does not protect you. What Ohio does NOT give is the larger half of the answer: no right of access for an outside organiser, no right to a meeting room, no right to post notices or canvass doors, no duty to recognise a tenant association and no duty to meet or bargain with one. 'Tenant association', 'tenants association' and 'tenant organization' appear nowhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Administrative Code chapters or the Constitution searched for this entry, and 'dealing collectively' appears in exactly two sections - R.C. 5321.02 and the park counterpart. So you may make neutral rules for common rooms and noticeboards and apply them to every group alike. Two more things. R.C. 5321.03 lets you still bring a possession action notwithstanding the retaliation rule on the grounds it lists, including rent default and holdover, so organising is no shield against an ordinary case. And discrimination law runs alongside: it is unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone who aided or encouraged another in exercising a fair-housing right (R.C. 4112.02(H)(12)), or to discriminate against someone who opposed an unlawful discriminatory practice or took part in a proceeding (R.C. 4112.02(I)). The Ohio Constitution's right to assemble (art. I, Section 3) binds the General Assembly, not you.

title: A Trespass Warning Is Not an Ohio Route to Possession
bodyText: Whether a trespass warning does anything for you in Ohio depends on who you are warning, and the first answer is the one that costs landlords money. Against a tenant - or a former tenant - it does nothing and is dangerous. R.C. 5321.15(A) says no landlord of residential premises shall initiate any act, including termination of utilities or services, EXCLUSION FROM THE PREMISES, or threat of any unlawful act, against a tenant 'or a tenant whose right to possession has terminated', for the purpose of recovering possession, other than as provided in Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321. The statute expressly covers the person whose tenancy has already ended, so you cannot convert a holdover into a trespasser by serving a notice and calling the police. Doing so makes you liable for all damages caused to that person together with reasonable attorney's fees (R.C. 5321.15(C)), and that fee award is statutory, so the Ohio rule voiding fee agreements does not protect you. What you do have is two court routes, not one. Chapter 1923 is the fast summary action in the municipal court, with its three-day notice and listed grounds. Chapter 5303 is the ordinary civil action for recovery of real property in common pleas, and its pleading burden is light: a legal estate, entitlement to possession, and that the defendant unlawfully keeps you out of possession, without stating how your estate is derived (R.C. 5303.03). That second route is the answer for an occupant who never was your tenant and for whom Chapter 1923 may give you no ground at all. One risk before choosing it: R.C. 5303.07 lets the parties invoke the occupying claimant sections, R.C. 5303.08 to 5303.17, which can require a successful plaintiff to pay an occupant for improvements made in good faith under colour of title before taking possession. Those sections protect only an occupant who obtained title without fraud or collusion and holds under a source R.C. 5303.08 lists - record title, a deed, an execution or tax sale, or a court-ordered sale. A squatter or a guest claiming only occupancy does not qualify, but take advice if the occupant shows you a deed. Against a true non-tenant in a common area you control, a written warning is a genuine tool - but its terms are not in the landlord-tenant law. Ohio's general criminal trespass offence is R.C. 2911.21. It covers a person who, 'without privilege to do so', recklessly enters or remains after notice given 'by actual communication', by posting or by fencing, or who negligently fails to leave when the owner or occupant, or their agent, tells them to (R.C. 2911.21(A)(3), (4)). The statute requires no written form. Your tenant is also an occupant who can give a guest privilege, so whether your warning overrides the tenant's invitation is a question only case law settles; warn only for areas you control. Cautious course, and follow it even if you are sure of your ground: never treat anyone who is or was your tenant as a trespasser; deal with a problem guest through the tenant's own statutory duties of keeping persons there with their consent from damaging the premises and from disturbing neighbours' peaceful enjoyment (R.C. 5321.05(A)(6) and (A)(8)), and through the eviction grounds for breaching those duties or a written lease term; give any warning to a genuine non-tenant in writing, naming the person, the date, the areas covered and the reason, with a copy to the tenant whose guest it concerns; and take possession only through a court.

title: Ohio Never Makes You Show a Tenant a Certificate of Occupancy - and Its Only CO Statutes Are About Hotels
bodyText:
Nothing in Ohio law makes you give a tenant a certificate of occupancy, state in the lease that one exists, or disclose that one does not. There is no Ohio counterpart to the states that make a lease unenforceable, or the rent uncollectable, where no certificate has been issued. R.C. 5321.04 lists your statutory duties and none is a disclosure duty; R.C. 5321.18's owner-and-agent identity is the only thing Ohio requires a residential lease to contain. No Ohio statute conditions a tenancy, a rent demand or an eviction on holding a certificate.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'occupancy' 36, 'license' 555, 'disclose' 55, 'disclosure' 44, 'shall contain' 62 and 'shall state' 29, so the subject area is amply held. 'certificate of occupancy' returns exactly three sections and all three are in the hotel chapter - R.C. 3731.01, 3731.04 and 3731.041. 'occupancy permit' returns two, both motor-vehicle provisions. 'notify the tenant' returns nothing.

Where Ohio's certificate of occupancy actually comes from, and why you cannot look it up here. Those hotel sections show the mechanism: a structure is 'approved pursuant to a valid certificate of occupancy issued by the building official having jurisdiction' against a use-and-occupancy classification adopted by the board of building standards under R.C. 3781.10 - residential group R-1 for transient occupancy, R-2 for non-transient. So in Ohio the certificate is a local building-department instrument issued under the state Building and Residential Codes, and those codes are administrative rules (Ohio Administrative Code 4101:1 and 4101:8) that are not in this library's corpus, alongside R.C. Chapter 3791, which is not held either. Any duty to obtain, post or produce a certificate for an ordinary dwelling lives there or in your city's housing code, which this library flags and does not resolve. Two things in the held chapters are worth knowing anyway: R.C. 3781.11(C) makes a building constructed, altered or repaired otherwise than in accordance with the statutes or the board's rules 'a public nuisance', R.C. 3781.15 allows its 'construction, use, or occupation' to be enjoined, and R.C. 3781.031 requires the enforcing agency to proceed by adjudication order or stop-work order; and R.C. 3781.01 confirms a municipality may add its own regulations on top.

The real Ohio exposure in this area is not a disclosure - it is being in the wrong licensing regime. Chapter 3731 requires a state fire marshal licence for every hotel or SRO facility, renewable annually, and R.C. 3731.03(B) provides that no such facility 'shall be maintained, conducted, or advertised without a license'. Two definitions can catch a landlord who thinks of the building as apartments. An 'extended stay hotel' under R.C. 3731.01(A)(3) is a structure of more than five dwelling units held out as offering temporary residence for pay, whose certificate of occupancy approves both R-2 non-transient dwelling features and all the R-1 transient features, and which the fire marshal has approved for extended stay. A 'residential hotel' under R.C. 3731.01(A)(4) is a structure of more than five dwelling units approved through a valid certificate of occupancy as having both sets of features and held out as offering non-transient dwelling units for pay 'for a minimum stay of more than thirty days'. And R.C. 3731.03(G)(1) bars a licensed hotel or SRO operator from also operating an apartment house, apartment, lodging house or rooming house in the same structure unless that part has been constructed as, and approved by the building official as being, a separate building or is separated to the code's occupancy-separation standard.
