So if you are running short-stay or furnished units, or mixing uses in one structure, the certificate your building holds is what decides which regime you are in - and getting it wrong is a licensing problem, not a disclosure problem.

Practical course. Obtain and keep the certificate for your own protection, check which use-and-occupancy classification it names before you let the unit on short stays, and disclose voluntarily if a tenant asks. R.C. 5321.06 lets you say anything in the lease not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or another rule of law, but do not promise that the premises comply with any code - R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) already obliges you to comply with the applicable codes, and R.C. 5321.13(A) means you cannot shrink that duty by agreement anyway.

title: Ohio Does Not Bar Rent After a Condemnation - It Bars You From Re-Renting at All
bodyText:
Ohio has no statute making rent uncollectable because the unit has been condemned, posted or ordered vacated, and no statute making you repay rent already taken. It has no condemnation-of-premises regime at all. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this review 'unfit', 'uninhabitable', 'unfit for human habitation', 'vacate order' and 'order to vacate' return nothing; 'condemn', 'condemned' and 'condemnation' return three, one and one hit, all about unserviceable military stores and underground storage tanks; all eight hits for 'placard' are motor-vehicle provisions; and 'abate rent', 'rent abatement', 'not collect rent' and 'shall not be liable for rent' return nothing at all. The power to condemn or placard a dwelling in Ohio sits in the building code and in city housing codes, which R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) expressly leaves outside Chapter 5321's preemption and which this library flags rather than resolves.

Do not read that as permission, because Ohio's actual sanction is worse than a rent bar. R.C. 1923.15 provides that during any proceeding involving residential premises under the eviction chapter the court may order an appropriate governmental agency to inspect the premises; and if the agency determines and the court finds conditions violating R.C. 5321.04 or R.C. 4781.38, and the premises have been vacated or are to be restored to you, 'the court may issue an order forbidding the re-rental of the property until such conditions are corrected.' That is not an abatement of this tenant's rent - it is the loss of the unit's entire income until you fix it. If instead the court lets the tenant stay, it may order the conditions corrected; and if the tenant caused them, it may award you the reasonable cost of correction.

Three other routes take the rent away from you without any condemnation. The rent-escrow remedy: once the tenant has given written notice under R.C. 5321.07(A) and you have not remedied within a reasonable time or thirty days, whichever is sooner, the tenant may deposit all rent with the clerk of court, who holds it in a separate escrow account (R.C. 5321.08), and you get it back only by applying under R.C. 5321.09 - on the ground that the condition has been remedied, that the tenant did not comply with the notice requirement or was not current in rent, or that there was no violation at all. The tenant may also ask the court to reduce the periodic rent until you remedy the condition, or to use the deposited rent to do the work. A tenant sued for nonpayment can counterclaim under R.C. 1923.061(B) for anything recoverable under the lease or Chapter 5321, and 'If no rent remains due after application of this division, judgment shall be entered for the tenant or resident in the action for possession.' And R.C. 3767.41 lets a court appoint a receiver over a building found to be a public nuisance - a definition that includes a building 'otherwise no longer fit and habitable' - who then collects the rents instead of you.

One principle underlies all of it, and it is the Ohio answer to the question this topic asks. R.C. 5321.13(E) provides that no rental agreement, and no assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument of your interest in it, 'may permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with section 5321.04 of the Revised Code', and R.C. 5321.13(A) makes that unwaivable. Ohio does not bar the rent by statute; it refuses to let the rent be separated from the duty. So a lease term entitling you to full rent regardless of the unit's condition, or regardless of a public order against it, is the wrong place to put your protection.

Not searched, and the bound on everything above: Ohio Administrative Code 4101:1 (the Building Code) and 4101:8 (the Residential Code) are not in this library's corpus, R.C. Chapter 3791 is not held, and city housing codes - which are where a vacate order or a placard actually comes from, and which may themselves bar rent - are flagged and not resolved. Check your city's housing code before accepting rent on a posted unit.

title: A Lien From Work Your Tenant Ordered
bodyText:
A contractor your tenant hires can file a lien, and the sentence that decides whose property it hits is worth reading slowly. R.C. 1311.02 gives a lien to anyone who performs work or furnishes material for an improvement 'undertaken by virtue of a contract, express or implied, with the owner, part owner, or lessee of any interest in real estate', and makes it a lien 'upon the improvement and all interests that the owner, part owner, or lessee may have or subsequently acquire in the land or leasehold to which the improvement was made'. Two things follow. A tenant's own contract can generate a lien - 'lessee' is named twice - and what the lien reaches is expressed in terms of the interests of the party who contracted, so a tenant's contractor is reaching the tenant's leasehold rather than your fee.

Treat that as the likely reading and not as a guarantee. The sentence names all three capacities together, and the sections that would settle it were not read in this review. The practical course is the one that does not depend on the answer: require your written consent before a tenant has any work done, say in the lease that you do not consent to any lien against your interest, and keep the right to pay off and recover a lien a tenant causes. Do not write that the tenant will pay your attorney's fees or legal costs, because R.C. 5321.13(C) recognises no agreement to pay either party's attorney's fees, in the lease or in any other agreement between you.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, where this subject is simply not present - control term 0 sections and 'mechanic's lien' 0, 'mechanics lien' 0 and 'materialman' 0, against 'landlord' 34, 'leasehold' 6 and 'improvement' 28 - plus R.C. 1311.02 read in full outside it. R.C. 1311.01, 1311.03, 1311.04's notice of commencement and the rest of R.C. 1311.04 to 1311.14 were not read, nor were R.C. 1311.55 to 1311.57 or 1311.71 to 1311.80. Those are also where any protective step for an owner - a posted or recorded notice that the fee is not subject to a lien - would live. No Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: Your Tenant Is a Party to a Taking
bodyText:
Your tenant is a party to an Ohio taking, not a bystander, and that is the thing to know before an agency contacts you. R.C. 163.01(E) defines 'owner' for Ohio's appropriation chapter as 'any individual, partnership, association, or corporation having any estate, title, or interest in any real property sought to be appropriated', and (F) defines the property that may be taken to include 'any estate, title, or interest' in it. A leasehold is an estate in real property, so a tenant is an owner in their own right: entitled to the good faith offer an appropriating agency must make before it begins (R.C. 163.01(J), required by R.C. 163.04(B)), entitled to appear, and entitled to compensation for the leasehold itself. You do not speak for your tenant and cannot settle their claim with yours. Two other points from the definitions are worth knowing: the case goes to the common pleas or probate court of a county where the property lies (R.C. 163.01(D)), and 'public use' excludes a taking for conveyance to a private commercial enterprise, for economic development, or solely to increase public revenue, unless one of three exceptions applies, of which the practical one is a blighted parcel or a blighted area proved by a preponderance of the evidence (R.C. 163.01(H)(1)).

What Ohio law does not do is tell you how the lease ends or how an award is split. Nothing in Chapter 5321 mentions a taking, so the lease governs - and a lease that says nothing leaves both of you arguing. Decide in the lease what happens on a total taking, on a partial taking, and who may claim what.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, 'eminent domain' 1, 'condemnation' 1, 'taking' 53, 'appropriat' 484, every relevant hit checked and none a landlord-tenant provision, against 'landlord' 34 - plus R.C. 163.01 read in full outside it. The rest of Chapter 163 was not read: in particular the section apportioning an award among separate estates in one parcel, the deposit-and-possession section, and any section on a taking's effect on an existing lease. Ohio Const. art. I, section 19 was not read either, nor any case law.

title: Ohio Makes You Tell a New Tenant Nothing About a Foreclosure - and the Near-Miss Is a Land Contract
bodyText:
In the 37 Revised Code chapters searched below, Ohio imposes no duty to tell a prospective or sitting tenant that the property is in foreclosure, that your lender has served a notice of default, or that a foreclosure complaint has been filed. R.C. 5321.04 lists your statutory obligations as an Ohio landlord and no limb of it is a disclosure duty of any kind. The only thing Ohio requires a residential lease to contain is the owner's and the owner's agent's name and address under R.C. 5321.18 - which is why that is the only Ohio clause in this library carrying a statutory disclosure basis. There is no pre-lease notice, no notice within a set number of days of service, no required form of words, and no tenant right to end the lease or recover a penalty because you did not mention it.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections. 'disclose' returns 55 sections, 'disclosure' 44, 'shall contain' 62, 'shall state' 29, 'pending' 62 and 'foreclosure' 19, so the subject area is amply held and the tool was answering; 'notify the tenant', 'in writing to the tenant', 'prior to occupancy', 'before signing' and 'notice of default' return nothing at all, and the only two hits for 'prospective tenant' are the fair housing definitions in R.C. 4112.01 and the manufactured-home-park rental agreement section R.C. 4781.40, whose lots are outside Chapter 5321 anyway under R.C. 4781.01(W) with R.C. 5321.01(C) - a park's 'residential premises' is the LOT and the park's grounds, not a dwelling unit. Not searched: Ohio's residential-foreclosure chapter 2308, the mortgage chapter 1322, and city ordinances, which this library flags and does not resolve.

The near-miss is worth knowing because it shows Ohio knows how to write this duty when it wants to. R.C. 5313.02(A)(16) requires a land installment contract to contain 'a statement of any pending order of any public agency against the property'. That is a sale instrument, not a lease, and it is about agency orders rather than foreclosures - but it is the one place in this body of law where Ohio makes a property owner disclose a pending proceeding to the person taking occupancy. If you are selling on a land contract rather than letting, that duty is real.

One Ohio notice does run, and it runs to you, not from you. R.C. 1349.78 requires a written notice to you at least thirty days before a foreclosure action is filed - but only where the debt is secured by a mortgage lien on your residential real property that is not in first position and has been accelerated or is in default. A first-mortgage foreclosure gets no notice under this section; whether other Ohio or federal law requires one was not researched for this row.

Disclose anyway, and do it in writing. Nothing stops you: R.C. 5321.06 lets a lease carry any term not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or another rule of law. There are three practical reasons. A tenant who learns mid-tenancy that the home is being sold out from under them is the tenant who stops paying and defends the eviction. Federal law, not Ohio law, is what actually governs what happens to that tenancy after the sale - see this library's row on the federal thirty-day notice to vacate - and a tenant who was told up front is far less likely to argue about it. And if you take a year's rent in advance on a property you know is being foreclosed, you are closer to a misrepresentation claim than to a statutory violation, and Ohio's silence is no answer to that.

title: Ohio's Foreclosure Chapter Never Mentions Tenants - Which Cuts Both Ways
bodyText:
The remarkable thing about Ohio's judicial-sale law is its silence. Across all one hundred and one sections of Chapter 2329, the chapter that governs execution against property and judicial sales, the words 'tenant', 'lessee', 'rental agreement' and 'occupant' do not appear once. So Ohio gives a tenant no statutory protection at a foreclosure sale - no lease survival, no conversion to a tenancy at will, no redirection of rent to the purchaser, no sixty- or ninety-day notice, and no tenant right of redemption. Redemption in Ohio belongs to three people and a tenant is none of them: the judgment debtor, who may redeem at any time before confirmation by depositing the judgment plus costs and interest at eight per cent on the purchase money (R.C. 2329.33); the judgment creditor and the first lienholder, each within fourteen days of a minimum-bid auction, with the first lienholder winning a conflict (R.C. 2329.311); and the judgment creditor on a prosecutor-forced sale (R.C. 2329.071(C)). The deed carries only 'all the estate and interest of the person whose property the officer so professed to sell and convey' (R.C. 2329.37) - the former owner's interest, not the tenant's. And only a 'permanent leasehold estate renewable forever' is a leasehold that can itself be levied on and sold (R.C. 2329.01(A)), so an ordinary residential lease is not leviable property.

Getting possession after the sale. R.C. 1923.02(A)(3) lets a purchaser bring the summary forcible entry and detainer action 'In sales of real estate, on executions, orders, or other judicial process, when the judgment debtor was in possession at the time of the rendition of the judgment or decree, by virtue of which the sale was made.' Read that condition before you rely on it: it is satisfied where the former owner was living there, and on its face it is not satisfied where a tenant rather than the judgment debtor held possession when judgment was rendered. In that case your grounds are R.C. 1923.02(A)(5), an occupier without colour of title where you have the right of possession, or (A)(6), any other unlawful and forcible detention - or the slower route, an ejectment action under Chapter 5303, which R.C. 5321.15(A) names as lawful. Either way you serve the R.C. 1923.04(A) notice three or more days before filing, and if you are recovering residential premises it must carry the conspicuous statutory wording. Never shut off a utility or change a lock: R.C. 5321.15(A) and (C).

Buying at an Ohio sale, as a landlord. R.C. 2329.271 makes the purchaser give the selling officer identifying information, and the duty is heavier if you intend to rent the property out: division (A)(1)(d) requires a statement of whether you intend to use it as residential rental property, and (A)(1)(c) requires an entity purchaser of residential rental property to name a trustee, executor, general partner, member, manager, officer or associate 'with the provision that the purchaser be readily accessible through the identified contact person'. 'Residential rental property' there means what it means in R.C. 5323.01 - so the same county-population test. No post office box is allowed as the mailing address; your email, telephone and payment-device details are confidential under (B)(2) but the rest is a public record; and (C) exempts the plaintiff or a lienholder party to the action. Expect also that an open house may have been held before the sale if the property was vacant or abandoned (R.C. 2329.272).

Losing the property, as the borrower. One Ohio notice runs in your favour and it is narrow: R.C. 1349.78 requires, not less than thirty days before a foreclosure action is filed, a written notice mailed to your residential address - but only where the debt is secured by a mortgage lien on your residential real property that is not in first position and has been accelerated or is in default. The notice must be in at least twelve-point type and give the collector's contact details, the amount of the debt, a statement of your right to engage an attorney, and statements about Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 bankruptcy relief; on written request the owner of the debt must give you the note and the loan history. There is a bona-fide-error safe harbour, and a cause of action that cannot be a class action. A first-mortgage foreclosure gives you none of this. Separately, R.C. 2329.071 lets the local political subdivision or the county prosecutor force a sale twelve months after a foreclosure decree on residential real property, with a minimum bid equal to the unpaid taxes and court costs - so a stalled foreclosure is not a stalemate you can rely on.

The rent while all this happens. A lender taking an assignment of rents does not take them clean: R.C. 5321.01(B) makes any person authorised to manage the premises or to receive the rent a landlord, and R.C. 5321.13(E) stops any assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument of your interest in the rental agreement from permitting receipt of rent free of the R.C. 5321.04 duties. A court-appointed receiver has it harder still for your tenants: R.C. 3767.41(F) lets the receiver collect rents, re-let and evict tenants outright.

Federal law is the limb that actually protects tenants here, and Ohio's does not. This library's row on the federal thirty-day notice to vacate under the CARES Act sets out that duty; do not treat it as an Ohio rule. One further federal statute, the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, is the one that in other states gives a bona fide tenant the rest of the lease term and ninety days' notice after a foreclosure sale; it has NOT been reviewed in this library and nothing here should be read as stating its terms. If you are buying a tenanted property at an Ohio sheriff's sale, or are the lender taking one back, get advice on it before serving any notice - the state silence described above is not permission.

What Ohio does not have at all, across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this review: no equity-skimming statute, no foreclosure-rescue or foreclosure-consultant regulation, no cancellation right for a homeowner who sells and stays on as the buyer's tenant, and no requirement that a sale-leaseback contract recite the lease terms. 'equity skimming', 'foreclosure rescue', 'foreclosure consultant', 'leaseback', 'deed in lieu' and 'short sale' each return nothing. Chapter 2308, Ohio's residential-foreclosure chapter, is not in this library's corpus and was not read, and both R.C. 2329.01(B)(3) and R.C. 2329.33 point into it - so the absences above are bounded by what was searched.

title: Ohio Has an Alien Land Filing - On the Owner, Not on the Lease
bodyText:
Ohio has a nonresident-alien land statute, and almost nobody knows it is there. Under R.C. 5301.254 every nonresident alien who acquires an interest in Ohio real property of more than three acres, or worth more than one hundred thousand dollars, must file with the Secretary of State within thirty days a report giving name, citizenship, the location of the property, its acreage and its intended use, with a five dollar fee. Division (C) extends the same duty to a corporation or other entity in which one nonresident alien holds at least ten per cent, or several together hold at least forty per cent, with a twenty-five dollar fee. Division (D) requires an updated filing within thirty days of a change, and division (F) makes non-compliance enforceable by the county prosecuting attorney or the Attorney General.

Read what that is and what it is not. It is a reporting duty on an acquirer of land. It does not prohibit a foreign person from owning or leasing Ohio real property, it does not void anything, it imposes nothing on a lease, and it gives no party a right against the other. Ohio has no foreign-adversary acquisition ban of the kind several states enacted recently, no leasehold carve-out, and no provision making a non-complying leasehold void: across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library, 'nonresident alien', 'foreign adversary' and 'foreign person' return nothing, the six hits for 'alien' are unrelated, and the Ohio Constitution contains no alien land provision. So for a residential lease there is nothing to disclose and nothing to obtain.

One unsettled point you should not guess at. R.C. 5301.254 attaches to acquiring 'an interest in' Ohio real property, and a lease is an interest in real property in Ohio - R.C. 5301.01(A) speaks of a 'lease of any interest in real property' and the statute of frauds at R.C. 1335.04 of a 'lease, estate, or interest'. Whether a nonresident-alien tenant taking a leasehold over three acres or worth more than one hundred thousand dollars is therefore inside R.C. 5301.254 is not answered by the words of the section, and no case law was reviewed. For an ordinary house or apartment the question will not arise. If you are letting acreage, a farmhouse on land, or a high-value property to a foreign national, or letting to a foreign-owned company for staff housing, get advice before signing rather than assuming the filing is somebody else's problem.

Finally, do not turn any of this into a screening rule. Ohio's fair housing law, R.C. 4112.02(H), makes it an unlawful discriminatory practice to refuse to sell or rent, or to discriminate in the terms of a rental, because of national origin or ancestry. A nationality or citizenship question put to an applicant is its own exposure - see this library's rows on protected-class inquiries and on immigration-status questions. The filing duty in R.C. 5301.254 runs against an acquiring owner; it is not a reason to treat a foreign tenant differently.

title: No Ohio Duty to Show a Tenant Your Open Code Orders - But an Agency Finding Hands Them the Escrow Key
bodyText:
Ohio requires no disclosure of an outstanding inspection order, code-violation notice, abatement order, stop-work order or condemnation order to a prospective or sitting tenant. R.C. 5321.04 sets out your statutory duties and none is a disclosure duty; R.C. 5321.18's owner-and-agent identity is the only thing Ohio requires an Ohio residential lease to contain. There is no form to hand over, no attachment, no acknowledgment to sign and no penalty for silence.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'inspection' 115 and 'inspect' 147, 'disclose' 55 and 'disclosure' 44, and 'adjudication order' 6, so the subject area is amply held. 'outstanding order' and 'notify the tenant' return nothing; 'code violation' returns three sections (R.C. 3731.07 hotels, R.C. 4781.41 manufactured-home parks and R.C. 5321.07) and 'notice of violation' two (the fire marshal's citation power and the accessibility-law notice), none of them a tenant disclosure; and the two hits for 'prospective tenant' are the fair housing definitions and the manufactured-home-park rental agreement section.

Now the part that matters more than the disclosure question. An open agency finding gives your tenant a shortcut into rent escrow that does not depend on proving you breached anything. R.C. 5321.07(A) gives the tenant the written-notice-then-escrow route on three separate triggers, and the third is this: 'if a governmental agency has found that the premises are not in compliance with building, housing, health, or safety codes that apply to any condition of the premises that could materially affect the health and safety of an occupant'. So once an inspector has made that finding, the tenant can give you the R.C. 5321.07(A) notice specifying the code violations, and if you have not remedied within a reasonable time or thirty days, whichever is sooner, deposit the rent with the clerk, ask the court to reduce the rent, ask to spend the deposited rent on the repair, or terminate. You will not get that rent released without satisfying R.C. 5321.09. Treat an open order as a live financial exposure, not a filing problem.

And you will not keep it quiet in a nuisance action, because Ohio serves your tenant. In a R.C. 3767.41 public-nuisance action the complaint and notice of hearing must be served on the owner and all other interested parties under the Rules of Civil Procedure, and R.C. 3767.41(A)(4) defines 'interested party' to include a tenant. The same section lets a tenant, a neighbour, a municipality, a township or a nonprofit housing organisation start the action in the first place. Separately, under R.C. 1923.15 the court in an eviction may order an agency to inspect, and on a finding of conditions violating R.C. 5321.04 may forbid you from re-renting the unit until they are corrected. The orders reach your tenant through the courts whether or not you hand them over.

Two near-misses show Ohio can write this duty. R.C. 5313.02(A)(16) requires a land installment contract - a sale instrument, not a lease - to contain 'a statement of any pending order of any public agency against the property'. And R.C. 3781.031(A) requires the enforcing department or agency to issue an adjudication order or stop-work order, which goes to the person charged, not to the occupant.

So disclose voluntarily, in writing, with the order attached. R.C. 5321.06 permits it, you are not conceding a breach by describing a condition, and the alternative is a tenant who discovers the order from a city inspector and goes straight to the clerk of court. Bound: Ohio Administrative Code 4101:1 and 4101:8 are not in this library's corpus, R.C. Chapter 3791 is not held, and city housing codes - which often do impose their own notice or posting duties - are flagged and not resolved here.

title: Ohio Requires No Landlord Insurance - But Its Statutes Assume You Carry It, and One Lets You Get the Premium Paid
bodyText:
No Ohio statute makes a residential landlord carry liability insurance, name a minimum amount, carry a bond instead, or prove coverage to anybody. R.C. 5321.04 lists your statutory duties and insurance is not among them. Ohio's rental registration chapter, which does impose a real filing duty in counties over two hundred thousand in population, is a filing duty only: all five sections of Chapter 5323 were read and none conditions registration, or anything else, on holding insurance - so the pattern some states use, a mandatory landlord policy tied to municipal registration, has no Ohio counterpart at state level.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'insurance' returning 80 sections, 'bond' 93 and 'surety bond' 9, so the subject area is amply held and the tool was answering. 'proof of insurance', 'maintain insurance', 'shall carry insurance', 'insurable interest' and 'certificate of insurance' return nothing at all. All six hits for 'liability insurance' were inspected and none is a landlord duty: they are a nursing-home operator on a transfer of operation, two petroleum underground-storage-tank fund provisions, two motor-vehicle registration sections and a manufactured-housing installer licence. Within Chapter 5321 the word 'insurance' appears exactly once.

That one appearance is worth knowing. R.C. 5321.10(A) provides that where you have brought an action for the release of rent your tenant has deposited with the clerk of court, the court may release part of it to pay 'the periodic interest on a mortgage on the premises, the periodic principal payments on a mortgage on the premises, the insurance premiums for the premises, real estate taxes on the premises, utility services, repairs, and other customary and usual costs of operating the premises as a rental unit'. So Ohio law treats your insurance premium as a customary and usual cost of operating a rental, and if your rent is sitting in escrow you can ask for it to be released to pay that premium - the court weighing the rent from the building's other units, the cost of operating them and the cost of remedying the condition. The statute assumes you insure; it simply does not compel it.

Two reasons to carry it anyway, both from Ohio law. R.C. 5321.13(D) refuses to recognise any agreement by a tenant to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of yours arising under law, or to indemnify you for that liability or its related costs - and unlike some states there is no common-areas exception. So you cannot transfer your own exposure to the tenant by drafting, and your insurer is the only place that exposure can go. And under R.C. 3767.41(F)(2) a court-appointed receiver over a building found to be a public nuisance pays 'insurance premiums' out of the building's income as an expense of conserving it, and the receiver's approved spending becomes a first lien on your building ahead of your mortgage - so if you stop insuring, somebody else may insure at your expense and at a very high priority.

The bound on all of the above. Ohio's insurance code is Title 39 of the Revised Code and is not in this library's corpus, so it was not searched. That matters less than it sounds: Title 39 regulates insurers and the terms of policies, and a duty imposed on a landlord would sit in Chapter 5321 or Chapter 5323, which were read in full. What this review cannot tell you is what an Ohio insurer may lawfully require of you or cancel you for. Nor does it resolve city ordinances: this library flags municipal rental licensing and insurance requirements and does not resolve them, and some Ohio cities do operate their own rental registration schemes - check yours before concluding you need no coverage.

title: Ohio Gives You No Landlord's Lien, Bars You From Seizing Anything, and Exempts the Deposit in Your Hands
bodyText:
Ohio has no statutory landlord's lien on a residential tenant's goods and no distress for rent. Across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this review, 'lien for rent', 'distress for rent', 'innkeeper' and 'lien upon the goods' return nothing, and the single hit for "landlord's lien" is R.C. 1309.109(D)(1), which says Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code 'does not apply to ... A landlord's lien, other than an agricultural lien'. That is a carve-out from the secured-transactions chapter, not a grant of a lien - read it as proof that Ohio knows the concept and has not given you one.

And the prohibition is explicit. R.C. 5321.15(B): 'No landlord of residential premises shall seize the furnishings or possessions of a tenant, or of a tenant whose right to possession has terminated, for the purpose of recovering rent payments, other than in accordance with an order issued by a court of competent jurisdiction.' Note three things in those words. It reaches a former tenant as well as a current one. It is not limited to locked-out tenants - any seizure for rent is caught. And R.C. 5321.15(C) makes you liable in a civil action for all damages caused to the tenant 'together with reasonable attorneys fees' - fees by statute, which the usual Ohio ban on fee agreements does not touch, because that ban is on agreements. R.C. 5321.13(A) means you cannot contract out of any of this.

Taking a consensual security interest instead is not the workaround it looks like. A lease term granting you a security interest in the tenant's household goods is not a landlord's lien arising by law; it is a consensual security interest and Article 9 does govern it. It is not a purchase-money security interest, so it is not perfected on attachment under R.C. 1309.309 and would need a filed financing statement; R.C. 1309.204(B)(1) stops an after-acquired property clause from reaching consumer goods given as additional security unless the tenant acquires rights in them within ten days after you give value; and although R.C. 1309.609(B)(2) normally lets a secured party take possession without judicial process if it acts without breach of the peace, R.C. 5321.15(B) withdraws exactly that from a residential landlord recovering rent. So you would be perfecting an interest you still could not enforce without going to court. Federal consumer-credit rules on nonpossessory security interests in household goods were not reviewed here and are a further risk.

What a court order gets you is bounded by exemptions, and those cannot be waived. R.C. 2329.66(A)(4)(a) exempts the tenant's interest up to five hundred and twenty-five dollars in any particular item and ten thousand seven hundred and seventy-five dollars in aggregate value in household furnishings, household goods, wearing apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, musical instruments, firearms and hunting and fishing equipment held primarily for personal, family or household use, with a further one thousand three hundred and fifty dollars for jewellery. R.C. 2329.66(A)(3) names you directly: the tenant's interest up to four hundred dollars in 'cash on hand, money due and payable, money to become due within ninety days, tax refunds, and money on deposit with a bank, savings and loan association, credit union, public utility, landlord, or other person, other than personal earnings' is exempt - so the deposit sitting in your hands is exempt money, and a money judgment does not simply absorb it. Those are the statute's figures, not a landlord's: R.C. 2329.66(B) has the Ohio Judicial Conference adjust every dollar amount in the section on the first of April in each third calendar year after 2010, by the increase in the consumer price index for all urban consumers over the preceding three years, rounded to the nearest twenty-five dollars, and publish a memorandum in the Register of Ohio - so check the current memorandum before relying on any number here. And R.C. 2329.661(B) provides that no promise, agreement or contract shall be made that would waive the exemption laws of this state, and that every one, insofar as it seeks to, is void.

So the Ohio route to a tenant's property is a money judgment and then execution through the court, subject to those exemptions - and the writ of restitution in an eviction gets you the unit, not an answer about what is left in it. Delete any lien, seizure, lock-up, self-help-sale or security-interest clause from an Ohio lease. What is left to you is worth stating plainly: sue for the rent, apply the deposit under R.C. 5321.16, and recover your actual damages.

title: Ohio Does Require You to Register - With the County Auditor, in the Big Counties Only
bodyText: Ohio has a statewide rental registration law, and most landlords have never heard of it. Chapter 5323 of the Revised Code applies to 'residential rental property', which it defines as real property in a county whose population exceeds two hundred thousand by the most recent decennial census, on which there is at least one dwelling unit rented solely for residential purposes - and it covers a mobile home park or other site where lots are rented for parking a manufactured home, mobile home or recreational vehicle used solely as a residence. A hotel and a college or university dormitory are excluded. If your property is in one of those counties, you must file with the county auditor your own name, address and telephone number; the street address and permanent parcel number of the property; and, if the property is owned by a trust, estate, partnership, limited liability company, association, corporation or other business entity, the name, address and telephone number of the trustee, executor, general partner, member, manager, officer or associate. You must update the filing within sixty days after anything in it changes. An agent you have appointed to manage the property may file or update for you. Notice three things. First, this is a filing duty and nothing more: there is no licence, no certificate, no inspection, no approval to obtain, nothing you must do before you let the unit, and nothing in Chapter 5323 gives a tenant any right at all - no termination right, no rent defence, no penalty payable to the tenant. Second, the penalty runs against you, not against the tenant: under R.C. 5323.99 the county auditor may impose on the property a special assessment of not less than fifty dollars and not more than one hundred fifty dollars for failing to file or update, appealable to the county board of revision. It is your own default, so do not treat it as a reimbursable tenant charge. Third, there is a real benefit in R.C. 5323.04: the filing is a public record, and an owner who complies 'shall be deemed to be in full compliance with any request by the state or any political subdivision to that owner for information that is identical to the information filed with the county auditor'. So a city demand for the same owner-contact information is already answered by your county filing. Two separate duties sit next to this one. R.C. 5323.03 requires an owner who resides outside Ohio to designate an in-state agent for service of process - covered in its own row. And R.C. 5321.18 requires the owner's and agent's name and address to be in the written lease itself, which is a different obligation with a different sanction. One more sits in the business-entity law: if you rent under a trade name or fictitious name, you must register it with the Secretary of State or report its use within thirty days of first use, and you cannot bring an eviction in that name until you do (R.C. 1329.01(D), 1329.10(B)); and an out-of-state corporation or LLC must be licensed or registered with the Secretary of State before it transacts business in Ohio (R.C. 1703.03, 1706.511(A)) - see `edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-oh`. Finally, nothing here resolves city rental licensing: R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) leaves local housing, building, health and safety codes outside Chapter 5321's preemption, so a municipal rental registration or licensing ordinance may still apply on top. This library flags city ordinances and does not resolve them - check your city.

title: Ohio Has No Lease Registry - and Only One Housing Instrument Must Be Recorded
bodyText:
There is no lease registry in Ohio and nothing to file a residential lease with. Nothing in Chapter 5321 asks you to record or register a lease, nothing conditions any right on having done so, and no statute makes an unrecorded residential lease invalid between you and your tenant. The only recording rule anywhere near a tenancy is a formalities threshold at three years: R.C. 5301.08 says sections 5301.01 to 5301.45 'do not affect the validity of any lease ... of any other lands for any term not exceeding three years or require that lease to be acknowledged or recorded', so a lease of three years or less needs no notary and no recording, while a longer term should be signed by you and acknowledged before a notary (or a judge, clerk of a court of record, county auditor, county engineer or mayor) and recorded. That is the formalities row's subject, not a registration regime.

The instrument Ohio really does make you record is the one landlords confuse with a long lease. A land installment contract - an agreement under which the buyer pays by instalments while you keep title as security, and which by its terms is not to be fully performed within one year (R.C. 5313.01(A)) - must by R.C. 5313.02(C) be recorded within twenty days of signing and a copy delivered to the county auditor, must contain the sixteen provisions listed in R.C. 5313.02(A), and must conform to the formalities required for deeds and mortgages. If you are drafting a rent-to-own or lease-purchase arrangement, decide deliberately which instrument you are creating: a land installment contract carries recording, content, mortgage and forfeiture rules a lease does not, and R.C. 5313.07 and 5313.08 govern how you get the property back.

Two things to register instead of the lease. First, if your property is in an Ohio county over two hundred thousand in population, R.C. 5323.02 makes you file owner and parcel information with the county auditor - not the lease, but a real filing duty, and it has its own row. Second, R.C. 5321.18 makes the owner's and agent's name and address go in the written lease itself, which is where Ohio puts the information other states put on a register.

One limb of this question has not been answered. Whether a tenant's possession under an unrecorded lease gives a later buyer or lender notice of the tenancy is governed by Ohio's recording statute, R.C. 5301.23 to 5301.25, which is not in this library's Ohio corpus and has not been read. R.C. 5313.02(C) names R.C. 5301.25 as the recording provision, which is how we know it is the right place to look. If you hold a lease longer than three years, or are selling or refinancing a tenanted property and need to know whose interest wins, that is the section to get advice on - and recording a long lease, or a memorandum of it, is the cautious course even though no statute requires it.

title: Live Out of State? Ohio Makes You Name Someone Here to Take Court Papers
bodyText:
If you own Ohio rental property and you live outside Ohio, R.C. 5323.03 makes you designate an individual who resides in Ohio to serve as your agent for the acceptance of service of process in any legal action or proceeding in the state. You designate in whatever manner the county auditor of the county where the property is located determines, and you then file with that auditor, in writing, the agent's name, address and telephone number. There is one way out: if you already designated and still maintain a statutory agent for service of process with the Secretary of State as a condition of being authorised to do business in Ohio - which an out-of-state company or LLC registered here will have done - you instead file with the county auditor a certified copy of the designation document you filed with the Secretary of State. Either way something gets filed with the auditor; there is no version of this where you do nothing.

Four limits and one trap. The duty only reaches 'residential rental property' as Chapter 5323 defines it, which means property in an Ohio county whose population exceeds two hundred thousand by the most recent decennial census, so in a smaller county there is no state designation duty at all. The agent must be an individual who resides in Ohio - not a company, and not a post box. The agent is for service of process only: Chapter 5323 does not make the agent responsible for repairs, rent or notices, and does not make you liable for the agent's acts. And the penalty is yours: R.C. 5323.99 lets the county auditor impose on the property a special assessment of not less than fifty and not more than one hundred fifty dollars for failing to satisfy the designation requirement or to file the designation document, appealable to the county board of revision.

The trap is a different section. R.C. 5321.18(A) requires every written lease to state the name and address of the owner and of the owner's agent, and where the owner or agent is a corporation, partnership, limited partnership, association, trust or other entity, 'the address shall be the principal place of business in the county in which the residential property is situated or if there is no place of business in such county then its principal place of business in this state', including the name of the person in charge. An out-of-state entity owner with no Ohio place of business cannot satisfy that on its own terms - so appoint an Ohio manager or agent and put that Ohio address and that person's name in the lease. R.C. 5321.18(C) is why it matters: fail to give the owner-and-agent information and you waive your right to receive the tenant's R.C. 5321.07 and 5321.08 notices, which means the tenant can go straight to rent escrow without giving you the cure window.

What Ohio does not do. There is no Ohio requirement that an out-of-state owner employ an Ohio-licensed real estate broker, no provision barring you from suing a tenant until a Chapter 5323 agent designation is on file (an out-of-state company is different - see below), and nothing in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters held for this library imposing income-tax withholding on rent paid to a nonresident owner. That last point is bounded: Ohio's income tax is Chapters 5747 and 5733, which were not reviewed, so confirm your withholding and composite-return position with a tax adviser rather than reading this as tax advice.

Out-of-state companies and trade names. An out-of-state corporation must hold a Secretary of State licence before it transacts business in Ohio, must keep an Ohio designated agent for service of process, and may not maintain any action in any Ohio court - an eviction included - until it is licensed (R.C. 1703.03, 1703.041(A), 1703.29(A)). An out-of-state LLC must register with the Secretary of State, naming an Ohio statutory agent, before it transacts business here, and until it does it may not maintain a proceeding to collect its debts, such as unpaid rent, though the court may stay the case until it registers (R.C. 1706.511(A), (B)(3), 1706.515(A), (B)). Owning real property is not by itself transacting business for an LLC (R.C. 1706.512(A)(9)); whether leasing it out is, is a case-law question, so register before you file. A licensed or registered company whose agent cannot be found can be served through the Secretary of State (R.C. 1703.19, 1706.09(H)(2)). An individual owner makes no such appointment, but an Ohio court may exercise jurisdiction over you in a case arising from your interest in Ohio real property (R.C. 2307.382(A)(8)). And if you rent under a trade name or fictitious name, register or report it first: until you do, you cannot sue in that name (R.C. 1329.10(B)).

title: You May Require Renter's Insurance in Ohio - What You May Not Do Is Make It Cover You
bodyText:
Ohio does not regulate renter's insurance in a residential tenancy, and the whole of the answer sits in two sections of Chapter 5321.

The permission. R.C. 5321.06 lets a landlord and tenant include in a rental agreement any terms and conditions not inconsistent with or prohibited by Chapter 5321 or any other rule of law. So requiring the tenant to carry renter's insurance is simply a lease term, and Ohio sets no minimum amount, no maximum, no proof deadline, no grace period, no notice before you force-place a policy, and no cap on an administrative charge for doing so. The figure in your lease is your figure, not the statute's, and R.C. 5321.14's unconscionability test is the only general ceiling. Ohio also imposes no advisory - there is no required written statement that you will not insure the tenant's property, and no required flood or coverage notice before signing. Say it anyway: telling the tenant in plain words that your insurance does not cover their belongings is the sentence that prevents the argument later, and this library's tenant-insurance clause opens with it.

The prohibition, and this is the limb that catches most borrowed lease language. R.C. 5321.13(D) provides that no agreement by a tenant to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law, or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or its related costs, shall be recognised in any rental agreement or in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant - and R.C. 5321.13(A) makes that unwaivable. There is no common-areas exception, unlike some states. So an insurance clause is void to the extent it is really an indemnity. Three forms to avoid: requiring the tenant's policy to cover your liability or your negligence; requiring the tenant to name you as an additional insured in respect of your own acts; and requiring a waiver of the insurer's subrogation rights against you for your own negligence. Requiring the tenant to be named as the insured, to carry a stated liability limit for the tenant's own acts, to give you evidence of coverage, and to name you as an interested party or certificate holder so that you are told if the policy lapses, is a different thing and is lawful - it tells you about the policy without making it your policy. And keep R.C. 5321.13(C) in mind: no agreement to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees is recognised, in the lease or in any other landlord-tenant agreement, so do not attach a fee-shifting tail to an insurance covenant.

Two practical traps. Nothing the tenant insures reduces what you owe: R.C. 5321.04's duties are yours and R.C. 5321.13(A) stops you shrinking them by agreement, so an insurance requirement is not a repair strategy. And if you collect money up front in connection with insurance rather than charging for a cost you have incurred, watch R.C. 5321.01(E), which defines a security deposit as 'any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under a rental agreement' - deliberately broad, and the reason several other charges in this library turn out to be deposit money in Ohio.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'insurance' 80 sections, 'insurance policy' 5, 'insurer' 4, 'subrogation' 3 and 'indemnify' 9, so the subject area is held and the tool was answering. Both forms of the regime's own noun return nothing: "renter's insurance" 0 and 'renters insurance' 0. So do 'additional insured', 'waiver of subrogation', 'force-placed', 'proof of insurance', 'certificate of insurance', 'insurable interest', "tenant's personal property" and 'personal property of the tenant'. Within Chapter 5321 the word 'insurance' appears exactly once, in R.C. 5321.10's list of operating costs a court may release escrowed rent to pay. Bound: Ohio's insurance code is Title 39 of the Revised Code and was not searched; it regulates insurers and policy terms rather than lease terms, but it is what would govern an insurer's conduct, and city ordinances are flagged here and not resolved.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers in Ohio - The Statute Follows Control, Not the Deed
bodyText:
Ohio has no sale-or-transfer section in its landlord-tenant chapter. There is no statutory notice you must give the tenant when you sell or change managers, no statutory release from your obligations when you do, no successor-liability provision, no estoppel-certificate statute, and no seller-disclosure duty owed to a sitting tenant. What Ohio has instead are four provisions that work by control rather than by title, and they are the ones to plan around.

First, whoever takes control becomes a landlord. R.C. 5321.01(B) defines 'landlord' as 'the owner, lessor, or sublessor of residential premises, the agent of the owner, lessor, or sublessor, or any person authorized by the owner, lessor, or sublessor to manage the premises or to receive rent from a tenant under a rental agreement.' A new management company, a lender collecting rents, a receiver - each is a landlord with Chapter 5321 duties from the moment it is authorised to manage or to take the rent. Second, you cannot sell or pledge the rent away from the repair duty: R.C. 5321.13(E) provides that a rental agreement, or the assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument of the landlord's interest in the rental agreement, may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with R.C. 5321.04, and R.C. 5321.13(A) makes that unwaivable. Third, the lease has to name the right people: R.C. 5321.18(A) requires the owner's and the owner's agent's name and address in every written lease, and R.C. 5321.18(C) makes the sanction for not providing that information a waiver of your right to receive the tenant's R.C. 5321.07 and 5321.08 notices - so a tenant whose lease names a long-gone manager can go straight to rent escrow. Give written notice of the change and paper it, even though no statute compels it. Fourth, if your property sits in an Ohio county over two hundred thousand in population, R.C. 5323.02(C) gives you sixty days after any change to update the owner information filed with the county auditor.

The deposit is the real exposure and it has its own row. Ohio has no statute moving deposit liability to a buyer and no safe harbour for doing it properly, so the thing that protects you is the purchase and sale agreement - itemise the deposits, put them on the rent roll, and get assumption or a price credit in writing. Do not try to solve this with lease language: R.C. 5321.13(D) refuses to recognise any tenant agreement exculpating or limiting a liability of the landlord arising under law, so a clause purporting to release you on sale is not a reliable shield.

Two more things to expect. Showings for a sale are an entry, not a special right: R.C. 5321.04(A)(8) requires reasonable notice of intent to enter and entry at reasonable times, with twenty-four hours presumed reasonable, and R.C. 5321.04(B) gives the tenant damages, injunctive relief and attorney's fees, or termination, for an entry in violation of it. And a change of hands can be involuntary: under R.C. 3767.41(F) a court-appointed receiver over a building found to be a public nuisance may take possession and control, 'establish and collect rents and income, lease and rent the building and the property, and evict tenants' - Ohio does not protect a sitting residential tenant from a receiver, and the receiver's approved spending becomes a first lien ahead of your mortgage.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections; 'purchaser' 73, 'successor' 41, 'transferee' 18 and 'conveyance' 22 all checked, with none a residential sale-or-transfer provision; 'sale of the premises' and 'assignment of the rental agreement' return nothing; and in Chapter 5321 the word 'sale' appears only once, in R.C. 5321.20's rent-control findings. Not reviewed: R.C. 5302.30 (Ohio's residential property disclosure form, which runs to a purchaser rather than a tenant) and R.C. 5301.23 to 5301.25 (recording, and whether an unrecorded lease binds a later buyer), neither of which is held here.

title: How an Ohio Receivership Actually Runs - and the One Moment You Can Still Stop It
bodyText:
This library already tells you that a tenant or a neighbour can put your building into receivership under R.C. 3767.41. This row is the procedure, because knowing the sequence is how you keep control of your building.

Who can start it, and where. A municipal corporation, a township, a neighbour, a tenant or a nonprofit corporation that has improving housing conditions in the county or municipality as one of its goals may apply in a civil action to enforce a local building, housing, air pollution, sanitation, health, fire, zoning or safety code, or in a civil action for abatement. 'Neighbour' is wide: any owner of property within five hundred feet, including someone buying under a land installment contract or a duly executed purchase contract, and any occupant of a building within that distance. The claimant is not liable for the receiver's costs, expenses or fees. If your municipal court has a housing or environmental division, R.C. 1901.181(A)(1) gives it exclusive jurisdiction over these actions, and R.C. 3767.41 overrides anything in the municipal court chapter that conflicts with it.

The steps. The complaint and a notice of the hearing are served on you as owner and on all other interested parties - which R.C. 3767.41(A)(4) defines to include your tenants, mortgagees and lienholders - and if service is refused or unclaimed, the papers are posted conspicuously on the building. The hearing comes no sooner than twenty-eight days after service. If the property is subsidized housing, the claimant must first give you sixty days' written notice specifying the defective conditions, served at the management office or where tenants pay rent, with an attempt to serve the owner of record as well; and the judge must find the property is not a public nuisance if HUD's real estate assessment center scored it seventy-five or higher out of a hundred in the preceding twelve months and conditions have not significantly changed since.

Then the fork, and this is the moment that matters. If the judge finds the building is a public nuisance and finds you have not previously been given a reasonable opportunity to abate, or were given one and did not refuse or fail, the judge may only issue an injunction requiring you to abate - and you get up to thirty days to comply, extendable for good cause. If instead the judge finds you were given a reasonable opportunity and refused or failed, you lose the initiative entirely: the judge must then offer your mortgagees, lienholders and other interested parties, in order of priority of title, the chance to do the work, on proof of ability, a viable financial and construction plan and posted security. Only if none is willing or able, or one takes it on and does not proceed with due diligence, is a receiver appointed - and the receiver must itself have produced a plan costing the labour, the projected income and expenses, the financing and, if rehabilitation is not feasible, demolition. So the whole of your leverage sits in abating when you are first asked.

What the receiver can do to your building. Take possession and control, operate and manage it, establish and collect the rents, re-let it, and evict tenants. Pay operating expenses, taxes, insurance and a managing agent. Pay pre-receivership mortgages. Remove abandoned personal property by court order. Give custody back to you or to a mortgagee. And issue notes secured by mortgages the judge approves, which rank ahead of the receiver's own claims and among themselves by order of recording. The receiver is not personally liable except for misfeasance, malfeasance or nonfeasance, and is paid fees as in a mortgage foreclosure receivership. Approved expenditures and fees become a first lien on the building and land, superior to all prior and subsequent liens and encumbrances including taxes and assessments, once approved by judgment and a certified copy of the entry is recorded within sixty days.

How it ends. Once the receiver reports and the judge confirms the nuisance is abated, the receiver or any interested party may ask for a sale; at the hearing the burden is on you or any objector to prove by a preponderance that the benefits of not selling outweigh selling. Proceeds go first to the receiver's notes, then its unreimbursed expenses and fees, then a selected interested party's approved expenditures, then delinquent taxes and public charges, and only then to pre-receivership mortgages and liens - so your lender, and anything you hoped to recover, sits last. If the costs of the receivership are not paid in full within three days of a declaration that the nuisance is abated, the judge may order a sale on that ground alone. The purchaser's title is incontestable and clear of unsatisfiable state and local tax liens, while all other liens, a properly filed federal tax lien and recorded easements and covenants survive. The judge keeps continuing jurisdiction to review the building's condition, and a demolition will only be ordered if the interested parties requesting it have paid the costs. One carve-out, and it is narrow: 'building' does not include a building occupied by its owner that contains three or fewer residential units.

title: Ohio Has No 'Actual Notice' Standard - It Has One Open Notice and One Closed One
bodyText:
Ohio's landlord-tenant law never uses an 'actual notice' standard, so the question other states answer - may the parties agree an extra way of achieving actual notice, such as a text message - does not arise here in that form. The phrase 'actual notice' appears only twice anywhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters reviewed for this library, in a Medicaid fraud lien provision and in the housing-discrimination civil action, and neither is a tenancy delivery rule. There is no Ohio provision deeming a notice received, no provision letting the lease designate an agreed method that counts as service, and no safe-harbour list.

What Ohio has instead is a split, and the split is what you need to work with. The OPEN notice is R.C. 5321.17: either party 'may terminate or fail to renew' a week-to-week tenancy 'by notice given the other' at least seven days before the termination date, and a month-to-month tenancy by thirty days' notice before the periodic rental date. 'Notice given the other' is all it says - no writing, no method, no proof rule, and that is true even of the mandatory three-day drug-activity termination in R.C. 5321.17(C), which speaks only of 'giving a notice of termination'. The CLOSED notice is R.C. 1923.04(A): the notice to leave that must precede an eviction may be given only by certified mail return receipt requested, by handing a written copy to the defendant in person, or by leaving it at the defendant's usual place of abode or at the premises. That is a court-procedure prerequisite, and your lease does not get to add a fourth method to it.

So your lease can do useful work on the open notices - name an address, name an email, say that notice may be given by any of several routes - and the limit is one-directional. R.C. 5321.13(A) says no provision of Chapter 5321 may be modified or waived by any agreement except the duty-shift in its division (F). Adding a permitted route is not a modification, because the chapter prescribes none. Making your route the ONLY way the tenant may give a R.C. 5321.17 notice takes away something the chapter gives, and is void. Write it as 'notice may be given by any of the following', never 'notice is effective only if'.

There is a sleeper in the same family that costs landlords real money. R.C. 5321.07(A) says the tenant's written repair complaint - the notice that starts the thirty-day clock and opens the rent-escrow route - 'shall be sent to the person or place where rent is normally paid.' Wherever your lease sends the rent is therefore also where the notice that can put your rent in a court account arrives. If rent goes to a lockbox, a bank, an online portal or a third-party processor, a repair notice delivered there has been delivered. Name a person and an address that someone actually reads, keep R.C. 5321.18's owner and agent information current, and remember that failing to give that information waives your right to this notice altogether - which sounds like a relief and is the opposite, because it lets the tenant go straight to escrow without giving you the cure window.

Two related points are carried elsewhere so this row does not repeat them: whether a notice may be delivered electronically at all, and on what conditions, and which Ohio notices your lease may change and which it may not.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - not the whole Revised Code, and no court rules or forms.

title: Ohio's Adverse-Proceeding Notices Nearly All Run to the Owner - Nobody Has to Tell Your Tenant, and Nobody Has to Tell You About Theirs
bodyText:
Ohio has no general rule requiring notice of a proceeding that threatens a tenancy - not from you to the tenant, and not from the tenant to you. What it has is a short set of specific duties, and almost all of them run in one direction: to the OWNER.

Where Ohio does require notice of an adverse proceeding. If you own a condominium unit and rent it out, R.C. 5311.19(B)(1) lets the unit owners association evict your tenant for breaching the declaration, bylaws or rules - and it must bring that action as your agent, in YOUR name. R.C. 5311.19(B)(2) gives you at least ten days' written notice of the intended eviction, and R.C. 5311.19(B)(3) charges the costs and reasonable attorney's fees to you as a special assessment and a lien on your unit. Ten days is the whole of your warning, so keep the association's notice address current and read what it sends. If your rental is a lot in a planned community, R.C. 5312.11 lets the owners association assess your lot for costs caused by the willful or negligent act of an occupant, tenant, guest or invitee, with divisions (C) and (D) requiring written notice to YOU describing the violation and the proposed charge, a right to a hearing before the board, and no levy before a requested hearing is held. And if someone petitions to put your building into receivership as a public nuisance, R.C. 3767.41(B)(2) requires the complaint and a notice of the hearing date and time to be served on the owner and all interested parties under the Rules of Civil Procedure, with posting on the building if service is refused, and the hearing may not be held until at least twenty-eight days after service.

The one adverse proceeding where the tenant is notified in their own right is a taking. R.C. 163.01(E) defines 'owner' as anyone 'having any estate, title, or interest' in the property, and (F) brings 'any estate, title, or interest' within the property appropriated. A leasehold is an estate, so your tenant is an owner for Ohio's appropriation procedures and is entitled to the agency's good-faith offer directly. You are not the conduit and you cannot assume you will hear first.

And the gap, which is the part worth planning for: a forced sale. Ohio's execution chapter runs to one hundred and one sections and never uses the word 'tenant' or the word 'occupant'. Nothing requires a foreclosure plaintiff, a judgment creditor or a purchaser to give a tenancy-specific notice, and R.C. 1923.02(A)(3) then lets a purchaser at a sale of real estate on execution bring an eviction against a judgment debtor who was in possession when judgment was rendered. So a proceeding brought against you can end with a stranger seeking possession from your tenant, and a proceeding or lien aimed at your tenant can surface without anyone telling you. Two limbs could not be read and you should treat them as open: whether a foreclosure plaintiff must name or serve an occupant, which lives in Revised Code Chapter 2323 (R.C. 2323.07 is the foreclosure and judicial sale section), and the notice rules for a tax foreclosure. Neither chapter is held in this library and neither was fetched.

What to do about it. There is no statutory way to make a tenant forward a notice of proceedings affecting the property, so the lease has to create the duty - this library carries a clause for exactly that, and it is worth using, because without it you have nothing. Be clear-eyed about its limits: breach of it carries no statutory damages-and-fees award in Ohio, since the award in R.C. 5321.05(C)(1) attaches only to the statutory tenant duties, and R.C. 5321.13(C) refuses to recognise any agreement to pay your attorney's fees. It is an ordinary lease breach: your actual damages are recoverable (R.C. 5321.12), and breach of a written lease term is a possession ground (R.C. 1923.02(A)(9)), but neither is likely to be worth much here. The clause buys you early warning more than a claim. Pair it with your own monitoring: watch the county recorder and the clerk of courts for your own parcels rather than relying on being told.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - not the whole Revised Code, and no court rules.

title: Ohio's Consumer Sales Practices Act Does Not Reach Your Lease - But It Can Reach What You Sell Alongside It
bodyText:
Ohio has a full consumer protection regime - the Consumer Sales Practices Act in R.C. Chapter 1345, with Attorney General enforcement, rulemaking under R.C. 1345.05 and the deceptive-acts rules in Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3 - and a residential lease sits outside it. R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a 'consumer transaction' as 'a sale, lease, assignment, award by chance, or other transfer of an item of goods, a service, a franchise, or an intangible' to an individual for personal, family or household purposes. The word 'lease' is in the definition, which is why people get this wrong; what can be leased is goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible. Real property is not in the list, and the exclusions that follow carve out utilities, home construction service contracts, accountants, lawyers, doctors, dentists and veterinarians without ever mentioning a landlord. The Act misses your lease by omission, not by exemption. The Attorney General's 109:4-3 rules contain no 'landlord', no 'tenant', no 'lessor' used as a landlord and no 'rental agreement' at all, and across Chapters 1345 and 1349 the word 'landlord' never appears.

So the answers to the usual questions are all no. Ohio's consumer statutes do not list leaving blank spaces at signing or failing to give a copy at signing as unlawful practices - neither phrase appears anywhere in the thirty-seven chapters reviewed here. There is no Ohio provision making a lease induced by a deceptive practice 'unenforceable by the lessor', and no guarantor question arising from one. Where the Act does apply, R.C. 1345.02(A) bars any unfair or deceptive act in connection with a consumer transaction 'whether it occurs before, during, or after the transaction', and R.C. 1345.09 gives the consumer rescission or actual economic damages plus up to five thousand dollars in noneconomic damages, trebled to three times actual damages or two hundred dollars, whichever is greater, where the practice had already been declared deceptive by rule or by a published court decision. Those are serious remedies, which is why the boundary matters.

And the boundary is not the same as your business. The Act follows the transaction, not the person: if you also sell or lease goods or services to your residents - furniture or appliance rental, a laundry or valet-trash service contract, a renter's-insurance or deposit-alternative product, a resident-benefits package, moving or cleaning services - that transaction can be a consumer transaction and you can be a 'supplier' for it even though the lease itself is not. Price, bill and describe those products as carefully as a retailer would, and keep them documented separately from the rent.

Two cautions. First, no Ohio appellate decision is in this library, so this row rests on statutory text alone; whether an Ohio court has drawn the line differently in a particular setting was not researched, and a submetered utility resold by a landlord is a genuinely unsettled case because the Act's own exclusion is keyed to utility-company definitions. Second, a separate consumer statute does touch tenancies once, in your favour: R.C. 1349.52(L)(3) relieves a consumer reporting agency of the duty to place a security freeze on a database used solely for criminal-record, loss-history, fraud, employment-screening or tenant-screening information - so a tenant's credit freeze does not necessarily stop a tenant-screening report drawn from such a database. That is the only place a tenancy is mentioned in either consumer chapter.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections - Chapter 1345 (68 sections) and Chapter 1349 (60 sections) among them - plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters including 109:4-3. Not the whole Revised Code, and no case law.

title: Ohio Dictates Almost Nothing About What Your Lease Says - Three Items, and Only One Is Mandatory
bodyText:
Ohio prescribes lease content in one section and one section only. R.C. 5321.18(A) says every written rental agreement for residential premises shall contain the name and address of the owner and the name and address of the owner's agent, if any - and where the owner or the agent is an entity, that address must be the principal place of business in the county where the property sits, or if there is none there, the entity's principal place of business in Ohio, with the name of the person in charge. If the tenancy is oral, R.C. 5321.18(B) makes you deliver the same information in a written notice at the start of occupancy. The sanction in R.C. 5321.18(C) is why this is not a formality: fail to give it and you waive the tenant's R.C. 5321.07 and 5321.08 notices, so the tenant can go to rent escrow without ever giving you a cure window.

Two more items are conditional, not mandatory. If you are a party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and you want to keep the rent-escrow exemption, R.C. 5321.07(C) makes you say so in the written rental agreement - omit it and you lose the exemption. And if you are a college or university letting to your own student tenant, R.C. 5321.031 makes the written rental agreement specify the conditions under which it may be terminated and the institution's notice and hearing procedures.

Everything else people expect is absent. Nothing requires the start and end dates to appear on the first page, or anywhere in particular. Nothing requires the lease to state the rent, the term, the deposit, the parties' signatures, a page count or a table of contents, and nothing requires a particular order, caption or type size. R.C. 5321.06 is why: the lease may carry any terms the parties agree that are not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or another rule of law, and the chapter almost never says what the terms must look like. The near-miss is worth knowing because it shows what a content rule looks like when Ohio writes one: R.C. 4781.51 requires a manufactured-home-park rental agreement to carry the identity information and, in ten-point boldface type, a prescribed paragraph telling the resident which sections protect them. A park lot is outside Chapter 5321, though not for the reason usually given: R.C. 4781.01(W) makes a park's 'residential premises' the LOT and its grounds, while R.C. 5321.01(C) reaches a dwelling unit, and sections 4781.36 to 4781.52 are a complete parallel code for park lettings. None of it reaches an ordinary rental.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - not the whole Revised Code. Outside Chapter 5321 the formalities that do bite are a signature and acknowledgment for a term over three years and the writing needed to sue on a term over one year; those are covered separately.

title: Ohio Never Makes You Give the Tenant a Copy - Which Is a Problem for You, Not for Them
bodyText:
No Ohio statute requires you to give a residential tenant a copy of the signed lease. There is no delivery duty, no deadline, no acknowledgment to collect, and - because there is no duty - no provision making a failure to deliver a defence to enforcement, a bar to suing, or a ground for the tenant to terminate. The only thing Ohio makes you put in the tenant's hands about the agreement is the owner's and the agent's name and address, which R.C. 5321.18 requires in the written lease itself, or as a separate written notice at the start of occupancy if the tenancy is oral.

That is worth knowing because the absence cuts against you. Two of your most important rights turn on what the lease says and therefore on your ability to prove the tenant was bound by it. R.C. 5321.16(B) lets you apply the deposit to damages from the tenant's noncompliance 'with section 5321.05 of the Revised Code or the rental agreement' - and the 'or the rental agreement' limb is only as good as your proof of the terms, which is hard to make against a tenant who was never given them. R.C. 1923.02(A)(9) gives you an eviction ground for breach of an obligation imposed by a WRITTEN rental agreement, which again puts the document in evidence. Nothing stops you from closing the gap yourself: R.C. 5321.06 lets the lease carry a receipt and acknowledgment term, and the companion clause in this library does exactly that.

The contrast shows what an Ohio copy duty looks like when the legislature writes one. R.C. 5313.02(A) makes every land installment contract be executed in duplicate with a copy provided to both the vendor and the vendee, and R.C. 5313.02(C) makes the vendor record it and deliver a copy to the county auditor within twenty days. Nothing of the kind exists for a lease.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters, including the Attorney General's deceptive-acts rules - not the whole Revised Code. One limb was not read and is open: whether a licensed Ohio real estate broker or property manager owes a delivery duty to the tenant under the licensing law. That is Revised Code Chapter 4735, which this library does not hold and which could not be fetched; R.C. 4735.55 (agency agreements, including leases over eighteen months) is the section named there. If you manage under a licence, check your licensing obligations separately - the answer here is only that the landlord-tenant chapter imposes nothing.

title: Nothing in Ohio Has to Be Initialled - and the Only Lease Signature Ohio Ever Requires Is Yours
bodyText:
No Ohio statute requires a tenant to initial, separately sign, or separately acknowledge any part of a residential lease. There is no clause Ohio singles out for a set of initials, no provision making a term unenforceable because it was not initialled, and no provision making a term enforceable because it was. Ohio also prescribes no capitalisation, no minimum type size and no conspicuousness standard for anything in a residential lease - the one place the Revised Code does that for a letting is R.C. 4781.51(D), a manufactured-home-park provision requiring a prescribed paragraph in ten-point boldface type, and Park lots sit outside Chapter 5321 on their own definitions - R.C. 4781.01(W) makes a park's 'residential premises' the LOT, and sections 4781.36 to 4781.52 are a separate code for them.

The surprising part is the other direction. Chapter 5321 nowhere requires the tenant to sign the lease at all, because R.C. 5321.01(D) brings an oral rental agreement inside the chapter. The only Ohio signature requirement that touches a lease runs against YOU: R.C. 5301.01(A) requires a lease of an interest in real property to be signed by the lessor and the signing acknowledged before a notary or one of the other named officials - and R.C. 5301.08 lifts that for any term not exceeding three years. So for an ordinary one-year lease Ohio requires no signature from anyone, and for a term over three years it requires your signature and your acknowledgment, not the tenant's initials.

Use initials anyway, by choice rather than by rule. R.C. 5321.06 lets your lease carry them, and they are the cheapest evidence that a particular term was read - which matters in Ohio precisely because nothing makes you give the tenant a copy and because R.C. 5321.14 lets a court decline to enforce an unconscionable term. Put them next to the terms a tenant is most likely to dispute later: the deposit deduction provisions, pet and smoking rules, the entry provisions, any automatic-renewal term, and any addendum.
