Do not put them next to anything that reads as a waiver of a Chapter 5321 right, because R.C. 5321.13(A) voids that whether it is initialled or not, and initials next to a void term do nothing except show you meant it.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - not the whole Revised Code. City rental codes were not reviewed.

title: Ohio Tells You What the Notice Must Say and Nothing About What Else It May Say - Which Is Where Landlords Lose
bodyText:
Ohio prescribes a floor for the notice to leave and no ceiling. R.C. 1923.04(A) requires every landlord notice to recover residential premises to contain its three sentences 'printed or written in a conspicuous manner', and says nothing at all about what else the notice may carry. No Ohio provision limits the content of a notice to vacate, forbids extra language, requires a reason, or voids a notice for saying too much. The phrases that would do that - 'notice to vacate', 'additional language', 'demand for rent' - appear nowhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters reviewed here. So the risk is not that Ohio bans something; it is that nothing protects you from what you add.

Three things routinely added to an Ohio notice cause trouble. First, pay-or-quit language. Ohio gives a tenant no statutory right to cure a nonpayment, and R.C. 1923.04(A)'s notice is a notice to LEAVE, not a demand for rent. Offering a cure window you do not have to offer, and then accepting the money, can undo the notice - taking rent after serving it is the classic way an Ohio landlord loses a case. Second, a stated reason. Nothing requires one, and a reason you state becomes something the tenant can contest, and something a court can weigh against R.C. 5321.02's retaliation bar. Third, naming the wrong people: no Ohio eviction may name a minor tenant as a defendant where a parent or adult guardian is also named. Keep the notice to the prescribed sentences, the premises, the date and your identity.

One structural trap in the same section. R.C. 1923.04(B) says that service of the notice required by R.C. 5321.17(C) - the mandatory three-day drug-activity termination - 'constitutes compliance with the notice requirement of division (A) of this section', and so does a R.C. 5313.06 land-contract forfeiture notice. But division (A)'s prescribed language is required of 'Every notice given under this section', and a R.C. 5321.17(C) notice is given under a different section. Read literally, you can satisfy (A) with a notice that does not carry (A)'s words. Do not run that experiment: include the prescribed paragraph in any notice you expect to found an eviction, since adding it costs nothing and omitting it risks the case.

On the other half of the topic, Ohio has no prohibition on altering the unit while a notice to vacate is pending - no provision bars work that makes a unit uninhabitable, and 'uninhabitable' does not appear in these chapters at all. It gets to a similar place by three other routes, and you should treat them as the answer. Your R.C. 5321.04 duties keep running: nothing in Chapter 5321 suspends them because you have served a notice or filed a case. R.C. 5321.15 bars self-help outright - no lock change, no utility shutoff, no removing the tenant's belongings - and the only lawful routes to possession are Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321. And R.C. 5321.02 makes retaliatory conduct unlawful, which is exactly how a court will read work timed to make a unit unlivable after a tenant complained. A tenant can also raise defences and counterclaims during the case under R.C. 1923.061, so the conduct arrives in front of the same judge deciding possession.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - not the whole Revised Code, and no court rules, local court forms or city rental codes.

title: Ohio Does Not Make You List the Terms That Favour You - It Voids Them Instead
bodyText:
Some states run a plain-language consumer-contract regime on residential leases: a readability test, a front-page statement listing every term that restricts the tenant or waives a tenant right, an optional route to have the form pre-approved by the attorney general, and a dollar figure above which the regime stops applying. Ohio has none of the four. There is no consumer-contract statute reaching a lease, no statement of consumer restrictions, no front-page or first-page requirement anywhere in Ohio lease law, no process for submitting a lease form to the Attorney General or any other office for approval, and no dollar threshold switching anything on or off. Do not put a 'statement of consumer restrictions' heading in an Ohio lease; it points at a regime that does not exist here and invites a tenant to argue the list was incomplete.

The reason is structural. R.C. 1345.01(A) builds the Consumer Sales Practices Act on a 'consumer transaction' in 'an item of goods, a service, a franchise, or an intangible', so a lease of real property is outside it by omission, and the Attorney General's deceptive-acts rules made under that Act - Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3 - contain no 'landlord', 'tenant', 'lessor' or 'rental agreement' at all. With no jurisdiction there is no form review, which is why Ohio has no preapproval route.

Ohio took the opposite approach to landlord-protective terms: rather than require you to disclose them, it voids the ones it objects to. R.C. 5321.13 makes no provision of Chapter 5321 modifiable or waivable by any agreement except the one-way duty-shift in its division (F), refuses to recognise any agreement to pay either party's attorney's fees, bars a warrant of attorney to confess judgment, and bars any tenant agreement exculpating, limiting or indemnifying your liability arising under law. R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause. So the Ohio equivalent of a waiver list is a prohibition list, and it operates whether or not the lease discloses anything.

One Ohio statute does the exact thing this topic describes, and it is not yours. R.C. 4781.51(D) requires a manufactured-home-park rental agreement to carry, in ten-point boldface type, a prescribed paragraph telling the resident that their rights and the operator's rights are protected by named sections of the Revised Code. That is Ohio's only prescribed lease paragraph with a type size attached, and Park lots sit outside Chapter 5321 on their own definitions - R.C. 4781.01(W) makes a park's 'residential premises' the LOT and its grounds, while R.C. 5321.01(C) reaches a dwelling unit - so it does not reach an ordinary rental.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters including 109:4-3 - not the whole Revised Code, and no city rental code.

title: Ohio Has No Plain-Language Law - It Gave a Judge a Veto Instead
bodyText:
Ohio has no plain-language or readable-contract statute of any kind, and none that reaches a residential lease. There is no readability test, no reading-grade standard, no requirement that the lease be divided into captioned sections or carry a table of contents, no minimum type size, no dollar ceiling or threshold that switches such a regime on, and no state office that reviews or approves a lease form.

Ohio's consumer statutes are not a back door, and it is worth knowing exactly why, because the definition reads as though they might be. R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a 'consumer transaction' as 'a sale, lease, assignment, award by chance, or other transfer of an item of goods, a service, a franchise, or an intangible' to an individual for personal, family or household purposes. The word 'lease' is right there - but look at what can be leased: goods, a service, a franchise, an intangible. Real property is simply not in the list, and the long set of express exclusions that follows carves out utilities, home construction contracts, accountants, lawyers, doctors, dentists and veterinarians without ever needing to mention a landlord. The Consumer Sales Practices Act misses your lease by omission, not by exemption, which also means there is nothing for a court to read narrowly. The Attorney General's deceptive-acts rules made under that Act, Ohio Adm.Code 109:4-3, contain no 'landlord', no 'tenant', no 'lessor' used as a landlord and no 'rental agreement' at all. Nor is there an Ohio counterpart to the consumer-contract statutes some states use: Chapter 1349's provisions run to sale escrows, residential mortgages, security-breach notices, high-volume online sellers and age verification, not to leasing a home.

What Ohio put in place of a readability rule is a judge. R.C. 5321.14 lets a court that finds a rental agreement or any clause in it unconscionable refuse to enforce it or limit its application, and R.C. 5321.13 flatly voids the worst terms whatever words they are dressed in. So the discipline on confusing drafting is retrospective and judicial rather than prospective and statutory: nobody will tell you in advance that your lease is too hard to read, and a court can decline to enforce the term you most relied on. Draft plainly because the only test is the one applied after the dispute starts, and keep defined terms, cross-references and double negatives out of the clauses that do the real work - deposit deductions, fees, renewal, entry and termination.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, together with the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters, which include the Attorney General's 109:4-3 rules - not the whole Revised Code, and not any city rental code.

title: Ohio's Complete List of Lease Disclosures Is Short - and Adding a Purchase Option Can Change the Statute You Are Under
bodyText:
Here is everything an Ohio residential tenancy makes you disclose, and the list is genuinely this short. One mandatory item: R.C. 5321.18 requires the owner's and the agent's name and address in every written rental agreement, delivered as a written notice at the start of occupancy if the tenancy is oral, and R.C. 5321.18(C) punishes a failure by waiving the tenant's R.C. 5321.07 and 5321.08 notices to you. One conditional item for your own benefit: if your rental agreements cover three or fewer dwelling units, R.C. 5321.07(C) makes you state that fact in the written lease to keep the rent-escrow exemption. One institutional item: R.C. 5321.031 makes a college or university letting to its own student tenant specify in the written agreement the conditions for termination and the institution's notice and hearing procedures. And one federal item, the lead-based-paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing.

What Ohio does not require. There is no notice of whether the unit is covered by a just-cause or rent-increase law - Ohio has neither, and R.C. 5321.19 preempts local rent control. No state-published form has to be the first page of the lease, or anywhere in it. No state agency publishes a tenant-rights summary you must hand over or have signed. Nothing has to be attached to the rental agreement as an exhibit.

Now the trap in adding an option. If your tenant merely has an OPTION to buy, R.C. 5313.01(A) says in terms that option contracts for the purchase of real property are not land installment contracts, so Chapter 5313 does not reach you. But if the arrangement is one where you agree to convey title and the occupant agrees to pay a purchase price in installments while you hold title as security, and it cannot be fully performed within a year, it is a land installment contract whatever you call it - and then R.C. 5313.02 imposes sixteen required provisions (parties' current mailing addresses, signing dates, legal description, contract price, separate fees, down payment, principal balance, each installment's amount and due date, the interest rate and how it is computed, encumbrances, a deed promise, evidence of title, a mortgage-default credit, a recording promise, tax responsibility and any pending public-agency order), requires execution in duplicate with a copy to each party, and requires you to record it and deliver a copy to the county auditor within twenty days. The forfeiture route then runs on R.C. 5313.06 rather than on an eviction notice. Draft the option as an option, keep the rent and the option price separate, and do not let a lease-purchase drift into an installment sale by accident.

One limb could not be read and you should treat it as open: whether granting a purchase option makes you a 'seller' owing Ohio's property-condition disclosure statement, and when it would be due. That duty is in Revised Code Chapter 5302, usually cited as R.C. 5302.30, which this library does not hold and which could not be fetched in this review - so nothing here says you owe it or that you do not. What was proved inside the thirty-seven chapters held here, 1,953 sections, is that no provision in them imposes a property-condition disclosure on a landlord or on a lessor granting an option. Ask a title company or counsel before you sign a lease-option.

title: No Ohio Rental Guide to Hand Over - Ohio Writes That Duty for Nursing Homes and Car Dealers, Not Landlords
bodyText:
Ohio does not require you to give a prospective tenant a state-published rights-and-responsibilities guide before signing, at renewal, or ever. There is no such guide, no delivery duty, no signed acknowledgment to collect and keep, and no consequence for not providing one - no fine, no tenant defence, and nothing suspending your right to sue. The reason is checkable: Chapter 5321 names no administering agency. Across its twenty-three sections no department and no director appears, and the only 'agency' it mentions is a governmental agency that has found a code violation. No Ohio office is told to publish a tenant guide, so there is nothing for a delivery duty to attach to.

Ohio does write exactly this duty elsewhere, which is how you can be sure the omission is deliberate rather than an oversight. For a nursing home, R.C. 3721.12(A)(3) makes the administrator furnish each resident and sponsor, prior to or at the time of admission, a copy of the statutory residents' rights, a written explanation of named sections, the home's policies and procedures, the home's rules, and a list of the addresses and telephone numbers of the county board of health, the county department of job and family services, the state departments of health and medicaid, the offices of the department of aging and any Ohio nursing home ombudsman programme - and R.C. 3721.12(B) makes written acknowledgment of receipt part of the resident's record. That is the full guide-and-acknowledgment pattern, and R.C. 5321.01(C)(2) expressly puts Chapter 3721 homes outside 'residential premises', so none of it reaches you.

Two Ohio provisions look adjacent and are not the same duty. R.C. 5321.07(C) does make you tell the tenant something about the law, but it runs in YOUR favour: if your rental agreements cover three or fewer dwelling units and you want to keep the rent-escrow exemption, say so in the written lease, or deliver written notice of it at the start of an oral tenancy - omit it and you lose the exemption. And R.C. 5321.18 makes you give the owner's and the agent's name and address, which is information about you, not a summary of the law.

The only state-written words about a tenant's rights that Ohio ever puts in your hands arrive at the end of the tenancy. R.C. 1923.04(A) requires every landlord notice to recover residential premises to carry, printed or written in a conspicuous manner: 'You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance.'

A plain written summary of Ohio's deposit rules, repair and escrow route, entry notice and termination notice periods is still worth giving - it cuts disputes and costs nothing - but write it yourself, mark it clearly as your own summary and not a state document, and do not let it contradict the lease.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - not the whole Revised Code, and no city rental code.

title: Who Ohio's Landlord-Tenant Law Covers - Ten Exclusions, Four Section-Level Carve-Outs, and a Hotel Problem
bodyText:
Chapter 5321 applies to 'residential premises', which R.C. 5321.01(C) defines as a dwelling unit for residential use and occupancy, the structure it is part of, the facilities and appurtenances in it, and the grounds, areas and facilities for tenants generally or promised to the tenant. It expressly INCLUDES a dwelling unit owned or operated by a college or university. It excludes ten things: (1) prisons, jails, workhouses and other places of incarceration, including halfway houses and residential arrangements required as a community control or post-release control sanction or as parole; (2) hospitals and similar medical institutions, and homes licensed under Chapter 3721; (3) tourist homes, hotels, motels, recreational vehicle parks, recreation camps, combined park-camps, temporary park-camps and similar facilities 'where circumstances indicate a transient occupancy'; (4) elementary and secondary boarding schools where room and board is part of tuition; (5) orphanages and similar institutions; (6) farm residences furnished with the rental of at least two acres for agricultural production by an occupant; (7) dwelling units subject to Chapter 3733; (8) occupancy by an owner of a condominium unit; (9) certain 501(c)(3) single-room-occupancy facility stays; and (10) 501(c)(3) emergency shelters for transient occupants.

Read exclusion (7) carefully, because it is widely misread. Chapter 3733 of the Revised Code is AGRICULTURAL LABOR CAMPS - eleven sections, R.C. 3733.41 to 3733.99. It is not the manufactured-home-park chapter, and it never was the limb this exclusion pointed at: before 2023 the exclusion read 'sections 3733.41 to 3733.49', which are the labour-camp sections, and the budget act broadened it to the whole chapter at the same time as the park provisions moved out to Chapter 4781. So (7) excludes agricultural-labour-camp housing. Manufactured-home-park lots are outside Chapter 5321 for a different reason: R.C. 4781.01(W) defines a park's 'residential premises' as the LOT and the park's grounds and facilities, not a dwelling unit, and R.C. 4781.36 to 4781.52 is a complete parallel code for park lettings with its own obligations, rent deposits, security-deposit rule, unconscionability test and lease-content requirement. If you rent out a HOME inside a park rather than a lot, do not assume you are in the park regime; take advice.

Scope also narrows inside the chapter, not only at its door. R.C. 5321.07(C) takes the rent-escrow section away from a landlord who is a party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units AND says so in the written lease, and R.C. 5321.07(D) takes it away entirely for a dwelling unit occupied by a student tenant. R.C. 5321.031 then adds a termination-and-hearing regime that applies only where a college or university lets to its own student tenant.

Now the hotel problem, which matters if you run extended-stay or furnished lettings. The (C)(3) exclusion is QUALIFIED: it reaches hotels and motels 'where circumstances indicate a transient occupancy'. A hotel licence does not satisfy that on its own. R.C. 3731.01(A)(6) defines 'transient' as not more than thirty days, and R.C. 3731.01(A)(4) defines a 'residential hotel' as one offering NON-transient dwelling units 'for a minimum stay of more than thirty days' - so a residential hotel is, by its own definition, not a place of transient occupancy. R.C. 3731.01(A)(1) also says 'hotel' does not include apartment houses, apartments or other similar places of permanent personal residence, lodging houses, rooming houses or dormitories, and R.C. 3731.01(B) says the hotel chapter does not apply at all to apartment buildings and other structures in which all the units are residential premises. Worse for the assumption, R.C. 3731.041 lets a licensed TRANSIENT hotel keep a guest for up to two hundred seventy continuous days in up to forty per cent of designated rooms if it installs an approved fire alarm and detection system - so a very long stay inside a transient hotel is expressly contemplated by the hotel chapter, while the circumstances of that stay look nothing like transient occupancy. The cautious course, and the one to run your business on until a court says otherwise: where an occupant's stay is in substance non-transient - the unit is their residence, the stay runs past thirty days, rent is periodic - treat them as a tenant with full Chapter 5321 rights, give the R.C. 5321.17 termination notice and the R.C. 1923.04(A) notice to leave, and go to court for possession rather than locking a door. R.C. 5321.15 makes self-help unlawful and the downside of guessing wrong is a damages claim, not a cheaper eviction.

One genuine divergence to carry with you: the county rental-registration chapter draws its lines differently. R.C. 5323.01(A) takes 'hotel' straight from R.C. 3731.01 and R.C. 5323.01(E) says 'residential rental property' does not include a hotel or a college or university dormitory, with NO transient-occupancy qualifier - and (D) and (E) confine the whole chapter to counties over two hundred thousand by the most recent decennial census. So the same building can be inside Chapter 5321 and outside Chapter 5323, and a college dormitory is inside Chapter 5321 and outside the registration duty.

Finally, four things Ohio does NOT do. No term-length exclusion: none of the ten (C) exclusions turns on how long the lease runs, so a long residential lease is still inside the chapter. No lease-date gating: no Chapter 5321 duty applies only to agreements entered into on or after a date. No local-adoption mechanism: Chapter 5321 applies statewide, and R.C. 5321.19 preempts local measures regulating rental-agreement rights the chapter regulates, preserving only housing, building, health and safety codes, rent for premises the subdivision itself owns, and voluntary-incentive programmes. And no 'multiple dwelling' definition at all - Ohio sets its small-landlord lines by other numbers.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - not the whole Revised Code, and no city rental code. Leases on or within a reservation or on trust land were NOT researched and are a question of federal and tribal law, not Ohio law.

A correction to the count: there are four of these section-level carve-outs, not two, and three of them concern a student tenant. R.C. 5321.07(C) withdraws the rent-escrow section from a landlord party to agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units who gives notice of that fact, and (D) withdraws it for a unit occupied by a student tenant. R.C. 5321.03(C) adds that the landlord's possession grounds in that section 'does not apply to a dwelling unit occupied by a student tenant'. And R.C. 1923.02(D) goes furthest: 'This chapter does not apply to a student tenant as defined by division (H) of section 5321.01 of the Revised Code when the college or university proceeds to terminate a rental agreement pursuant to section 5321.031 of the Revised Code' - the whole forcible entry and detainer chapter, withdrawn. So a college or university terminating its own student tenant's agreement under R.C. 5321.031 is outside chapter 1923 altogether and proceeds under the notice-and-hearing procedures the lease must specify.

title: Ohio's Statute of Frauds Bars the Lawsuit, Not the Tenancy - and It Says Nothing About Giving the Lease Back
bodyText:
Ohio's statute of frauds works differently from how landlords assume, and the difference decides cases. R.C. 1335.05 says no action shall be brought to charge a defendant on a contract or sale of lands or an interest in them, 'or upon an agreement that is not to be performed within one year from the making thereof', unless the agreement or a memorandum of it is in writing and signed by the party to be charged. Read that carefully: it bars the ACTION, not the agreement. An oral two-year tenancy is not void in Ohio - R.C. 5321.01(D) brings an oral rental agreement squarely inside the landlord-tenant chapter, with all your duties and all the tenant's - you simply may be unable to sue on it. R.C. 1335.04 is the other limb: no lease, estate or interest of freehold or term of years in land 'shall be assigned or granted except by deed, or note in writing, signed by the party assigning or granting it', or by an agent authorised in writing, or 'by act and operation of law'. So the grant and any assignment need a signed writing, and note that last escape clause, which is wider than people expect.

Two gaps worth knowing. First, R.C. 1335.04 names assigning and granting; it does not name a SURRENDER. Nothing in it expressly requires a writing for a tenant to give the leasehold back, which is one more reason to take a written, dated surrender rather than keys and a conversation - and to say in the lease that a surrender must be in writing. Second, the Revised Code contains no part-performance provision; whether paying rent and taking possession takes an oral long lease out of R.C. 1335.05 is a case-law question, and no Ohio case law was reviewed here.

Ohio has no long-lease exclusion. Several states cut leases of five years or more, or seven, out of their landlord-tenant act. Ohio does not: R.C. 5321.01(C)'s ten exclusions from 'residential premises' are about the TYPE of occupancy - prisons, hospitals and Chapter 3721 homes, transient hotels and camps, boarding schools, orphanages, two-acre farm residences, units subject to Chapter 3733, a condominium owner's own occupancy, and two categories of charitable facility - and not one of them turns on how long the term is. A thirty-year residential ground lease and a one-year apartment lease are both inside Chapter 5321.

What the term length does change is formalities. A lease of three years or less needs no acknowledgment and no recording; above three years R.C. 5301.01(A) requires your signature acknowledged before a notary, a judge, a clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer or a mayor, and the lease should be recorded. The companion row in this library carries those thresholds. One limb could not be read and you should treat it as open: whether an unacknowledged long lease is merely unrecordable or actually ineffective against a later good-faith purchaser or a foreclosure buyer. That turns on R.C. 5301.25, in Revised Code Chapter 5301, which this library does not hold and which was not fetched. What was proved from inside the thirty-seven chapters held here is that no provision in them makes a lease invalid for want of a writing, acknowledgment or recording.

Finally, the practical teeth. R.C. 1923.02(A)(9) gives you an eviction ground for breach of an obligation 'imposed upon them by a written rental agreement' - so with an oral tenancy you have no general lease-breach ground at all. And if your lease-option drifts into an installment sale, R.C. 5313.07 takes forfeiture away from you once the buyer has paid for five years or more, or has paid twenty per cent of the price, and makes you foreclose instead. Put it in writing, signed, every time.

title: Ohio Prescribes a Rights Statement for a Car Lease and a Trailer Lot - Not for a Home
bodyText:
No Ohio statute requires a statement of tenant rights with a residential lease. Nothing has to be attached as the lease's first page, nothing has to be signed page by page, no state agency publishes a statement for you to deliver, and nothing bars you from suing a tenant until you have provided one. Ohio prescribes no first page, no page-by-page signature and no attachment to a residential rental agreement of any kind.

The omission is deliberate, and two Ohio statutes show what the legislature writes when it wants this. For a motor vehicle, R.C. 1345.74(A) makes the manufacturer, directly or through the dealer or lessor, provide the consumer 'a written statement on a separate piece of paper, in ten-point type, all capital letters' in substantially a prescribed form - 'IMPORTANT: IF THIS VEHICLE IS DEFECTIVE, YOU MAY BE ENTITLED UNDER STATE LAW TO A REPLACEMENT OR TO COMPENSATION' - and for a leased vehicle it must be given at the time the lease agreement is executed. For a manufactured-home-park lot, R.C. 4781.51(D) makes every written rental agreement carry, in ten-point boldface type, a prescribed paragraph telling the resident that their rights and the park operator's are protected by named Revised Code sections. So Ohio knows how to require a separate-sheet, fixed-type-size, prescribed-words rights statement at lease execution; it simply has never done it for housing. Park lots sit outside Chapter 5321 on their own definitions - R.C. 4781.01(W) makes a park's 'residential premises' the LOT - so neither provision reaches you.

The only prescribed tenant-rights language Ohio ever puts in a landlord's hands comes at the end. R.C. 1923.04(A) requires every landlord notice to recover residential premises to contain, printed or written in a conspicuous manner: 'You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance.' Get that language wrong and your eviction is at risk. The one thing Ohio requires in the lease itself is the owner's and the agent's name and address under R.C. 5321.18, and failing to give it waives your right to the tenant's repair and escrow notices.

Practical consequence: if you use a multi-state lease template, strip out any 'Statement of Tenant Rights' page, any 'state-required disclosure' heading and any instruction to initial each page in the Ohio version. Those pages invite a tenant to argue you adopted a standard Ohio does not impose, and an incomplete adopted summary is worse than none.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - not the whole Revised Code, and no city rental code.

title: Ohio Never Makes You Translate a Lease - But Advertising in One Language and Leasing in Another Is a Fair-Housing Problem
bodyText:
Ohio imposes no translation duty on a residential landlord. There is no requirement to provide the lease in the tenant's language, no requirement triggered by advertising or negotiating in another language, no certified-translation rule, no provision giving a translated version equal standing with the English text, and no rule about which version prevails if the two differ. Ohio also prescribes no lease language at all beyond the owner-and-agent identity in R.C. 5321.18, so there is nothing for a translation duty to attach to. The only prescribed words a landlord must use are in the eviction notice under R.C. 1923.04(A), and that provision requires them 'printed or written in a conspicuous manner' with no language requirement of any kind.

Ohio does write a Spanish-language duty in one place that touches housing, which shows the omission is a choice. For agricultural labor camps, R.C. 3733.45(B) makes the licensor distribute posters carrying the state monitor advocate's toll-free number and information 'in English and Spanish', with at least one posted in a conspicuous place within the camp. That duty falls on the Director of Health, not on the camp operator's lease, and labour-camp dwelling units are excluded from Chapter 5321 by R.C. 5321.01(C)(7). Nothing comparable exists for an ordinary rental.

Where the real Ohio exposure lies is fair housing, not translation. R.C. 4112.02(H) makes it unlawful to discriminate in housing on the basis of national origin or ancestry, among other protected classes. Nothing in it requires you to translate anything - but a practice that advertises and negotiates in one language and then presents a lease the applicant cannot read, or that offers different terms, a different deposit or a different process depending on the language an applicant speaks, is evidence of national-origin discrimination rather than a translation failure. So the safe practice is consistency: use the same lease, the same figures and the same process for everyone, and if you market in a second language, be ready to walk a tenant through the English lease in that language or let them bring their own interpreter. If you do provide a translation voluntarily, say in the lease which version governs, because Ohio law will not answer that for you - and expect a court to read any ambiguity against the drafter.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, together with the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters, which include the Ohio Civil Rights Commission's housing and discrimination rules - not the whole Revised Code, and no city rental code or language-access ordinance.

title: Ohio Has No Truth in Renting Act - Half of One Is Buried in Chapter 5321
bodyText:
'Truth in renting' is Michigan's statute and New Jersey's, not Ohio's. Ohio has no act of that name and no statute doing either of the two things those acts do. There is no required notice telling the tenant that the lease is a binding legal document or that state law establishes rights the lease cannot take away, no state-published statement of tenant rights you must hand over or attach, and no penalty, fine or civil liability for failing to deliver one.

The structural reason is worth knowing because it also answers several related questions: Chapter 5321 names no administering agency at all. Across its twenty-three sections no department and no director appears; the only 'agency' it mentions is a governmental agency that has found a code violation, in R.C. 5321.02 and R.C. 5321.07. Nobody in Ohio government is charged with publishing a rental guide, prescribing a lease form, reviewing one, or distributing a rights statement - so there is nothing for a delivery duty to attach to.

What Ohio does have is the enforcement half of the idea, without the disclosure half. R.C. 5321.13 is a prohibited-terms list: no provision of the chapter may be modified or waived by any oral or written agreement except the one-way duty-shift in its division (F); no warrant of attorney to confess judgment; no recognised agreement to pay either side's attorney's fees, in the lease or any other landlord-tenant agreement; and no tenant agreement exculpating, limiting or indemnifying your liability arising under law. R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause. R.C. 5321.20 records the General Assembly's own policy findings about residential rental law. Put together, Ohio protects the tenant by striking terms rather than by making you announce them - which means the compliance work is in your drafting, not in a notice you attach.

The near-miss is a different chapter. R.C. 4781.51(D) requires a manufactured-home-park rental agreement to carry a prescribed paragraph in ten-point boldface type telling the resident which Revised Code sections protect their rights and the operator's. That is the closest thing in Ohio law to a truth-in-renting notice, and Park lots sit outside Chapter 5321 on their own definitions - R.C. 4781.01(W) makes a park's 'residential premises' the LOT - so it is not available to you and not required of you.

Searched: the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters in this library, 1,953 sections, plus the Ohio Constitution and the held Administrative Code chapters - not the whole Revised Code, and no city rental code.

title: No Ohio Rule on Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText:
Ohio imposes no state standard here, and that is the answer rather than a gap: zoning in Ohio is local, and the state's zoning statutes are enabling - they grant power to counties, townships and municipalities rather than setting a rule you can look up. Nothing in Ohio requires a landlord to permit an accessory dwelling unit, nothing bars a lease from prohibiting it, and R.C. 5321.06 lets a lease carry any term not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or another rule of law, with R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability the only ceiling. So your lease decides, and the local code decides what the building may lawfully contain.

Two Ohio provisions are worth holding in mind because they cut in opposite directions. R.C. 5321.19(A) preempts a local measure that 'regulates the rights and obligations of parties to a rental agreement that are regulated by this chapter' - so a city cannot rewrite your lease terms. But R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) expressly preserves local housing, building, health and safety codes and ordinances, which is where an occupancy standard or a limit on what a dwelling may contain actually lives. The practical consequence is that the binding rule for this subject is a city or township one, and this review flags local ordinances rather than resolving them. Check the zoning and housing code for the specific municipality or township before you rely on anything.

A caution about reading Ohio statutes in this area. R.C. 5104.054 says a type B family child care home 'shall be considered to be a residential use of property for purposes of municipal, county, and township zoning' - words that look as though they override a lease. They do not: the section binds zoning authorities and nobody else. Expect the same shape from any other Ohio provision in this family.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, 'accessory dwelling' 0, 'unrelated' 7, 'family' 82 and 'occupancy' 36, every relevant hit checked and none of them a state occupancy limit or a dwelling-unit mandate, against 'landlord' 34 - plus the section index of R.C. Chapter 519, the township zoning enabling chapter, which contains no occurrence of 'accessory' and nothing catchlined for an accessory dwelling unit, an occupancy limit or a definition of family. That is a bounded search: only the index of chapter 519 was searched, not every section body, and R.C. Chapters 303 (county) and 713 (municipal) were not searched at all. No city or township ordinance was reviewed, and no Ohio case law.

title: Converting to Condominiums: 120 Days' Notice and No Eviction
bodyText:
If you convert a rented building to condominiums, Ohio gives your sitting tenants real rights and you cannot evict them to clear the way. R.C. 5311.25(G) requires the developer to give each tenant written notice of not less than one hundred twenty days before the conversion or intended conversion, and - this is the part that bites - 'during which time the tenant may not be evicted to accommodate or facilitate the sale of any unit if the tenant is not in default under the tenant's terms of tenancy'. It also requires you to offer each tenant an option to buy the unit they occupy, exercisable within not less than ninety days after notice, at a price no higher than the price at which the unit will be offered to the general public for the following one hundred eighty days. The ninety-day and one hundred twenty-day periods may run at the same time, and a tenant may waive them - but only in writing. Where two or more tenants share a unit, the option goes to them jointly.

The duty is written as the developer's, which matters less than it sounds: in a conversion the landlord usually is the developer or is selling to one, so plan on it being yours. Getting it wrong is expensive on the sale side rather than the tenancy side - under R.C. 5311.27 a contract executed in violation of R.C. 5311.25 is voidable by the purchaser for fifteen days, with a full refund of deposits and closing costs, the floor on damages is five hundred dollars for each violation against each purchaser plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and the Attorney General may sue or bring a class action where substantial numbers are affected.

Two things this is not. It is not a notice duty on an ordinary sale - selling a rented building to one buyer triggers none of this, and nothing in Ohio requires you to tell a tenant you are selling. And it is not a disclosure to tenants of the condominium documents: R.C. 5311.26's disclosure statement runs to a prospective purchaser, not to a tenant, which the association-disclosure row explains.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, 'conversion condominium' 0 and 'condominium' 5, none of them a conversion provision, against 'landlord' 34 - plus R.C. 5311.25 and R.C. 5311.27 read in full outside it, chapter 5311 not being held. The rest of chapter 5311 and all of chapter 5312 were not read, and no Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: Ohio Has No Rule On Who Keeps The Charger - But One Tenant Duty Decides It If Your Lease Does Not
bodyText:
Ohio says nothing about what happens to electric vehicle charging equipment when the tenancy ends. There is no removal right, no removal duty, no restoration standard, no notice period, no formula for buying the equipment out, and no provision deciding whether a charger a tenant paid for stays with the building. Settle it in the lease, because Ohio will not settle it for you - R.C. 5321.06 lets you agree any term not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or another rule of law.

The gap is not neutral, and the reason is a tenant duty most leases never think about in this context. R.C. 5321.05(A)(6) makes the tenant personally refrain, and forbid anyone on the premises with their permission from, 'intentionally or negligently destroying, defacing, damaging, or removing any fixture, appliance, or other part of the premises'. If the charger has been wired in and has become a fixture, a tenant who unbolts it and takes it has breached that duty - and R.C. 5321.05(C)(1) then gives you actual damages together with reasonable attorney's fees, awarded by the statute itself rather than by agreement, which matters because R.C. 5321.13(C) voids any agreement to pay attorney's fees. Ohio has no trade-fixture statute, so whether a particular installation is a fixture is a question of fact nothing in the chapter answers.

So write the three answers down. Say who owns the equipment at the end of the term. If the tenant is to remove it, say so and say the tenant restores the surface, the conduit and the panel, because R.C. 5321.16(B) lets you apply the deposit to damages for the tenant's noncompliance with R.C. 5321.05 'or the rental agreement' - the rental-agreement limb is what makes an agreed restoration standard recoverable from the deposit. And say what happens if equipment is simply left: Ohio gives you no safe harbour for dealing with left-behind property, which the abandoned-property entry explains.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'security deposit' 8, 'fixture' 23 and 'restoration' 8 proving the subject area is held. 'Electric vehicle', 'charging station', 'charger', 'trade fixture' and 'remove any fixture' all return 0. Bound: R.C. ch. 4928 was not read and is not held; Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 and 4101:8 are not held, so no code requirement for making an installation safe on removal could be read; city permit rules are flagged, not resolved.

title: Ohio Puts No Conditions On An EV Charger You Install - And No Price Rule On The Power You Sell Through It
bodyText:
Ohio attaches no requirements to an electric vehicle charger at a rental property. There is no registration, no permit at state level, no accuracy or certification standard, no price-posting duty and no cap on what you may charge a tenant for the electricity that goes through it. Nor is there anything the other way: Ohio gives a tenant no right to install one and puts no duty on you to permit or accommodate one. That means the installation, who owns the equipment, who pays for the power and how it is measured are all lease terms, under R.C. 5321.06, with R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability the only general ceiling on a figure. The figure you charge is yours, not the statute's.

Three things still bite, and none of them is an EV rule. First, if you supply the charger it is an electrical fixture you supplied, so R.C. 5321.04(A)(4) makes you keep it in good and safe working order, and R.C. 5321.13(A) stops you contracting out of that. Second, anything you take up front in connection with a charger rather than as payment for a cost you have already incurred is caught by R.C. 5321.01(E)'s deliberately broad definition of a security deposit - 'any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under a rental agreement' - and then the whole of R.C. 5321.16 applies to it. Third, the physical work is governed by the building and electrical codes R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) makes you comply with, and by city permit rules.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'landlord' 34 and 'electricity' 7 proving the tool was answering and the subject area is held. 'Electric vehicle', 'electric vehicle supply', 'charging station', 'charging equipment', 'charger', 'weights and measures', 'measuring device', 'kilowatt', 'submeter', 'submetered', 'net metering' and 'customer-generator' all return 0 sections. BOUND, and it matters here: R.C. Chapter 4928, which governs net metering, customer-generators and interconnection with the utility, was not read and is not held; that is a utility-customer question rather than a lease question, so it cannot create a tenant right against a lease term, but it is the chapter that would answer whether reselling power through a charger makes you a supplier. Ohio's weights-and-measures chapter was likewise not read. Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 and 4101:8 (the Building and Residential Codes, which carry the electrical requirements) are not held, and city EV and permit ordinances are flagged here, not resolved.

title: A Charger In A Shared Parking Area Is A Common-Area Duty You Cannot Hand Back
bodyText:
Ohio has no shared-area charging law. Nothing allocates a common parking area between tenants who want to charge, requires you to make a space available, sets a queue or a time limit, lets a tenant install equipment in a shared area over your objection, or tells you how to divide the cost. All of that is yours to set under R.C. 5321.06.

What Ohio does supply is the part landlords get wrong. R.C. 5321.01(C) defines the residential premises to include 'the grounds, areas, and facilities for the use of tenants generally or the use of which is promised the tenant', so a shared parking area is part of the premises, and R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) makes you keep all common areas of the premises in a safe and sanitary condition. Put a charger, a cable or a bollard in that area and its condition is inside that duty. R.C. 5321.13(A) says no provision of the chapter may be modified or waived by agreement, and R.C. 5321.13(F) lets duty-shifting run one way only - you may assume a tenant's R.C. 5321.05 duties, but a tenant cannot assume yours. So a clause making the tenant responsible for keeping shared charging equipment safe does not move that duty, and a clause making the tenant indemnify you for a claim arising out of it is barred outright by R.C. 5321.13(D), which has no common-areas exception. If the charger is in the tenant's own exclusive space and you did not supply it, you are on much better ground.

What to do instead: permit a shared-area installation only by a written agreement that is explicit about who owns the equipment, who may use it, who carries the insurance on it, how a trailing cable is kept out of a walkway, and who pays the electricity - and keep the inspection and upkeep of the shared area in your own hands, because Ohio will not let you give it away.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'common areas' 4, 'alteration' 28 and 'improvement' 28 proving the subject area is held and the tool was answering. 'Electric vehicle', 'charging station', 'charger', 'parking space', 'shared area' and 'assigned parking' all return 0. Bound: R.C. ch. 4928 was not read and is not held, and it is a utility-customer chapter rather than a lease chapter; Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 and 4101:8 are not held, so the electrical and clearance requirements for an installation could not be read; city parking and permit ordinances are flagged, not resolved.

title: Ohio Has No Guaranty Statute For A Lease - Which Means The Guaranty's Own Words Are The Whole Of Your Protection
bodyText:
No provision found in this review limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a separate guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, conditions a guaranty on being written on or referring to the lease, or caps anything you may take from a guarantor. 'Guarantor', 'cosigner' and 'co-signer' do not appear in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched, and Chapter 5321 never mentions a guarantor at all. So whether the guaranty survives into a renewal, an extension, a rent increase or a holdover is decided by what the guaranty says and by Ohio contract law - not by statute. Say it expressly: name every renewal, extension, modification including a rent increase, and any holdover period, or expect an argument that the guarantor's promise ended with the original term.

The cautious course, on two points.

First, get the guarantor's own signature on a writing. R.C. 1335.05 bars an action on an agreement 'not to be performed within one year from the making thereof' unless the agreement, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged. Most lease guaranties are of that kind. Its first limb, on a promise to answer for another person's debt, separately requires the guarantor's signed writing (see the last paragraph), so a signed writing from the guarantor is mandatory, not merely prudent. Have the guarantor acknowledge receiving a complete copy of the lease.

Second, do not import fee-shifting or indemnity language into an Ohio guaranty. R.C. 5321.13 keys its prohibitions to agreements 'between a landlord and tenant', and a guarantor is not a 'tenant' as R.C. 5321.01(A) defines one - someone 'entitled under a rental agreement to the use and occupancy of residential premises to the exclusion of others'. Read literally, that puts a landlord-guarantor agreement outside the prohibited-terms list. But a guaranty secures the tenant's obligations, and R.C. 5321.13(C) means the tenant has no enforceable obligation to pay your attorney's fees, so on that head there is nothing to guarantee; and whether a court would let a landlord reach through a guarantor what R.C. 5321.13(A) stops it reaching through the tenant is a question no section in this review answers. Keep the guaranty to the tenant's own enforceable obligations - rent, late charges the lease validly imposes, utilities, and damages for the tenant's breach - and leave out any warrant of attorney to confess judgment, any fee-shifting tail, and any indemnity of your own liability.

One trap with money. Ohio caps no deposit, so there is no cap to work round, but R.C. 5321.01(E) defines a security deposit as 'any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under a rental agreement' - which money a guarantor puts up plainly is. R.C. 5321.16's duties then run, and that section speaks only of 'the tenant': it is the tenant who must give you a forwarding address and the tenant who recovers for a breach. Rather than create that puzzle, take the deposit from the tenant and let the guarantor fund it, so the statutory counterparty is never in doubt.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'landlord' 34, 'surety' 31 and 'renewal' 267 proving the subject area is held and the tool was answering. 'Guarantor' 0, 'cosigner' 0, 'co-signer' 0, 'answer for the debt' 0, 'extension of the term' 0; 'guaranty' returns a single section, an underground-storage-tank financial-responsibility definition. BOUND: R.C. Chapter 1335, Ohio's statute of frauds, is not held in this review. R.C. 1335.04 and 1335.05 were read whole from outside it, including the suretyship limb quoted in the last paragraph. No Ohio case law was reviewed, and Ohio contract law on the reach of a guaranty into a renewal is case law.

What Ohio does require, and it is the one thing to get right: a guaranty must be in writing and signed by the guarantor. R.C. 1335.05 says no action shall be brought 'upon a special promise, to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another person ... unless the agreement upon which such action is brought, or some memorandum or note thereof, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged therewith'. A guaranty of a tenant's rent is exactly that promise, so an oral guaranty, or one the guarantor never signed, gives you nothing to sue on. The same section separately bars an action on an agreement 'not to be performed within one year' absent a signed writing, so a guaranty covering a term longer than a year needs the signature on both counts. Get it signed at the outset, get a fresh signature if the guaranty is to carry into a renewal or a new term rather than relying on the original wording to stretch, and keep the signed original.

One limit worth knowing in your favour: R.C. 5321.13(C) refuses to recognise any agreement to pay the landlord's or the tenant's attorney's fees, in a rental agreement 'or in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant'. A guarantor is not a tenant, so that wording does not reach a landlord-guarantor agreement on its face - but a guaranty of the tenant's obligations can only deliver what the tenant actually owes, and the tenant owes no fees, so there is nothing there to guarantee. A separate promise by the guarantor to pay your fees sits outside the section's words; this library does not offer one, because no Ohio authority tests it.

title: Letting Inside An Ohio Association: The Association Evicts In Your Name, And Bills You
bodyText:
Ohio gives an association real power over your tenancy, and it runs through you rather than around you. Four things follow, and the order matters.

The association can start an eviction, but it is your case. R.C. 5311.19(B)(1) lets a unit owners association initiate eviction proceedings under Chapters 5321 and 1923 for a breach of the association's covenants, conditions or restrictions - but 'the action shall be brought by the unit owners association, as the unit owner's agent, in the name of the unit owner.' You are the plaintiff of record. Every Chapter 1923 prerequisite is still yours to satisfy, including the notice to leave the premises with its prescribed wording, and R.C. 5311.19(B)(1) opens 'Except as otherwise provided in the declaration or the bylaws', so read yours before you assume the power exists at all.

You get ten days' warning - use it. R.C. 5311.19(B)(2) requires the association to give the unit owner at least ten days' written notice of the intended eviction action, in addition to anything Chapters 5321 and 1923 require. That is your window to cure the problem with the tenant yourself, and it is cheaper than the alternative, because R.C. 5311.19(B)(3) charges the costs of the eviction action, 'including reasonable attorney's fees', to the unit owner as a special assessment against the unit and a lien on it. In a planned community the parallel is R.C. 5312.11(A), which lets the association assess the lot for enforcement assessments, for enforcement costs, and for costs of maintenance, repair or replacement incurred because of the willful or negligent act of an owner or occupant 'or their family, tenants, guests, or invitees', attorney's fees and court costs included. R.C. 5312.11(C) and (D) then give you - the owner - written notice describing the violation and the proposed charge, a right to a hearing before the board, and no levy until a requested hearing has happened. Ask for the hearing.

Your tenant is already bound, and you still have to hand over the rules. R.C. 5311.19(A) binds 'All unit owners, their tenants, all persons lawfully in possession and control of any part of a condominium property' to the covenants, conditions and restrictions in the deed, the declaration, the bylaws or the association's rules - directly, whether or not the lease says so - and makes a violation grounds for the association or any unit owner to sue for damages, injunctive relief or both, with court costs and reasonable attorney's fees in both types of action. That fee award comes from the statute, not from an agreement, which is why it survives R.C. 5321.13(C). Nothing requires you to give the tenant the rules, but a tenant cannot obey rules they have not seen, so give them and say in the lease that you did.

When the money comes back to you, call it damages, not indemnity. The assessment under R.C. 5311.19(B)(3) or R.C. 5312.11(A) is your liability arising under law, and R.C. 5321.13(D) refuses to recognise any tenant agreement to indemnify you for such a liability or its related costs - with no common-areas exception. Recover the same money as damages for the tenant's breach of a lease term requiring compliance with the association's rules, which R.C. 5321.06 lets you include and R.C. 5321.16(B)'s 'or the rental agreement' limb lets you take from the deposit. The distinction is drafting, not semantics.

Three things Ohio does not do, on the sections read: it does not cap an association's lease-approval or applicant fee, it does not authorise an association to hold a deposit from your tenant, and it does not let an association collect rent directly from your tenant when you are behind on assessments - so do not borrow a clause written for Florida, Utah or Michigan. If an association does require a deposit from your tenant and you collect it, note R.C. 5321.01(E): a security deposit is 'any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under a rental agreement', and once it is money held by you, the whole of R.C. 5321.16 attaches to it.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'landlord' 34, 'condominium' 5 and 'assessment' 34 proving the tool was answering; 'unit owners association' and 'owners association' return 1 section each (the sex-offender notification section, not an association power), 'homeowners association' and 'planned community' return 0, and 'association fine' 0. BOUND, and it is the whole limit of this entry: Chapters 5311 and 5312 are not held in this review. R.C. 5311.19, 5311.26 and 5312.11 were read in full from outside it, and everything above rests on those three sections and on Chapter 5321. This is not a claim about either chapter as a whole, and the sections that would carry an assessment lien, a conversion notice or a rental restriction were not read. Your own declaration and bylaws can change much of this and are private documents no review can resolve for you.

title: No Minimum Type Size For An Ohio Lease - And The One Rental Agreement Ohio Does Set Typography For Is A Storage Unit
bodyText:
Nothing sets a minimum type size for an Ohio residential lease, prescribes a font, requires a block in capitals or boldface, dictates where a clause must sit on the page, or attaches an evidentiary sanction to any of it. There is no Ohio counterpart to the New York rule that makes an unreadably small printed contract inadmissible. Your lease's typography is your choice, under R.C. 5321.06, and R.C. 5321.14's unconscionability test is the only thing that could ever reach it - which is a reason to set type generously rather than minimally.

Ohio plainly knows how to prescribe typography, and it does it four different ways, which is what makes its silence on leases meaningful rather than accidental. R.C. 1345.032 requires a solicitation for copies of deeds to carry its statement 'in at least twenty-four-point type'. R.C. 1349.78(B) requires a written notice to be 'printed in at least twelve-point type'. R.C. 4112.021(B)(1)(g) takes a different approach again, requiring a creditor to print or firmly attach a prescribed Ohio civil rights notice to each credit application 'in a type size no smaller than that used throughout most of the application form' - a relative standard rather than a point size. R.C. 1349.26(A) requires a creditor's covered-loan disclosures to be 'in conspicuous type size', which is neither a measurement nor a relative test but a standard of appearance. And for the eviction notice Ohio drops type altogether and goes to a verbal standard: R.C. 1923.04(A), R.C. 1923.06(B) and R.C. 1923.12 each require their prescribed language to be 'printed in a conspicuous manner', with no size attached.

The closest Ohio comes to what this topic asks about - typography deciding whether a term works - is in a different kind of rental agreement entirely. R.C. 5322.06(A) provides that where a self-storage rental agreement limits the value of personal property that may be stored, 'that limit is the maximum value of the stored property, provided that the provision is printed in bold type or underlined in the rental agreement.' Typography there is a condition of the term's effect. Ohio wrote that rule for storage facilities and did not write it for residential leases - so do not import it, and do not assume a bolded or underlined clause in a residential lease gains anything legally. It gains readability, which is worth having for its own sake.

One unresolved point worth knowing, because it is bigger than type size. R.C. 4112.021 applies to a 'creditor', defined in (A)(2) as any person who regularly extends, renews or continues credit, with 'credit' defined in (A)(1) as the right to defer payment of a debt. Whether a residential landlord taking a rental application is a creditor for that section is not settled by the text, and no case law is in this review. Rent in Ohio is normally payable in advance rather than deferred, which points away from it, but the question also controls (B)(1)(f), which would require a written statement of the specific reasons for rejecting an application when the applicant asks in writing within sixty days. Treat it as open, and if you reject applicants in writing anyway you will never need the answer.

'Point type' 4, 'type size' 2, 'boldface' 9, 'bold type' 1, 'capital letters' 5, 'legible' 3, 'underlined' 1 - each set opened, and not one of them reaches a residential lease. Chapter 5321 contains no typographic requirement at all. No Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: Ohio Prescribes No Parking Notice To Your Tenant - The Only Prescribed Parking Notice Goes On A Sign
bodyText:
Ohio has no parking-rules notice regime for a residential tenancy. Nothing requires you to deliver parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, prescribes a heading or a form of words for them, limits changing them during the term, limits what vehicle information you may demand, or makes a parking permit expire with the lease. Your parking rules are lease rules, which R.C. 5321.06 lets you include, and changing them mid-term is governed by your own rule-change term - this library's Ohio house-rules clause already carries that notice period as {{rule_change_notice_days}}, so use that one rather than inventing a second parking-specific period.

The only parking notice Ohio actually prescribes is a sign, and it is not addressed to your tenant. Where accessible parking locations must be designated, R.C. 3781.111(C) requires every designating sign to be mounted on a fixed or movable post or otherwise fixed vertically so that the distance from the ground to the bottom edge is not less than five feet; and for any sign posted or replaced on or after October 14, 1999, a notice stating the fine applicable for parking there without entitlement must be affixed to the sign's surface or next to it. R.C. 3781.111(E) makes it an offence for the owner of such a building or facility to fail to mark those locations or to fail to maintain the markings and signs, and R.C. 3781.99(A) prices it: a warning for a first offence, then a fine of twenty-five dollars for each parking location that is not properly marked or whose markings are not properly maintained. Those are the statute's figures, not yours. Whether your property must designate accessible parking at all depends on the building-code rules adopted under R.C. 3781.111(A), which were not available here.

Two other parking duties that are easy to miss. Your tow-away signs are prescribed by statute down to their dimensions, and getting them wrong makes the tow unlawful - the towing entry sets that out. And R.C. 4501.05 reaches 'keepers of garages, parking lots, or other places where motor vehicles of any kind are stored or left for repair or for any other purpose', requiring anyone who knows or becomes aware that a vehicle left there bears 'bullet marks, gunshot marks, blood stains, or marks or evidence of any crime' to report the facts immediately to municipal police, the county sheriff or a state highway patrol trooper, on penalty of a forfeiture of up to one hundred dollars. If you run the lot, read that as reaching you.

One caution on the information you collect. Nothing in Ohio limits asking a tenant for a vehicle description, plate number or proof of registration. But if your permit process also captures a driver's licence or state identification card number alongside the tenant's name, you are holding 'personal information' as R.C. 1349.19(A)(7)(a) defines it, and the breach-notification duty in that section attaches - a duty R.C. 1349.19(H) makes unwaivable. Collect the plate, not the licence number, unless you need it.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'parking' 14, 'license plate' 313 and 'vehicle registration' 264 proving the subject area is held and the tool was answering. 'Parking rules' returns 0. Every one of the fourteen 'parking' hits was opened; none is a notice to a tenant. Bound: Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 is not held, so the rules deciding which properties must designate accessible parking could not be read; R.C. chs. 4511 and 4513, which carry the traffic and towing provisions, are not held either; city parking and permit-parking ordinances are flagged here, not resolved.

title: No Ohio Occupancy Limit in a Single-Family Zone
bodyText:
Ohio imposes no state standard here, and that is the answer rather than a gap: zoning in Ohio is local, and the state's zoning statutes are enabling - they grant power to counties, townships and municipalities rather than setting a rule you can look up. Nothing in Ohio requires a landlord to permit a particular number of unrelated occupants, nothing bars a lease from prohibiting it, and R.C. 5321.06 lets a lease carry any term not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or another rule of law, with R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability the only ceiling. So your lease decides, and the local code decides what the building may lawfully contain.

Two Ohio provisions are worth holding in mind because they cut in opposite directions. R.C. 5321.19(A) preempts a local measure that 'regulates the rights and obligations of parties to a rental agreement that are regulated by this chapter' - so a city cannot rewrite your lease terms. But R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) expressly preserves local housing, building, health and safety codes and ordinances, which is where an occupancy standard or a limit on what a dwelling may contain actually lives. The practical consequence is that the binding rule for this subject is a city or township one, and this review flags local ordinances rather than resolving them. Check the zoning and housing code for the specific municipality or township before you rely on anything.

A caution about reading Ohio statutes in this area. R.C. 5104.054 says a type B family child care home 'shall be considered to be a residential use of property for purposes of municipal, county, and township zoning' - words that look as though they override a lease. They do not: the section binds zoning authorities and nobody else. Expect the same shape from any other Ohio provision in this family.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, 'accessory dwelling' 0, 'unrelated' 7, 'family' 82 and 'occupancy' 36, every relevant hit checked and none of them a state occupancy limit or a dwelling-unit mandate, against 'landlord' 34 - plus the section index of R.C. Chapter 519, the township zoning enabling chapter, which contains no occurrence of 'accessory' and nothing catchlined for an accessory dwelling unit, an occupancy limit or a definition of family. That is a bounded search: only the index of chapter 519 was searched, not every section body, and R.C. Chapters 303 (county) and 713 (municipal) were not searched at all. No city or township ordinance was reviewed, and no Ohio case law.

title: A Tenant's Bankruptcy Is Federal - But Ohio Has Opted Out Of The Federal Exemption List, And That Changes What You Can Collect
bodyText:
FEDERAL: a tenant's bankruptcy is a case under Title 11 of the United States Code. Title 11 is not part of this review and its terms are not stated here - what the filing does to your lease, to a pending eviction and to a claim for unpaid rent is a federal question, and it is the question to take to counsel first.

What Ohio contributes is the exemption side, and it is more than most landlords expect. R.C. 2329.662 is the whole of it in one sentence: 'Pursuant to the "Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1978," 92 Stat. 2549, 11 U.S.C.A. 522 (b)(1), this state specifically does not authorize debtors who are domiciled in this state to exempt the property specified in the "Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1978," 92 Stat. 2549, 11 U.S.C.A. 522 (d).' Ohio is an opt-out state. An Ohio-domiciled tenant in bankruptcy uses Ohio's own list in R.C. 2329.66, not the federal schedule - so the figures that decide what a creditor can reach are the Ohio figures, and R.C. 2329.66(A)(17) preserves exemptions under other federal statutes while expressly excluding the Bankruptcy Act's own.

Three parts of that list are written for bankruptcy specifically, and they are easy to miss. R.C. 2329.66(A)(18) exempts the person's aggregate interest in any property up to one thousand seventy-five dollars, and says that division 'applies only in bankruptcy proceedings' - a wildcard available in bankruptcy and nowhere else. R.C. 2329.66(D)(1) fixes the valuation date: in bankruptcy, a person's 'interest' is determined 'as of the date a petition is filed with the bankruptcy court commencing a case under Title 11 of the United States Code', rather than at the appraisal or writ date that governs everything else. And R.C. 2329.66(B) has the Ohio Judicial Conference adjust every dollar amount in the section every three years on the first of April and publish the memorandum in the Register of Ohio - so read the current memorandum, because the numbers above are the ones the section carried when this entry was written and they move.

Two things that matter directly to you. The security deposit in your hands is exempt money, up to the (A)(3) figure for money on deposit with a landlord among others - the exemption-waiver entry sets that out and explains why no lease term can waive it, R.C. 2329.661(B) making every promise, agreement or contract void insofar as it seeks to waive Ohio's exemption laws. And Ohio gives you no bankruptcy-specific eviction provision at all: the word does not appear anywhere in Chapter 1923, so nothing in Ohio's forcible entry and detainer chapter stays, accelerates or alters an eviction because of a filing. Ohio's only statutory eviction stay is the active-duty one in R.C. 1923.062, and the delay routes are set out in the hardship-stay entry. Any stay arising from the bankruptcy itself is federal.
