'Automatic stay', 'executory contract', 'debtor in possession' and 'discharge of the debt' all return 0, which is the expected result for a federal regime. Bound: Title 11 of the United States Code was not read and nothing above states its terms; the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure were not read; no Ohio case law was reviewed; and the remaining Ohio exemption sections, R.C. 2329.67 to 2329.70, were not read.

title: Ohio Uses Three Different Fault Tests For Tenant Damage - And The Escrow Statute Has No Fault Test At All
bodyText:
Ohio gives you a damage remedy, but it changes shape depending on which section you are standing on, and the differences decide how your clause should be worded.

The duty. R.C. 5321.05(A)(6) makes the tenant 'personally refrain and forbid any other person who is on the premises with his permission from intentionally or negligently destroying, defacing, damaging, or removing any fixture, appliance, or other part of the premises'. Note the two limits: the fault standard is intention or negligence, and the people covered are the tenant and those on the premises with the tenant's permission. A vandal, a trespasser or an uninvited visitor is outside it.

The remedy, and it is better than most. R.C. 5321.05(C)(1) gives you 'any actual damages that result from the violation together with reasonable attorney's fees', and says that remedy is in addition to terminating the agreement, suing for possession, or obtaining injunctive relief. Those fees come from the statute, not from an agreement, which is why they survive R.C. 5321.13(C)'s refusal to recognise any agreement to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees - so do not put a fee-shifting sentence in your damage clause. It would be void, and you already have the award.

The second route, and a wider cast of people. The deposit. R.C. 5321.16(B) lets you apply the deposit to past due rent and to 'the amount of damages that the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with section 5321.05 of the Revised Code or the rental agreement.' That 'or the rental agreement' limb is what makes your own damage standard - which may reach any occupant or household member, not only someone there with permission - recoverable from the deposit. And a third formulation again: R.C. 5321.03(A)(2) lets you sue for possession notwithstanding the retaliation bar where the code violation complained of 'was primarily caused by any act or lack of reasonable care by the tenant, or by any other person in the tenant's household, or by anyone on the premises with the consent of the tenant'. Three sections, three different tests. Match your clause to the one you intend to rely on, and if you want the wider cast of people, you need the words in the lease.

Two things Ohio does not have, and both surprise people. There is no statutory casualty or untenantability termination right - 'untenantable' appears nowhere in the thirty-seven chapters searched - so there is nothing for tenant fault to be an exception to. Your termination after a fire comes from your own casualty clause, and lost rent is recoverable as contract damages, with no Ohio mitigation statute to limit you. And the rent-escrow statute has no tenant-fault bar at the door: R.C. 5321.07(B) conditions the tenant's escrow, rent-reduction and termination remedies only on your failure to remedy after written notice and on the tenant being current in rent. A tenant who caused the condition can still start an escrow over it. Fault counts at the end instead: if the court finds the condition resulted from the tenant's act or omission, R.C. 5321.09(D) makes the tenant liable for your damages and costs, with attorney's fees if the tenant intentionally acted in bad faith. You cannot answer the escrow with a no-abatement clause, because R.C. 5321.13(A) makes no provision of the chapter modifiable or waivable - your answers are that release-and-damages application, a possession action under R.C. 5321.03(A)(2), or the three-or-fewer-units exclusion in R.C. 5321.07(C), which works only if you gave the notice the exclusion requires.

One last word on wear and tear: Chapter 5321 never uses the phrase. The limit on what you may charge is simply that the amount must be damages you actually suffered from the tenant's noncompliance with R.C. 5321.05 or the lease.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'landlord' 34, 'actual damages' 14 and 'occupant' 38 proving the tool was answering. 'Untenantable' 0; 'wear and tear' 2 and 'normal wear' 1, none of them in Chapter 5321; 'casualty' 4, none landlord-tenant; 'intentionally or negligently' 2, one of them R.C. 5321.05. Bound: no Ohio case law was reviewed, and the measure of damages for injury to real property in Ohio is case law rather than statute.

title: Ohio Says Nothing About A Claim On The Tenant's Policy - And The Protection It Does Give Runs Only One Way
bodyText:
Ohio has no rule about insurance claims in a tenancy. Nothing requires a tenant to make a claim, sets a period for notifying a loss, allocates insurance proceeds between you and the tenant, decides who repairs with them, or regulates subrogation between a landlord and a tenant. Nothing makes a tenant an implied co-insured on your policy, and Ohio has no collateral-source rule reducing what you may recover because somebody's insurer paid. All of that is lease drafting under R.C. 5321.06.

The asymmetry is the thing worth knowing, because landlords assume Chapter 5321 is even-handed here and it is not. R.C. 5321.13(D) protects the tenant from you: no tenant agreement to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of yours arising under law, or to indemnify you for it, is recognised - in the lease or in any other agreement between you - and R.C. 5321.13(A) makes that unwaivable. So a clause telling the tenant to look first to their own policy for a loss you caused is exculpation in substance and fails however it is worded. Nothing in the chapter runs the other way. R.C. 5321.05(C)(1) gives you actual damages together with reasonable attorney's fees for a tenant's breach of any R.C. 5321.05 duty, and R.C. 5321.16(B) lets you apply the deposit to damages for the tenant's noncompliance with R.C. 5321.05 'or the rental agreement'. Your own insurer's subrogated claim against the tenant stands on that same footing: Ohio gives the tenant no statutory waiver of subrogation and no co-insured status to hide behind.

So draft the claims mechanics, which are lawful, and leave the risk-shifting alone. Require prompt written notice of any loss, damage or injury at the property. Require the tenant to cooperate with your insurer's investigation and to give you a copy of the policy and of any claim correspondence affecting the property. Require the tenant not to settle or release a claim that affects your interest without your written consent. Ask to be named an interested party or certificate holder so you are told if the policy lapses - which tells you about the policy without making it your policy. Do not attach a fee-shifting tail to any of it, because R.C. 5321.13(C) refuses to recognise any agreement to pay the landlord's or the tenant's attorney's fees.

Two pointers rather than repetition. What you may and may not require of the policy itself - additional insured, waiver of subrogation, force-placement - is set out in the renter's-insurance entry, and the lease covenant is in this library's tenant-insurance clause. And Ohio does not make you carry insurance at all, though a court may release escrowed rent to pay your premium, which the landlord-insurance entry covers.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'insurance' 80 and 'claims' 74 proving the subject area is amply held and the tool was answering. 'Co-insured' 0, 'coinsured' 0, 'collateral source' 0, 'notice of loss' 0, 'additional insured' 0. 'Proof of loss' returns one section, a fire-marshal provision; 'insurance proceeds' returns one, inside the nuisance-receivership section; 'subrogation' returns three, none between a landlord and a tenant. Bound: Title 39 of the Revised Code, Ohio's insurance code - including its fire-insurance chapter and any unfair-claims-practices or prompt-payment provisions - was not searched. That is where a claims-handling or claims-timing rule would live, and it binds insurers rather than lease terms. No Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: You May Require An Ohio Tenant To Use A Portal - But Moving Rent Into It Moves The Repair-Notice Address Too
bodyText:
Ohio has no tenant-portal statute. Nothing requires you to offer a portal, forbids you requiring one, caps a portal or convenience fee, obliges you to accept cash or a paper cheque, or regulates what the portal may collect. 'Portal' appears once in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched and it is a Medicaid provision. So a requirement to pay rent and sign documents through a portal is a lease term under R.C. 5321.06, with R.C. 5321.14's unconscionability test the only general ceiling and the fee your figure, not the statute's.

The finding that matters, and it is the one nobody drafts for. R.C. 5321.07(A) is the tenant's rent-escrow route, and it says the tenant's written notice of your failure to repair 'shall be sent to the person or place where rent is normally paid.' If rent is normally paid through your portal, the portal is a place where rent is normally paid - so a tenant who posts a repair complaint there has a real argument that the statutory notice has been given, and your thirty days under R.C. 5321.07(B) start running. Somebody must read the portal's message channel daily and escalate anything that looks like a repair complaint, and your portal must not drop messages or cap attachments. A notice you never saw still starts the clock.

Three more Ohio constraints, each belonging to an entry of its own rather than repeated here. Your tenant keeps a right to refuse to transact electronically that a lease term cannot waive, which the electronic-notices entry sets out - so give a non-electronic way to pay and a paper route for notices, and name them in the lease. Do not serve the notice to leave the premises through the portal: R.C. 1923.04(A) sets its own methods and email is not among them. And if you take money up front in connection with the portal - a setup charge that is refundable, or a credit balance held against future rent - R.C. 5321.01(E) catches it as 'any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under a rental agreement' and the whole of R.C. 5321.16 then applies.

Two more practical points. A portal is a database of personal information. The moment it holds a tenant's name with a bank account number and its security or access code, or with a driver's licence or state identification card number, you are inside R.C. 1349.19 - which requires notification of a security breach 'in the most expedient time possible but not later than forty-five days' after discovery, makes any waiver of the section 'contrary to public policy and ... void and unenforceable', and is enforced by the Attorney General. Collect what you need and no more. And because Ohio requires no rent receipt at all, the portal's ledger is in practice your only proof of payment - keep it, export it, and do not let a change of software lose it.
