'Portal' 1 and 'paper copy' 0; 'convenience fee' 1 and 'legal tender' 1, both opened and neither reaching a tenancy. Bound: R.C. Chapter 1306, Ohio's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, is NOT in this review - the electronic-notices entry carries it and this entry does not restate or re-verify it. No Ohio case law was reviewed, and city ordinances are flagged, not resolved.

title: An Ohio Tenant Has No Right To See Their File - And Exactly One Record You Must Hand Over
bodyText:
Ohio gives a residential tenant no right of access to their own tenancy records. There is no right to inspect or copy the file, no rent-ledger duty - not on request, not inside a nonpayment notice, and not on a records request - no record-retention period for a landlord, and no requirement to keep records in any particular form. 'Ledger', 'rent ledger', 'tenant record', 'inspect and copy' and 'records request' return nothing across the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters searched. And Ohio requires no rent receipt either, which is the reason your own ledger is usually the only evidence that rent was paid: keep it, back it up, and do not let a change of software lose it.

The one record Ohio makes you give a tenant is the deposit itemisation. R.C. 5321.16(B) requires any deduction from the security deposit to be 'itemized and identified by the landlord in a written notice delivered to the tenant together with the amount due, within thirty days after termination of the rental agreement and delivery of possession.' Miss it and R.C. 5321.16(C) exposes you to the amount wrongfully withheld again, plus reasonable attorney's fees. Beyond that, the only other thing Ohio makes your lease carry is the owner's and any agent's name and address, and - if you are party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and want the rent-escrow exclusion - the notice of that fact.

Ohio's data-security statute does reach you, and it is narrower than people assume. R.C. 1349.19 applies to any 'person' owning or licensing computerized data that includes personal information, and a landlord conducting business in Ohio is one. 'Personal information' in R.C. 1349.19(A)(7)(a) means an individual's name together with one or more of exactly three things: a social security number; a driver's licence or state identification card number; or an account, credit or debit card number combined with and linked to a required security code, access code or password - and only where those elements are not encrypted, redacted or altered so as to be unreadable. An ordinary tenant file contains all three kinds, so the duty attaches. On discovering a breach you must notify affected Ohio residents 'in the most expedient time possible but not later than forty-five days' after discovery, and notify the nationwide consumer reporting agencies as well if more than a thousand residents are involved. R.C. 1349.19(H) makes any waiver of the section 'contrary to public policy and ... void and unenforceable', so no lease term can shed it, and the Attorney General enforces it. Encryption or redaction is the practical answer: data that is unreadable is outside the definition.

What the statute does not reach. Ohio imposes no written-information-security-program duty on a landlord - 'data security', 'written information security' and 'security program' all return nothing in the chapters searched. And a biometric template is not on R.C. 1349.19(A)(7)(a)'s list of three. The word 'biometric' returns zero across all thirty-seven chapters, the Administrative Code chapters and the Fire Code rules held here, so a landlord holding a fingerprint or face template for door access has no R.C. 1349.19 notification duty for that template - while still having one for the social security, licence and account numbers in the same file. Treat that as a gap in the statute rather than permission: the template is still data you are holding for your own convenience.

One limit on what you may record at all. Ohio Adm.Code 4112-5-04(B) says that making and maintaining records of a housing applicant's race, colour, religion, sex, military status, familial status, ancestry, disability or national origin does not breach the discrimination chapter where the records are made in conformance with the instructions or requirements of a government agency or court administering a programme to eliminate discrimination - and that such records 'shall be gathered and maintained in such a fashion as to preclude their inadvertent or deliberate use for discriminatory purposes and to avoid possible misinterpretation by applicants of the purpose for which such data will be used.' Read that the right way round: it is a safe harbour, which means that outside it, making or keeping such a record is itself the prohibited act. The inquiry-and-record ban entry sets out the statute.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections, plus the Administrative Code chapters and Fire Code rules held - control term 0 sections, with 'record' 316, 'personal information' 4 and 'breach of the security' 1 proving the subject area is held and the tool was answering. Bound: R.C. Chapter 1354, Ohio's Data Protection Act, which creates a voluntary cybersecurity-programme affirmative defence, is NOT in this review and was not read; FEDERAL: the Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. 1681, governs what you may do with a consumer report and was not researched. No Ohio case law was reviewed and city ordinances are flagged, not resolved.

title: Charging Separately For Parking Is Allowed In Ohio - What It Does Not Do Is Create A Second Contract Outside Chapter 5321
bodyText:
Ohio neither requires nor forbids unbundling parking from rent. There is no duty to offer parking, no duty to include it, no cap on what you may charge for it, no rule on whether the charge counts as rent, and no notice period for changing it. R.C. 5321.06 lets you put the term in the lease and R.C. 5321.14's unconscionability test is the only general ceiling, so the monthly figure is yours, not the statute's.

The mistake to avoid is thinking that a separate parking agreement sits outside the landlord-tenant chapter. Three definitions close that door. R.C. 5321.01(C) brings into the residential premises 'the grounds, areas, and facilities for the use of tenants generally or the use of which is promised the tenant' - so a lot or space whose use you promise the tenant is part of the premises however you price it, and R.C. 5321.04(A)(3) then makes you keep it safe and sanitary as a common area. R.C. 5321.01(D) defines a rental agreement as any agreement, written or oral, that establishes or modifies 'the terms, conditions, rules, amount of rent charged or paid, or any other provisions concerning the use and occupancy of residential premises' - which a parking agreement about a promised area does. And R.C. 5321.13's prohibitions apply not only in the rental agreement but 'in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant', so a side licence cannot carry an attorney-fee clause, a confessed judgment, or an exculpation or indemnity of your own liability. Unbundling changes the price, not the regime.

Two practical consequences. Money you take up front in connection with parking - a space deposit, an access-card deposit, a refundable gate-fob charge - is caught by R.C. 5321.01(E)'s definition of a security deposit as 'any deposit of money or property to secure performance by the tenant under a rental agreement', and the whole of R.C. 5321.16 then applies to it, including the thirty-day itemised notice. And because Ohio has no rule on whether a fee counts as rent, your lease should say which it is: if the parking charge is rent, nonpayment is a default in the payment of rent and the eviction and late-fee machinery follows it; if it is not, say so, and collect it as a separate contract debt. Do not leave it to be argued.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review, 1,953 sections - control term 0 sections, with 'parking' 14, 'appurtenances' 5 and 'grounds, areas' 2 proving the tool was answering and the subject area is held. 'Parking space', 'parking fee' and 'license to use' return 0, and 'separate agreement' returns 1 section that has nothing to do with a tenancy. Every one of the fourteen 'parking' hits was opened and none regulates charging for it. Bound: Ohio Adm.Code 4101:1 and 4101:8 are not held, so any code requirement for the number or dimensions of spaces could not be read, and city zoning and parking-minimum ordinances are flagged here, not resolved.

title: No Ohio Lease Needs A Government Officer's Approval To Be Valid
bodyText:
Nothing in Ohio makes a residential lease wait for a government officer's signature. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library, there is no communal, tribal, village or native land-tenure regime, no land commission or land court with power to approve a lease, and no provision making rent or possession conditional on an approval that has not yet been given. The words 'communal land', 'tribal land', 'trust land', 'land tenure' and 'usufruct' return nothing; the only uses of 'tribal' are convictions in a tribal court for sex-offender and arson registration, and the only uses of 'communal' are a hotel's shared kitchen and bath and a licence-plate fund.

So your Ohio lease is valid when the parties make it. R.C. 5321.06 lets a landlord and tenant include any terms not inconsistent with chapter 5321 or another rule of law, and R.C. 5321.01(D) brings even an oral agreement inside the chapter. The only officer who ever touches an ordinary residential lease is a notary, and only on length: a lease of more than three years must be signed by the lessor and acknowledged before a notary, a judge, a clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer or a mayor, and should then be recorded, while a lease of three years or less needs neither acknowledgment nor recording. That is a formality, not an approval, and nobody reviews your terms.

Two cautions. If you ever let land held in trust for a federally recognised tribe, the approval regime you are looking for is FEDERAL, not Ohio - do not try to answer it from state law or from this library, and get counsel. And a county rental-registration filing, where it applies, is a filing about the property and the owner; it is not an approval of the lease and no lease waits on it.

title: The Miscellaneous Questions Ohio Simply Does Not Answer
bodyText:
This entry gathers the odds and ends. Each item below was searched for in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules held for this library, and the bounded claim is exactly that: we found no provision there, which is not the same as a claim about every word of Ohio law. Details, citations and the search terms are in the linked entries.

ABSENT - no provision found. There is no communal, tribal or village land-tenure regime and no officer's approval needed before a lease is valid. There is no usufruct: Ohio decides who the landlord is by who lets, manages or takes the rent, so a limited-interest owner who lets carries every ordinary duty. No lease has to state what district the property sits in, and no tenant gets a vote in one. There is no work card, permit or registration for housing staff, and nothing extra for age-restricted housing - though a licensed care home is a different regime with mandatory records checks. There is nothing at all about housing someone who works for you: no signed occupancy disclosure, no duty to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, no sponsored-worker filing. There is no incentive of any kind for letting to a veteran, and the only veteran preference Ohio writes binds a public housing authority. There is no rent-reporting law: nothing makes you report rent to the credit bureaus, nothing stops you, and nothing makes you warn a tenant first. There is no rule about a refused subsidy inspection, no proration or abatement of rent for a bad condition, and no late-fee rule for a subsidised tenancy. A government shutdown changes nothing. And there is no Ohio tenant protection Act - no rent cap, no just-cause regime, so no cap notice, no exemption notice, and nothing with an expiry date to diary.

PRESENT, and worth knowing, because the gaps are not the whole picture. A college or university letting to its own student must state the conditions of termination and its notice and hearing procedures in the written agreement, and that letting is outside the eviction chapter. Complying with federal servicemember rights is one of your statutory duties. A deployed tenant can get a ninety-day court stay, unless you let fewer than four premises. If you hold a tenant's name with a social security, licence or account number, you owe breach notification within forty-five days and no lease can waive it. Recording a tenant's social security or telephone number in connection with a payment needs consent and a legitimate purpose. Housing two or more families engaged in agriculture is an agricultural labor camp needing an annual licence. And project-based subsidised housing of more than four units has its own habitability floor inside the nuisance-receivership statute.

TWO ITEMS ARE ANSWERED IN THEIR OWN ENTRIES, not here. A farm tenant and the tenant's children living on the land may hunt on it without a hunting licence (R.C. 1533.10(C)). And Ohio's sales tax reaches lodging only where a hotel furnishes it to transient guests, so it does not reach a residential lease (R.C. 5739.01(B)(2)).

title: Outside The Landlord-Tenant Title: What We Checked, What Is Genuinely Missing, And What Nobody Has Read Yet
bodyText:
Ohio's landlord-tenant chapter is short, so most of the answers a landlord needs sit in other parts of the Revised Code. This entry says which of those this review reached and which it did not, because the difference matters: a subject we searched and did not find is a real gap you can rely on, and a subject nobody has read is not.

WHAT WE SEARCHED. Thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and several Administrative Code chapters, covering landlord-tenant and eviction; the forcible-entry chapter and the municipal courts; civil rights and the housing-discrimination rules; consumer sales practices and consumer protection; land installment contracts; self-storage; county rental registration; manufactured homes and parks; unclaimed funds; secured transactions; execution against property and exemptions; nuisances including building receivership; building standards and the Fire Marshal with the Ohio Fire Code rules; nursing homes; recreational vehicle parks and camps; hotels; agricultural labor camps; metropolitan housing authorities; drugs and controlled substances; arson, search warrants, offences against justice, sentencing, parole and the sex-offender registry; executors and claims against estates; motor vehicles and titles; Medicaid; and the National Guard and organised militia.

ABSENT, on that search. There is no summary remedy against a squatter or an unauthorised occupant: the words do not appear, and what you have instead is the eviction chapter's ground against an occupier of lands or tenements without colour of title, plus the ordinary ejectment action. There is no duty to give a receipt for rent, in cash or otherwise, anywhere - not in the landlord-tenant chapter and not in the consumer chapters either. Registration is not a precondition to a possession judgment: no section of the eviction chapter refers to the rental-registration chapter at all, and the only sanction for not registering is a special assessment of between fifty and one hundred fifty dollars imposed by the county auditor and appealable to the board of revision. That is county rental registration only. Ohio's trade-name and company statutes, which were outside the search above, can stop you suing: if you rent under a trade name or fictitious name, you must register it with the Secretary of State or report its use within thirty days of first use, and you may not commence or maintain an action in that name until you do, though once you comply the action may go forward (R.C. 1329.01(D), 1329.10(B)); an out-of-state corporation that should hold a Secretary of State licence to transact business here may not maintain any action in any court until it obtains one and pays a two-hundred-fifty-dollar forfeiture (R.C. 1703.03, 1703.29(A)); and an out-of-state LLC transacting business here must register with the Secretary of State, and until it does it may not maintain a proceeding to collect its debts, such as unpaid rent, though the court may stay the case rather than dismiss it (R.C. 1706.511(A), 1706.515(A), (B)). Owning real property is not by itself transacting business for an LLC (R.C. 1706.512(A)(9)); whether letting it out is, is a case-law question (see `edu-nonresident-owner-agent-oh`). And Ohio has no biometric privacy statute.

NOT LOCATED - these are not absences, and must never be quoted as any. Whole chapters that bear on a tenancy were outside this review and could not be fetched: ejectment, which the landlord-tenant chapter itself names as one of only three lawful routes to possession; conveyances and recording; condominiums and planned communities; arbitration; sales and use tax, and municipal income tax; hunting and fishing; emergency management; interest and the statute of frauds; limitations of actions; mechanics' liens; eminent domain; domestic violence protection orders; small claims and garnishment; public records; record sealing; utilities and the Public Utilities Commission's rules; public health, lead and swimming pools; child care; the Building and Residential Codes; and the base text of the International Fire Code, which is copyrighted and published on no state site. Several of these have been read section by section and are cited in the entries that needed them; the rest are open questions, named in those entries, with the chapter and section written out so they can be chased. City ordinances are flagged throughout this library and never resolved.

title: Your Farm Tenant Needs No Hunting Licence
bodyText:
Your farm tenant can hunt on the land without a hunting licence, and that is worth knowing before you assume a licence requirement does the work of a lease term. R.C. 1533.10(C) ends with this sentence: 'The tenant and children of the tenant, residing on lands in the state, may hunt on them without a hunting license.' The same division exempts a resident owner and the owner's parents, children of any age and grandchildren under eighteen; a non-resident owner and the spouse and children living with them, where that owner's own state extends the same courtesy to Ohioans; and an individual member of a limited liability company or partnership of three or fewer members, or a trustee or beneficiary of a trust with three or fewer trustees and beneficiaries, that owns the land.

Two limits matter. It is an exemption from the licence, not from everything: division (F) says the section does not authorise taking deer or wild turkeys without the separate permit under R.C. 1533.11, ducks, geese or brant without a wetlands habitat stamp under R.C. 1533.112, or trapping fur-bearing animals without a fur taker permit under R.C. 1533.111 - and this review did not determine whether a tenant needs those. And it reaches the tenant and the tenant's children only, not guests.

What it means for your lease: the exemption is not a right against you. R.C. 5321.06 lets the lease prohibit hunting, confine it to seasons, require proof of insurance or bar firearms altogether, with R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability the only ceiling. If you want any of that, write it down - because the tenant needs no licence, there is nothing to withhold and no permission to refuse. Note too that a farm residence let with two or more acres for agricultural production by the occupant is outside Chapter 5321 entirely under R.C. 5321.01(C)(6), so on many farm lettings the landlord-tenant chapter is not doing the work at all and the lease is doing all of it.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, 'hunt' 7 and 'wild' 18, every hit checked and none a landlord-tenant provision, against 'landlord' 34 - plus R.C. 1533.10 read in full outside it. R.C. 1533.11, 1533.111, 1533.112 and 1533.17 were not read, nor were R.C. 1533.18 and 1533.181 (recreational-user immunity) or R.C. 1531.02, and no Ohio case law was reviewed.

title: Ohio Neither Makes You Report Rent To The Credit Bureaus Nor Stops You - The Rules That Bite Are Federal
bodyText:
Ohio has no rent-reporting law. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library, nothing requires a landlord of any size to offer positive rent reporting, nothing gives the tenant an election or a signature block for one, nothing forbids requiring a tenant to join a reporting programme, and nothing makes you notify a tenant in writing before you report a late payment. The phrases 'rent reporting', 'credit bureau' and 'credit score' do not appear at all.

That does not make reporting a free action, because the regime that governs it is FEDERAL: the Fair Credit Reporting Act. Report rent - positive or negative - and you become a furnisher of information to a consumer reporting agency, with federal accuracy, dispute-investigation and correction duties that Ohio law does not displace and that are not set out here. Get them checked before you report anything, not after a tenant disputes it. The same goes for any third-party rent-reporting service you sign up to: read what it promises to do in your name.

Four Ohio points do touch the subject. If you keep a tenant's name together with a social security number, a driver's licence or state identification number, or an account or card number with its security code, you are holding 'personal information' and R.C. 1349.19 makes you notify affected Ohio residents of a security breach, and any waiver of that section is void - the confidential-information entry carries it. R.C. 1349.17 restricts recording a tenant's social security or telephone number in connection with a payment by cheque or card unless you have a legitimate business purpose and the tenant's consent and you keep it from third parties. An Ohio security freeze will not block your screening: R.C. 1349.52(L)(3)(e) excuses a reporting agency from placing a freeze on a database used solely for tenant screening. And Ohio's Consumer Sales Practices Act does not reach your lease, because R.C. 1345.01(A) defines a consumer transaction by goods, a service, a franchise or an intangible and says nothing about real property - so do not expect a state consumer claim here, and do not assume one cannot arise out of a separate service you sell alongside the tenancy.

title: No Ohio Tax on the Rent Your Tenant Pays
bodyText:
Ohio puts no tax on the rent your tenant pays. The sales tax reaches occupancy of real property in exactly one place: R.C. 5739.01's definition of a 'sale' includes '(2) All transactions by which lodging by a hotel is or is to be furnished to transient guests', and nothing else in that definition touches real property - the only other mention of it is the definition of 'premises' as the place where a seller operates. A residential lease is not a taxable sale, so there is no rent tax to collect, no registration to make and nothing to add to the rent.

What you do pay is tax on your side of the transaction: real property tax, which R.C. 5321.10(A) lists among the 'customary and usual costs of operating the premises as a rental unit', and income tax on the rental income, including any municipal income tax where the property or your business is located. Those are costs of operation, not charges on the tenant - and the way Ohio lets you recover a rise in them is through rent, under R.C. 5321.02(C)'s reference to 'increasing the rent ... to reflect an increase in other costs of operation'. See the tax escalation clause rather than trying to bill a tax to a tenant as a tax.

One boundary worth knowing if you let anything short-stay. The sales tax limb turns on 'transient guests', and R.C. 3731.01(A)(6) makes transient thirty days or less while (A)(4) makes a 'residential hotel' non-transient by definition. So a long-stay occupant is not a transient guest, their lodging is not a taxable sale, and - separately - they look like a tenant under Chapter 5321 rather than a hotel guest. The tax line and the tenancy line fall in the same place, which is convenient but means a hotel licence does not change either answer.

Searched: the 37 Revised Code chapters in this review - control term 0 sections, 'sales tax' 3, 'excise tax' 1, 'gross receipts' 0, 'lodging tax' 0 and 'transient occupancy' 2, every hit checked and none a tax on residential rent, against 'landlord' 34 and 'tax' 413 - plus R.C. 5739.01's definition of 'sale' searched on its own page outside the corpus. The rest of chapter 5739, chapter 5741 (use tax) and chapter 718 (municipal income tax) were not read. Municipal income taxes are a city matter this review flags rather than resolves, and a city lodging or short-term-rental excise is a real possibility it did not examine.

title: Ohio Issues No Work Card For Housing Staff - But Crossing From Age-Restricted Apartments Into Care Changes Everything
bodyText:
Ohio has no work card, work permit, registration or licence for people who work in rental housing, and nothing extra for age-restricted housing. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library, 'work card', 'work permit', 'background check', 'caretaker' and 'resident manager' return nothing at all. Age-restricted letting is a fair-housing idea in Ohio, not a licensing one: R.C. 4112.024(E) lifts the familial-status limb of the state fair-housing section for housing determined under the federal Fair Housing Amendments Act to be designed and operated to assist elderly persons, for housing intended for and solely occupied by people sixty-two or older, and for housing intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person fifty-five or older per unit as determined under that federal Act. Note what that is: permission to restrict by age, resting on a FEDERAL determination, with not a word about staff.

The real line to watch is the one between letting and caring. If what you operate is a home licensed under R.C. Chapter 3721, or an adult day-care program on the same site as one, a mandatory screening regime switches on. R.C. 3721.121 requires the chief administrator to request a Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation criminal records check on every applicant under final consideration for a full-time, part-time or temporary position involving direct care of an older adult - sixty or older - with fingerprints, FBI information where the applicant cannot show five years' Ohio residence, and a bar on employing anyone who refuses. It then forbids employing a person convicted of any offence on a long list in division (C)(1), unless the Director of Health's personal-character rules permit it, requires termination if the check does not come back within sixty days of a conditional hire, and gives you a real benefit: under division (H) you cannot be found negligent solely for having relied in good faith on the report, or for a good-faith conditional hire, or for employing under those character standards. The fee is yours, and you may pass it to the applicant only on the notice division (D)(2) prescribes and only where Medicaid does not reimburse it.

And a chapter 3721 home is not a chapter 5321 letting at all - R.C. 5321.01(C)(2) takes hospitals, similar medical institutions and chapter 3721 homes out of 'residential premises'. So if you are running independent-living apartments, screen your staff as a matter of judgment, not because Ohio makes you; if you are providing direct care, you are in a different regime with different duties. Two companion entries cover general staff screening and key control; this one covers only the senior-housing question.

title: A Government Shutdown Changes Nothing About Ohio Rent - And The Tenant Who Asks For Time Needs Your Agreement, Not A Statute
bodyText:
Ohio has no shutdown provision. The word 'shutdown' appears in none of the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Constitution or the administrative rules searched for this library, 'moratorium' and 'federal employee' return nothing, and no act of the 135th or 136th General Assembly - every one of which was searched for this pass - creates a rent deferral, a grace period, a late-fee suspension or an eviction bar for a government worker whose pay stops. Rent stays due on the day the lease says, your late fee runs if the lease provides one, and the eviction route is unchanged.

Two Ohio facts make that harder for the tenant than landlords expect. Ohio gives no statutory right to cure a nonpayment: the notice that starts an eviction is a notice to leave, not a pay-or-quit notice. And a delayed payment the tenant was counting on is no defence - the benefit-delay entry in this library sets that out, along with the fact that a tenant who wants the case put off must usually bond the rent. A tenant whose pay has stopped therefore has nothing to point at except your goodwill.

Which makes the goodwill worth documenting. If you agree to take the rent late or in instalments, put it in a dated written agreement that says exactly what is deferred, when it is payable, that the rest of the lease is unchanged and that you are not waiving anything. Be careful on two points Ohio does police: accepting rent after you have served a notice can void the notice, and no provision of the landlord-tenant chapter can be modified or waived by agreement, so a side letter cannot touch your duties or the deposit rules. And do not expect a city to help: Ohio preempts local measures that regulate the rights and obligations of parties to a rental agreement, with findings attached, so a municipal shutdown rent measure would be on very thin ground - though city measures are always worth checking and this library never resolves them.

The one thing this review could not read is R.C. Chapter 5502, emergency management and the Governor's emergency powers - R.C. 5502.21, 5502.22, 5502.24 and 5502.30. A federal shutdown is not a declared disaster, so it is unlikely to be the answer here, but if an emergency were ever declared those are the sections that would say what could be suspended. Nothing else in Ohio law does.

title: No Ohio Lease Has To Say What District The Property Is In, And No Tenant Gets A Seat Because Of It
bodyText:
Nothing in Ohio makes you tell a tenant that the property sits inside a special district, a taxing district, an improvement district or any other sub-county body, and nothing gives a tenant a vote or a seat on one because they live there. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library, the phrase 'special district' does not appear at all, 'assessment district', 'sanitary district' and 'community authority' return nothing, and no provision requires a district statement in a lease or a notice to an occupant. Ohio's short list of lease disclosures has no entry for it.

The nearest thing Ohio has is worth knowing because it is the one district-like body that touches rental property. Ohio preempts local measures that regulate rental-agreement rights, but it preserves voluntary incentive programs including community reinvestment areas under R.C. 3735.65 to 3735.70. Where a municipality, limited home rule township or county designates such an area, R.C. 3735.69(A) requires a community reinvestment area housing council, and the seats are appointments - by the mayor, the legislative authority, the planning commission, township trustees or county commissioners - with two further members who need only be residents of the subdivision. There is no tenant seat, no election, and nothing that follows your tenant into the lease. That council inspects exempted properties annually and hears appeals; if you have taken an abatement on a rental you own, it is the body that can revoke it, which is a reason to know it exists.

Two related matters are covered by their own entries rather than repeated here: you owe a tenant no statement of what share of the rent goes to property tax, and your county rental-registration duty in the larger counties is enforced by a special assessment against the property rather than by anything in the lease. If you want a tenant to know about a district - a lighting assessment, a levy on the ballot - say so as a courtesy, not as a required disclosure, and do not write it as though the tenant acquires rights in it.

title: Ohio Has A Student-Housing Regime - And It Only Works If The College Owns The Building
bodyText:
Ohio has real student-housing law, and everything in it turns on one definition. A 'student tenant' under R.C. 5321.01(H) is a person who occupies a dwelling unit owned or operated by the college or university at which the person is a student, under a rental agreement contingent on that student status. If you are a private landlord letting near a campus, your tenants are not student tenants however many classes they take, and none of what follows applies to you: you are an ordinary Ohio landlord with the ordinary duties, the ordinary notice, and the ordinary eviction route.

Where the institution is the landlord, four things change. R.C. 5321.031 requires the written rental agreement to specify the conditions under which it may be terminated and to specify the institution's notice and hearing procedures - the only lease-content requirement in chapter 5321 besides the owner and agent identity disclosure, and the clause entry for this topic carries it. The institution may only terminate mid-term after a hearing that finds a violation of a lease term or of the code of conduct or other policies, preceded by written notice and otherwise complying with its own disciplinary-hearing procedures. R.C. 1923.02(D) then takes chapter 1923 away entirely when a college or university terminates under R.C. 5321.031, so the hearing replaces the eviction case rather than preceding it. And two sections drop out: R.C. 5321.07(D) withdraws the tenant's rent-escrow remedy for a unit occupied by a student tenant, and R.C. 5321.03(C) withdraws the landlord's possession grounds in that section as well.

A college unit is otherwise squarely inside the chapter - R.C. 5321.01(C) says 'residential premises' includes a dwelling unit owned or operated by a college or university - so the repair duties, the deposit rules and the prohibited-terms list all still bind the institution. Note the neighbours: R.C. 5321.01(C)(4) excludes an elementary or secondary boarding school where room and board is part of tuition, R.C. 5323.01(E) excludes a college or university dormitory from county rental registration, and R.C. 4112.022(D) makes disability discrimination in assigning institutional housing an unlawful discriminatory practice.

Beyond that, Ohio has nothing. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library, no provision regulates per-bed or by-the-bedroom letting, semester or academic-year terms, a student co-signer or guaranty, summer storage, or anything else about letting to students privately. Those are lease terms you set under R.C. 5321.06, with R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability the only general ceiling.

title: Ohio Writes No Rule About A Subsidy Inspection - But It Does Give The Housing Authority An Entry Power, And Your Lease Is The Only Place Refusal Has A Consequence
bodyText:
Nothing in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution or the administrative rules searched for this library says what happens if an inspection required by a rent-subsidy programme is refused - by you or by your tenant. There is no Ohio provision suspending the subsidy, abating the rent, creating a breach, or giving either of you a remedy. That subject belongs to FEDERAL programme rules and to your own assistance contract, and neither is in this library: get them read, because the sanction for a failed or refused inspection is in them.

Three Ohio provisions do bear on it. First, a metropolitan housing authority has its own statutory entry power. R.C. 3735.31(A) lets an authority conduct investigations into housing and living conditions, enter any buildings or property in order to conduct its investigations, and subpoena witnesses, books and papers. Read it as a reading rather than a settled rule - the section grants the authority's corporate powers and says nothing about a private owner's refusal or about a warrant - but do not assume an authority inspecting your building is there only by your permission.

Second, the ordinary access machinery is all Ohio gives you against a tenant who will not let the inspector in. Your tenant must not unreasonably withhold consent for you to enter to inspect the premises, make repairs or exhibit the unit, and if the tenant breaches that you may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees, terminate, sue for possession, or get an injunction compelling access. You still owe the tenant reasonable notice of your own entry, and entering in breach of that, entering unreasonably, or making repeated harassing demands hands the tenant damages, an injunction, fees or the right to terminate. The entry and remedy entries in this library carry the detail.

Third, and this is the one landlords underrate: refusing an inspection can cost you a statutory defence. Ohio's nuisance-receivership statute gives subsidized housing - a property of more than four units receiving project-based assistance under the listed federal programmes - a sixty-day written notice before an abatement action and deems the property not a public nuisance where the federal assessment centre has scored it seventy-five or higher out of a hundred in the preceding twelve months and conditions have not significantly changed. No inspection means no score, and no score means no safe harbour. The receivership entry sets this out.

So the practical answer is to write it into the lease. The eviction chapter gives you a ground for a tenant's breach of an obligation imposed by a written rental agreement, and that is the only route by which an inspection refusal becomes a possession case. State the tenant's duty to permit and cooperate with any inspection required by a housing programme, and the notice you will give.

title: Ohio Prorates Nothing For A Bad Condition - And In A Subsidised Tenancy The Tenant Can Only Escrow Their Own Share
bodyText:
Ohio has no rent-abatement or proration rule of any kind, subsidised or not. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library, 'rent abatement', 'abatement of rent' and 'withhold rent' return nothing at all; every use of 'abatement' is the abatement of a nuisance, and every use of 'proration' is a vehicle tax. Nothing reduces the rent automatically because a unit falls below a standard, and nothing apportions a reduction between a tenant's share and a subsidy.

What Ohio has instead is a court-supervised escrow, and the habitability entries in this library set it out. In outline: the tenant gives you written notice of the defect at the place rent is normally paid; if you have not remedied it within a reasonable time or thirty days, whichever is sooner, and the tenant is current in rent, the tenant may deposit the rent with the clerk of court, apply for an order making you remedy it, apply for an order reducing the periodic rent until you do, apply to have the deposited rent spent on the repair, or terminate. So a reduction exists, but a judge grants it - it is not something the tenant may take, and not something you should concede by instalments.

Now the subsidy point, and read it as a reading of the words rather than a settled rule. The escrow division lets the tenant deposit 'all rent that is due and thereafter becomes due the landlord'. In a subsidised tenancy the tenant pays only the tenant portion; the assistance payment comes from the housing authority under a separate contract to which the tenant is not a party. So what a tenant can put into court is their own share, and your exposure in an Ohio escrow case is correspondingly smaller than the full contract rent - while the fate of the assistance payment is decided by the FEDERAL programme rules and your assistance contract, not by the Ohio court. Those rules, which this library does not hold, are where any abatement, withholding or termination of the subsidy for a failed inspection actually lives, and they can take away far more than the tenant's share. Have them read.

Two further Ohio points. Project-based subsidised housing of more than four units has its own habitability floor inside Ohio's nuisance-receivership statute, which measures the property against the federal physical-condition standards and can put it into receivership - the receivership entry carries it. And the escrow route does not reach every landlord: it is withdrawn from a landlord who is party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and who gave written notice of that fact, and from a unit occupied by a college's own student tenant.

title: No Ohio Late-Fee Rule For A Subsidised Tenancy - And The Only Figure You Can Charge Late On Is The Tenant's Own Share
bodyText:
Ohio says nothing about late fees in a subsidised tenancy. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library there is no cap, no grace period, no rule about charging a fee on an assistance payment that arrives late, and no rule about the tenant's portion. 'Late charge', 'grace period', 'tenant portion' and 'tenant share' return nothing, and the only late-fee statute Ohio has written is for self-service storage units, not homes. So your fee is a lease term: permitted because the lease may contain any term not inconsistent with the landlord-tenant chapter or another rule of law, with unconscionability the only general ceiling and the figure yours to justify rather than the statute's. The general late-fee entry carries this.

Two things follow that are specific to a subsidy, and they are the useful part. First, the amount. Your tenant owes the tenant portion; the assistance payment is owed by the housing authority under a separate contract that your tenant is not a party to. Charging the tenant a late fee calculated on the full contract rent, or charging the tenant because the authority paid you late, is charging them for someone else's default - keep any fee tied to the tenant's own share and to the tenant's own lateness, and say so in the lease.

Second, the real constraint is not Ohio's. FEDERAL programme rules and your assistance contract govern what you may charge a subsidised tenant and when, and they are not in this library. In practice they are stricter than Ohio, and a fee your Ohio lease permits may still breach them. Have them read before you set the figure, and remember that Ohio gives you no protection in the other direction either: no provision of the landlord-tenant chapter may be modified or waived by any oral or written agreement, so nothing you sign with a tenant or an authority can buy you out of the Ohio duties that do apply.

title: Ohio Imposes No General Duty To Keep Tenant Information Private - And Three Narrow Duties That Do Bind You
bodyText:
Start with the gap, because it is wide. Neither Ohio's landlord-tenant chapter nor its eviction chapter contains the word 'confidential' or 'confidentiality' at all. Nothing in them bars you from disclosing a tenant's information, requires the tenant's consent before you do, limits what you may collect, sets a retention period, or tells you to destroy a file when the tenancy ends. Ohio has no biometric privacy statute either - 'biometric' returns nothing across all thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library - so fingerprint entry, face recognition at a door and the like are unregulated by Ohio statute. Treat that as exposure rather than freedom: you can still be sued in contract or in tort, and your vendors' contracts and your insurer will have views.

Three duties do bind you. First, breach notification. R.C. 1349.19 reaches any person, including a business entity doing business in Ohio, that owns or licenses computerised data containing 'personal information' - a tenant's first name or initial and last name together with an unencrypted social security number, driver's licence or state identification number, or an account or card number with its security code. If that is accessed and acquired by an unauthorised person and causes or is reasonably believed to cause a material risk of identity theft or other fraud, you must tell every affected Ohio resident as soon as possible and in no case later than forty-five days, by written, electronic or telephone notice. A vendor holding the data for you must tell you expeditiously. A breach touching more than a thousand Ohio residents also has to be reported to the nationwide consumer reporting agencies. There is a cheaper substitute-notice route if you have ten employees or fewer and notice would cost over ten thousand dollars, but it means a quarter-page newspaper advertisement weekly for three weeks, your website and local media - budget accordingly. Any waiver of the section is void, so no lease term can contract out of it, and the Attorney General enforces it.

Second, payment data. R.C. 1349.17 restricts recording the other party's social security or telephone number when payment is made by credit card agreement, cheque or draft: you need a legitimate business purpose, which includes collection, and the tenant's consent, and you must not pass the number to a third party except for collection or use it to market unrelated goods. Taking a card number in lieu of a deposit to secure payment on default, loss or damage is expressly allowed. Third, driver data. If you obtain a tenant's information from the Bureau of Motor Vehicles - for a tow, a vehicle or a screening - R.C. 4501.27(C) lets an authorised recipient resell or redisclose it only for a use that section permits, and its definition of personal information includes the address, telephone number, social security number and photograph.

So your practical rule is: collect the minimum, encrypt what you keep (encrypted data falls outside the definition), keep it out of anything you file or forward, and answer third-party requests with a 'no' unless a subpoena or the tenant's written authority says otherwise. Three related entries carry their own subjects: a tenant's access to their own file, your portal and electronic notices, and the address confidentiality programme, where re-disclosing an address you obtained through the Secretary of State is a crime.

title: Housing Someone Who Works For You In Ohio: No Disclosure Duty, No Exit Rule, And Two Regimes You Can Fall Into By Accident
bodyText:
Ohio writes nothing about an ordinary employment-linked letting. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library there is no signed disclosure of occupancy and vacating conditions to give a resident employee, no duty to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, no rule that occupancy ends with employment or that it survives, and no sponsored-worker rent filing. The words 'caretaker', 'resident manager', 'incident of employment', 'in lieu of wages' and 'furnished by the employer' do not appear anywhere in it.

So your own paperwork decides everything, and the definitions decide which law you are in. R.C. 5321.01(A) makes a tenant a person entitled under a rental agreement to the use and occupancy of residential premises to the exclusion of others, and R.C. 5321.01(D) counts an oral agreement as a rental agreement. Housing a caretaker or a manager with no agreement at all does not keep you out of trouble; it leaves you arguing about what was agreed, with every chapter 5321 duty applying if a court finds an agreement and no deposit rule, notice or termination machinery to help if it does not. Write a rental agreement, put the rent in it even where the rent is part of the pay package, say in terms that occupancy ends when the employment ends and how many days the occupant then has, and keep the two documents separate so that dismissing the employee does not look like evicting the tenant.

Two regimes catch the unwary. First, if you house two or more families or five or more people who are engaged in or intend to engage in agriculture or related food processing - 'whether occupancy is by rent, lease, or mutual agreement', so free housing counts - that is an agricultural labor camp, and R.C. Chapter 3733 takes it out of chapter 5321 altogether. You must apply to the Director of Health for a licence before the fifteenth of April each year, no camp may be operated without one, a hotel licence is expressly no substitute, and operating in breach is a minor misdemeanour. Second, the ethics statutes: Ohio had to pass a special provision, R.C. 3735.43, before a metropolitan housing authority could give a police officer free housing without falling foul of the public-contract and improper-compensation sections. If you or your employee hold any public position, free or discounted housing needs advice before it is offered.

One point in your favour on removal. If the occupant turns out not to be a tenant at all, Ohio still gives you a court route and not a self-help one: the eviction chapter reaches 'an occupier of lands or tenements, without color of title' where you have the right of possession, and ejectment in the common pleas court is the second route. Never change the locks on someone who works for you.

title: Ohio Has No Rent-Cap Exemption To Claim - But It Does Have One Exemption You Lose If The Lease Does Not Say So
bodyText:
In states with a rent cap and a just-cause regime, a landlord who falls inside an exemption - a new building, a single-family home separately alienable from any other dwelling, an owner who is a natural person - usually has to say so in a prescribed paragraph of the lease, and loses the exemption if the paragraph is missing. Ohio has nothing of the kind, because it has nothing to be exempt from: no rent cap, no just-cause regime, and a statute that preempts a city from creating either. 'Exemption notice', 'notice of exemption', 'rent cap' and 'separately alienable' return nothing in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library.

Do not keep an exemption paragraph in an Ohio lease on the theory that it is harmless. A statement that this tenancy is exempt from a rent cap tells the tenant about a regime that does not exist, invites an argument about what you promised, and in a lease that otherwise borrows a cap paragraph it is worse than useless. The companion notice entry says the same of the main paragraph.

But Ohio does have one exemption that works exactly the way the question describes, and landlords lose it constantly by not drafting for it. The tenant's rent-escrow remedy does not apply to a landlord who is a party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and who gives written notice of that fact in a written rental agreement - or, for an oral tenancy, delivers written notice of it to the tenant at the time of initial occupancy. No notice, no exemption: the remedy stays available however few units you let. The three-or-fewer-units clause in this library is the paragraph, and the habitability entries explain what the exemption does and does not reach, which is less than it sounds - it leaves the damages claim, the counterclaim in your own eviction and the court-ordered inspection untouched.

One other Ohio provision is a lease-content requirement rather than an exemption, and it runs only where a college or university lets to its own student: the written agreement must state the conditions of termination and the institution's notice and hearing procedures. The student-housing entries carry it. Beyond those two, Ohio hooks almost nothing to what your lease says.

title: There Is No Ohio Tenant Protection Act - Do Not Put A Rent-Cap Or Just-Cause Notice In An Ohio Lease
bodyText:
Some states require a specific paragraph in the lease telling the tenant that the rent is capped by a formula and that the tenancy can only be ended for stated causes. Ohio has no such Act, no such cap, no such cause list and therefore no such notice. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library, 'tenant protection' and 'rent cap' return nothing; 'rent increase' appears in exactly one place, and it is the definition Ohio wrote in order to forbid rent control by cities rather than to impose one. Ohio preempts local measures regulating the rights and obligations of parties to a rental agreement, including rent control and rent stabilisation, and the preemption entry carries it; the no-general-just-cause entry carries the eviction side.

So nothing is required, and this matters more than it sounds: if your lease is adapted from a California or Oregon form, take the notice out. A paragraph saying the rent may rise only by a stated percentage, or that you will only terminate for cause, is not harmless surplus in Ohio. It is a term of your own lease, and your lease binds you - you would have given the tenant a contractual rent cap and a contractual just-cause regime that Ohio never imposed, enforceable against you for the term. Ohio's lease freedom cuts both ways.

What Ohio does require in a lease is very short, and the disclosures entry lists it. The only form of words Ohio prescribes for an ordinary tenancy is in the notice that starts an eviction, not in the lease. And Ohio sets no rent-increase notice period at all, so if you want notice obligations before a rise, they have to come from your own lease - which is a reason to draft that clause deliberately rather than by inheritance.

title: Nothing In Ohio's Landlord-Tenant Law Expires - What Changes It Is Amendment, And That Needs Watching Instead
bodyText:
In some states the core tenant-protection statute carries a dated repeal, so a landlord has to diary the year it lapses. Ohio has nothing to diary. The word 'sunset' appears nowhere in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Constitution or the administrative rules searched for this library; no section of the landlord-tenant chapter, the eviction chapter, the civil rights chapter or the county rental-registration chapter contains an expiry or cessation clause; and the one 'this section expires' in the whole corpus is a transitional provision in the secured-transactions chapter. Ohio can write an expiry when it wants one - it just has not written one here. The landlord-tenant chapter dates from 1974 and its core sections still carry 1974 effective dates.

The currency risk is amendment, not expiry, and it is real. In the last three years alone: the 2023 budget act rewrote the definitions section, the retaliation-exception section and one of the eviction sections; a 2025 act changed the eviction chapter so that no action may name a minor tenant where a parent or guardian is also named; a 2026 bill that would have added a submetered-utility disclosure to your statutory duties passed both houses and was vetoed, so it is not law and the duties section is unchanged; and the cannabis chapter was renumbered wholesale, which breaks every citation to the old one. None of that announces itself in the statute you read last year.

So the discipline that replaces a sunset diary is this. When you rely on a section, read the two lines the official site prints with it - the effective date and the act that last changed it - and note them. Check them again before you rely on the section in a dispute. Where a statute incorporates an outside standard by a frozen citation, read the citation rather than the current edition of the standard, which the frozen-standard entry explains. And treat a vetoed or pending bill as not law until its status page says otherwise.

title: Ohio Has No Usufruct - It Decides Who The Landlord Is By Who Lets And Who Collects
bodyText:
Usufruct is a civil-law idea and Ohio does not use it. In the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Ohio Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library, the words 'usufruct', 'usufructuary', 'naked owner' and 'life tenant' do not appear once, and there is no provision about a lessor whose own right to the property is temporary or limited.

What Ohio does instead is define the landlord functionally, and that is the answer to the question. R.C. 5321.01(B) makes a 'landlord' the owner, lessor or sublessor of residential premises, the agent of any of them, or any person authorised by any of them to manage the premises or to receive rent from a tenant. R.C. 1923.01(C)(2) repeats the same structure for the eviction chapter. Nothing in either definition asks what quality of title you hold. So if you let the unit, manage it, or take the rent, you are the landlord and you carry every duty in R.C. 5321.04, the deposit rules, and the prohibited-terms list - whether you own the fee, hold a life estate, hold under a lease of your own and sublet, or act for a trust or an estate. Your tenant sues you, not whoever holds the paper title.

The practical risk is the other half, and Ohio's statutes do not address it: a letting cannot outlast the interest it comes out of. If your own right to the property ends - a life estate ends, a head lease ends, a trust distributes - the lease you granted has no statute to save it, and no Ohio provision found here tells the tenant that, gives the tenant a remedy for it, or requires the lease to disclose it. If you are letting out of an interest that is not a fee simple, say in the lease where your authority comes from and when it ends, keep the term inside it, and take advice before granting anything longer. Note separately that an assignment or grant of a leasehold needs a signed writing in Ohio, and a lease running more than three years must be acknowledged before a notary or other named officer.

title: Ohio Pays You Nothing For Renting To A Veteran - And A Veterans Discount Is Not The Safe Gesture It Looks Like
bodyText:
No Ohio provision found in the thirty-seven Revised Code chapters, the Constitution and the administrative rules searched for this library gives a private landlord any incentive - a tax credit, a payment, a grant, a guarantee, a deposit waiver or a preference - for letting to a veteran or a servicemember, and none requires you to give a veteran a preference. The only veteran preference Ohio writes is R.C. 3735.42, and it binds a metropolitan housing authority: among applicants equally in need and eligible for the dwelling at the rent involved, the authority must prefer families of veterans and of people in active military or naval service, including families of the deceased, except as its federal financial-assistance contract provides otherwise. That is an obligation on a public authority, not an offer to you. R.C. 3735.62 lets five or more veterans form a nonprofit corporation to build residences for sale to its own members, which is a route to ownership and not a rental incentive, and R.C. 3781.05 is a 1953 plumbing rule for federal veterans' emergency housing.

What Ohio does impose on you is a duty, in one line most landlords have never read: R.C. 5321.04(A)(10) makes it a landlord obligation to comply with the rights of tenants under FEDERAL: the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which the section cites as 117 Stat. 2835, 50 U.S.C. App. 501. Those rights are federal and are not restated here - get them checked before you act against a servicemember tenant. Ohio separately gives a deployed tenant a court stay of an eviction, which the eviction-delay entry sets out, and that one does not reach a landlord operating fewer than four residential premises.

Now the trap in the gesture. Ohio's fair-housing section makes military status a protected class, and it is drawn narrowly: military status means a person's status in service in the uniformed services as that phrase is defined for military-leave purposes, which is framed around performing duty - active duty, training, full-time National Guard duty - so a discharged veteran is not plainly inside it, while a serving reservist plainly is. The section prohibits refusing, denying or making housing unavailable because of military status, and it does not say 'adversely'. A 'veterans discount' or a reserved-for-veterans unit therefore distinguishes between applicants on exactly the ground the statute names, and nothing in Ohio shields a private landlord the way R.C. 3735.42 authorises an authority. If you want to do something for veterans, take advice first, and in the meantime market to them, advertise where they will see it, and keep your criteria and your rent the same for everybody.

title: Ohio Does Not Recognise a Confession-of-Judgment Clause in a Lease
bodyText: Ohio bars the clause outright. R.C. 5321.13(B): 'No warrant of attorney to confess judgment shall be recognized in any rental agreement or in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant for the recovery of rent or damages to the residential premises.' So a cognovit paragraph in a form lease does nothing in Ohio. The bar also reaches a side agreement, such as a separate note for back rent, because it covers 'any other agreement between a landlord and tenant'. The tenant cannot agree around it, because no provision of Chapter 5321 may be modified or waived by agreement (R.C. 5321.13(A)). Manufactured home parks have the same rule between a park operator and a resident (R.C. 4781.47(B)). Delete the paragraph from any form you use. To collect rent or damages, sue for them; you may join a claim for past-due rent and damages to the eviction case (R.C. 1923.081). See 'edu-exculpation-indemnity-ban-oh', which covers this rule alongside the exculpation ban.

title: Ohio Does Not Recognise Exculpatory or Indemnity Clauses in a Lease
bodyText: Ohio does not recognise a lease clause that excuses or limits your liability, or makes the tenant indemnify you for it. R.C. 5321.13(D): 'No agreement by a tenant to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or its related costs shall be recognized in any rental agreement or in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant.' That covers 'Landlord is not liable for' clauses, releases, hold-harmless terms and indemnity promises, wherever in the lease they sit. Adding 'to the extent permitted by law' does not save one, because the statute refuses to recognise the agreement at all. The tenant cannot waive the rule, since no provision of Chapter 5321 may be modified or waived by agreement (R.C. 5321.13(A)). A court may also refuse to enforce, or may limit, any clause it finds unconscionable when made (R.C. 5321.14(A)). Manufactured home parks have the same rule for a park operator (R.C. 4781.47(D)). What still protects you is the tenant's own liability for damage the tenant, or someone there with the tenant's permission, causes (R.C. 5321.05(A)(6), (C)(1)), plus renter's insurance and your own liability cover. See 'edu-exculpation-indemnity-ban-oh' for more.

title: Ohio's Landlord-Tenant Chapter Cannot Be Waived, Except in One Direction
bodyText: Ohio has one non-waiver rule for the whole landlord-tenant chapter. R.C. 5321.13(A): 'No provision of this chapter may be modified or waived by any oral or written agreement except as provided in division (F) of this section.' Division (F) allows one move only: you may agree to take on a tenant duty under R.C. 5321.05, other than the drug-law duty in (A)(9). Nothing lets the tenant take on one of your duties. R.C. 5321.13(E) adds that no rental agreement, assignment or security instrument may let anyone receive rent free of the duty to comply with R.C. 5321.04. The rule covers only Chapter 5321. The three-day notice to leave sits in Chapter 1923, which has no non-waiver section of its own; see 'edu-notice-to-quit-waiver-oh'. Separately, a court may refuse to enforce, or may limit, a clause it finds unconscionable when made (R.C. 5321.14(A)). A restriction on displaying the flags R.C. 5321.131 protects is unconscionable by statute (R.C. 5321.131(D)). Manufactured home parks have a parallel rule (R.C. 4781.47(A), (F)). One rule runs against you instead. If your written lease omits the owner's name and address, and any agent's, the notices to you required under R.C. 5321.07(A) and 5321.08(A) are waived (R.C. 5321.18(A), (C)). See 'edu-one-way-delegation-oh' for the duty-shifting rule in more depth.

title: Ohio Repair Remedies: Rent Escrow Through the Court, and Getting It Released
bodyText: Ohio gives a tenant no repair-and-deduct right. The remedy runs through the court. If you fail a duty under R.C. 5321.04 (other than the (A)(9) drug-eviction duty) or under the lease, or a government agency finds a code violation that could materially affect health and safety, the tenant may give you written notice. It goes to the person or place where rent is normally paid (R.C. 5321.07(A)). If you do not remedy the condition within a reasonable time, or within thirty days, whichever is sooner, a tenant who is current in rent may do one of three things (R.C. 5321.07(B)). The tenant may deposit rent with the clerk of the municipal or county court, ask the court to order the repair (with a rent reduction or use of the deposited rent for the repair), or terminate the rental agreement. The clerk must notify you of a deposit and may charge one per cent of it as costs (R.C. 5321.08(A), (D)). To get the money released, R.C. 5321.09 gives you four grounds. If the condition is remedied, apply to the clerk, who releases the rent, less costs, once the tenant confirms in writing (R.C. 5321.09(A)(1)). Otherwise apply to the court: the tenant gave no proper notice, was not current in rent when deposits began, there was no violation, or the condition is remedied (R.C. 5321.09(A)(2), (3)). The tenant is a party, and trial is held within sixty days unless the court continues it for good cause (R.C. 5321.09(B)). If the condition was the tenant's own doing, or the tenant intentionally acted in bad faith, the tenant owes your damages and costs, plus reasonable attorney's fees for bad faith (R.C. 5321.09(D)). While your action is pending, the court may release part of the rent for mortgage payments, insurance, real estate taxes, utilities, repairs and other usual operating costs (R.C. 5321.10(A)). It weighs the rent from other units, their operating costs and the cost of the repair (R.C. 5321.10(B)). The remedy does not apply if you are party to agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units and say so in the written lease, or to a unit a student tenant occupies (R.C. 5321.07(C), (D)). See 'edu-habitability-escrow-oh' and 'repair-escrow-exemption-notice-oh'.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Ohio follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (R.C. 1303.40). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (R.C. 1301.308(B)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Ohio's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (R.C. ch. 5321 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Ohio's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
